pages.title: Guides for translators and translation agencies
pages.h1: Guides for translators and translation agencies
pages.meta_description: Practical guides on certifying a translation, translator credentials, CAT tools and translation memory, production workflow, and running a translation practice.
pages.body_html:
These guides are for working translators and the agencies that employ them: how to certify a translation so the receiving authority accepts it, what credentials are worth holding, which tools move a document through production without destroying its layout, and what the work is worth.

Certifying a translation

Accuracy statements, certification wording, what notarisation adds and when it is wanted.

Credentials

ATA certification, sworn and court-appointed status, and what each is accepted for.

Tools and translation memory

CAT tools, translation memory, TMX and XLIFF, and what to use instead of the expensive incumbents.

Production workflow

Layout, OCR, word counts, quality assurance and post-editing.

Running your practice

Rates, quoting, and finding clients.
pages.excerpt: Written for the people who produce and certify translations, not for the people who need one.

pages.title: Certificate of translation accuracy: what it must say
pages.h1: Certificate of translation accuracy
pages.meta_description: What a certificate of translation accuracy has to contain, who signs it, and which authorities accept it.
pages.body_html: A certificate of accuracy is the translator's signed statement that the translation is complete and faithful.

pages.title: Who can certify a translation?
pages.h1: Who can certify a translation?
pages.meta_description: Whether a translator may certify their own work, and when a notary or a sworn translator is required instead.
pages.body_html: In the UK and the US a translator may certify their own work. Other jurisdictions appoint sworn translators.

pages.title: AI Localization: How Translators and Agencies Run the First-Draft + Human-Certification Workflow
pages.h1: AI Localization: How Translators and Agencies Run the First-Draft + Human-Certification Workflow
pages.meta_description: AI localization pairs LLM first drafts with human review and certification. See how translators run the workflow, price it at $0.10–$0.25/word, and QA it.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is AI localization inside a translator's production workflow?
  • How does AI localization actually work, step by step?
  • What are the real benefits of AI localization for an agency?
  • What are the challenges and limitations translators hit with AI localization?
  • What AI localization tools and platforms do agencies actually use?
  • How does AI localization change pricing and margins for a translation agency?
  • What are the best practices for running AI localization at agency quality?
  • What common misconceptions about AI localization do agency buyers get wrong?

Inside professional production, "AI localization" is not a tool category — it is a four-stage lane that sits in front of human review and certified sign-off. Translators and agency owners who treat it as a first-draft layer, not a replacement, keep the margin and the accountability.

How it works

What is AI localization inside a translator's production workflow?

1

How is AI localization different from traditional machine translation (MT)?

AI localization uses large language models that accept glossaries, style guides, and segment context, where traditional neural machine translation translates string-by-string without those inputs. First-draft fluency rises. The human-review requirement for certified or high-stakes content does not change.

DimensionTraditional NMTLLM-based AI localization
Context windowOne segmentSegment plus neighbors, glossary, style guide
Terminology controlWeakTerm-base entries respected per call
Register and toneFlatShaped by style guide prompt
Best fitCommodity volume, high-resource pairsMarketing-adjacent, UI, product copy with context
Human review requirementMandatory for certified workMandatory for certified work

2

Where does AI localization sit in the four-tool stack a localization manager runs?

AI first-draft engines are one of four tool categories a localization manager runs, alongside CAT platforms, translation management systems, and QA tools. They cut per-word production cost before the human certification review, not instead of it. For the full tool-category framework, see Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

  • CAT platforms — segment-level production surface for the post-editor.
  • Translation management systems — workflow, vendor orchestration, and engine routing.
  • QA tools — pre-delivery checks and LQA scoring.
  • AI first-draft engines — LLMs and NMT routed per segment with quality scores.

AI localization also sits inside the broader product and app lane. For the parent cluster, see How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying.

How does AI localization actually work, step by step?

AI localization runs as a four-stage lane: an LLM pre-translates source segments with glossary and context injected, TM and term-base rules enforce approved renderings, a human translator post-edits at $0.04–$0.08 per source word, and LQA samples the output using MQM-style error typology before release or certification. Certified lanes add a fifth stage: a human translator signs the certificate of accuracy.

Stage 1 — How does the LLM produce the first draft?

The TMS routes each segment to a selected engine with the term base, style guide excerpts, and surrounding segments passed as context. The engine returns a draft tagged with a confidence or quality score per segment. Engines in rotation include GPT-4-class LLMs, Claude, tuned NMT models, DeepL, and Google Translate NMT.

The context-passing checklist we enforce on every pre-translate call:

  • Locked term-base entries for brand, product, and regulated vocabulary.
  • Style guide excerpts covering tone, register, and person.
  • Screenshots or segment neighbors for ambiguous short strings.
  • Content-type metadata so the TMS applies per-engine routing with historical quality scores.

Stage 2 — How do translation memory and term base override the draft?

Translation memory leverage overwrites AI output wherever a 100% or in-context exact match exists, and locked term-base entries force approved renderings for brand terms, product names, and regulated vocabulary. This step alone resolves most terminology errors before a human sees the file. Translation memory stays authoritative over the LLM, not the other way around.

Stage 3 — What does human post-editing (MTPE) look like on an AI draft?

A qualified translator opens the segments in the CAT editor and applies full MTPE: fixing meaning errors, tightening fluency, correcting locale conventions, and rewriting culturally loaded passages. Standard review billing is $0.04–$0.08 per source word. Locale conventions include dates, currency, address formats, phone number masks, and punctuation.

What error categories does the post-editor hit most often on LLM output?

The most common errors on LLM first drafts are terminology drift, over-literal idioms, hallucinated additions in long segments, and inconsistent register across adjacent segments. Each maps to an MQM error category used in LQA sampling:

  • Accuracy — hallucinated additions, omissions, mistranslation.
  • Fluency — awkward phrasing, grammar, over-literal idiom.
  • Terminology — drift against the locked term base.
  • Locale convention — dates, currency, address, number format.
  • Style — register and tone inconsistency across segments.

Stage 4 — How does LQA sign off an AI-assisted project?

LQA samples segments at $40–$90 per 1,000 words using an MQM-style typology: accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style. The reviewer scores severity, calculates an error-points-per-1,000-words figure, and gates release against the per-lane threshold. Certified and regulated lanes carry stricter thresholds than marketing or product copy. ISO 17100:2015 remains the benchmark LQA frameworks reference.

Stage 5 — When does a human translator still have to certify?

For certified translations — USCIS filings, court evidence, academic credentials, medical records — a credentialed human translator must sign the certificate of accuracy on every page. AI generates the draft. The signature, the professional liability, and the regulatory acceptance stay human. USCIS certified translation prices sit at $0.10–$0.25 per word or $25–$150 per standard page of about 250 words, and the certificate is mandatory on every page.

Why us

How much does AI localization actually cut turnaround time?

Automation and AI first-draft systems have compressed turnaround from days to hours without removing the human certification step. A 10,000-word application string file that took three days end-to-end now runs same-day on an AI-pre-translate + MTPE lane. The post-edit and LQA steps still take real human hours — they just start sooner.

Where do the cost savings land in the per-word stack?

Raw translation drops because the human role moves from first-pass to post-edit — billed at $0.04–$0.08 per source word versus $0.10–$0.25 for full translation. LQA stays at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and project management holds at 10–15% of project value.

Cost lineTraditional laneAI-assisted lane
Translation / post-edit (per source word)$0.10–$0.25 (full translation)$0.04–$0.08 (MTPE)
LQA (per 1,000 words)$40–$90$40–$90
Project management10–15% of project10–15% of project
ToolingAmortized per projectAmortized per project
Certified sign-off (where required)Human translator signsHuman translator signs

How does AI localization protect brand voice across locales?

Agencies protect brand voice by passing the style guide, approved tone-of-voice samples, and a locked glossary into every pre-translate call, and by storing brand memories in vector stores the LLM retrieves per segment. Consistency across languages improves because the same guardrails bind every engine call. For how this plays out on product pages, see Product Localization: How Translators and Agencies Deliver It.

How does AI localization compress time to market for multi-locale launches?

Parallel LLM drafting across all target locales simultaneously collapses the sequential hand-off model. Multi-locale launch cycles move from weeks to days — a concrete differentiator when pitching enterprise clients with hard go-live deadlines. The release step still needs locale metadata and search-visibility work; see Localization SEO: How Translators Make Localized Pages Rank for the hreflang and metadata layer AI does not handle.

What are the challenges and limitations translators hit with AI localization?

AI localization still breaks on five production realities: low-resource language pairs, missing segment context, transcreation and marketing copy, regulated or certified content requiring named-translator liability, and culturally loaded imagery or idiom. Each demands a human translator in the loop, not around it.

Why do low-resource language pairs still require human translators?

LLMs and NMT engines are trained on uneven corpora, so low-resource pairs return drafts with high hallucination rates and poor terminology coverage. Examples include English into less-digitized African, Indigenous, or minority languages. Human translators carry the load, often without usable AI pre-translate at all.

How does missing context break AI first drafts?

LLMs translate segments without seeing the UI, the surrounding paragraph, or the user's path through the product. Agencies mitigate this by passing screenshots, segment neighbors, and content-type metadata into the pre-translate call. Ambiguous short strings — buttons, labels, menu items — still need human disambiguation.

Which content types does AI localization fail outright on?

AI localization fails on transcreation, culturally loaded imagery, regulated medical and legal copy requiring named liability, and any content where the translator's professional signature carries legal weight. These stay on human-only or human-led lanes. For how the transcreation tier is priced and scoped, see Define Transcreation: What It Means Inside a Translator's Workflow.

  • Transcreation — marketing slogans, campaign headlines, poetry.
  • Regulated medical and legal copy — warnings, dosages, clauses, depositions.
  • Certified translations — USCIS, court, academic credentials, medical records.
  • Culturally loaded imagery descriptions — tone, taboo, metaphor.

Why can't AI assume professional liability for certified translations?

A certified translation requires a competent human translator to sign a certificate of accuracy attesting the translation is complete and correct — a legal act. For USCIS filings this certificate is mandatory on every page, and an LLM cannot be the signatory. AI accelerates production. It does not accept accountability.

What AI localization tools and platforms do agencies actually use?

Agencies combine four tool categories: CAT editors with AI pre-translate, translation management systems with LLM routing, LQA tools with MQM typology, and the LLM engines themselves. The TMS picks the engine per segment based on content type, language pair, and historical quality scores.

CategoryRole in the AI laneExamples
CAT editorSegment-level post-edit surface with TM and term-base enforcementSDL Trados, memoQ, Phrase
Translation management systemWorkflow, vendor routing, per-engine quality scoresXTRF, Plunet, memoQ, Lokalise
LQA toolMQM-style error scoring and release gatingMQM-based scorecards inside the TMS
LLM / NMT engineFirst-draft generation per segmentGPT-4-class, Claude, DeepL, Google Translate NMT

What belongs in an AI-enabled localization management platform?

A localization management platform combines translation memory, term base, project and workflow management, repo and CMS connectors, machine translation routing with per-engine quality scores, LQA tooling, and reporting on throughput and leverage. The MT routing layer with per-engine quality scores is what makes it AI-enabled rather than merely MT-aware.

How do agencies pick which LLM to route a segment to?

Routing is driven by content type, language pair, and historical per-engine quality scores stored in the TMS. UI strings route to a fast general engine. Marketing copy routes to a brand-tuned LLM with retrieval over vector-stored brand memory. Regulated content either skips AI entirely or routes to a domain-tuned engine with mandatory human review.

How do agencies select the right AI localization tool for their content mix?

No single platform wins every content type, language pair, or volume tier. Evaluate tools against the actual segment mix — legal, marketing, UI strings — and run parallel quality tests before committing a production workflow to any one LLM or TMS integration. Score the output with the same MQM typology used in LQA so the comparison is like-for-like.

Pricing

How does AI localization change pricing and margins for a translation agency?

AI localization compresses per-word translation on commodity volume but opens margin on review and LQA. The published cost base — translation $0.10–$0.25 per word, review $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA $40–$90 per 1,000 words, PM 10–15%, tooling amortized per project — reshapes depending on whether the agency re-prices around post-edit bundles or keeps selling raw output. Review and LQA rise in share of margin even as raw translation compresses.

What does an AI-assisted multi-locale program cost end to end?

A mid-size multi-locale program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end, with AI pre-translate shifting the mix toward review and LQA rather than translation. TM leverage, turnaround speed, and certification requirements move the number inside that band.

Line itemShare of a 5-language, 50,000-word program
MTPE (post-edit) @ $0.04–$0.08 / source word$10,000–$20,000 per locale, pre-leverage
LQA @ $40–$90 per 1,000 words$2,000–$4,500 per locale
Project management10–15% of project value
Tooling (TMS, CAT, LLM calls)Amortized per project
Certified sign-off (where required)Per-page certificate billed separately

How do agencies re-price when the first draft is free?

The margin move is to sell post-edit + LQA bundles rather than per-word translation. Translators bill $0.04–$0.08 per source word for MTPE, LQA runs $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and PM stays at 10–15% of project value. Agencies that keep quoting commodity per-word translation on AI output lose margin to clients who learn the engine is free.

Get a quote

What are the best practices for running AI localization at agency quality?

Agencies that run AI localization well do seven things: lock the term base, maintain a current style guide, pass context into every pre-translate call, pick engines per content type, keep translation memory authoritative over AI output, sample with MQM-style LQA, and keep certified lanes human-signed.

  1. Lock the term base before any AI pre-translate call runs.
  2. Keep the style guide current and pass excerpts as system prompt.
  3. Pass screenshots, segment neighbors, and content-type metadata as context.
  4. Route per engine by content type and historical quality score.
  5. Apply TM matches before the LLM call; let 100% and in-context matches override AI output.
  6. Sample LQA with MQM categories and gate release against per-lane thresholds.
  7. Reserve certified lanes for human translators who sign the certificate of accuracy.

Why are glossaries and style guides the single biggest quality lever?

Glossaries and style guides are the biggest quality lever because they are the only context the LLM reliably respects across every segment. A locked term base enforces approved renderings. A style guide passed as system prompt holds register, person, and tone across thousands of segments without drift.

How does translation memory stay authoritative over AI output?

Translation memory stays authoritative when the TMS applies TM matches before the LLM call and locks 100% and in-context exact matches. The LLM pre-translates only the residual segments. The post-editor sees TM provenance per segment so legacy approved wording is never overwritten by a fresher but inconsistent AI draft.

What segments should agencies route to a human translator from the start?

Agencies route transcreation, legal clauses, medical warnings, marketing headlines, culturally sensitive imagery descriptions, and all certified-translation lanes to human translators from the start. These segments either carry legal liability or depend on cultural judgment the LLM cannot source.

About

What common misconceptions about AI localization do agency buyers get wrong?

Buyers get four things wrong: that AI replaces human translators, that AI is error-free, that AI handles any language pair equally, and that AI output can carry a certification signature. Each of these assumptions breaks down the moment it meets professional production reality, and acting on any one of them introduces quality, legal, or cost risk into a live project.

  • "AI replaces human translators." AI localization is, by definition, a first-draft practice: a large language model generates an initial translation that human translators then post-edit, QA, and certify. Roles shift — translators spend more time on MTPE and LQA than on raw drafting — but they do not disappear. Certified, legal, medical, and transcreation work remains entirely human-driven, and post-editing itself is a skilled task priced at roughly $0.04–$0.08 per source word precisely because it demands linguistic judgment, not just proofreading.
  • "AI is error-free." Hallucinations, terminology drift, over-literal idiom rendering, and register inconsistency are routine outputs from any LLM, even one supplied with a glossary and style guide. Professional workflows catch these failures through a structured LQA pass — typically priced at $40–$90 per 1,000 words — using an MQM-style error typology that categorises every defect by type and severity. Without that gate, undetected errors ship to market.
  • "AI handles any language pair equally." High-resource pairs — Spanish, French, German, Japanese — carry years of training data and deliver reliable first drafts. Low-resource pairs collapse in quality: coverage gaps widen, terminology consistency drops sharply, and human post-editing effort rises significantly, often approaching the cost of full translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word.
  • "AI output can carry a certification signature." This is the most consequential misconception. Every certified translation submitted to USCIS, a court, or an academic institution requires a competent human translator to personally sign the certificate of accuracy on every page. AI is the drafter; the human translator is the accountable signatory. No AI system can fulfill that legal and professional obligation, and no agency should imply otherwise to a client.

Correcting these four assumptions early in a client conversation protects project quality, sets accurate budget expectations, and ensures compliance when certified output is required. The average market rate for professional translation sits around $0.22 per source word, and AI localization workflows deliver real savings — but only when buyers understand that human oversight is the mechanism that makes those savings safe to capture.
