pages.title: Agile Localization: How Translators and Agencies Work Inside Sprint Cycles
pages.h1: Agile Localization: How Translators and Agencies Work Inside Sprint Cycles
pages.meta_description: Agile localization embeds translation into sprint cycles so strings flow from the repo to the TMS continuously, with human review and LQA inside each release.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is agile localization from a translator's and agency's perspective?
  • How does the agile localization workflow run inside a sprint?
  • What core technologies and tools make agile localization work?
  • What are the key benefits of agile localization for translators and agencies?
  • How do quality gates survive a two-week sprint cadence?
  • How do agencies price agile localization versus traditional project work?
  • What breaks an agile localization program and how do agencies respond?
  • Frequently asked questions

Translation agencies that still batch strings into weekly handoffs lose the sprint-shaped work to shops that have re-engineered their production floor around merge events. This page covers how translators and agencies restructure intake, roles, cadence, quality gates, and billing to deliver certified-grade output inside a client's two-week release train — without breaking the ISO 17100-aligned quality line. For the broader program this delivery model sits inside, see How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying.

What is agile localization from a translator's and agency's perspective?

Agile localization is a production method where translators work inside the client's sprint cycle: strings flow from the source repo into a TMS continuously, micro-jobs replace batch POs, and localized builds trail the English release by hours instead of weeks. For agencies, the model collapses the gap between dev merge and locale ship.

The operating shift touches five production levers at once:

  • Intake: connector-driven string flow, not emailed XLIFF packages.
  • Job size: micro-jobs of 10–200 strings, not multi-thousand-word POs.
  • Roles: PM moves from dispatch to exception handling.
  • Billing: retained capacity against an SLA, not per-PO quoting.
  • Quality: review and LQA run in parallel inside the sprint, not after.

How does agile localization differ from traditional waterfall translation handoff?

In waterfall, strings are exported once per release, translated offline, and reimported weeks later. In agile localization, every merge pushes new or changed strings to the TMS, translators pick micro-jobs sized in minutes, and locales ship on the same sprint as source.

DimensionWaterfall localizationAgile localization
String intakeBatch export per releaseWebhook on merge, diff-based
Job size5,000–50,000 words per PO10–200 strings per micro-job
Release-trail deltaWeeks to months behind sourceHours behind source
PM workQuote, dispatch, chase filesMonitor queues, resolve blockers
Billing framePer-PO quotingRetained capacity with overage
TM update cadencePer batch closePer approved segment

In-sprint timing and release-trail mechanics are documented further in Product Localization: How Translators and Agencies Deliver It.

When does a project actually need agile localization?

A project crosses into agile localization when four triggers appear together: a release cadence under two weeks, more than 500 new or changed strings per sprint, more than six active target locales, and in-app experimentation that spawns strings outside the main release train.

  1. Release cadence under two weeks. Batch handoff cannot keep up with the merge rate.
  2. 500+ changed strings per sprint. Volume justifies a connector instead of manual exports.
  3. 6+ active locales. Coordination cost of parallel waterfalls exceeds a single continuous pipeline.
  4. In-app experimentation. A/B copy, feature flags, and in-product messaging ship between releases.

In-tool experimentation is one of the loudest triggers; see How Pendo Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know for the string-flow pattern when copy ships outside the main release train.

How it works

How does the agile localization workflow run inside a sprint?

1

How do strings move from the developer's repo into the translator's queue?

Strings move via a TMS connector: when a developer merges new or changed resource files, a webhook fires, the TMS diffs the keys, creates micro-jobs for only the affected segments, and routes them to the pre-assigned linguist pool for that locale. The repo stays untouched by translators; the TMS stays authoritative.

Common stacks for the source side include GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket, with CI pipelines handling the merge trigger. For a frontend-framework example, see React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline. For broader multi-locale orchestration, see Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

2

What does a translator's day look like under agile localization?

A translator's day under agile localization is a feed of micro-jobs — typically 10 to 200 strings each, sized in minutes — picked from a shared queue, with translation memory and glossary pre-loaded, screenshots or Figma context attached, and an SLA counting down per job.

  • Queue view: micro-jobs ranked by SLA, locale, and client priority.
  • Context panel: screenshot, Figma frame, or in-app route for the string.
  • TM and term base: pre-loaded per locale, with match percentages visible.
  • AI first-draft: pre-filled for post-editing on new segments.
  • Submit path: segment moves to reviewer, then to LQA sampling pool.

3

How does the PM role change in an agile localization setup?

The PM role shifts from job dispatch to exception handling and capacity planning: instead of issuing POs and chasing files, the PM watches queue health, resolves context questions, reroutes blocked segments, and forecasts linguist capacity against the client's roadmap.

A PM's day under this model includes five recurring tasks:

  • Monitor queue depth and SLA burn-down per locale.
  • Resolve translator context queries routed through the TMS.
  • Reroute segments blocked by mutating source copy or missing assets.
  • Forecast linguist capacity against the next 2–3 sprints of client roadmap.
  • Report LQA scores per locale to the client and the quality lead.

What core technologies and tools make agile localization work?

Agile localization relies on four core technology layers: a translation management system with Git/CI connectors, a shared translation memory and term base per locale, AI first-draft and machine translation engines (DeepL, GPT-class, NMT), and webhook-driven integrations with GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket for real-time string sync.

LayerFunctionOwner
TMS with connectorsSystem of record; routes micro-jobsAgency
Translation memory + term baseLeverage and terminology consistencyAgency (per locale)
AI first-draft / NMTPre-translation upstream of human reviewAgency
Repo + CI webhooksTrigger diff and micro-job creation on mergeClient dev team

What role does the TMS play as the system of record?

The TMS is the single system of record for every string, variant, and status: translators never touch the repo, developers never hand-edit locale files, and every change — source, translation, approval, LQA score — is logged against the segment ID for audit.

That audit trail is what lets ISO 17100-aligned agencies defend a per-segment chain of custody when a certified lane runs through an agile pipeline. Multi-locale governance of the same system of record is covered in Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

How does translation memory change under continuous flow?

Translation memory under continuous flow is updated per approved segment, not per batch, so leverage climbs sprint over sprint. Agencies govern one TM and one term base per locale across all client lanes to keep match rates stable and prevent fragmentation.

Per-segment updates have three operational effects:

  • Leverage rises inside the same sprint, not after a batch close.
  • Terminology drift is caught the moment a reviewer rejects a term.
  • Fragmentation across sub-projects collapses when the TM is shared, not forked.

Where does AI first-draft and machine translation fit in the pipeline?

AI first-draft and machine translation sit upstream of human review: the engine pre-translates every new segment, TM overrides exact and high-fuzzy matches, and translators post-edit the AI output rather than translating from scratch — compressing turnaround without removing the human sign-off.

The stacking order is fixed: TM match → AI pre-translate on no-match → human post-edit → reviewer → LQA sample. Engines in common use include DeepL, GPT-class large language models, and domain-tuned NMT. CI-integrated branch flows that feed these engines are documented in Computer Software Localization: How Translators and Agencies Ship It.

Why us

What are the key benefits of agile localization for translators and agencies?

Agile localization delivers four measurable benefits to the production side: predictable linguist utilization through retained capacity, higher TM leverage from continuous updates, faster time-to-locale that justifies premium SLAs, and a PM workload that scales sub-linearly with string volume.

  • Predictable utilization: reserved hours smooth the sawtooth of PO cycles.
  • Higher TM leverage: per-segment updates raise match rates faster.
  • Faster time-to-locale: locales trail source by hours, supporting premium SLAs.
  • Sub-linear PM load: queue monitoring scales better than per-PO dispatch.

How do quality gates survive a two-week sprint cadence?

Quality gates survive agile cadence by running in parallel, not in series: review at $0.04–$0.08 per source word checks every segment, and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words samples output against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 covering accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style.

What does the LQA scorecard check per sprint?

The LQA scorecard checks sampled segments against five error categories — accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style — with severity weights that convert raw defects into a per-locale score that must clear the pass threshold before the sprint build ships.

CategoryChecksSeverity weights
AccuracyMistranslation, omission, additionMinor / Major / Critical
FluencyGrammar, punctuation, spellingMinor / Major
TerminologyTerm base adherence, consistencyMinor / Major
Locale conventionDate, number, currency, address formatMinor / Major
StyleRegister, tone, brand voiceMinor / Major

Do certified lanes (USCIS, legal) break under agile cadence?

Certified lanes do not break under agile cadence when LQA stays a blocking gate and the certificate of accuracy remains mandatory per page. USCIS filings still price at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard page, with notarization an optional $10–$50 line item — sprint pressure is absorbed through parallel reviewer pools, not by skipping gates.

Three operational rules keep the certified lane intact:

  • LQA sampling runs on every certified-lane sprint, not every other one.
  • Reviewer pools are expanded in parallel when volume spikes.
  • Per-page certificate of accuracy and sign-off are issued before the build cuts, not after.

Pricing

How do agencies price agile localization versus traditional project work?

Agencies price agile localization in four stacked line items on a retained-capacity frame: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and PM at 10–15% of project value — with AI pre-translate shifting the mix toward review and LQA rather than translation.

Line itemRateBasis
Translation (post-edit on AI draft)$0.10–$0.25 / source wordPer word, per locale
Review$0.04–$0.08 / source wordEvery segment, per locale
LQA$40–$90 / 1,000 wordsSampled against MQM scorecard
Project management10–15% of project valueRetained capacity + exception handling
Certified sign-off (USCIS)$25–$150 / pagePer page, with notarization $10–$50 optional

What does a mid-size agile localization program cost end-to-end?

A mid-size multi-locale program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end, with AI pre-translate shifting the mix toward review and LQA rather than translation. Variation tracks TM leverage, turnaround SLA, and whether certified sign-off is in scope.

Three variables move the budget inside that band:

  • TM leverage: a mature TM at 40%+ fuzzy-and-above match compresses translation cost.
  • Turnaround SLA: 24-hour SLAs carry a premium over 72-hour SLAs.
  • Certified scope: adding per-page certification raises the per-locale floor.
Get a quote

What breaks an agile localization program and how do agencies respond?

Agile localization programs break in five predictable ways: missing context on new strings, source copy that keeps changing after translation, connector drift between repo and TMS, reviewer burnout on micro-job cadence, and locale-specific QA bugs that only surface in staging builds.

  • Missing context: enforce screenshot or Figma link on every new string key.
  • Mutating source copy: lock copy at sprint start or price re-translations as overage.
  • Connector drift: run a scheduled key-parity check between repo and TMS.
  • Reviewer burnout: cap micro-job queue depth per reviewer per day.
  • Locale QA bugs: ship pseudo-localization builds to staging each sprint.

How is a readiness check run against a prospective agile localization client?

A five-row readiness check scores a prospect before an agile retainer is signed: connector availability for the client's stack, internationalization hygiene (externalized strings, no hard-coded dates), string-volume floor above 500 per sprint, in-tool context delivery (screenshots or Figma links), and a budgeted LQA line.

RowCheckPass criterion
1Connector availabilitySupported TMS connector for the client's repo and CI
2i18n hygieneExternalized strings; no hard-coded dates, numbers, or currency
3String-volume floor500+ new or changed strings per sprint
4Context deliveryScreenshots or Figma frames attached per string key
5LQA budget line$40–$90 per 1,000 words line item approved

Per-locale emission on the published output still follows standard tagging: ISO 639-1 language codes with optional ISO 3166-1 country codes, for example hreflang="es-MX" and hreflang="pt-BR", applied per locale build.

Frequently asked questions

What are the best practices for doing localization (software)?

The best practices for software localization center on integrating translation work directly into the development sprint cycle rather than treating it as a post-release afterthought. Key practices include: internationalizing the codebase first (i18n) so strings are externalized and context-tagged before any translation begins; assigning a dedicated localization engineer or LSP contact to each sprint; committing to continuous localization by pushing new or changed strings to translators within 24–48 hours of a string freeze; and using translation memory (TM) to avoid re-translating repeated UI strings across sprints, which typically reduces per-word costs by 20–40%. For certified content — such as in-app legal notices, compliance disclosures, or onboarding documents — first-draft automation tools can compress turnaround from days to hours, keeping pace with two-week sprint cadences without sacrificing quality or certification requirements.
pages.excerpt: Agile localization embeds translation into sprint cycles so strings flow from the repo to the TMS continuously, with human review and LQA inside each release.

pages.title: Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide
pages.h1: Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide
pages.meta_description: Application localization is the end-to-end process of adapting an app's strings, UI, formats, and cultural references for a specific locale — here is how
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is application localization from the translator's side of the desk?
  • How does the application localization process run from brief to release?
  • What should translators know about resource files, placeholders, and ICU plurals?
  • How much does text expansion affect application localization layout?
  • When does a project move from waterfall to continuous application localization?
  • What does app store metadata localization require from translators?
  • How do agencies price application localization work?
  • What are the common application localization pitfalls agencies see?
  • Which tools do translators and agencies use for application localization?
  • Where does application localization sit inside the broader localization program?
  • Frequently asked questions

Application localization is the production discipline this guide treats from the translator's and agency's seat — the string file open in the editor, the translation memory feeding leverage, the character budget printed next to each segment, and the LQA scorecard that signs off the release. The pages that rank for this term speak to buyers; this one speaks to the people doing the work.

What is application localization from the translator's side of the desk?

Application localization is the end-to-end adaptation of an app's strings, UI layout, media, number and date formats, and cultural references for one target locale, delivered by translators and reviewers working inside resource files, translation memory, and a staging build the developer merges back into the repo. The translator's desk holds five artifacts — resource bundle, TM, term base, style guide, and a pseudo-loc or staging build — not a Word document.

For the canonical cross-discipline definition, see our guide on what localisation means and how professionals define it. Four facts frame the seat:

  • The deliverable is a locale-stamped resource file, not prose.
  • The source is externalized by the dev team before the translator touches it.
  • Context arrives as screenshots, character limits, and segment IDs.
  • Quality is scored per 1000 words against a weighted rubric at release.

What does an application localization project actually contain?

An application localization project contains five artifacts the translator inspects before quoting: the extracted resource bundle, the project translation memory, the client term base, the locale style guide, and the pseudo-localization or staging build used for in-context review.

ArtifactWhat to check before quoting
Resource bundle (.xliff, .json, .strings, strings.xml)Segment count, placeholder density, character limits attached, context fields populated
Translation memoryLeverage report: ICE, 100%, 95–99%, 85–94%, no match — drives the discount schedule
Term baseEntries per locale, forbidden terms, enforcement set to hard-fail in the editor
Style guideRegister, address form (tú/usted), punctuation, number and date conventions
Pseudo-loc or staging buildTruncation hotspots, hard-coded strings, RTL readiness, encoding sanity

How does application localization differ from software localization and website localization?

Application localization is the subset of software localization scoped to a shipping end-user app — iOS, Android, desktop, web app — while website localization covers browser-rendered marketing and content sites, and broader software localization also covers back-office, embedded, and SDK layers. For the sibling discipline, see Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.

  • Application: compiled or packaged binary, resource bundles, store metadata, release train.
  • Website: CMS strings, SEO metadata, continuous publishing, no store review.
  • Software (broad): back-office consoles, SDK docs, embedded firmware strings, EULAs.

How does UX writing and UI copy affect the translator's brief?

UX copy carries strict character limits and tone constraints that shape every segment decision. Button labels, error messages, and onboarding tooltips must preserve the UX intent — a 12-character English CTA cannot become a 24-character German phrase on an iOS primary button. Translators treat each segment as a UI component, not a sentence.

How it works

How does the application localization process run from brief to release?

1

What does the internationalization (i18n) handoff look like?

The internationalization handoff is the point where developers deliver a build whose strings, dates, numbers, and layouts are externalized and locale-ready, so translators can work without touching code. For the engineering-side deep dive, see Internationalization (i18n) Explained for Language Professionals, and for a framework example, see How to Add i18n to an Astro Site.

Internationalization is the prerequisite that makes localization possible — it is the engineering step that externalizes strings and locale-dependent code so translators can work without touching source. Four handoff artifacts tell the translator whether i18n is complete:

  • Resource files with no concatenated sentences.
  • Date, number, and currency rendering via locale APIs, not hard-coded.
  • Plural handling via ICU MessageFormat or platform equivalent.
  • Layout that reflows for text expansion and RTL mirroring.

2

How are strings extracted and delivered to the translator?

Strings are extracted into locale resource files and delivered as a CAT or TMS job with source context, screenshots, and character limits attached per segment. The common formats are .strings and .stringsdict on iOS, strings.xml on Android, .resx on .NET, .properties and .po on cross-platform back ends, and .json or .xliff as the TMS interchange format. For framework-specific pipelines see React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline and JavaScript Localization Libraries Compared for Translation Professionals.

3

Where does pseudo-localization fit in the workflow?

Pseudo-localization fits between extraction and translation as a dev-side stress test that inflates strings and swaps characters to expose hard-coded text, truncated UI, and encoding bugs before any human translation money is spent. Our dedicated reference, Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds, covers the test-build mechanics in full — this page treats it as a gate, not a tutorial.

4

What happens during in-context review on the staging build?

During in-context review the translator or reviewer opens the staging build with locale forced on, walks every screen, and files per-string issues against the segment ID in the TMS. Four issue types dominate the ticket queue:

  • Truncation on primary CTAs, tab bars, and form labels.
  • Wrong register — formal where informal was briefed, or vice versa.
  • Placeholder drift that compiles but renders a raw token.
  • Misleading icon pairing where the translated label contradicts the glyph.

5

What does linguistic quality assurance (LQA) check at release?

Linguistic quality assurance checks five categories at release — accuracy, terminology, style, locale conventions, and functional integrity — scored against a weighted rubric that produces a per-1000-word error count.

LQA categoryWeightWhat it catches
Accuracy30%Mistranslation, omission, addition against source
Terminology20%Term base violations, inconsistent brand terms
Style15%Register, voice, style guide drift
Locale conventions15%Dates, numbers, currency, address format, punctuation
Functional integrity20%Placeholder, tag, plural branch, character-limit breakage

Agencies quote a pass rate of under 10 errors per 1000 words at major/critical severity. Regulated verticals tighten the bar — see What Financial Localization Requires Beyond Standard Translation and How Pharma Localization Works and What It Demands from Translators for sector-specific adjustments to the locale-conventions row.

About

What should translators know about resource files, placeholders, and ICU plurals?

Translators handling application localization work inside locale resource files that carry placeholders, plural rules, and markup — breaking any of them crashes the build. Five integrity checks belong in every QA pass:

  1. Placeholder presence — every {name}, %s, %@ in source appears in target.
  2. Positional order — %1$s and %2$s indices preserved or correctly reordered.
  3. Plural branch coverage — every CLDR category required by the target language filled.
  4. HTML and XML tag balance — <b>…</b>, <link>…</link> opened and closed.
  5. Escape consistency — \" and \n handled per the file format's rules.

These five breakages drive roughly 80% of post-handoff bug tickets.

Which resource file formats appear most often in app projects?

The resource file formats translators see most often are platform-mapped and tool-mapped per project:

Platform / roleFile formatNotes
iOS.strings, .stringsdictUTF-16 by default; .stringsdict carries plural rules
Androidstrings.xmlPlural tags, escape rules for apostrophes
.NET.resxXML with name/value pairs and comments
Cross-platform back end.po, .properties, .jsonGettext, Java properties, JSON key-value trees
TMS interchange.xliff, .tmxRound-trips the segment plus metadata

How do placeholders behave in iOS, Android, and ICU syntax?

Placeholders behave differently per platform: iOS uses printf-style %@ and %1$@ positional tokens, Android uses %s with explicit indices, and ICU MessageFormat uses named {variables} with select and plural branches. Mixing syntaxes in a translation unit breaks compile. For iOS specifically, see SwiftUI Localization: A Practical Guide for App Translators.

How are ICU plurals and gender branches translated correctly?

ICU plurals and gender branches are translated by filling every CLDR category the target language requires, not by copying the English singular/plural pair. The ICU MessageFormat syntax uses named {variable} placeholders with select and plural branches. Named example counts:

  • English — 2 forms: one, other.
  • Russian — 4 forms: one, few, many, other.
  • Polish — 3 forms: one, few, many.
  • Arabic — 6 forms: zero, one, two, few, many, other.
  • Chinese and Japanese — 1 form: other.

Pricing

How much does text expansion affect application localization layout?

Text expansion changes app layout by target language. German strings grow about 35% over English, Russian 30%, Spanish 25%, French 20%, while Chinese and Japanese contract about 40%. Translators quote character budgets per segment to protect buttons, tabs, and iOS navigation bars from truncation. For UI-specific depth, see UI Localization: Constraints, Pitfalls, and Best Practices.

Target languageExpansion vs EnglishCommon UI pain points
German+35%Tab bars, primary CTA buttons, form field labels
Russian+30%Toasts, iOS navigation bar titles, menu items
Spanish+25%Buttons, onboarding tooltips
French+20%Buttons, settings labels
Chinese (Simplified)-40%Visual balance, line-height tuning — see Chinese Localization: What Makes It Harder Than Most Projects

Which UI elements break first when strings expand?

The UI elements that break first are iOS tab-bar labels, Android bottom navigation, primary CTA buttons, form field labels, and single-line toast messages. All five carry hard character limits a translator respects per segment, and all five surface in pseudo-loc before any real translation ships.

How do right-to-left languages change the layout brief?

Right-to-left languages like Arabic and Hebrew mirror the layout: navigation flips, icon chirality reverses, number sequences stay left-to-right inside RTL paragraphs. Translators flag any UI element whose meaning depends on direction — a back arrow, a progress bar, a chevron on a list row — so the dev team mirrors or swaps the asset per locale.

Get a quote

When does a project move from waterfall to continuous application localization?

A project moves to continuous localization when four triggers appear together: a release cadence under two weeks, more than 500 new or changed strings per sprint, more than six active target locales, and in-app experimentation that spawns strings outside the main release train. For the delivery model, see How Continuous Localisation Works and When to Offer It, and for experiment-driven string flow, see How Pendo Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.

  1. Release cadence under two weeks.
  2. Over 500 new or changed strings per sprint.
  3. More than six active target locales.
  4. In-app experimentation generating strings between releases.

What changes operationally in a continuous localization setup?

In a continuous localization setup, strings flow from the repo to the TMS automatically via a connector, translators work on micro-jobs sized in minutes, and the agency bills on retained capacity or per-word with an SLA on turnaround, not on one-off POs. The PM role shifts from job dispatch to exception handling and capacity planning.

How do translation memory and term base behave under continuous flow?

Under continuous flow the translation memory updates after every merged segment and the term base is enforced as a hard check in the editor. Translation memory stores approved segments per client and locale and drives leverage percentages that discount per-word pricing. The term base locks brand terminology per locale and fails the segment at save when violated. Translators see leverage and terminology status in real time instead of in a weekly export.

What does app store metadata localization require from translators?

App store metadata localization requires the translator to deliver eight fields per locale, each with its own length limit and ASO constraint. For the website SEO sibling discipline, see How to Apply SEO Principles When Localizing a Website.

FieldiOS limitGoogle Play limit
Title30 characters50 characters
Subtitle30 characters—
Promotional text170 charactersShort description 80 chars
Keywords100 characters— (ranks on full description)
Full description4000 characters4000 characters
"What's New"4000 characters500 characters
Screenshot captionsPer-image overlayPer-image overlay
In-app purchase display names30 characters55 characters

Promotional text and screenshot captions often cross into transcreation — see Transcreation Defined: How It Differs from Translation for the rate and workflow difference. For the marketing-lane framing, see What Localization in Marketing Means — and How to Deliver It.

How do iOS App Store and Google Play metadata requirements differ?

The iOS App Store exposes a dedicated keywords field capped at 100 characters while Google Play has no keywords field and ranks the full description instead. Translators adapt the same source brief into two different ASO shapes per locale — tight keyword packing for iOS, keyword-density prose for Play.

How are keywords localized without machine-translating them?

Keywords are localized by researching the target-locale search terms with store analytics or an ASO tool, then selecting the 100-character set that matches intent. This step is distinct from translating the English keyword list and is billed by the hour, not by the word.

Pricing

How do agencies price application localization work?

Agencies price application localization on a per-source-word base rate ($0.10–$0.25 USD for European targets, higher for low-resource locales) plus line items for placeholder-dense segments, in-context review hours, LQA passes, pseudo-loc rebuilds, and ASO metadata. Continuous retainers replace per-job pricing above a defined string volume.

What line items belong on an application localization quote?

The line items that belong on an application localization quote are eight, priced per locale:

Line itemUnitTypical US agency range
TranslationPer source word$0.10–$0.25
ReviewPer source word$0.04–$0.08
In-context reviewPer hour$60–$120
LQAPer 1000 words$40–$90
Project management% of job10–15%
TMS connector setupFlat$300–$1,500 one-time
Pseudo-loc rebuildFlat per build$150–$500
ASO metadata per localeFlat$120–$350

Placeholder-dense segments carry a surcharge of 15–25% because the editor time per word rises sharply when every string carries two or more tokens. Adjacent application types — games, for instance — price differently; see How to Localise a Godot Game for Multiple Languages and How Video Game Localization Works and What Clients Expect.

How does machine translation post-editing (MTPE) change the rate card?

Machine translation post-editing changes the rate card by splitting the per-word rate into a lower raw-MT line and a human post-edit line, with the combined price typically 50–70% of full human translation when the engine quality and domain fit have been tested on the client's own strings first. MTPE on untested engines prices at full human rates because the editor rewrites rather than edits.

Get a quote

What are the common application localization pitfalls agencies see?

The common application localization pitfalls agencies see are five recurring failures: hard-coded strings missed by i18n, concatenated sentences that break grammar in target locales, context-free segments quoted at full rate, placeholder drift surviving to production, and ASO metadata translated without keyword research. For the dedicated anti-pattern treatment, see Bad Localization: What Goes Wrong and How to Avoid It.

How are concatenated strings handled when the dev team cannot refactor?

When the dev team cannot refactor concatenated strings, the translator flags each affected segment, requests a single-sentence rewrite in English, or negotiates per-locale rewording that preserves grammatical agreement. The translator never silently reorders the fragments — gender, case, and verb agreement collapse when a target language inflects differently from English.

What goes wrong when context is missing from the resource bundle?

When context is missing from the resource bundle, translators guess the register, part of speech, and screen placement — producing segments that compile but read wrong in-app. The downstream cost is LQA failure, bug tickets, and rework that exceeds the initial translation fee. The PM fix is to require a screenshot or developer comment on every segment before the job opens.

Which tools do translators and agencies use for application localization?

Translators and agencies use three tool categories: translation management systems (Crowdin, Phrase, Lokalise, Transifex, Smartling) that host the project, CAT editors (Trados Studio, memoQ, OmegaT, Wordfast) that host the translation work, and QA utilities (Xbench, Verifika, LQA scorecards) that gate release. For a Crowdin-specific drill-down, see How Translators and Agencies Work Inside Crowdin.

What does a TMS do that a CAT tool does not?

A TMS adds the project layer a CAT tool lacks: repo connectors, string lifecycle tracking, in-context editors, multi-translator assignment, pseudo-loc generation, and ASO metadata hosting. The CAT tool is the segment editor; the TMS is the production system around it.

  • TMS scope: repo sync, job routing, in-context, roles, analytics, store metadata.
  • CAT scope: segment, TM leverage, TB enforcement, QA checks, bilingual export.
  • QA utility scope: cross-file checks for terminology, placeholders, numbers, consistency.

Where does application localization sit inside the broader localization program?

Application localization sits as one of six delivery lanes inside a broader localization program: product app, website, marketing content, support knowledge base, legal and compliance documents, and in-product video. Each lane carries its own SLA, tooling, and reviewer pool, but all six share one term base and style guide per locale. For the program framing, see How Enterprise Localization Programs Are Structured and Run and Building a Localisation Strategy That Agencies Can Execute.

Sibling lanes and adjacent scopes translators are routinely moved across:

  • Website — Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.
  • E-commerce platforms — How Shopify Localization Works and What It Means for Your Agency, How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.
  • Marketing and content — Content Localisation: How to Adapt Material That Goes Beyond Text.
  • Services with no physical product — Localizing Services: What Changes When There's No Physical Product.

How is ROI measured on an application localization program?

ROI on an application localization program is measured against four metrics tracked per locale: install uplift, 7-day retention delta, average revenue per paying user, and support ticket deflection. The baseline is captured on the English-only build before the first locale ships. For the full reporting treatment, see How to Measure and Present the ROI of Localization Work.

Application localization costs $0.10–$0.25 per source word for European target locales on the translation line, plus review, in-context, LQA, PM, and ASO metadata line items. A 10,000-word app launching in five locales commonly lands between $8,000 and $20,000 for the first release, before continuous-localization retainers kick in.

Frequently asked questions

What does app localization mean?

App localization means adapting a software application's content, interface, and functionality so it feels native to a specific target locale — not just translating strings, but also formatting dates, currencies, plurals, and culturally sensitive imagery. For translators and agencies, this typically involves working with resource files (e.g., .strings, .xml, .json) exported by developers, translating UI strings within tight character limits, and returning files that slot directly back into the codebase. Certified translation teams may also need to handle in-app legal disclosures or terms of service that require formal certification alongside the standard linguistic work.

What is localization in apps?

Localization in apps is the end-to-end process of making a mobile or desktop application fully usable and culturally appropriate for a new language-market combination. It goes beyond UI string translation to include locale-specific number and date formatting, right-to-left layout support, app store listing copy, push notification text, and any regulated content (such as medical or legal disclaimers) that may require certified translation. For agencies producing certified translations, app localization projects often arrive as bundled file packages requiring both linguistic accuracy and format-exact file return so the developer can rebuild the app without reformatting.

What is the software localization process?

The software localization process typically follows five stages: content extraction, translation and adaptation, engineering/DTP, quality assurance, and delivery. Developers first export translatable strings into resource files; translators then work on those files — often inside a CAT tool or TMS — before the localized files are reintegrated and tested in-app. For certified translation contexts, an additional certification or notarization step is inserted after linguistic QA. Turnaround for a mid-sized app (5,000–20,000 words) typically runs one to three weeks depending on language pair, complexity, and whether certification is required.

How is localization different from translation?

Translation converts text from one language to another, while localization adapts the entire user experience — text, visuals, formats, and cultural references — so the product feels locally made. A translator renders words accurately; a localizer also adjusts idioms, resizes UI elements for text expansion (German can run 30–40% longer than English), converts units, and flags culturally inappropriate imagery. In certified translation production, the distinction matters because a certified translation guarantees linguistic accuracy of a specific source document, whereas localization is an iterative, engineering-adjacent workflow that rarely carries a single certification stamp over the whole product.

What does localization mean in software?

In software, localization (often abbreviated L10N) means configuring an application to display content correctly and culturally appropriately for a specific locale, identified by a language-region code such as fr-CA or zh-TW. This covers UI text, error messages, help documentation, date/time and number formats, currency symbols, keyboard input handling, and sometimes right-to-left text rendering. For translators delivering work into software pipelines, it also means respecting placeholder syntax (e.g., %s, {0}), character limits, and file encoding requirements so that translated strings integrate without breaking the build.

What does localization mean in simple terms?

In simple terms, localization means making a product feel like it was built for a specific country or language community — not just translated, but truly local. Think of it as the difference between a menu that says "USD 5.00" everywhere versus one that automatically shows "€5,00" in Germany with the correct decimal convention. For translation professionals, localization is the discipline that combines linguistic skill with technical file-handling so that apps, websites, and documents work correctly in every target market.

What is an example of localization?

A clear example of localization is a medical app originally built in US English being adapted for the Brazilian Portuguese market. The work involves translating all UI strings, converting date formats from MM/DD/YYYY to DD/MM/YYYY, replacing Fahrenheit references with Celsius, adjusting dosage units where relevant, and — for any patient-facing regulatory disclosures — producing certified translations accepted by Brazil's ANVISA. The app store listing copy and push notifications are also rewritten for Brazilian idiom, not just word-for-word translated from European Portuguese.

How much does localization cost?

App localization costs vary widely, but translators and agencies typically charge between $0.10 and $0.30 per source word for standard language pairs, with less common pairs or certified content running higher. A 10,000-word app might cost $1,000–$3,000 per language in translation alone, plus engineering, DTP, and QA fees that can add 20–50% to the total. Certified translation of specific in-app documents (terms of service, medical disclaimers) is usually priced per page or per document rather than per word, ranging from $25 to $100+ per page depending on complexity and jurisdiction.

What are the best practices for localizing software and products?

Key best practices include internationalizing the codebase before localization begins (separating hard-coded strings into resource files), providing translators with context through screenshots or a style guide, setting and enforcing character limits for UI strings, and running in-context QA on the live build rather than only on raw files. For certified translation elements within an app — such as legal terms or regulatory notices — agencies should maintain a clear audit trail linking the source document version to the certified output. Using translation memory and glossaries across projects cuts costs and ensures brand-term consistency over time.

How does localization work?

Localization works by separating content from code so that translatable text can be swapped out without rewriting the application logic. Developers export resource files (e.g., strings.xml for Android, Localizable.strings for iOS), hand them to translators or agencies, and then reintegrate the returned files for each target locale. Translators work on those files using CAT tools that display source and target side by side, flag repeated segments, and enforce glossaries. Quality assurance is then done both on the raw files (checking formatting tags and placeholders) and inside the running application (checking text display, truncation, and cultural fit).

How can I localize my iOS app?

To localize an iOS app, developers use Xcode's built-in localization workflow: marking UI strings with NSLocalizedString, exporting an XLIFF file per target language, sending those files to translators, and reimporting the translated XLIFF before building. As a translator or agency receiving iOS localization work, you'll most often handle XLIFF or .strings files, need to respect variable placeholders like %@ and %1$d, and work within character limits imposed by the UI. If any in-app content — such as privacy policies or medical disclaimers — requires certified translation, those should be scoped and delivered as a separate certified document alongside the standard localization files.
pages.excerpt: Application localization is the end-to-end process of adapting an app's strings, UI, formats, and cultural references for a specific locale — here is how translators and agencies actually deliver it.

pages.title: Bad Localization: What Goes Wrong and How to Avoid It
pages.h1: Bad Localization: What Goes Wrong and How to Avoid It
pages.meta_description: Bad localization is translated content that fails in-market — wrong meaning, broken UI, cultural misses, or editorial overreach. Here are the causes, examples
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What counts as bad localization, and what does not?
  • What are the common causes of bad localization?
  • What are the most famous bad localization examples?
  • What does good localization look like, for contrast?
  • How can translators and agencies avoid bad localization on their side?
  • Frequently asked questions

Localization fails on release when a production team cannot defend what shipped. The failures split into five distinct classes, each routed to a different owner on the production floor, and each catchable at a specific workflow gate the translator or agency controls.

What counts as bad localization, and what does not?

Bad localization is a released build that fails in-market through linguistic error, engineering breakage, cultural misfire, undisclosed editorial rewriting, or process gaps. A tight deadline or a liberal-but-disclosed adaptation does not qualify. The defining trait is failure the production team cannot defend when a reviewer, a client, or a source-literate fan asks what changed and why.

The scope matters. One wrong noun in one segment is a defect in a line. A released product where translation, engineering, culture, editorial judgment, or process broke together is bad localization. The failure is at the system level.

How does bad localization differ from a bad translation?

A bad translation is a sentence-level error; bad localization is a system-level failure where translation, engineering, culture, editorial judgment, or process broke together on release. Translation is sentence-level transfer of meaning between languages. Localization is the full locale-fit build — engineering, culture, legal, layout, and editorial — assembled around that transfer. For the full definition, see Define Localization: What the Term Means in Professional Translation.

Is any cultural adaptation automatically bad localization?

Cultural adaptation is not bad localization when the change is disclosed, scoped by the style guide, and signed off by an in-market reviewer. It becomes bad localization when the team cannot name what was changed, why it was changed, or who approved it. The failure is silence, not liberty.

What are the common causes of bad localization?

Five production classes cause bad localization: linguistic errors from context-starved translators, engineering breakage from poor i18n, cultural misfires without an in-market reviewer, undisclosed editorial rewriting, and process gaps where no gate caught the problem. Each class routes to a different owner on the team, and each is catchable at a specific gate before release.

Which bad-localization failure maps to which production owner?

Each failure class has one accountable owner: linguistic to the translator, engineering to the developer, cultural to the in-market reviewer, editorial overreach to the editorial lead, process to the PM. The table pairs the symptom, the owner, and the workflow gate that would have caught it.

Failure classSymptomOwnerGate that catches it
LinguisticWrong register, wrong part of speech, mistranslated segmentTranslatorContext pack with screenshots on every segment
EngineeringHard-coded strings, UI overflow, placeholder driftDeveloperPseudo-localization at sprint zero
CulturalWrong iconography, invalid legal reference, offensive marketing claimIn-market reviewerIn-market reviewer sign-off per locale
Editorial overreachUndisclosed rewriting, appropriateness edits, inserted dialogueEditorial leadStyle guide with disclosure clause
ProcessMissing gate, late context, no QA passPMLQA threshold under 2 errors per 1000 words

What linguistic failures count as bad localization?

Linguistic failures are context-free segments translated at the wrong register, wrong part of speech, or wrong screen placement. The translator receives a string with no screenshot, no developer comment, and no record of where the string renders. The result is a grammatically correct line that reads wrong in the running product.

  • Button labels translated as full sentences.
  • Error messages written in a formal register that mismatches the product voice.
  • Variable names like "user" translated as the common noun instead of the role.
  • Gender agreement broken because the segment hid the subject.

The downstream cost is LQA failure and rework that exceeds the original translation fee.

What engineering failures count as bad localization?

Engineering failures include hard-coded strings, concatenated sentences that cannot reorder for Japanese or German, missing plural categories, placeholder drift, and UI that breaks under 15–30% text expansion into German, Russian, and Arabic. These originate upstream of the translator but ship as bad localization to the user. For the full inventory and the pipeline fixes, see i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds. Framework-specific patterns live in React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

What cultural failures count as bad localization?

Cultural failures ship when no in-market reviewer sees the build before release. The symptoms are untranslated puns, color or iconography that reads wrong in the target market, legal references that do not exist in the target jurisdiction, and marketing claims that insult the audience the brand is trying to enter. The owner is the in-market reviewer, and the gate is a per-locale sign-off with authority to block release.

What editorial overreach counts as bad localization?

Editorial overreach is undisclosed rewriting: appropriateness edits, inserted dialogue, removed jokes, or ideological softening that the production team cannot point to in the style guide. The failure is the lack of disclosure, not the fact that a change was made. Four undisclosed moves recur:

  1. Lines inserted that do not exist in the source.
  2. Jokes removed because a reviewer judged them inappropriate without logging the judgment.
  3. Character voice flattened to a house editorial style the client never signed.
  4. Ideological softening of source dialogue outside the style guide scope.

Each becomes defensible the moment the editorial lead logs the change, the reason, and the reviewer who approved it.

What process failures count as bad localization?

Process failures are missing gates: no pseudo-localization sprint-zero checkpoint, no context pack with screenshots, no in-market reviewer sign-off, and no LQA threshold enforced before release. Each missing gate is traceable to a specific clause in the localization strategy document. Build the clauses in from the first scoping call, as described in Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs.

What communication breakdowns between teams cause bad localization?

When developers, translators, editors, and QA testers operate in silos, errors compound across handoffs. Poor communication is a root process failure that spawns linguistic, engineering, and cultural mistakes at once. A developer ships a string without context. The translator guesses. The editor polishes the guess. The QA tester never sees the source. The build goes out broken, and no single owner can trace the failure.

The fix is a shared context channel per project — not a wiki, not a dead inbox — with named roles and query turnaround under 24 hours.

What are the most famous bad localization examples?

The famous bad localization examples are "All Your Base Are Belong To Us" from Zero Wing, "I Am Error" from Zelda II, "This Guy Are Sick" from Final Fantasy VII, the One Piece and Pokémon anime cuts, and recent script controversies in Final Fantasy Remake, Rebirth, and XVI. Each one maps to one of the five failure classes above.

Which video-game examples define bad localization?

Zero Wing, Final Fantasy IV, Zelda II, Pro Wrestling, Ghostbusters, X-Men Arcade, Final Fantasy VII, Resident Evil Revelations, Contra 3, and Metal Gear produced the English-language lines fans still quote decades later. Each line is a linguistic failure that no in-market reviewer caught.

  • Zero Wing — "All Your Base Are Belong To Us."
  • Final Fantasy IV — "You spoony bard!"
  • Zelda II — "I Am Error."
  • Final Fantasy VII — "This guy are sick."
  • Metal Gear — "I feel asleep."
  • Pro Wrestling — "A winner is you."
  • Ghostbusters (NES) — "Conglaturation !!!"
  • X-Men Arcade — "Welcome to die!"
  • Resident Evil Revelations — stilted shipboard dialogue.
  • Contra 3 — malformed cutscene lines.

For the production economics behind this category, see Video Game Localization: What Translators and Agencies Need to Know.

Which anime and manga examples define bad localization?

Anime examples center on One Piece, Naruto, and Pokémon dubs where cuts, renamed characters, and substituted cultural references confused viewers. The One Piece 4Kids dub cut whole episodes and renamed items. Pokémon dubs replaced onigiri with jelly donuts on screen. More recent flashpoints — Dragon Maid and Prison School — triggered the modern anti-localization backlash by making undisclosed appropriateness edits that fans traced line-by-line.

Which recent games show the modern localization backlash?

Final Fantasy Remake, Rebirth, and XVI, together with recent Trails/Falcom releases, are the current flashpoints. Fans with source-language access compare English scripts line-by-line and flag perceived liberties. The earlier Trails in the Sky 1–3 releases escaped the same scrutiny — the "just happy it came west" audience of that era accepted liberties that the current source-literate audience rejects. The content did not get worse; the audience changed, and disclosure did not catch up.

Does bad localization happen outside Japanese-to-English?

Bad localization is not limited to the Japanese-to-English pipeline. Portuguese and other non-English players report the same five failure classes in Nintendo Switch titles and SaaS products. The debate concentrates on English because the audience is largest, not because the problem is. High-friction locale pairs each produce their own failure patterns — see Chinese Localization: What Makes It Harder Than Most Projects for one example.

What does good localization look like, for contrast?

Good localization is faithful to source meaning, disclosed where it adapts, and signed off by an in-market reviewer against an MQM-style rubric scoring under 2 errors per 1000 words. 999 (Nine Hours, Nine Persons, Nine Doors) is the standard reference for creative, source-faithful adaptation that fans still praise. The script localized puzzles, honorifics, and wordplay without silently rewriting the story. Every creative liberty was traceable to a design need the team could name.

That is the test. A localization is defensible when the production team can name the change, the reason, and the reviewer who signed off.

How can translators and agencies avoid bad localization on their side?

Translators and agencies avoid bad localization by owning five production gates: a context pack with screenshots on every segment, pseudo-localization before translation money is spent, a term base and style guide with a disclosure clause, in-market reviewer sign-off, and an LQA threshold enforced at release under 2 errors per 1000 words.

Which workflow gates catch bad localization before release?

Five gates catch bad localization before release:

  1. Pseudo-localization at sprint zero — covered in full in Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds.
  2. Context pack with a screenshot or developer comment on every segment before the translation job opens.
  3. Style guide with a disclosure clause for every non-literal change.
  4. In-market reviewer sign-off per locale, with authority to block release.
  5. MQM-style LQA pass scoring under 2 errors per 1000 words against a weighted rubric.

How does disclosure prevent the editorial-overreach failure class?

A disclosure clause in the style guide requires every non-literal change to be logged with the reason and the reviewer who signed off. Fans and clients tolerate adaptation when the production team can defend it. The editorial failure is silence, not liberty. A one-line log entry per change — "line 412: joke adapted for US audience, approved by [reviewer]" — converts an overreach into a defensible edit.

What quality threshold separates acceptable from bad localization?

The release threshold used by production teams is under 2 errors per 1000 words against a weighted MQM-style rubric covering accuracy, terminology, regulatory compliance, and readability, with pass/fail checks on regulatory boilerplate and locked brand terms. The rubric is applied by a reviewer who did not translate the segment. Builds above the threshold go back to the translator before release, not after.

Translation is sentence-level transfer of meaning between languages; localization is the full locale-fit build around that transfer, including engineering, culture, legal, layout, and editorial judgment. A perfect translation can still ship as bad localization when the surrounding build breaks.

Frequently asked questions

What is localization in translation?

Localization is the process of adapting a translated text so it feels natural and appropriate within the target culture, not just linguistically accurate. Where translation converts words from one language to another, localization goes further: it adjusts idioms, humor, cultural references, date formats, units of measure, legal conventions, and tone. For certified translation production, this distinction is critical — a certified document must be accurate and legally equivalent, meaning localization choices must never distort meaning or omit content required by the certifying standard.

What's the difference between translation and localization, and does that distinction matter?

Translation converts content from a source language into a target language; localization adapts that content to fit the target culture's norms, expectations, and context. The distinction matters enormously in professional and certified translation work. A birth certificate or legal contract requires precise equivalence — over-localization that paraphrases or omits source content can invalidate certification. In marketing or software, under-localization produces content that reads as foreign and awkward. Knowing when each approach applies is a core competency for translators and agencies producing certified documents alongside general content.

What does localization mean?

Localization means adapting content — text, visuals, formatting, and cultural references — so it resonates naturally with a specific target locale, not just a target language. It goes beyond word-for-word translation to account for cultural sensitivities, regional spelling conventions (e.g., British vs. American English), legal terminology norms, and even layout considerations like text expansion. For translation professionals, localization is a defined workflow stage that follows or runs parallel to translation and requires separate quality-assurance checks from linguistic accuracy reviews.

What are common issues with localization — what does 'bad localization' mean?

Bad localization means the adapted text fails either the source or the target audience — it is inaccurate, culturally tone-deaf, inconsistent, or editorially altered beyond its mandate. Common failure modes include mistranslated idioms rendered literally, culturally specific humor that lands as offensive or nonsensical, omitted or added content that changes meaning, and inconsistent terminology across a document set. For certified translation production specifically, bad localization can mean a document fails legal validation, mistranslated amounts or dates, or certifications that are challenged or rejected by authorities.

How do you preserve meaning across languages without either being too literal or too liberal?

Preserving meaning requires a calibrated approach: stay close to the source structure where precision is legally or technically required, and adapt culturally loaded elements where literal rendering would obscure the intent. Professional translators use techniques such as functional equivalence (finding a target-culture concept that carries the same communicative weight), back-translation review, and terminology management to keep consistency. For certified translations, the governing standard — whether NAATI, ATA, or ISO 17100 — sets the boundaries: the text must be complete, accurate, and certifiably equivalent, leaving limited room for liberal interpretation.

How do you overcome translation and localization problems?

Overcoming localization problems starts with clear scope definition — establishing upfront whether the project requires strict equivalence (as in certified translation) or cultural adaptation (as in marketing copy). Concrete steps include building and enforcing client-approved glossaries, using translation memory tools to ensure consistency across large document sets, applying structured QA checklists, and having a second qualified linguist review for both accuracy and cultural fit. For certified translation workflows, using a platform that produces structured first drafts helps reduce the risk of omissions or formatting errors that typically account for a large share of revision cycles.

Why do localizers change things that seem 'not appropriate' — who authorized those changes?

Localizers make cultural adaptation decisions based on a brief, style guide, or editorial mandate provided by the client or publisher — ideally. Problems arise when those guardrails are absent or loosely defined, leaving individual translators or editors to make judgment calls about appropriateness with no documented authority. In certified translation, this issue is less common because regulatory standards explicitly prohibit unauthorized omissions or additions. In commercial localization, the solution is a clear, signed-off localization brief that specifies exactly which elements may be adapted and which must remain faithful to the source.
pages.excerpt: Bad localization is translated content that fails in-market — wrong meaning, broken UI, cultural misses, or editorial overreach. Here are the causes, examples, and the production-side fixes

pages.title: Business Localization: How Agencies Deliver Multi-Locale Programs for Corporate Clients
pages.h1: Business Localization: How Agencies Deliver Multi-Locale Programs for Corporate Clients
pages.meta_description: Business localization is the agency-side practice of adapting a client's corporate content — contracts, financial reports, websites, HR, marketing — into each
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is business localization from the agency's side of the desk?
  • What are the core components of a business localization deliverable?
  • What are the key benefits a corporate client buys when commissioning business localization?
  • What are the steps to build a business localization program on the agency side?
  • How much does a business localization program cost in USD?
  • What does business localization look like in practice? (US → EU example)
  • What are the hardest problems in running a business localization program?
  • What tools and TMS platforms carry a business localization program?
  • Frequently asked questions

Business localization is the agency-side production program that adapts a corporate client's contracts, financial reports, HR policies, compliance material, website, marketing, and certified filings into each target locale under one term base, one style guide, and lane-specific SLAs. A mid-size program covering 5 languages × 50,000 words budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end, built on translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and project management at 10–15% of project value. For the term's canonical scope, see Define Localization: What the Term Means in Professional Translation, and for the sibling app lane see How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying.

What is business localization from the agency's side of the desk?

Business localization is the agency-side practice of adapting a corporate client's contracts, financial reports, HR policies, compliance material, website, marketing, and certified filings into each target locale under one term base, one style guide, and lane-specific SLAs. The program replaces ad-hoc translation purchases with a repeatable production system that scales predictably as locale count grows. One shared term base governs all seven lanes per locale, ensuring that the entity name on a signed contract matches the one on the homepage footer and in the HR handbook. One locale style guide governs tone, date formats, currency presentation, and legal register across every deliverable in that market.

Localization is a comprehensive process that involves far more than converting text from one language to another. Translation changes language; localization adapts language, culture, legal format, UX, imagery, currency, and date formats simultaneously. That distinction matters on the production floor because each adaptation layer requires a different specialist and a different QA gate — a linguist alone cannot close the gap between a US-formatted financial statement and one accepted by a German commercial registry.

The seven production lanes carry distinct SLAs:

  • Contracts — certified line, named-translator attestation.
  • Financial reports — regulated figures, locked boilerplate.
  • HR policies — employee-facing, bilingual review.
  • Compliance materials — statutory wording.
  • Website and app — UI strings, hreflang, DTP.
  • Marketing — campaign copy, image QA gate.
  • Certified filings — USCIS, sworn, apostilled output.

How does business localization differ from translation and internationalization?

Translation converts text between languages, internationalization engineers software to accept any locale, and business localization is the per-locale delivery program that uses both to adapt corporate content to each market's legal, cultural, and operational expectations. Internationalization — abbreviated i18n — is the engineering preparation that happens before any locale-specific work begins; localization is the per-locale adaptation delivered against that preparation. The three terms describe three different jobs on the production floor, and conflating them leads to scope gaps, missed regulatory requirements, and mismatched deliverable formats.

DisciplineWho delivers itWhat it changes
TranslationLinguist in CAT toolLanguage only
Internationalization (i18n)Engineering teamCode accepts any locale
Business localizationAgency program managerLanguage, culture, legal format, UX, imagery, currency, dates

When does a client need a formal business localization program?

A client needs a formal business localization program once it operates in more than 2–3 active locales simultaneously, or once certified output such as USCIS filings, sworn translations, or apostilled documents enters the deliverable mix. Below that threshold, per-project purchase orders work adequately. Above it, drift in terminology, pricing, and turnaround forces governance — different vendors use different entity names, figures appear in inconsistent formats, and certified stamps from unvetted translators get rejected by receiving authorities. The formal program exists precisely to prevent those failure modes at scale.

What are the core components of a business localization deliverable?

A business localization deliverable has seven core components: contracts, financial reports, HR policies, compliance materials, website and app content, marketing assets, and certified filings — each produced against one shared term base and one locale style guide. The shared-asset model prevents the certified contract from using different corporate-entity names than the marketing site, and it prevents HR documents from adopting a tone that contradicts the brand voice established in campaign copy. Every component is a distinct production lane with its own specialist pool, QA gate, and pricing band.

Localization succeeds or fails based on meticulous attention to detail across each of these components. A weak link in any single lane — an untranslated UI string on the app, a figure presented in the wrong decimal convention on a financial report, or a stock photograph that reads as foreign on a localized landing page — undermines the entire market entry investment.

The shared-asset model prevents the certified contract from using different corporate-entity names than the marketing site. For the production model behind the shared assets, see Service Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Deliver.
