Which content lanes carry the heaviest certified-translation load?

Three lanes carry most of the certified load: incorporation and contract documents, financial statements for cross-border filings, and HR or compliance records for employee transfers, all requiring a signed certificate of accuracy on every page. The certified lane prices at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard 250-word page, with optional notarization at $10–$50 when the receiving authority requests it.

What role do website, app, and marketing lanes play in corporate localization?

Website, app, and marketing lanes carry the client's public-facing content: landing pages, product UI strings, campaign copy, and visual assets, each adapted against the same term base used in the legal lanes. The same corporate entity name appears on the signed contract, in the HR handbook, and on the homepage footer. Cross-reference Localization in Marketing: What Translators and Agencies Deliver for the marketing lane in isolation.

Where does image and visual localization fit?

Image and visual localization sits inside the marketing and website lanes as a QA gate covering photography, iconography, color symbolism, and on-screen text in graphics. It is the step most commonly skipped in multilingual campaigns, and the one most likely to break buyer trust in-market. Stock photography that reads as US-coded on an EU landing page undercuts every translated word around it. The gate runs late in the lane but blocks release.

Should business name and brand marks be localized?

Business name and brand marks are localized when the source name carries unintended meaning, misreads phonetically, or fails local registration rules — a decision that affects legal registration, consumer trust, and local SEO discoverability in the target territory. Business name localization is a trust and discoverability signal, not a cosmetic choice. The brand mark enters the term base as a locked entry per locale, so no reviewer accidentally translates it mid-document.

5–

What are the key benefits a corporate client buys when commissioning business localization?

A corporate client buys five concrete benefits: legally admissible documents in each jurisdiction, consistent brand voice across markets, measurable conversion lift on localized web and marketing content, lower regulatory risk on cross-border filings, and faster market entry per new locale. Each benefit maps to one or more lanes in the production program, and together they represent the business case for moving from ad-hoc translation purchasing to a governed localization program.

Legal admissibility — certified lane output is accepted by the receiving authorities the client files with, because each certificate carries a named translator's attestation and, where required, a notarization stamp costing

What are the steps to build a business localization program on the agency side?

1

How is scope defined across the seven lanes?

Scope is defined lane by lane: each content surface is counted, word volumes are forecast per locale, and certified lanes are isolated because they add per-page certificate requirements, locked boilerplate, and named-translator attestation that other lanes do not carry. A 50,000-word scope split across 5 locales is 250,000 output words, not 50,000. Certified pages are counted as pages, not words, inside the same forecast.

2

How do term base and style guide carry across lanes?

One term base and one locale style guide govern every lane in a given locale, so the certified contract uses the same corporate entity names and legal phrasing as the marketing site and the HR handbook. Cross-lane terminology drift is eliminated at source. The term base lives in the TMS, is reviewed per locale, and is updated by the lead reviewer, not by individual linguists.

3

What quality gates audit the program?

Two gates audit the program: review at $0.04–$0.08 per source word checks every segment, and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words samples output against a scorecard aligned to ISO 17100, with certified lanes carrying a mandatory sign-off on the certificate of accuracy. Review covers 100% of segments. LQA samples a statistical slice and scores against error categories.

Pricing

How much does a business localization program cost in USD?

A mid-size business localization program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end, built from translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and project management at 10–15% of project value.

Cost lineRateMid-size program (5 × 50,000 words)
Translation$0.10–$0.25 / source word$25,000–$62,500
Review$0.04–$0.08 / source word$10,000–$20,000
LQA$40–$90 / 1,000 words$2,000–$4,500
Project management10–15% of project valueRolled into total
End-to-end range—$25,000–$75,000

What does the certified-translation line cost inside the program?

The certified-translation line prices at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard 250-word page, with a certificate of accuracy signed by a competent translator required on every page and optional notarization at $10–$50 when the receiving authority requests it. Pricing matches the lane's standalone market rate, and the certificate boilerplate is locked in the term base.

How does AI pre-translation shift the cost mix?

AI pre-translation shifts the cost mix away from raw translation and toward review and LQA, so the mid-size $25,000–$75,000 program keeps roughly the same ceiling but spends more of it on human verification and scorecard sampling than on first-pass drafting. The headline rate per word drops. The reviewer load rises. The LQA sampling rate often rises alongside, because machine output errors cluster differently from human output errors.

Get a quote

What does business localization look like in practice? (US → EU example)

A US company expanding into the EU commissions the same corporate contract in German, French, Polish, and Spanish; each version carries a sworn or certified translator's stamp valid in its jurisdiction, with date formats, legal terminology, notarization conventions, and document layout adjusted to meet each country's official requirements. The four versions share one term base, one style guide family, and one project manager — meaning a single change to the source entity name propagates correctly across all four certified documents rather than requiring four separate correction rounds.

Locale identifiers for the four markets follow BCP 47 format, pairing an ISO 639-1 language code with an ISO 3166-1 country code: de-DE, fr-FR, pl-PL, and es-ES. The TMS stores every segment against those tags, and the multilingual site references each locale URL pair using the matching hreflang code — a configuration detail that is set once in the program and inherited by every subsequent content update in those markets.

  • German (de-DE) — sworn translator (beeidigter Übersetzer) stamp; dates in DD.MM.YYYY format; decimal comma convention on all financial figures.
  • French (fr-FR) — traducteur assermenté stamp registered with a court of appeal; space as thousands separator; GDPR-specific consent language in HR policies.
  • Polish (pl-PL) — sworn translator entered on the Ministry of Justice list; legal register conforming to Polish Civil Code article references.
  • Spanish (es-ES) — traductor jurado appointed by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs; locale style guide distinguishes es-ES from es-MX and es-AR to avoid register mismatches across the client's other markets.

The same program simultaneously localizes the client's EU landing pages, ensuring that visual assets — photography, iconography, and on-screen graphics — pass the image QA gate before any locale goes live. A German landing page that carries US-coded stock photography undermines the certified legal work produced in the same program. All four markets enter production on the same intake cycle, releasing sequentially as each lane clears its QA gate rather than waiting for a single waterfall handoff.

The planning model behind this example sits in Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs.

What are the hardest problems in running a business localization program?

Four problems break programs: complex-script locales that force layout re-engineering, image and visual QA skipped under schedule pressure, platform-specific ERP localization in markets with limited vendor support, and the architectural debate over whether localization data belongs in presentation or domain logic.

How do Japanese, Chinese, and Arabic locales affect layout?

Japanese, Chinese, and Arabic locales force layout re-engineering because character height, line-wrap behavior, and right-to-left flow break grids designed for Latin scripts, so the production budget shifts from translation to DTP, UI redesign, and QA. CJK characters stack tighter vertically and wrap differently. Arabic reverses the entire layout axis. Mirror padding, icon direction, and form-field order all flip.

How does ERP localization work in markets like the Philippines?

ERP localization in markets like the Philippines routes through Microsoft-certified partners for Dynamics 365 Business Central, because statutory reporting, tax, and audit formats require locale extensions that Microsoft does not ship directly, and the translation agency sits inside the partner's delivery chain. Business Central localization in such markets is partner-gated. The agency delivers the language and terminology layer; the certified partner delivers the statutory extension.

Should localization data live in presentation or domain logic?

Localization data lives in the presentation layer for display strings and formats, and in the domain or business logic for currency math, tax rules, certified-document fields, and legal clauses — because those values change the result of the computation, not just how it is rendered. A currency symbol belongs in presentation. A VAT rate belongs in domain logic. A certified-document attestation field belongs in domain logic, because its wording is legally operative.

What tools and TMS platforms carry a business localization program?

A business localization program runs on a translation management system that centralizes term base, translation memory, and workflow across all seven lanes, with CAT editors handling segment-level work, LQA scorecards gating release, and connectors integrating with e-commerce platforms, headless CMSs, and ERP systems. The TMS is the single source of truth for every locale's shared assets — when a product name changes in the term base, every in-progress segment across every lane flags for review automatically, rather than propagating an error through dozens of separate files.

Internationalization is the engineering foundation that makes TMS-driven localization possible: the development team prepares the codebase to accept any locale before the first translation segment is created, and the TMS then delivers localized strings back into that prepared structure. Without that preparation, each new locale requires bespoke engineering work that erodes the cost and speed advantages of the program.

  • Term base — locked corporate terminology per locale; brand marks stored as do-not-translate entries.
  • Translation memory — segment reuse across lanes and projects, compressing per-word cost on repetitive legal boilerplate.
  • Workflow engine — enforces the translation → review → LQA → sign-off sequence per lane SLA.
  • Connectors — push/pull integrations with Shopify, headless CMS, Business Central, Git, and document management systems.
  • LQA scorecard — error categories aligned to ISO 17100; priced at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated and run as a blocking gate before client delivery.
  • Reporting dashboard — project management overhead of 10–15% of project value is tracked against time logged per lane, giving the program manager a real-time cost position.

How do locale identifiers get configured?

Locale identifiers follow BCP 47, pairing an ISO 639-1 language code with an optional ISO 3166-1 country code — for example, es-MX for Mexican Spanish or fr-FR for metropolitan French — and every alternate URL on a multilingual site references itself and its siblings using the same hreflang codes. The TMS stores all content against the BCP 47 tag, not against a free-text locale name, which means that a client adding es-AR (Argentine Spanish) to an existing es-ES program inherits the shared term base and translation memory immediately rather than starting from zero. Correct BCP 47 tagging also ensures that search engines serve the right locale variant to users in each territory, supporting the local SEO discoverability that business name and brand localization decisions depend on.

Six questions recur across corporate localization engagements: product vs business localization, the simple definition, synonyms, benefit summary, internationalization overlap, and when to escalate to a certified lane.

Frequently asked questions

What is localization in business?

In business, localization is the end-to-end process of adapting a product, service, or piece of content so it feels native to a specific target market — covering language, currency, legal requirements, and cultural norms. For agencies handling multi-locale corporate programs, this means coordinating certified translation, desktop publishing, terminology management, and quality assurance across multiple language pairs simultaneously. A single enterprise rollout might span 20+ locales, requiring strict style guides, glossaries, and ISO 17100-compliant workflows to keep output consistent and certifiable.

What is localization in simple words?

Localization means making content look and feel as if it was originally created for a specific country or region, not just translated word-for-word. Beyond swapping languages, it involves adapting dates, units of measure, legal disclaimers, imagery, and tone. For translation professionals, the practical result is a deliverable that passes both linguistic review and the client's in-country validation — something a bare machine-translation draft alone cannot achieve without skilled post-editing.

What is product localisation?

Product localisation is the process of adapting a software application, physical product, or digital service so it meets the language, regulatory, and cultural expectations of each target market. It covers UI strings, on-screen help, packaging, legal inserts, and any certified documentation required for market entry. For translation agencies, product localisation programs typically involve iterative file handoffs — developers export resource files, translators and reviewers process them, and engineers re-integrate them — making scalable first-draft production a key efficiency lever.

What is internationalization and localization?

Internationalization (i18n) is the engineering practice of designing a product so localization (l10n) can be applied without re-engineering the core — for example, externalizing all user-facing strings and supporting Unicode. Localization is then the market-by-market adaptation work that follows. For agencies producing certified translations, the distinction matters because well-internationalized source content arrives in clean, segmented formats that translation memory tools and CAT environments handle efficiently, reducing per-word cost and turnaround time.

What are the benefits of localization?

Localization increases market reach, regulatory compliance, and customer trust in every territory a business enters. For corporate clients commissioning multi-locale programs, the measurable benefits include faster regulatory approval when certified documents meet local legal standards, reduced customer-support volume when UIs are accurately adapted, and stronger brand consistency across regions. For the agencies and translators delivering those programs, systematic localization workflows — with translation memory, glossaries, and structured QA — also reduce per-word cost on repeat projects by reusing previously approved segments.

What's the difference between translation and localization for a product?

Translation converts text from one language to another, while localization adapts the entire product experience — including layout, imagery, legal content, and cultural references — for a specific market. A translated software string might be linguistically correct yet still confuse users if number formats, date conventions, or UI space constraints are ignored. For certified translation producers, the difference is practical: a certified translated document meets legal equivalence requirements, whereas full product localization may additionally require desktop publishing, font changes, and in-country legal review beyond the translator's scope.

What are the different types of localization?

The main types of localization are software/UI localization, document and legal localization, marketing and multimedia localization, website localization, and game localization. For agencies serving corporate clients, legal and document localization is the most compliance-sensitive category, often requiring certified translations with translator declarations, notarization, or apostilles depending on the target country. Marketing localization sits at the other end of the spectrum, prioritizing cultural resonance and brand voice over formal equivalence.

How much does localization cost?

Professional localization costs typically range from $0.10 to $0.35 per source word for translation, with certified translation commanding a premium — often $0.20–$0.40 per word or a flat per-page rate of $50–$150 depending on language pair and certification requirements. Total program costs scale with the number of locales, file complexity, DTP needs, and QA rounds. Agencies using CAT tools and translation memory can significantly reduce costs on high-volume or repeat projects by leveraging fuzzy and 100% matches, sometimes cutting effective per-word rates by 30–50% on iterative content.

What is an example of localization?

A classic example is a multinational corporation adapting its employee handbook for markets in France, Brazil, and Japan — not just translating the text but also replacing references to at-will employment with locally compliant termination clauses, adjusting leave entitlements to match statutory minimums, and obtaining certified translations for submission to local labor authorities. For a translation agency, this single project requires language-pair specialists, certified translators with relevant subject-matter expertise, and a QA process that verifies legal accuracy against each country's current regulations.

What are the best practices for localizing software and products?

Best practices include internationalizing the source product before localization begins, maintaining a centralized termbase and style guide per language, using translation memory to enforce consistency and control costs, and running in-context linguistic QA rather than reviewing strings in isolation. For agencies producing certified elements within a larger software localization project — such as end-user license agreements or regulatory inserts — it is essential to keep certified document workflows separate from agile UI localization cycles, since certification requirements impose fixed review and sign-off steps that cannot be compressed to match sprint timelines.

What happens to layout and design when you localize into Japanese or other complex languages?

Text expansion or contraction can significantly disrupt layouts when localizing into languages like Japanese, Arabic, or German, requiring desktop publishing rework after translation. Japanese, for example, may use vertical text flow in certain document types, requires specific font choices, and can produce text that is 10–30% shorter than English by character count but may need more line space due to glyph complexity. For agencies delivering certified translations in these languages, DTP is often a billable post-translation phase, and translators must flag layout-breaking segments during QA rather than after final formatting.

How do I start a localization/translation agency focused on a specific language pair like English to Bahasa?

Starting a focused translation agency requires building a vetted roster of qualified translators for your language pair, establishing a clear service scope — including whether you will offer certified translations — and implementing a CAT-tool and QA workflow from day one. For an English-to-Bahasa (Indonesian or Malay) agency, certified translation demand is driven by immigration, legal, and government procurement sectors, so understanding the relevant national certification standards (e.g., sworn translator credentials in Indonesia) is critical. Agencies typically launch with freelance capacity and move to in-house staff once volume justifies fixed costs.

pages.meta_description: A CAT tool is a desktop or cloud segment editor where translators work on bilingual segments with translation memory, term base, QA checks, and audit trail.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • Key points
  • What is a CAT tool?
  • What does a CAT tool actually do during translation?
  • What are the main features of a CAT tool?
  • What are examples of CAT tools translators actually use?
  • Where does the CAT tool sit in the broader translation stack?
  • Why do certified translation lanes depend on the CAT tool's audit trail?
  • What are the limits of a CAT tool — and where does the workflow break?
  • How we use the CAT tool, and what we refuse to do with it
  • Frequently asked questions

A CAT tool is the segment-editor layer a working translator sits inside all day — the screen that splits a source file into rows, pulls translation memory and machine translation into each one, and writes every keystroke to a bilingual audit trail. It is layer 2 of a seven-layer production stack, between the TMS that routes the job and the certifier who signs the exported file. This page defines what the tool is, what it does during production, and why the certified lane cannot be run without one.

Key points

  • A CAT tool is desktop or cloud software that segments a source document and lets a human translator edit each segment against translation memory, a term base, and inline QA checks — it never produces autonomous output the way an MT engine does.
  • CAT stands for Computer-Assisted Translation. The tool works segment by segment, keeping the human translator in control of every decision while the software surfaces matches, flags terminology, and enforces QA rules in real time.
  • At the center of every CAT tool is Translation Memory — a database that stores previously approved segment pairs and replays them automatically whenever the same or a similar source segment appears again. The first time a translator works on a new domain they will see most segments return as "New," but that proportion drops steadily as approved content accumulates in the TM over successive projects.
  • In a seven-layer localization stack, the CAT tool occupies Layer 2 — sitting above the TMS (Layer 1) that routes work and stores TM/TB data centrally, and below the MT engine (Layer 3) that can feed raw first-draft output back into the editor for post-editing.
  • memoQ and SDL Trados Studio are the two CAT tools most paired with a TMS on ISO 17100-aligned certified lanes, because both carry a segment-level audit trail and a reliable offline working mode — both requirements for legally defensible certified translation delivery.
  • The standard client-agreed fuzzy-match threshold for TM pre-translation is 75%: segments that match an existing TM entry at or above that score are pre-populated before the translator opens the file.

    • A CAT tool is desktop or cloud software that segments a source document and lets a translator edit each segment against translation memory, a term base, and inline QA checks.
    • CAT stands for Computer-Assisted Translation — the tool assists a human translator segment by segment and does not translate autonomously the way an MT engine does.
    • memoQ and SDL Trados Studio are the CAT tools paired with a TMS on ISO 17100-aligned certified lanes, because both carry segment-level audit trail and offline working mode.
    • US per-word production grid: translation $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard.
    • The standard client-agreed fuzzy threshold for TM pre-translation inside the editor is 75% match.

    5–

    What is a CAT tool?

    A CAT tool is desktop or cloud software that splits a source document into segments and lets a translator edit each one against translation memory, term base hits, and inline QA checks, writing every change to a bilingual audit trail. It is one entry in a compared set covered in CAT Tools Compared: How Translation Memory Software Works, and it is distinct from both the TMS that routes the project and the MT engine that drafts first-pass output.

    What does a CAT tool actually do during translation?

    A CAT tool segments the source file, pre-populates each target segment from translation memory and machine translation, enforces the term base, runs inline QA checks on numbers, tags and placeholders, and exports a clean bilingual file back to the TMS. The seven steps a translator triggers inside the editor are:

    1. Open the project package handed down from the TMS.
    2. Let the tool segment the source by punctuation and tag rules.
    3. Accept TM leverage above the agreed fuzzy threshold.
    4. Post-edit the MT first draft segment by segment.
    5. Resolve term base flags as they appear in the target column.
    6. Clear every inline QA warning before locking the segment.
    7. Export the bilingual file and the clean target for review.
    The CAT tool workflow runs in 8 steps: the TMS delivers the source file; the CAT tool segments it; TM pre-fills matches at or above 75%; MT fills empty segments; the translator post-edits each segment; the term base and inline QA flags surface warnings; cleared segments are exported as a bilingual file; the review and LQA gate approves release. fills empty segments]
 D --> E[Translator post-edits each segment]
 E --> F[Term base + inline QA flags]
 F --> G{All warnings cleared?}
 G -- No --> E
 G -- Yes --> H[Bilingual export back to TMS]
 H --> I[Review and LQA gate]

    How does segmentation work inside the editor?

    The CAT tool breaks the source document into translation units — sentences — using segmentation rules keyed to punctuation, format tags, and language-specific exceptions, then displays each unit as an editable row. The segment-by-segment production surface is already described in detail on Localization Workflow: How Translators and Agencies Wire the Production Pipeline.

    How does translation memory leverage change the first-draft screen?

    Translation memory pre-fills segments that match stored past translations above the client-agreed fuzzy threshold — 75% — so the translator post-edits instead of typing from scratch. The CAT tool colour-codes exact, fuzzy, and no-match segments so the eye finds leverage first. The underlying mechanics are covered in How CAT Tools Use Translation Memory to Speed Up Your Work.

    How does the term base enforce approved terminology in real time?

    The term base holds client-approved renderings of product names, feature names, and regulated terminology. The CAT tool highlights source terms as the cursor enters each segment and flags deviations in the target as the translator types. The translator never alt-tabs to a glossary. Real-time term base flagging is covered Content Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce It.

    What inline QA checks run while the translator works?

    The CAT tool runs inline QA on numbers, dates, placeholders, tag integrity, double spaces, untranslated segments, inconsistent translations, and term base violations. The warnings appear beside each segment and must clear before export. The nine checks a certified lane will not release without are:

    • Number mismatches between source and target.
    • Date format drift against the locale convention.
    • Placeholder count and family consistency.
    • Tag integrity (opening/closing, order).
    • Double spaces and stray whitespace.
    • Untranslated segments left in the source language.
    • Inconsistent translations of the same source segment.
    • Term base violations against approved renderings.
    • Punctuation mismatches at segment boundaries.

    What are the main features of a CAT tool?

    A CAT tool bundles seven core features: segmentation, translation memory, term base, inline QA checks, bilingual export, concordance search, and a segment-level audit trail — each one tied to a specific stage of the production workflow.

    FeatureWhat it doesWorkflow stage it serves
    SegmentationSplits the source into translation units by punctuation and tag rules.Project open
    Translation memoryPre-fills segments from stored past translations at or above the fuzzy threshold.First-draft screen
    Term baseFlags source terms and enforces approved target renderings in real time.Translation
    Inline QA checksBlocks tag, number, placeholder and terminology errors segment by segment.Translation and review
    Bilingual exportWrites a source+target file that review tools and auditors can read.Delivery
    Concordance searchLooks up prior translations of substrings across the TM for context.Translation
    Segment-level audit trailRecords who changed each segment, when, and from what prior value.Certified-lane sign-off

    Which CAT tool features matter for certified translation production?

    Four CAT features gate certified work: segment-level audit trail, offline working mode, named-translator attestation on export, and a locked bilingual review view. memoQ and SDL Trados carry all four, which is why they are the pair agencies run on ISO 17100-aligned lanes. The deeper Trados breakdown is in Trados as a CAT Tool: Features, Costs, and Honest Trade-offs.

    What are examples of CAT tools translators actually use?

    Working translators and agencies use five main CAT tools: SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Phrase, OmegaT, and Wordfast — with memoQ and SDL Trados dominating certified and regulated lanes, and OmegaT holding the free open-source slot.

    ToolDeploymentLicenseCertified-lane fit
    SDL Trados StudioDesktop (Trados Team is cloud)PaidPrimary certified-lane choice
    memoQDesktop + cloud (memoQ cloud)PaidPrimary certified-lane choice
    PhraseCloud / browserPaidWeak for offline certified work
    OmegaTDesktopFree, open sourcePossible for low-stakes work
    WordfastDesktop + web (Wordfast Anywhere)Paid; Anywhere freeVaries by edition

    Which CAT tools are free or open source?

    OmegaT is the main free, open-source CAT tool used by professional translators. It carries TM, term base, and QA checks but lacks the vendor-support and ecosystem depth paid tools offer. The full capability-and-limit picture is in OmegaT for Professional Translators: What It Does and What It Lacks.

    Which CAT tools run in the browser (cloud / online)?

    Phrase and the cloud editions of memoQ and Trados Team run inside a browser, letting multi-translator projects share one TM in real time without local file transfer. The trade-off is weaker offline control for certified lanes. The day-to-day feature set is covered Phrase CAT Tool: Features Translators Use Every Day.

    Services

    Where does the CAT tool sit in the broader translation stack?

    The CAT tool is layer 2 of a seven-layer production stack: the TMS routes projects and stores TM; the CAT tool is the translator workbench; the MT engine produces first drafts; QA and LQA gate release; connectors move files; the certifier signs off. The broader program view is Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

    Why do certified translation lanes depend on the CAT tool's audit trail?

    Certified translation lanes depend on the CAT tool because the segment-level audit trail, bilingual review view, and offline file control produce the court-admissible chain of custody that USCIS filings, court exhibits, and registry submissions require. A cloud-only web editor cannot generate the same evidence. The four features a certifier checks before signing are:

    • Who edited which segment, with timestamps.
    • Prior-value history on every change.
    • A bilingual export locked against post-sign-off edits.
    • An offline working copy outside third-party cloud storage.

    What does USCIS-grade certified production cost per page when a CAT tool drives the lane?

    USCIS certified translation sits at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard page of about 250 words, with the certificate of accuracy mandatory on every page and notarization an optional $10–$50 add-on. The CAT tool's exported bilingual file becomes the attachment of record.

    Production stageUS rateWhat it buys
    Translation$0.10–$0.25 / source wordHuman translator working inside the CAT editor.
    Review$0.04–$0.08 / source wordSecond linguist checks every segment.
    LQA$40–$90 / 1,000 wordsSampled MQM-style score against ISO 17100 criteria.
    Certificate of accuracyMandatory, per pageTranslator attestation attached to delivery.
    Notarization$10–$50 (optional)Notary witnesses the translator's signature.
    Standard page$25–$150About 250 source words.

    How it works

    What are the limits of a CAT tool — and where does the workflow break?

    1

    Custom-nested JSON that the stock filter cannot parse, causing segments to be skipped or merged incorrectly.

    2

    Segment drift when the source file is re-exported or updated mid-project, invalidating existing TM matches and forcing re-analysis.

    3

    Mixed placeholder families (ICU + sprintf + Angular, for example) in a single file, which generate QA warnings the translator cannot clear without developer intervention.

    4

    Hard-coded line breaks that split grammatical sentences into fragments, degrading both TM leverage and output fluency.

    5

    Locked tags whose integrity check blocks export, stalling delivery until the tag structure is corrected in the source or the filter rule is overridden with project-manager sign-off.

    How we use the CAT tool, and what we refuse to do with it

    We treat the CAT tool as the evidence-producing layer of the certified lane, not as a translation engine. Every certified job runs through memoQ or SDL Trados on an offline working copy, with the segment-level audit trail enabled from the first segment and retained with the delivered bilingual file.

    We do not sign a certificate of accuracy from a cloud-only web editor that cannot produce a locked bilingual export and a per-segment edit history. The attestation names a human translator, and the file beneath it has to be defensible if a court or an immigration officer asks who changed what and when.

    We refuse to pre-translate below the 75% fuzzy threshold and present the output as a human draft. Below that cutoff the TM match is a distraction, not leverage, and quoting it inflates the leverage column on an invoice. The post-editor starts from an empty target, and the review gate is priced at $0.04–$0.08 per source word on every segment.

    We will not run a certified lane on a free CAT tool because our clients need a vendor-supported filter chain and a documented QA profile. OmegaT remains fit for low-stakes work; it is not what we attach a certificate of accuracy to.

    A CAT tool splits a source document into segments and lets a human translator edit each one against translation memory, a term base, and inline QA checks, with every change written to a bilingual audit trail.

    Frequently asked questions

    What are CAT tools for translators?

    CAT tools for translators are software applications that support the translation process by breaking source documents into segments and presenting them alongside a workspace for writing target-language equivalents. They store every translated segment in a Translation Memory (TM), so repeated or similar text is auto-populated in future projects. Most tools also integrate a termbase (glossary), quality-assurance checks, and — increasingly — machine translation engines. Common examples include SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Wordfast, Déjà Vu, and Smartcat.

    What does a cat tool do?

    A CAT tool splits a source document into sentence-level segments, displays them one at a time, and lets the translator write or edit the target text in a structured editor. It simultaneously queries a Translation Memory to surface matches from previously translated content — exact matches (100%) are reused as-is, while fuzzy matches (typically 75–99%) are presented as editable suggestions. Integrated termbases flag key terms, built-in QA checks catch omissions or inconsistencies, and the finished file is exported in the original format. The cumulative effect is faster throughput and higher consistency across a project.

    What is a CAT tool in translation?

    In translation, a CAT tool (Computer-Assisted Translation tool) is a professional productivity environment that combines a segmented editing interface, Translation Memory, terminology management, and QA automation in a single platform. It is distinct from machine translation: the human translator controls every decision, while the tool handles repetitive retrieval and format reconstruction. CAT tools are industry-standard in commercial, legal, technical, and certified translation workflows, and most translation agencies require deliverables to be produced in a supported CAT tool format (e.g., a Trados package or an XLIFF file).

    What is the phrase CAT tool?

    "CAT tool" is industry shorthand for Computer-Assisted Translation tool, a software category used by professional translators. The phrase distinguishes this class of productivity software — which keeps the human translator in control — from fully automated machine translation (MT) systems. In professional settings the phrase is used interchangeably with "translation environment tool" (TEnT) or "translation memory tool." You will encounter it in job postings, agency style guides, and ISO 17100 compliance discussions.

    What are CAT tools examples?

    The most widely used CAT tools in professional translation today are SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Wordfast Pro, Déjà Vu X, Smartcat, and Memsource (now Phrase). Each supports Translation Memory and termbase management as core features. Smartcat and Phrase are cloud-native SaaS platforms, while Trados and memoQ offer both desktop and server/cloud editions. Specialised tools such as OmegaT (open-source) and Transifex (software localisation) also fall into the broader CAT tool category.

    Which is better, Trados or memoQ?

    Neither is objectively better — the right choice depends on workflow, budget, and client requirements. SDL Trados Studio has the largest market share and is the de-facto standard requested by large LSPs and enterprise clients, making it the safer choice if you want maximum compatibility. memoQ is widely preferred for its project-management features, more intuitive interface, and flexible licensing; it is especially popular in Europe. Both support XLIFF interchange, so files can be exchanged between them. Freelancers often hold licences for both tools.

    What is SMT and NMT?

    SMT (Statistical Machine Translation) and NMT (Neural Machine Translation) are two generations of automated translation technology that power the MT engines often embedded in CAT tools. SMT, dominant through the 2000s and early 2010s, used probabilistic models trained on parallel corpora to predict the most likely word sequences. NMT, which became mainstream around 2016–2017, uses deep neural networks (typically transformer architectures) to produce more fluent, context-aware output. Modern engines — including DeepL, Google Translate's neural mode, and ModernMT — are all NMT-based and significantly outperform legacy SMT systems on most language pairs.

    What are the two main types of translation?

    The two main types of translation are human translation and machine translation (MT). Human translation is performed entirely by a qualified linguist and is required for certified, legal, medical, and literary content where accuracy and accountability are non-negotiable. Machine translation uses algorithms (today predominantly neural models) to produce output automatically, as a first draft that a human post-editor then refines — a process called MTPE (machine translation post-editing). Within human translation, further distinctions are made between general, technical, sworn/certified, and literary translation.

    Where can I find CAT tools?

    CAT tools are available directly from their developers' websites: SDL/RWS for Trados Studio, memoQ for memoQ, Phrase for Memsource, and Smartcat.ai for Smartcat, among others. Most offer free trials of 30 days or a perpetually free tier (Smartcat). OmegaT is a fully free, open-source option downloadable at omegat.org. Professional translator communities such as ProZ.com and the SDL Community host comparison guides and discounted licences negotiated for freelancers. Some agencies provide licences to their regular contractors.

    Can I use Smartcat for free?

    Yes, Smartcat offers a permanently free plan for individual translators and small teams. The free tier includes unlimited Translation Memory storage, basic CAT editor access, and the ability to collaborate on projects. Paid plans add features such as advanced automation, MT integrations, and priority support, with pricing scaling by team size and monthly word volume. For freelancers doing occasional certified translation work, the free tier is often sufficient to manage standard projects.

pages.body_html:
On this page

  • Key points
  • Snapshot comparison
  • What is a CAT tool in translation and what does it actually do?
  • Which CAT tools do professional translators actually use?
  • How should translators compare CAT tools before picking one?
  • How do CAT tools change the economics of a translation project?
  • How do CAT tools fit into certified translation production?
  • What do CAT tools NOT do — and which tool covers each gap?
  • How we run the CAT layer, and what we will not do inside it
  • Frequently asked questions

CAT tools for translation sit at the segment-editing layer of professional production — the stage where translation memory leverage, term base enforcement, and QA checks decide throughput, per-word cost, and the audit trail certified lanes need. This page compares the six CAT tools working translators actually run and scores them against the lane each one bills. For the underlying definition and workflow mechanics, see CAT Tool: What It Is, What It Does Inside a Translator's Workflow.

Key points

  • A CAT tool is a segment-level editor that leverages translation memory, enforces a term base, runs inline QA checks, and exports a bilingual audit trail.
  • Translation memory leverage cuts effective per-word rates by 30–50% on iterative content, which turns a 5-locale × 50,000-word program priced at $25,000–$75,000 into a materially lower spend once TM is seeded.
  • US translation rates run $0.10–$0.35 per source word, review runs $0.04–$0.08 per word, and LQA scored to an ISO 17100-aligned scorecard runs $40–$90 per 1,000 words — CAT savings do not displace any of these.
  • Seat pricing spans $0 (OmegaT) to about $900 one-time (Trados Studio Freelance) and $27–$55 per user per month for Phrase and Smartcat professional tiers.
  • The client-agreed fuzzy match threshold on this workflow is 75%; below that, segments bill as no-match at the full per-source-word rate.

Snapshot comparison

Six CAT tools, scored on deployment, licensing, and the lane each one fits — this is the fast read before the detailed axes further down. Every tool in the table shares the same core loop: a segment-level editor that leverages translation memory, enforces a term base, runs inline QA checks, and exports a bilingual audit trail. Where they diverge is on deployment model, seat cost, and the workflow context each one was built to serve.

Seat cost is the first sorting axis: OmegaT costs nothing to license, Smartcat offers a free browser-based tier, and Wordfast Pro sits below Trados at roughly $460 one-time — all three serve translators whose project volume does not yet justify a heavier investment. Trados and memoQ occupy the professional desktop tier, each carrying the bilingual export format that agency vendor pools expect. Phrase is the only entry here that functions as both a CAT editor and a translation management system, making it the natural choice for distributed teams who need job routing and connector integrations alongside the segment editor.

What is a CAT tool in translation and what does it actually do?

A CAT tool is segment-level software that splits a source file into sentences, pre-fills matches from translation memory above the fuzzy threshold, enforces term base entries, runs inline QA checks, and exports a bilingual file that review and certified lanes audit downstream. The segment editor is the surface a translator spends the day in. Everything else — routing, vendor assignment, invoicing — happens outside it.

Five jobs sit inside the CAT tool itself:

  • Segmentation of the source into sentence-level units.
  • Translation memory lookup and pre-fill above the fuzzy threshold.
  • Term base enforcement with inline flags for banned or missing terms.
  • QA checks for placeholders, numbers, tags, and terminology drift.
  • Bilingual export (SDLXLIFF, XLIFF, TMX) preserving source-target pairing.

For the full component breakdown, see CAT Tool: What It Is, What It Does Inside a Translator's Workflow.

flowchart TD
 A[Source file in] --> B[Segmentation]
 B --> C{TM lookup}
 C -- Match above 75% --> D[Pre-fill segment]
 C -- Below 75% --> E[No-match, translate from scratch]
 D --> F[Term base check]
 E --> F
 F --> G[Inline QA checks]
 G --> H[Bilingual export for review and LQA]

Which CAT tools do professional translators actually use?

The CAT tools professional translators use day-to-day are SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Phrase (formerly Memsource), Wordfast Pro, Smartcat, Déjà Vu X, and OmegaT. They split cleanly between desktop editors (Trados, memoQ, Wordfast, OmegaT) and cloud-native platforms (Phrase, Smartcat) that agencies route jobs through.

What are the main desktop CAT tools: Trados, memoQ, Wordfast, OmegaT?

Desktop CAT tools install locally, keep translation memory on the translator's machine, and work offline — a fit for confidentiality-constrained certified work where files cannot leave the workstation.

  • SDL Trados Studio — the agency vendor-pool default. Freelance license runs about $900 one-time. SDLXLIFF is the format most LSPs ship. Deep coverage in Trados as a CAT Tool: Features, Costs, and Honest Trade-offs.
  • memoQ — desktop editor plus optional server. LiveDocs lets translators mine prior bilingual files as corpus without rebuilding TMs. Favored by freelancers who prioritize editor speed and a cleaner project view.
  • Wordfast Pro — cross-platform (Windows, macOS, Linux). Lower seat cost than Trados. Opens TXML and standard XLIFF.
  • OmegaT — open-source, free, Java-based. Supports TM and term bases. No vendor-signed bilingual export tooling by default, which matters for certified lanes. See OmegaT for Professional Translators: What It Does and What It Lacks.

What are the main cloud-native CAT tools: Phrase, Smartcat, memoQ cloud?

The main cloud-native CAT tools are Phrase, Smartcat, and memoQ cloud — each runs in a browser, shares live translation memory across vendors, and plugs into agency TMS routing.

  • Phrase (formerly Memsource) — cloud CAT and TMS hybrid, $27–$55 per user per month on professional tiers. Strong connector library. See Phrase CAT Tool: Features Translators Use Every Day and Phrase Alternatives Worth Considering for Your CAT Workflow.
  • Smartcat — cloud CAT with a free tier plus a vendor marketplace. Browser-based access suits freelancers without a Windows machine.
  • memoQ cloud — the hosted variant of memoQ server, same editor delivered as a service.

Are there free CAT tools worth using?

Free CAT tools worth using are OmegaT (open-source desktop), Smartcat's free tier, and Matecat — all three support translation memory and term bases, but none produce the signed bilingual audit trail certified lanes expect without manual rigging.

  • OmegaT — the only genuinely open-source option. Free download. Full TM, glossary, and QA check support.
  • Smartcat free tier — browser-based, limited to a cap on monthly words and a smaller feature set.
  • Matecat — browser-based, free, with public and private TMs.

Free is a budget decision, not a workflow one. The certified lane still needs the certificate of accuracy attached to every page, which is a document step, not a CAT feature.

How should translators compare CAT tools before picking one?

Translators compare CAT tools on seven axes: translation memory leverage model, term base enforcement, QA check library, file-format coverage, bilingual export fidelity, deployment (desktop vs cloud), and per-seat pricing — scored against the lane the translator actually bills. For the deeper buying-decision framework, see Choosing Translation Memory Software: What to Compare Before Buying.

  1. Translation memory leverage model — concordance search, fragment assembly, auto-propagation.
  2. Term base enforcement — inline flags, forbidden terms, morphology handling.
  3. QA check library — placeholders, numbers, tags, terminology, double spaces, length.
  4. File-format coverage — DOCX, IDML, SRT, XLIFF, PO, JSON, SDLXLIFF round-trip.
  5. Bilingual export fidelity — clean round-trip through review and back.
  6. Deployment — desktop vs cloud, offline capability, confidentiality posture.
  7. Per-seat pricing — one-time vs monthly, team vs freelance tiers.

CAT tool feature comparison table

The table below scores the six most-used CAT tools against the seven comparison axes a working translator checks before buying a seat.

Axis Trados memoQ Phrase Smartcat Wordfast Pro OmegaT
TM leverageDeepDeep + LiveDocsCloud-sharedCloud-sharedSolidBasic

File formats50+50+40+40+30+30+

What fuzzy match threshold should a CAT tool be set to?

A CAT tool's fuzzy match threshold is set at 75% — the client-agreed floor already used across our workflow — below which the segment is treated as a no-match and billed at the full per-source-word rate.

Decision rule for the threshold:

  • Raise above 75% (to 85%) on regulated content where every mismatch carries legal risk — the translator retypes more, so effective per-word cost goes up.
  • Hold at 75% for standard commercial content where the TM is well-maintained.
  • Lower below 75% only for first-pass drafts, never for billed segments, because low-match pre-fills slow the translator down more than typing from scratch.

How do CAT tools change the economics of a translation project?

CAT tools cut effective per-word rates by 30–50% on iterative content through fuzzy and 100% matches, turning a 50,000-word five-locale program that would price at

CAT tools cut effective per-word rates by 30–50% on iterative content through fuzzy and 100% matches, turning a 50,000-word five-locale program that would price at $25,000–$75,000 into a materially lower spend once translation memory is seeded. The savings compound at the translation line; they do not displace the review gate or the LQA scorecard downstream.

What do CAT tools cost per seat in the US?

CAT tool seat pricing in the US ranges from $0 (OmegaT) to roughly $900 one-time (Trados Studio Freelance) and $27–$55 per user per month for cloud editors like Phrase and Smartcat on professional tiers.

  • OmegaT — $0, open-source download.
  • Smartcat free tier — $0, with word caps.
  • Wordfast Pro — about $460 one-time.
  • memoQ translator pro — about $770 perpetual, plus annual support.
  • Trados Studio Freelance — about $900 one-time.
  • Phrase, Smartcat paid tiers — $27–$55 per user per month.

How do CAT tool savings interact with review and LQA gates?

CAT tool savings compound at the translation line ($0.10–$0.25 per source word) but do not displace the review gate ($0.04–$0.08 per word) or the LQA scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, which stay mandatory on certified lanes. A seeded TM lowers the translator's effective rate; it does not lower the reviewer's hourly check or the LQA sampler's defect scoring.

5,000–$75,000 into a materially lower spend once translation memory is seeded. The savings compound at the translation line; they do not displace the review gate or the LQA scorecard downstream. The mechanism is straightforward: every segment the TM resolves at or above the client-agreed fuzzy threshold — set at 75%, below which segments bill as no-match — is pre-filled automatically, reducing the translator's keystrokes and the buyer's effective rate simultaneously.

How do CAT tools fit into certified translation production?

CAT tools fit certified translation production as the segment editor that generates the bilingual audit trail a certified translator signs off on — the same file reviewed against the LQA scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 before the certificate of accuracy is attached to every page of a USCIS filing priced at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or

CAT tools fit certified translation production as the segment editor that generates the bilingual audit trail a certified translator signs off on — the same file reviewed against the LQA scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 before the certificate of accuracy is attached to every page of a USCIS filing priced at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard page.

memoQMQXLIFF, clean round-tripFullStrong

Procedure a certified lane runs through the CAT tool:

  1. Ingest the source file and segment it.
  2. Pre-fill from TM above the 75% fuzzy threshold.
  3. Human translator post-edits every segment.
  4. Term base check fires inline on every save.
  5. QA checks sweep placeholders, numbers, tags.
  6. Bilingual export passes to the reviewer.
  7. LQA sampler scores defects against the ISO 17100-aligned scorecard.
  8. Certified translator signs the certificate of accuracy for every page.

5–

What do CAT tools NOT do — and which tool covers each gap?

CAT tools do not route jobs, assign vendors, run cross-file consistency checks, or draft first-pass output — those gaps are filled by the translation management system, the standalone QA utility, and the AI first-draft engine that produces raw output before credentialed post-edit. Understanding where the CAT tool's scope ends is as important as understanding what it does: a translator or agency that expects one tool to cover all four categories will hit a wall at the project-management or cross-file consistency layer, because a segment editor is purpose-built for a single file's production loop, not the orchestration of a multi-vendor, multi-locale program.

The term base and inline QA checks built into a CAT tool operate within a single file session — they catch errors in spacing, number formatting, tags, and spelling as the translator works, and they enforce approved terminology against every saved segment. What they do not do is compare terminology consistency across fifty files delivered by ten different translators on the same program. That cross-file, cross-vendor consistency check is the job of a standalone QA utility, which ingests all delivered bilingual files and runs the check as a batch process after production is complete.

Four tool categories, four scopes:

Standalone QA utilityCross-file terminology, placeholder, number, and consistency checks across batch deliveriesNot a segment editor; runs post-production, not inline
AI first-draft engineFirst-pass raw output before credentialed human post-edit and reviewNot a replacement for the CAT editor's TM leverage or the human post-edit step

The boundary between TMS and CAT tool is blurring at the cloud-native tier: Phrase, for example, combines a segment editor with job routing and connector integrations on a single platform at

CAT tools do not route jobs, assign vendors, run cross-file consistency checks, or draft first-pass output — those gaps are filled by the TMS (Phrase, XTRF, Plunet), the QA utility (Xbench, Verifika), and the AI first-draft engine that produces the certified-translation first draft before human review.

TMSJob routing, vendor assignment, connectors, reportingXTRF, Plunet, Phrase (TMS side)

The multi-locale program view that ties these together sits Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

7–$55 per user per month, while desktop tools like Trados and memoQ rely on separate TMS software to handle the orchestration layer. For freelancers working solo, that separation rarely matters; for agencies running distributed multi-locale programs, the integration between the CAT editor and the TMS is a core operational dependency.

How we run the CAT layer, and what we will not do inside it

We treat the CAT tool as the editor our credentialed translator post-edits an AI first draft inside — not as a replacement for the translator and not as a source of certification. The segment editor pre-fills from TM above 75%, flags term base misses, and runs placeholder and number checks on every save. The reviewer sees the same bilingual file. The LQA sampler scores it against an ISO 17100-aligned scorecard before the certificate is written.

We will not sign a certificate of accuracy on raw CAT output. The CAT tool produces a draft; a credentialed human reads every segment against the source and signs for the translation, page by page. A QA utility pass covers cross-file terminology and placeholder consistency that the CAT tool cannot see on its own.

We will not lower the 75% fuzzy match threshold on billed segments. Below that line, the pre-fill slows the translator down more than typing from scratch, so we treat the segment as a no-match and bill it at the full per-source-word rate. The client-side math stays honest.

We will not use a cloud-only CAT tool on jobs where the source cannot leave the workstation. Desktop deployment is the baseline for those lanes. Confidentiality is a workflow setting, not a sales line.

The questions below cover the comparisons translators ask before committing to a CAT tool — Trados vs memoQ, whether Smartling counts, and whether CAT translators actually work in practice.

Frequently asked questions

What are CAT tools for translators?

CAT (Computer-Assisted Translation) tools are software applications that help human translators work faster and more consistently by segmenting source text and storing previously translated segments in a translation memory (TM). As a translator works, the tool automatically suggests matches from the TM for repeated or similar sentences, so they don't have to retranslate identical content. Most CAT tools also include a termbase (glossary), QA checks, and file-format handling for DOCX, XLIFF, PDF, and more. Leading examples include SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Wordfast, and Smartcat.

what is cat tools translation

CAT tools translation refers to the workflow in which a human translator uses Computer-Assisted Translation software to produce a target-language document segment by segment. The tool splits the source file into sentences or phrases, displays them one at a time in an editor, and offers TM matches, machine translation suggestions, and terminology hits to speed up the work. The translator reviews and edits each suggestion before confirming it. This process improves consistency across large projects and can meaningfully reduce turnaround time compared to translating in a plain word processor.

how to use cat tools for translation

To use a CAT tool, import your source file into the software, connect a translation memory and termbase relevant to your subject matter, then work through each segment in the editor. For each segment the tool displays any TM matches (shown as a percentage — 100% is an exact match, 75–99% is a fuzzy match) alongside machine translation suggestions; you accept, edit, or retranslate as needed. After finishing, run the built-in QA check for missed segments, number inconsistencies, or terminology errors, then export the translated file in the original format.

is google translate a cat tool?

No, Google Translate is not a CAT tool — it is a standalone machine translation (MT) engine. A true CAT tool combines a translation memory, termbase, segment editor, and QA features to support a human translator's workflow; Google Translate simply produces a raw automatic translation of whatever text you paste or type. That said, many CAT tools (such as Trados, memoQ, and Smartcat) can integrate Google Translate as an MT plug-in to provide suggestions inside the segment editor, but the CAT tool itself remains the working environment.

Which is better, Trados or memoQ?

Neither tool is universally better — the right choice depends on your workflow, budget, and client base. SDL Trados Studio dominates the market and is often required by large LSPs and agencies, making it the safer default if you work with many clients. memoQ is widely praised for its cleaner interface, stronger project-management features, and collaborative server environment, making it popular in-house at agencies. Trados perpetual licenses have historically started around €800–€900; memoQ's annual subscription runs roughly €600–€700. Many professional translators own both to stay compatible with all clients.

What is the best CAT tool for translation?

SDL Trados Studio is the most widely used CAT tool in the professional translation industry and is often considered the industry standard. memoQ is a close second and preferred by many agency project managers for its collaborative features. Wordfast is popular among freelancers for its lower cost and Word-based interface, while Smartcat and OmegaT offer free tiers that suit those starting out or working on tighter budgets. The "best" tool ultimately depends on your client requirements, the file formats you handle, and whether you need offline or cloud-based work.

What is SMT and NMT?

SMT (Statistical Machine Translation) and NMT (Neural Machine Translation) are two generations of automatic translation technology. SMT, dominant through the 2000s and early 2010s, generates translations by calculating the statistical probability of word and phrase pairings from large bilingual corpora. NMT, which became the industry standard from around 2016 onward, uses deep neural networks to model meaning at the sentence level, producing significantly more fluent and contextually accurate output. Engines like Google Translate, DeepL, and Microsoft Translator all run on NMT today, and most modern CAT tools can plug into them.

Is Smartling a CAT tool?

Smartling is a cloud-based translation management system (TMS) that includes CAT-tool functionality, but it is broader than a traditional CAT tool. It offers a web-based translation editor with translation memory, glossary, and MT integration — the core features of a CAT tool — but it is primarily designed for continuous localization workflows at enterprise scale, connecting directly to content platforms, code repositories, and marketing systems. Translators access projects through the browser rather than a desktop application, making it distinct from tools like Trados or memoQ while still supporting professional translation workflows.

Can I use Smartcat for free?

Yes, Smartcat offers a free tier that is genuinely usable for freelance translators and small teams. The free plan includes the cloud-based CAT editor, unlimited translation memories and glossaries, and access to Smartcat's marketplace for finding clients. Paid plans (aimed at agencies and enterprises) add features such as advanced automation, priority support, and higher volumes of MT characters. For a solo translator working on typical document volumes, the free tier is a practical starting point, though larger agencies will likely need a paid plan to manage multiple projects and users efficiently.

What are the five types of translation?

The five types most cited in professional translation contexts are literary, technical, legal, medical/scientific, and certified (or official) translation. Literary translation handles creative works such as novels and poetry. Technical translation covers manuals, engineering documents, and software. Legal translation deals with contracts, court documents, and legislation. Medical translation addresses clinical trials, labeling, and research. Certified translation — the most relevant type for this platform — requires the translator to attach a signed statement attesting to the accuracy and completeness of the translation, and is required for immigration, academic, or legal submission purposes.
