Term base enforcementOwnsStores shared TB—

Workflow context across the layers is How Translation Management Software Fits Into Your Workflow.

How do CAT tools interoperate across tool boundaries?

CAT tools interoperate through 3 open formats: XLIFF for bilingual segments in-flight, TMX for translation-memory exchange across tools, and TBX for term-base exchange. A project started in memoQ finishes in Trados when XLIFF round-trips cleanly without segment loss or tag damage.

The interoperability map in practice:

  • XLIFF 1.2 — accepted by Trados, memoQ, Phrase, Smartcat, OmegaT, MateCat, Wordfast.
  • XLIFF 2.0 — accepted by Trados, memoQ, Phrase, OmegaT; cloud platforms lag.
  • SDLXLIFF — native in Trados; imported by memoQ with occasional tag loss.
  • MQXLIFF — native in memoQ; imported by Trados with manageable fidelity.
  • TMX 1.4 — universal round-trip across every production-grade CAT tool.

  • TBX — accepted broadly but with vendor-specific extensions that need manual mapping.

Cloud-TMS to desktop-CAT round-trips are typical on Crowdin-run projects — see Crowdin Translation: How Translators and Agencies Run Projects Inside Crowdin.

Where does AI pre-translate fit inside the CAT tool?

AI pre-translate populates the target cell with an LLM or NMT draft before the translator touches the segment. The CAT tool scores confidence per segment, routes low-confidence segments to human post-edit, and holds the output for LQA sampling at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. The full first-draft-plus-human-certification shape is AI Localization: How Translators and Agencies Run the First-Draft + Human-Certification Workflow, and the Phrase-specific implementation What Phrase AI Does and Whether It Fits Your Workflow.

How do you choose a CAT tool for your own translation work?

Choose a CAT tool against 6 criteria: file-format breadth across your real client inputs, translation-memory and term-base interoperability through XLIFF and TMX, inline QA depth, pricing model, fit for your highest-value lane, and vendor lock-in risk measured by how cleanly projects export.

  1. File-format breadth across your real client inputs.
  2. TM and term-base interoperability through XLIFF and TMX.
  3. Inline QA depth — tag, number, terminology, punctuation, length.
  4. Pricing model — perpetual, subscription, or open source.
  5. Fit for your highest-value lane — certified, continuous software, or marketing.
  6. Vendor lock-in risk — tested by round-tripping a 20-segment file.

The companion buyer checklist is What a CAT Tool Set Includes and How to Pick One.

Which file formats do real translation clients send?

Match the CAT tool to the file formats your clients actually send. InDesign IDML and PDF for marketing agencies, DOCX and PPTX for corporate clients, XLIFF and JSON for software clients, and scanned PDFs with OCR for USCIS and legal filings.

Does the CAT tool round-trip XLIFF and TMX cleanly?

Test XLIFF and TMX round-trips before committing. Import a bilingual XLIFF from one tool, translate 20 segments, export, and re-import in the original tool. Segment loss, tag damage, or TM mismatches on round-trip signal vendor lock-in you will pay for later.

What does a CAT tool cost per translator per year?

CAT tool pricing in the US falls into 3 bands in 2025: perpetual desktop licences at $400–$900 one-time plus annual upgrades (Trados, memoQ), subscription cloud seats at $25–$80 per user per month (Phrase, Smartcat, Lokalise), and free open-source options (OmegaT, MateCat) with zero licence cost but no vendor support.

Pricing modelRepresentative toolsYear-one cost per seatTrade-off
Perpetual desktopTrados, memoQ, Wordfast$400–$900 + optional supportCapital outlay; full offline control
Cloud subscriptionPhrase, Smartcat, Lokalise, Smartling$300–$960 per user per yearLower entry; vendor dependency
Open sourceOmegaT, MateCat$0No vendor support; thinner QA

Does a CAT tool fit a certified-translation lane?

Certified-translation lanes require offline file control, named-translator attestation inside the bilingual export, and a documented chain of custody that cloud multi-tenant platforms struggle to prove. Desktop CAT workbenches remain the default for certified filings for USCIS, courts, and registries priced at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard page of about 250 words. The cloud-vs-desktop trade-off for working translators is weighed Cloud-Based CAT Tools Compared for Working Translators.

How do CAT tools change the economics of a translation project?

CAT tools change project economics on 3 axes. Translation-memory leverage discounts repeated and fuzzy-matched segments against the base $0.10–$0.25 per source word. Review at $0.04–$0.08 per word compounds that discount across the file. LQA sampling at $40–$90 per 1,000 words becomes the only quality gate that keeps the discount defensible.

How does the 75% fuzzy-match threshold set the discount grid?

The 75% fuzzy threshold is the floor below which TM matches are not leveraged. Above it, bands at 75–84%, 85–94%, 95–99%, 100% exact, and 101% in-context each carry a progressively steeper discount against the full per-word rate.

How does a mid-size program scale with CAT leverage?

A mid-size multi-locale program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words costs $25,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and certification requirements. The spread between the floor and the ceiling is almost entirely a function of how deeply the CAT tool's TM reuses prior output.

ScenarioTM leverage profilePer-locale cost (10,000 words)Program total (5 locales)
Cold start, no TM100% no-match$10,000–$15,000$50,000–$75,000
Second release30% leveraged, 70% no-match$7,000–$10,000$35,000–$50,000
Mature TM, continuous content60% leveraged, 40% no-match$5,000–$7,500$25,000–$37,500

What are the limits and failure modes of CAT tools?

CAT tools fail in 4 predictable modes.

  1. Tag damage on round-trip between desktop and cloud editors, especially when SDLXLIFF or MQXLIFF cross tool boundaries without lossless mapping.
  2. TM pollution when unapproved segments enter the memory and resurface as high-confidence matches on later projects.
  3. Term-base drift when multiple projects share one base without governance, and conflicting approved renderings accumulate.
  4. Over-reliance on fuzzy matches that read fluent in context but mistranslate the segment the client actually paid for.

What does a CAT tool look like at the segment level?

A specimen of the editing grid as the translator sees it — the surface where every other feature on this page converges in one view.

Frequently asked questions

What computer-assisted translation tools do professional translators actually use?

Professional translators most use SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Déjà Vu, Wordfast, and Smartcat as their primary CAT tools. These platforms share core features — translation memories (TMs), termbases, and segment-locking — but differ in price, collaboration features, and file-format support. Trados dominates agency workflows and is often required by large LSPs, while memoQ is favored for its project-management depth. Cloud-based tools like Smartcat and Phrase (formerly Memsource) are gaining ground for real-time team collaboration.

How is AI translation different from computer-assisted translation (CAT)?

AI translation (machine translation, or MT) generates a full translated text automatically, while computer-assisted translation (CAT) is a human-driven environment that presents segments for a translator to write or edit with tool-assisted support. CAT tools store approved translations in a translation memory and enforce terminology via a termbase, keeping the human in control of every decision. MT can be plugged into a CAT tool as a suggestion engine, but the two are architecturally distinct: one automates output, the other augments the human translator's productivity.

What is the main purpose of computer-assisted translation?

The main purpose of a CAT tool is to increase translator consistency and speed by recycling previously approved translations through a translation memory. When a new source segment matches or closely resembles a stored segment, the tool proposes the earlier translation as a fuzzy or exact match, reducing rework. For certified translation work, this is especially valuable: standard legal boilerplate, recurring government phrases, and document headers often repeat across files, and a well-maintained TM can cut active translation time on repeat content by 30–70%.

What are examples of CAT tools?

Well-known CAT tools include SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Wordfast Pro, Déjà Vu X, Smartcat, Phrase (Memsource), Lokalise, and OmegaT (open-source). Each segments source documents, stores approved translations in a TM, and manages project-specific termbases. Some, like Trados and memoQ, are desktop-first with cloud add-ons; others, like Smartcat and Lokalise, are fully cloud-native. OmegaT is free and popular among freelancers working on Linux or with tight budgets.

What are CAT tools for translators?

CAT tools are specialized software environments that break a source document into segments and present each one for a translator to translate, with real-time suggestions from a translation memory and termbase. They are not translation engines — the human writes every target-language segment, but the tool surfaces relevant prior work and flags terminology deviations. For certified translation producers, CAT tools also preserve document formatting and create auditable records of translator decisions, which supports quality-assurance workflows and revision tracking.

What are the disadvantages of machine translation?

Machine translation frequently produces fluent-sounding but factually or legally incorrect output, which is its most serious disadvantage for certified translation work. MT systems can mistranslate names, dates, document numbers, and legal terms in ways that are hard to spot on a surface read. They lack contextual judgment about register, jurisdiction-specific phrasing, and cultural conventions. Post-editing MT to certification standard often takes nearly as long as translating from scratch when the source document is complex or poorly OCR'd, erasing much of the speed benefit.

What is one major risk of machine translation?

The biggest single risk of machine translation is confident mistranslation — the system produces a grammatically smooth sentence that carries the wrong meaning, and the error goes undetected. In certified translation, this can invalidate a legal document, cause an immigration application to be rejected, or create liability for the certifying translator or agency. Unlike an obvious garbled output that prompts review, a fluent-but-wrong sentence can pass a quick scan and reach the end client uncorrected.

Which is better, Trados or memoQ?

Neither is universally better — the right choice depends on your workflow. Trados Studio has the largest market share among agencies and is the de facto standard requested by large LSPs, making it the safer choice if agency compatibility is a priority. memoQ offers a more intuitive project-management interface and is often preferred by in-house teams or agencies managing complex multilingual projects. Pricing is comparable for professional licenses (roughly $695–$900/year for a single translator seat), and both support XLIFF, bilingual Word, and most major formats used in certified translation.

Can I use Smartcat for free?

Yes, Smartcat offers a free tier that includes unlimited translation memory, basic CAT editor access, and a marketplace for finding work. The free plan covers most core CAT features a solo freelance translator needs, making it a practical entry point. Paid plans (starting around $50–$120/month depending on team size) unlock advanced automation, MT engine integrations, API access, and priority support. For certified translation agencies managing multiple translators, the paid tiers add workflow controls that the free plan lacks.

Which is the best cat tool for translation?

There is no single best CAT tool — the optimal choice depends on your volume, collaboration needs, and client requirements. SDL Trados Studio is the industry-standard choice for agency compatibility and file-format breadth. memoQ is widely preferred for project management and team use. Smartcat suits budget-conscious freelancers and small agencies with its free tier. For certified translation production at scale, the best tool is the one that integrates cleanly with your QA process, supports your file types, and matches the TM format your clients expect.

pages.title: Content Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce It
pages.h1: Content Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce It
pages.meta_description: Content localization is the end-to-end adaptation of marketing, editorial, and support content for a target locale, delivered by translators using TMs, term
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is content localization from the translator's side of the desk?
  • What are the key elements of content localization?
  • Why does content localization matter for businesses expanding into new markets?
  • What types of content get localized, and in what priority order?
  • What does the content localization workflow look like from the translator's desk?
  • How does the agency measure the success of content localization?
  • What are the biggest challenges of content localization, and how are they handled?
  • Frequently asked questions

Content localization is the production lane that takes a source asset — a landing page, a blog post, an email flow, a help article, a video — and ships it as locally authored copy in a target market. This guide is written from the translator's and agency's side of the desk, not the buyer's. It sits beside the sibling production lanes documented in Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide and Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.

What is content localization from the translator's side of the desk?

Content localization is the end-to-end adaptation of marketing, editorial, support, and multimedia content for one target locale, delivered by translators and reviewers using translation memory, a term base, a style guide, and an in-context review build the client publishes. The lane covers language, formats, imagery, cultural references, and legal disclaimers inside each asset.

The five production artifacts that enter the translator's workspace at kickoff are:

  • Externalized source content as XLIFF, Markdown, or a CMS export.
  • Translation memory for the language pair.
  • Client term base for product names and regulated terminology.
  • Locale style guide for tone, register, and formatting.
  • In-context review build on staging with real layout and imagery.

How is content localization different from translation?

Translation converts text from one language to another. Content localization adapts the full asset — copy, imagery, formats, cultural references, and legal disclaimers — so it reads as authored in the target market. The underlying i18n test discipline is covered in Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds, so this page does not re-explain it.

Where does content localization sit inside a broader localization program?

Content localization is one of six delivery lanes inside a broader localization program: product app, website, marketing content, support knowledge base, legal and compliance documents, and in-product video. Each lane carries its own SLA and reviewer pool. All six share one term base and one style guide per locale.

LanePrimary assetsShared with content lane
Product appUI strings, in-app messagesTerm base, style guide
WebsitePages, nav, SEO metadataTerm base, style guide, TM
Marketing contentCampaigns, blog, email, social, videoAll five artifacts
Support KBHelp articles, release notesTerm base, style guide, TM
Legal / complianceDisclaimers, privacy, claimsTerm base (locked segments)
In-product videoSubtitles, dubs, on-screen textTerm base, style guide, TM

What are the key elements of content localization?

The key elements of content localization are language adaptation, cultural references, date and currency formats, imagery and iconography, legal and regulatory disclaimers, SEO metadata, and in-context review — each delivered against a locale-specific style guide and term base.

ElementWhat the translator doesGoverned by
Language adaptationRewrites idioms, headlines, CTAsStyle guide, TM
Cultural referencesSwaps metaphors, holidays, humorImagery guidelines
FormatsApplies CLDR number, date, currencyCAT tool placeholders
ImageryFlags people, gestures, color meaningReviewer sign-off
Legal disclaimersLeaves locked segments untouchedLegal/compliance lane
SEO metadataTitle, description, slug per localeKeyword list, style guide
In-context reviewReads in staging layoutReview build

How does language adaptation differ from literal translation here?

Language adaptation rewrites idioms, headlines, and calls to action so they resonate with the target audience, rather than translating word-for-word. Translators work inside a CAT tool with TM leverage. The locale style guide sets tone, register, and reading level. A headline flagged as too formal for es-MX gets rewritten, not re-translated.

What cultural references and imagery need to change by locale?

Cultural references — holidays, sports metaphors, humor, product shots, people, hand gestures, and color symbolism — are swapped per locale against the client's imagery guidelines. Reviewers flag anything that reads as foreign, off-tone, or offensive. Common swap categories include:

  • Sports metaphors (baseball references out for most EU markets).
  • Holiday callouts (Thanksgiving out for non-US launches).
  • People shown (local models for hero images).
  • Hand gestures (thumbs-up and OK sign vary in meaning).
  • Color symbolism (white, red, and green read differently per market).

Markets with heavy cultural filtering are covered in Chinese Localization: What Makes It Harder Than Most Projects.

Which number, date, currency, and measurement formats get localized?

Number, date, time, currency, and measurement formats are localized to CLDR locale defaults. Translators apply these inside the CAT tool using locale-aware placeholders rather than typing values by hand.

Elementen-US sourcefr-FRes-ESja-JP
Currency$1,250.001 250,00 €1250,00 €¥1,250
DateMarch 5, 20255 mars 20255 de marzo de 20252025年3月5日
Time3:30 PM15:3015:3015:30
Measurement5 miles8 km8 km8 km
Name orderGiven FamilyGiven FamilyGiven FamilyFamily Given

How are legal disclaimers and regulatory language handled?

Legal disclaimers, privacy notices, and regulated-industry claims are not translated by the content linguist. They are routed to the legal and compliance lane, approved per jurisdiction, and dropped back into the content asset as locked segments. The content translator leaves those segments untouched at delivery.

What community and platform standards count as content localization?

Community standards — NSFW flair rules, geo-specific subreddit norms, and platform moderation thresholds — are a micro-layer of content localization. Geo-specific online communities (r/NRL for Australian rugby league, r/NFL for US football) carry their own flair and language rules. Automatic moderation systems routinely miss nationality-based harassment because the rules were written for one locale and never re-localized.

Why does content localization matter for businesses expanding into new markets?

Content localization matters because audiences convert on content that reads as locally authored — in their language, formats, and cultural register. Translated-but-not-localized content loses engagement, trust, and search visibility. It leaks revenue even when the product itself is ready.

What business outcomes does localized content drive?

Localized content lifts organic reach in target-language search, raises conversion on landing pages, improves support deflection in local-language KBs, and shortens sales cycles with regional messaging that resonates. The outcomes tracked are:

  • Organic sessions per locale against the source-language baseline.
  • Landing-page conversion rate per locale.
  • Support ticket deflection where KB content was localized.
  • Sales-cycle length with region-specific messaging.
  • NPS per locale, not global average.

How does dual-platform distribution change localization scope?

Dual-platform distribution splits one piece of content across audience segments with different formats, ad loads, and metadata. Dancing with the Stars Season 34 premiered on ABC September 16 with next-day streaming on Disney+ — the same episode shipped as two localized variants, not one. The content localization team delivers both.

What types of content get localized, and in what priority order?

The content types routinely localized are marketing campaigns, blog and editorial, product and category pages, email flows, social posts, video subtitles and dubs, and support knowledge-base articles. Priority is set by revenue impact per locale, source volume stability, and reuse through translation memory.

Content typeExternalizationTM leverageIn-context review path
Blog articleMarkdown or CMS exportMediumStaging preview URL
Long-form editorialCMS exportLowStaging preview URL
Email campaignHTML templateHigh (templates)Email render test
Social postSpreadsheet or JSONLowPlatform preview
Video subtitle / dubSRT or VTTMediumTimecoded playback
Knowledge-base articleXLIFF or MarkdownHighHelp center staging

How is marketing content localized differently from editorial?

Marketing content — campaigns, landing pages, ads — is transcreated. Headlines and CTAs are rewritten against brand voice per locale, often with two or three variants reviewed by the in-country marketer. Editorial content follows the style guide more literally. TM leverage is prioritized for consistency across the blog.

How are support KB articles and documentation localized?

Support KB articles and product documentation are localized with high TM leverage, strict term base enforcement, and a "translate on update" workflow that pushes delta segments to translators as the source changes. This is the support KB lane feeding content back into help centers. Changes to product names in the term base cascade through every published article.

CMS-driven editorial sits beside this: see How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know. Catalog and category pages for commerce sit in How Shopify Localization Works and What It Means for Your Agency.

How does video and multimedia fit into the content lane?

Video is localized through subtitles, closed captions, voice-over, or full dub, with the script running through the same TM and term base as written content. Imagery and on-screen text are swapped per locale. The final cut goes through in-context review before publishing.

How it works

What does the content localization workflow look like from the translator's desk?

1

What does the translator receive at project start?

The translator receives five artifacts at project start: the externalized source content, the TM for the language pair, the client's term base, the locale style guide, and access to the staging CMS or review build. Missing any one of the five stalls the kickoff. For externalization in a React stack, see React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

2

How does TM leverage and term base enforcement work on content assets?

TM leverage pre-translates repeated segments, exact matches, and fuzzy matches above a client-agreed threshold — typically 75%. The term base enforces approved renderings of product names, feature names, and regulated terminology. The CAT tool flags deviations in real time as the translator types.

3

How is in-context review performed on content assets?

In-context review happens on a staging environment or preview URL where the reviewer sees the translated content inside the final layout, with real images, CTAs, and spacing. Issues are logged against the segment, not the rendered page. Fixes flow back through the CAT tool and the TM so the next release inherits them.

4

How is quality scored at release?

Quality is scored per 1000 words against a weighted rubric at release. The score is handed to the client with the delivery, not kept internal.

Rubric axisWeightWhat it measures
Accuracy30%Faithful rendering of source meaning
Terminology compliance25%Term base adherence
Locale conventions20%CLDR formats, name order, address
Style guide adherence15%Tone, register, voice
Readability10%Reading level in target language

How does the agency measure the success of content localization?

Agencies measure content localization success on four axes: per-locale engagement and conversion against the source-language baseline, support ticket deflection, re-engagement cycles tied to region-timed content drops, and the per-1000-word QA score trend across releases.

What metrics are tracked per locale?

Per-locale metrics tracked are organic sessions, time-on-page, conversion rate, assisted-conversion share, support ticket volume per 1000 sessions, and NPS. Each is read against the source-language baseline for the same content type, not a global average.

MetricContent type scopeBaseline
Organic sessionsBlog, product pagesSource language, same page
Time on pageEditorial, KBSource language, same page
Conversion rateLanding pages, emailSource language, same campaign
Ticket deflectionSupport KBPre-localization volume
NPS per localeProgram-wideRolling 90 days

How do re-engagement cycles factor into measurement?

Re-engagement cycles — new content drops, seasonal updates, platform wipes, and region-timed events — pull audiences back on predictable schedules. Measurement that only looks at launch-week lift undercounts localized content. A rolling 90-day window captures the actual engagement curve.

What are the biggest challenges of content localization, and how are they handled?

The biggest challenges of content localization are cultural references that do not travel, source content written without internationalization in mind, inconsistent terminology across lanes, regulatory variance per market, and moderation gaps that miss nationality-based harassment on localized community platforms.

How do translators handle source content that was not internationalized?

Translators flag hard-coded strings, concatenated sentences, embedded images with on-screen text, and culture-specific jokes before translation starts. The content goes back to the author with an internationalization checklist. The agency rewrites the source in parallel against the style guide when a return trip is not possible.

How is terminology kept consistent across six localization lanes?

Terminology is kept consistent across lanes by one shared term base per locale, enforced inside the CAT tool for every lane — app, website, content, support KB, legal, video. Changes are proposed through a termbase RFC. The lead reviewer per locale approves promotion before the new rendering goes live.

Why do moderation systems fail on nationality-based content issues?

Automatic moderation systems fail on nationality-based harassment because the rulesets were written in one locale and never re-localized against the slurs, dog-whistles, and cultural flashpoints of other markets. A documented September 2026 incident on a gaming subreddit triggered zero automatic penalties despite repeated community reports.

The questions buyers and in-house teams most often ask about content localization are what it is, how it differs from translation, which content types to prioritize, what a localization specialist does, and what qualifies as a content localization example in the wild.

Frequently asked questions

What is content localization?

Content localization is the process of adapting source-language content so it feels native to a target market — not just translating words, but adjusting units of measure, date formats, imagery, legal references, and cultural conventions. For translators and agencies, this means going beyond a literal rendering to produce a version that reads as if it were written for that audience from the start. A certified translation, for example, must localize formal titles, credential names, and legal terminology to the conventions of the target country while preserving the legal equivalence of the original document.

What does localization mean?

Localization means transforming content from one linguistic and cultural context into another so it is fully appropriate for the target locale. In translation practice, this goes beyond word-for-word substitution: a translator localizes currency, date formats, idiomatic expressions, honorifics, and jurisdiction-specific legal language. For certified translations in particular, localization also requires mapping official titles and document structures to the formats recognized by the receiving authority — for instance, adapting a foreign birth certificate layout to meet USCIS or sworn-translator standards.

What does it mean to localize something?

To localize something means to reshape content so it is linguistically accurate and culturally appropriate for a specific target audience or region. For a translator, localizing a document involves replacing source-culture references with target-culture equivalents — swapping measurement systems, reformatting dates (e.g., DD/MM/YYYY vs. MM/DD/YYYY), adjusting formal registers, and ensuring legal or technical terminology matches the conventions of the destination country. On a certified translation, every localization decision must still preserve full semantic equivalence with the original.

What is a localization strategy?

A localization strategy is a structured plan that defines how, where, and to what depth content will be adapted for each target market. For translation agencies, this typically covers language-pair prioritization, style guides and glossaries per locale, quality-assurance workflows (translation, editing, proofreading — TEP), and decisions about which content tiers require certified or sworn translation versus general localization. A well-defined strategy also sets turnaround standards, technology choices (CAT tools, TMS, MT post-editing), and the certification or notarization requirements that vary by country and document type.

What does a localization job do?

A localization professional adapts content — documents, software, marketing materials, or legal texts — so it is linguistically and culturally fit for a target market. In a translation agency context, localization roles range from translator and editor to localization engineer and project manager. For certified document translation specifically, the translator must also apply the appropriate certification statement, match the target jurisdiction's formatting expectations, and often coordinate with notaries or apostille services. Turnaround requirements, quality standards, and certification rules vary significantly by language pair and destination country.

What are the differences between source language and target language in translation?

The source language is the original language of the document being translated, while the target language is the language into which it is rendered. In certified translation, this distinction carries legal weight: the translator attests that the target-language version is a complete and accurate representation of the source. Structural differences between languages — syntax, script direction, honorific systems, grammatical gender — mean a translator cannot work word-for-word; instead, they produce a target-language text that conveys the same meaning, register, and legal effect as the source.

What are the three types of translations?

The three broadly recognized types of translation are literary, technical/specialized, and general translation, though practitioners also distinguish a fourth — certified (or sworn) translation. Technical translation covers legal, medical, scientific, and financial documents and demands precise terminology management. Literary translation prioritizes style and voice. Certified translation is a formal category where the translator or agency attaches a signed statement of accuracy, making it legally acceptable to government bodies, courts, and academic institutions. Many agencies handle all three types but apply different workflows, rates, and QA standards to each.

What language is most in demand for translators?

Spanish consistently ranks as one of the highest-demand languages for translators in the United States, driven by immigration, legal, and healthcare document volume. Globally, Chinese (Mandarin), Arabic, French, German, and Portuguese also generate very high translation demand. For certified translation agencies, language demand closely tracks immigration patterns and trade relationships — USCIS document translation, for instance, sees especially high volume for Spanish, Chinese, Vietnamese, Tagalog, and Haitian Creole. Rare-language pairs command premium rates precisely because qualified certified translators are scarce.

How to set up a translation business?

Setting up a translation business requires establishing your legal entity, defining your service scope (general, certified, sworn, or localization), and building a vetted roster of qualified translators. For certified translation services specifically, you must understand the certification requirements of each target jurisdiction — U.S. agencies typically use a signed accuracy statement, while many European countries require sworn translators appointed by a court. Technology stack decisions — CAT tools, translation memory, TMS, and increasingly AI-assisted first-draft tools — directly affect throughput and margin. Agencies also need clear QA workflows (TEP or equivalent) and defined turnaround SLAs before taking on high-volume clients.

pages.title: Continuous Localization: How Translators and Agencies Run the Delivery Model
pages.h1: Continuous Localization: How Translators and Agencies Run the Delivery Model
pages.meta_description: Continuous localization pulls new strings from the repo on every merge, routes them through AI first-draft, review, and LQA, and ships locales hours behind
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • Key points
  • What is continuous localization and how does it work?
  • What are the key benefits of continuous localization for an agency?
  • When should a project move from waterfall to continuous localization?
  • How does continuous localization compare to traditional waterfall handoff?
  • What quality gates run inside a continuous localization lane?
  • How does an agency price a continuous localization program?
  • Which tools and platforms power continuous localization in practice?
  • How we run continuous localization lanes
  • Frequently asked questions

Continuous localization is the delivery model where translators and agencies receive commit-level string deltas from a client's repository through a TMS connector, process them as micro-jobs through AI first-draft, human review, and LQA, and return approved translations so the localized build trails the English source release by hours per merge. This page covers the production-floor mechanics an agency runs — the connector, the micro-job queue, the LQA gate against ISO 17100, the retained-capacity billing model, and the four triggers that force a project off waterfall — and sits inside our broader coverage of How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying.

Key points

  • Continuous localization pulls new and changed strings from the client's repository on every merge, routes them through AI first-draft plus human review plus LQA, and ships localized builds hours behind source — making it the natural delivery model for any team running CI/CD pipelines.
  • Four triggers force a move off waterfall: release cadence under two weeks, more than 500 new or changed strings per sprint, more than six active target locales, and in-app experimentation generating strings between releases.
  • Agency pricing stacks translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100.
  • Translation memory inside a continuous cycle trims per-word cost by 20–40%, and best practice pushes new strings to translators within 24–48 hours of string freeze — teams that apply this discipline have reported localization cycle time falling by more than 50%.
  • A mid-size program of 5 languages across 50,000 words lands at
    • Continuous localization pulls new and changed strings from the client's repository on every merge, routes them through AI first-draft plus human review plus LQA, and ships localized builds hours behind source.
    • Four triggers force a move off waterfall: release cadence under two weeks, more than 500 new or changed strings per sprint, more than six active target locales, and in-app experimentation generating strings between releases.
    • Agency pricing stacks translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100.

    • A mid-size program of 5 languages across 50,000 words lands at $25,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and certification requirements.

    5,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and certification requirements.

  • The PM role shifts entirely under continuous localization: instead of dispatching and tracking individual purchase orders, the PM focuses on exception handling and capacity planning across a standing translator pool.
  • Programs operating at full TM leverage have demonstrated human localization cost reductions exceeding 40% while simultaneously expanding language coverage — proving that cost discipline and scale are not mutually exclusive in the continuous model.

What is continuous localization and how does it work?

Continuous localization is the delivery model where a TMS connector pulls new and changed strings from the client's repository on every merge, routes them through AI first-draft, human review, and LQA inside the sprint, and returns approved translations so the localized build trails the English release by hours. The connector is persistent, the job queue is diff-based, and the reviewer pool stays on standby for sprint-aligned sampling. This model has become the standard delivery approach for software teams that have adopted CI/CD pipelines, because a waterfall handoff cannot keep pace with a weekly or faster deploy cycle. Teams that operate this way have reported localization cycle time falling by more than 50% and publishing delays collapsing from one to two weeks down to near-real-time — without adding internal headcount.

What is the difference between continuous localization and adjacent delivery models?

Continuous localization is one of four related but distinct concepts that come up in software localization conversations. Understanding the differences matters because each model implies a different contract structure, a different tool stack, and a different day-to-day workflow for the PM and the translator pool.

TermWhat it isWhen you offer it
Continuous localizationConnector-driven delivery mechanic that moves string deltas from repo to localized build within hoursWeekly or faster commit cadence with 500+ strings per sprint
Agile localizationSprint-cycle discipline that integrates translation work into development planningAny sprint-based engineering team, with or without a connector
Waterfall handoffSingle export per release, offline translation, re-importQuarterly or longer release trains with batch sign-off
In-sprint translationTranslation work scheduled inside the same sprint as the strings' developmentTeams running agile with a dedicated LSP contact per sprint

What does the string flow look like from commit to localized build?

On every merge the connector detects changed strings, pushes them into the TMS as a micro-job, assigns the micro-job to the translator pool, runs AI first-draft and human review, applies the LQA sampling gate, and writes the approved target strings back to the build within hours. The webhook fires on commit or merge from GitHub or GitLab, and the diff — not the full file — enters the queue. This diff-based architecture is what keeps micro-job sizes manageable: translators receive segments sized in minutes, not multi-day batches. React, Vue, and native mobile codebases are typical commit sources; the same pipeline logic applies to SaaS products that continuously ship in-app copy and experiment strings between formal releases.

The string flow runs in six steps: the developer merges to the repo, the webhook fires to the TMS, the diff is detected, a micro-job is created, AI first-draft runs, and the human translator reviews the draft before LQA sampling. D[Micro-job created in TMS queue]
 D --> E[AI first-draft runs]
 E --> F[Human translator reviews draft]
 F --> G{LQA sampling gate}
 G -- Pass --> H[Approved strings pushed back to build]
 G -- Fail --> F
 H --> I[Localized build ships hours behind source]

Who touches a string inside a continuous lane?

Four roles touch each string: the connector (automated), the AI first-draft engine, the human translator reviewing the draft, and the LQA reviewer sampling the output against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. The AI first-draft stage runs before human review on every micro-job, and the translator post-edits the draft rather than translating from scratch. This post-edit model is what makes the economics work: translation memory supplies matches, the AI fills gaps, and the human reviewer adds judgment — each role doing only what the previous layer does not. The LQA reviewer operates on a sampling basis calibrated to sprint volume, not on a full-file pass, which is what keeps the gate from becoming a bottleneck inside a high-frequency commit environment.

  1. Connector — detects the diff, creates the micro-job, carries metadata and context.
  2. AI first-draft engine — produces a seed translation leveraging TM and glossary.
  3. Human translator — reviews and post-edits every segment.
  4. LQA reviewer — samples output against the scorecard before build-back.

Why us

How much does translation memory reduce per-word cost in a continuous cycle?

Translation memory inside a continuous cycle reduces per-word costs by 20–40%, because repeated UI strings across sprints are not re-translated — only the diff is routed to the translator, and TM leverage is highest where micro-batches share vocabulary with prior merges. The glossary and style guide travel with the TM, and the AI first-draft engine pre-populates matches before the human translator touches the segment.

How does the retained-capacity billing model work?

Under continuous localization the agency bills retained monthly capacity or per-word with an SLA on turnaround, not one-off POs — the PM role shifts from job dispatch to exception handling and capacity planning, and the client secures guaranteed hours each sprint instead of waiting on a quote per release. Billing-model and PM-mode differences for multi-locale programs are documented on Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

When should a project move from waterfall to continuous localization?

A project moves to continuous localization when four triggers appear together: release cadence under two weeks, more than 500 new or changed strings per sprint, more than six active target locales, and in-app experimentation generating strings outside the main release train. One trigger alone does not justify the switch; the combination is what breaks file-based editing.

  1. Release cadence under two weeks. Waterfall handoff cannot keep pace with a bi-weekly or weekly release train.
  2. More than 500 new or changed strings per sprint. Manual export/import loses TM leverage at this volume.
  3. More than six active target locales. Coordination overhead across locales exceeds PM dispatch capacity.
  4. In-app experimentation generating strings between releases. A/B copy, feature flags, and in-product messaging spawn strings outside the main train.

What is the scaling threshold where an i18n-editor stops working?

An i18n-editor stops scaling at roughly 5,000 translation keys, four or more target locales, or any continuous-localization cadence that commits weekly — file-based editing loses TM leverage, has no reviewer gate, and cannot run the LQA sampling that certified lanes require under an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. See i18n-editor: What Translators Use to Edit JSON Translation Files for the scaling detail and when a TMS becomes mandatory.

How does continuous localization compare to traditional waterfall handoff?

Continuous localization moves string-level micro-batches through a repo connector on every commit and ships locales hours behind source; waterfall batches 5,000+ words per release cycle, exports once, translates offline, re-imports, and ships locales weeks or months behind source. The operational gap between the two models is not merely one of speed — it is a difference in how risk accumulates. Under waterfall, untranslated strings pile up invisibly between exports: a developer pushes a change on Monday, and by Thursday the French and German versions of that string may still be sitting in a manual export queue while the English build is already live. That latency compounds across every sprint, and by the time a release ships, the localized versions can be a full cycle behind.

What changes operationally for the PM and the translator pool?

Operationally, the PM moves from dispatch-and-track to exception handling and capacity planning, translators work on micro-jobs sized in minutes rather than multi-day POs, and the reviewer pool stays on standby for sprint-aligned sampling instead of one-shot batch review. This restructuring changes how capacity is contracted. Under waterfall, the agency scales up for each PO and then scales back down. Under continuous localization, a standing pool is retained across sprints, shifting billing to retained monthly capacity or per-word with an SLA. Teams that make this transition reduce publishing delays from one to two weeks to near-real-time., demonstrating that the operational change is not cosmetic — it fundamentally alters the relationship between source release and localized release. Translators in a continuous lane must also adapt their working habits: context arrives as micro-jobs with metadata rather than as packaged XLIFF files, and the translator's throughput expectation is measured against sprint velocity rather than weekly word counts.

What quality gates run inside a continuous localization lane?

Two quality gates run inside a continuous lane: review at $0.04–$0.08 per source word that checks every segment, and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words that samples output against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100, scoring accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style. The LQA gate is blocking — a failed sample sends the batch back to review before the build is pushed.

How is the LQA scorecard structured?

The LQA scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 scores five MQM defect categories — accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style — on sampled segments at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated, and runs as a blocking gate before the localized build is pushed to release.

CategoryWhat it scores
AccuracyMistranslation, omission, addition against source meaning
FluencyGrammar, spelling, punctuation in the target locale
TerminologyAdherence to the client glossary and TM entries
Locale conventionDates, numbers, currency, address format for the target
StyleRegister, tone, and style-guide compliance

How tight is the string-freeze-to-translator SLA?

Best practice is to push new or changed strings to translators within 24–48 hours of a string freeze — any longer and the sprint cadence breaks, because the reviewer and LQA gates still need to run before the localized build can trail the source release by hours.

Pricing

How does an agency price a continuous localization program?

A continuous localization program stacks four US-dollar line items: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated, and retained monthly capacity for PM and exception handling — with TM leverage trimming 20–40% off per-word spend across sprints. The retained capacity line item is the structural difference from waterfall pricing: because the translator pool and the PM are on standby between micro-jobs rather than spun up per project, that availability has a cost that sits outside the per-word rate. Programs that invest in TM leverage early — building glossary and TM while string counts are still manageable — have demonstrated human localization cost reductions exceeding 40% at scale, which means the up-front investment in TM infrastructure pays back quickly across a multi-sprint program.

A mid-size multi-locale program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words costs

What does a mid-size five-language program actually cost?

A mid-size multi-locale program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words costs $25,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and certification requirements — the floor applies to high-TM software strings, the ceiling to low-TM content with certified-lane LQA on every batch.

The billing model itself is a differentiator when pitching continuous against waterfall: retained monthly capacity with a per-word SLA gives the client budget predictability and gives the agency stable revenue, whereas per-PO waterfall billing creates revenue peaks and troughs that make capacity planning difficult for both sides. Agencies that articulate this trade-off concretely are better positioned to close continuous engagements with software clients who are already managing recurring SaaS operating costs and prefer predictable line items.

Computer-Assisted Translation Tools: The Working Translator's Field Guide

Which tools and platforms power continuous localization in practice?

Continuous localization runs on three tool layers: a TMS of record wired to the repo through GitHub or GitLab webhooks, a translation memory and glossary stored centrally, and an LQA scorecard tool that runs the ISO 17100-aligned sampling gate before build-back. The TMS is the system of record; the connector is the trigger mechanism; the TM is the economic engine that drives the 20–40% per-word cost reduction that makes the model financially sustainable at high commit frequency. This stack is the direct localization counterpart to the CI/CD pipelines that software teams have adopted to accelerate delivery — just as CI/CD automates build and test, the TMS connector automates string extraction, job creation, and build-back.

When does a lightweight editor stop being sufficient?

A simple i18n editor or file-based workflow is sufficient up to approximately 5,000 keys, four target locales, or a weekly commit cadence — beyond any of those thresholds, a full TMS connector becomes operationally necessary. Below those limits, manual string exports and spreadsheet-based review keep pace; above them, the volume and frequency of micro-jobs exceeds what any manual handoff handles without introducing the same latency problem that continuous localization eliminates. Agencies advising early-stage software clients track these three scaling signals and recommend a TMS migration proactively rather than reactively.

  • TMS of record — stores all translation memory, glossary, and job history; serves as the authoritative ledger for every string across every locale.
  • Repo connector — GitHub or GitLab webhook on commit or merge, diff-based micro-job queue; fires automatically without PM intervention.
  • Translation memory and glossary — stored centrally, consumed by AI first-draft and human review; primary driver of per-word cost reduction across sprints.
  • LQA scorecard tool — MQM-style, five error categories, aligned to ISO 17100; runs on a sampling basis calibrated to sprint volume.
  • CI/CD build-back integration — approved target strings written back into the pipeline for the next build, completing the automation loop without developer involvement.

How we run continuous localization lanes

We run continuous localization lanes where the client's repo is wired to a TMS via a webhook, and we deliver approved target strings back to the build within hours of the merge. Our AI first-draft runs on every micro-job and is post-edited by a human translator before the LQA gate — not instead of one.

We decline to ship raw AI output to a localized build, even on low-visibility strings. The LQA sampling gate aligned to ISO 17100 runs on every batch in a certified lane, and we refuse to skip it to hit a shorter SLA — the certification requirement is not compressible, only the cycle around it is.

We also refuse to quote a continuous program on a per-PO basis. The economics only work for the client and for us under retained monthly capacity with an SLA, because the PM mode is exception handling, not dispatch-and-track. A client asking for per-PO pricing on a weekly commit cadence is a client whose project belongs on waterfall or has not yet crossed the four-trigger threshold.

We will not claim universal acceptance of certified translations produced in a continuous lane. We prepare the certificate of accuracy and the sign-off; the receiving authority — a court, a registry, a regulator — decides acceptance, and we tell the client to check with theirs.

The questions below answer the operational edges that translators and agencies hit when they first move a client off waterfall and onto a continuous lane.

Frequently asked questions

What is continuous localization?

Continuous localization is a workflow model in which translation and localization work is released and updated in small, frequent increments rather than in large, periodic batches. Borrowed from continuous delivery in software development, it replaces the traditional "big-bang" release cycle — where all content is translated at once before launch — with an ongoing pipeline that processes new or changed strings as soon as they appear. For agencies and translators handling certified documents, this means integrating translation production, QA, and certification steps into a repeatable, near-real-time process that scales with client content velocity.
