    • AI post-editing is acceptable on repetitive UI strings and SKU attributes; human translation is required on claims-bearing product copy, regulated categories, and brand-voice marketing.
    • Scope translatable word counts from JSON, XML, YAML,.strings, and ARB exports — count string values only, not keys or structure.

    5,000–$75,000 depending on translation memory leverage and turnaround requirements.

  • AI post-editing is appropriate on repetitive UI strings and SKU-level attributes; human translation is required on claims-bearing product copy, regulated categories, and brand-voice marketing where regulatory or reputational risk is real.
  • Translatable scope comes from JSON, XML, YAML,.strings, and ARB exports — string values are counted, keys and structural markup are excluded.
  • Online retail is on track to surpass $6 trillion in global sales, and the majority of consumers prefer to buy in their own language — making localization a direct revenue lever, not a post-launch nicety.

What is e-commerce localization from the translator's and agency's side?

E-commerce localization is the production-side adaptation of an online store's catalog, storefront UI, checkout, currency, taxes, and SEO for one target market, delivered by translators against i18n-ready exports and audited through review and LQA gates. The surfaces are plural and the cadences differ — a theme release ships weekly, a catalog expansion ships quarterly, and a legal copy update ships on a regulatory trigger. The agency's job is to decouple these lanes so one does not block another.

Disambiguation — e-commerce localization vs adjacent terms

TermWhat it isWhen you need it
TranslationConverting source text into another language without changing commercial logic.Internal docs, segments inside a larger localization program.
Website localizationAdapting pages, navigation, SEO, and locale routing for a market.Content sites, marketing sites, non-commerce storefronts.
E-commerce localizationWebsite localization plus catalog, checkout, currency, taxes, payment methods, and consumer-law copy.Any site that transacts — D2C brands, marketplaces, Shopify stores.
App localizationLocalizing the strings, flows, and store listings of a native or hybrid application.iOS, Android, and desktop clients that connect to the same catalog.
TranscreationRewriting campaign and brand copy to carry concept and tone across markets.Hero copy, launch campaigns, taglines — priced off the per-word grid.

How is e-commerce localization different from generic website localization?

E-commerce localization adds catalog, pricing, checkout, tax, and payment surfaces on top of the pages, SEO, and locale routing that generic website localization already covers — the catalog alone can be the largest word-count surface in the entire program. Where Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project stops at CMS pages and hreflang, the e-commerce program also owns:

  • Product titles, descriptions, variants, specs, and category pages at SKU scale.
  • Local currency display with correct symbol placement — dollar signs replaced with euros for a DE storefront.
  • Preferred payment methods per market: SEPA and Klarna in Germany, iDEAL in the Netherlands, Alipay and WeChat Pay in China.
  • VAT and sales-tax display rules, customs copy, and shipping and returns policies adapted to each market's consumer law.
  • Order confirmations, shipping emails, help center articles, and the returns portal.

Where does e-commerce localization sit inside the broader localization program?

E-commerce localization sits as a CMS-specific sub-lane beneath website localization and alongside application localization, with sibling CMS deep-dives for each platform handling platform specifics. The most widely used CMS platforms are WordPress (powering roughly 40% of all websites), Shopify for commerce, Wix, Webflow, and Drupal — platform-level production detail lives on CMS Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce Multilingual Content Across Platforms. Shopify-specific surfaces — Markets, Translation API, Translate & Adapt, Liquid money filter, and metafields — are covered on How Shopify Localization Works and What It Means for Your Agency. Squarespace Commerce product fields and routes are covered on Squarespace Localization: How Translators Deliver Multilingual Squarespace Sites. For post-sale service surfaces — support macros, SLA copy, warranty terms — see Service Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Deliver.

flowchart TD
 A[Localization program] --> B[Application localization]
 A --> C[Website localization]
 C --> D[E-commerce localization]
 D --> E[Shopify sub-lane]
 D --> F[WooCommerce sub-lane]
 D --> G[Squarespace Commerce sub-lane]
 D --> H[Webflow Ecommerce sub-lane]

What are the key components of e-commerce localization?

The key components of e-commerce localization are the storefront UI, the product catalog, checkout and payment surfaces, local currency and tax display, locale-specific legal copy, customer support content, and multilingual SEO with hreflang — each produced on its own cadence and each carrying a different risk profile. The components map directly onto the three production lanes defined in the next section. Research consistently shows that the majority of consumers will not complete a purchase when the storefront presents information only in English, which means each component below is a conversion surface, not just a translation task.

ComponentLaneTypical AI-vs-human mix
Storefront UI, theme stringsStorefront UIAI + light post-editing
Product titles, descriptions, variantsCatalogHuman on claims; MTPE on SKU attributes
Checkout, currency, taxes, payment methodsTransactionalHuman review on all legal copy
Legal pages, returns, warrantiesTransactionalHuman translator with market expertise
Order confirmations, shipping emails, help centerTransactionalMTPE on templates; human on exceptions
Meta data, local keywords, hreflangCatalog + UIHuman on target keywords; config, not translation, on hreflang
Campaign and hero copyMarketing (adjacent)Transcreation, off per-word grid

How does the translator localize the storefront UI and theme strings?

Storefront UI localization adapts theme labels, navigation, buttons, filters, and error states against i18n-ready source files, with character-expansion checks per locale and locale routing confirmed before release. The translator works from the exported strings file — never from the live storefront — because in-context edits bypass version control and break the translation memory. German, for example, runs 25–35% longer than English on average, which means the tightest UI slot in the layout sets the character budget for the entire locale. Checks required before signoff include:

  • Character expansion validated against the tightest UI slot in the layout.
  • Placeholder integrity confirmed: {count}, {product_name}, and ICU plural forms preserved exactly as exported.
  • Locale routing verified on a staging domain or subfolder before production push.
  • Right-to-left mirroring tested on Arabic and Hebrew builds — layout, icons, and text direction all flip.
  • Date, time, number, and decimal-separator formats matching the target locale's conventions.

How does the translator localize product descriptions and the catalog?

Catalog localization rewrites product titles, descriptions, variants, specs, and category pages against a per-market glossary, with claims-bearing copy routed to human translators and SKU-level attributes handled by machine translation post-editing. The catalog is the largest word-count surface on any e-commerce project and also the surface with the highest translation memory leverage on recurring SKU updates — meaning the per-word cost drops substantially on the second and third update cycle once the TM is populated. Correct order of operations keeps quality consistent across thousands of SKUs:

  1. Lock a per-market glossary covering product category terms, ingredient names, unit conventions, and claim verbs before any translation begins.
  2. Split the export: SKU attributes such as color, size, and material go to MTPE; descriptive and narrative copy goes to human translators.
  3. Route claims-bearing categories — skincare, supplements, medical devices, food products — to human translators with regulatory expertise in the target market.
  4. Review translated output against the glossary; run an LQA sample before release.
  5. Push to the CMS and verify rendering on at least three device sizes and two browser locales before setting the page live.

How are checkout, local currency, payment methods, and taxes localized?

Checkout localization displays prices in local currency with correct symbol placement, surfaces the preferred payment methods for each market, applies the correct VAT or sales-tax display rules, and adapts shipping, returns, and customs copy to each market's consumer law. A US-to-Germany storefront, for instance, replaces USD with EUR and shifts to the symbol-after-amount placement convention standard in German retail contexts. Getting the currency display wrong — including the wrong decimal separator or an absent VAT line — erodes trust at the highest-intent moment in the purchase flow. Preferred payment methods vary sharply by market and must be surfaced, not buried:

  • Germany: SEPA direct debit, Klarna, PayPal, and credit card are the dominant methods.
  • Netherlands: iDEAL leads strongly, followed by Klarna and credit card.
  • China: Alipay, WeChat Pay, and UnionPay are the expected options; cards are secondary.
  • Global: Digital wallets are growing across all markets and require locale-specific display strings and flow copy.

VAT display rules, EU returns policy requirements, and customs disclosure copy each require human translators who know the target market's consumer law — not MTPE output reviewed by a generalist. A localized returns policy that misrepresents the statutory returns window creates legal exposure, not just a translation error.

How is multilingual SEO handled as a localization component?

Multilingual SEO localization covers target-market keyword research, localized meta titles and descriptions, localized heading and body copy, and correct hreflang configuration using ISO 639-1 language and ISO 3166-1 country pairs. The hreflang attribute uses pairs such as es-MX for Mexican Spanish or de-DE for German as spoken in Germany — a single es or de tag does not give search engines enough signal to serve the right locale. Keyword research is a human task: search volume and user intent differ materially between, say, es-ES and es-MX, and a word-for-word translation of English meta copy rarely matches what local users actually search. SEO localization is scoped separately from the catalog word count and is priced per locale rather than per word.

What are the best practices to get started on an e-commerce localization project?

Best practices to start an e-commerce localization project are to lock a per-market glossary and style guide, split the work into three production lanes, assign each lane's AI-vs-human mix, size the scope from the file-format export, and configure LQA against an ISO 17100-aligned scorecard before the first segment ships. Global online retail is on a trajectory that makes entering new language markets a structural growth decision rather than an optional experiment — and the majority of consumers across markets will not purchase from a storefront presented only in English. Starting with the right production architecture prevents the rework that compounds when glossaries, lane splits, and QA gates are retrofitted after launch. Steps in order:

  1. Pre-translation research: Map price sensitivity, cultural references, color symbolism, and competitive framing per target market before any string is exported.
  2. Lock the per-market glossary: Cover product category terms, ingredient names, claim verbs, and brand-protected terms. No translation begins without it.
  3. Lock the style guide: Document formality register (for example, Sie vs du in German), measurement units, date and number formats, and punctuation conventions per locale.
  4. Export and scope source strings: Pull JSON, XML, YAML,.strings, or ARB exports; count string values only — keys and structural markup are excluded from the word count.
  5. Split scope across three production lanes: Assign storefront UI, product catalog, and transactional/support content to separate queues with separate reviewer pools.
  6. Set the LQA scorecard: Configure defect categories and severity weights against ISO 17100 before the first lane goes live — retrofitting the scorecard after delivery creates disputes.
  7. Pilot one locale end-to-end: Run the full lane split, QA gates, and CMS push on one market before scaling to the full language list.

How should an agency split e-commerce localization into production lanes?

A clean split runs three decoupled lanes — storefront UI strings, product catalog, and transactional/support content — each with its own cadence, reviewer pool, and QA gate, so a theme release never blocks a catalog push and a regulatory update to the returns policy never delays a product launch. Coupling the lanes into a single workflow is the most common structural mistake agencies make on e-commerce programs: it creates bottlenecks, inflates cost-per-word by blending high-risk and low-risk content, and makes TM maintenance harder as the program scales.

LaneSurfacesAI-vs-human mixCadenceQA gate
Storefront UITheme strings, nav, buttons, filters, error statesAI + light post-editingWeekly or per theme releaseCharacter-expansion + placeholder integrity
Product catalogTitles, descriptions, variants, specs, category pagesHuman on claims; MTPE on SKU attributesQuarterly, with weekly SKU addsLQA sample vs glossary
Transactional / supportCheckout, legal, emails, help center, returns portalHuman review on all legal copyRegulatory trigger + release trainFull LQA against ISO 17100 scorecard

When is AI translation good enough and when does the lane require human oversight?

AI translation with light post-editing is appropriate on repetitive UI strings and SKU-level attributes, but human translators are required on claims-bearing product copy, regulated categories, and brand-voice marketing — because the risk on those surfaces is regulatory or reputational, not merely linguistic. A mislabeled ingredient claim or a mistranslated statutory returns period creates legal exposure that a post-editing workflow does not catch reliably at scale. The decision rule, applied per surface:

flowchart TD
 A[String to translate] --> B{Carries a product claim?}
 B -- Yes --> H[Human translator required]
 B -- No --> C{Regulated category?}
 C -- Yes --> H
 C -- No --> D{Brand voice marketing?}
 D -- Yes --> T[Transcreation lane]
 D -- No --> E{Repetitive UI or SKU attribute?}
 E -- Yes --> M[AI + light post-editing]
 E -- No --> R[Human review on MTPE output]

Transcreation on brand and campaign copy is priced hourly, per concept, or per variant — it does not fit the per-word model because the output is not a translation of the source but a market-native rewrite that shares little surface text with the original.

How does a D2C skincare or beauty brand split its workflow?

A D2C skincare brand entering its first non-English market runs AI post-editing on storefront UI and shipping copy, routes product descriptions and ingredient claims through a human translator with regulatory expertise, and locks a per-market glossary covering ingredient names and claim verbs before the first export. This split keeps cost down on the high-volume, low-risk surfaces while protecting the brand on the surfaces where a translation error creates a compliance problem. A worked split for a typical skincare launch:

  • AI + MTPE: Navigation labels, filter strings, cart UI, size selectors, order confirmation templates, shipping notification templates, and tracking update copy.
  • Human translation: Product description body copy, benefit claims, ingredient call-outs, directions for use, contraindication statements, and any copy referencing dermatological or clinical outcomes.
  • Human with legal review: Returns policy, statutory consumer rights notice, GDPR consent copy, and any market-specific labeling required by cosmetics regulation.
  • Transcreation: Hero banner headlines, campaign taglines, and brand story copy — priced per concept, not per word.

Pricing

How is e-commerce localization priced in the US?

In the US, e-commerce localization is priced in four stacked line items: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100, and transcreation off the per-word grid for campaign copy.

Line itemUS rateBasis
Translation$0.10–$0.25 / source wordPer lane, weighted by TM leverage
Review$0.04–$0.08 / source wordSecond-pass bilingual revision
LQA$40–$90 / 1,000 wordsMQM-style scorecard, ISO 17100-aligned
TranscreationHourly / per concept / per variantOff per-word grid
Engineering (file prep)HourlyExport, segmentation, placeholder protection

What does a mid-size multi-locale e-commerce program cost end-to-end?

A mid-size e-commerce localization program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words costs $25,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and whether certified lanes are in scope. The spread reflects:

  • TM leverage: 20–60% match rate on a repeat catalog push cuts the translation line item proportionally.
  • Turnaround: standard vs expedited rates diverge 25–40% on tight release windows.
  • Scope mix: three lanes at different human-vs-AI ratios land in different corners of the band.
  • Regulated categories: skincare, supplements, and medical devices require human translators with category expertise and command the top of the per-word range.

How does the LQA gate work on an e-commerce lane?

The LQA gate samples the translated output at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 — scoring accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style — and runs as a blocking gate before client delivery. The scorecard categorizes defects by severity (minor, major, critical) and type, producing a pass/fail against a quality threshold agreed in the SOW. ISO 17100:2015 is the framework the defect categorization aligns to.

Computer-Assisted Translation Tools: The Working Translator's Field Guide

How we run e-commerce localization lanes

Our production model treats e-commerce localization as three decoupled lanes — storefront UI, product catalog, and transactional/support content — because each surface carries a different risk profile, a different reviewer requirement, and a different QA gate. Collapsing them into a single workflow is how agencies introduce bottlenecks and hide cost drivers behind a blended rate. We don't do that.

On the storefront UI lane, we draft first-pass output from the i18n export the agency or client supplies, with all placeholders, ICU plurals, and HTML inline tags preserved exactly as they appear in the source file. The agency's reviewer then runs the human pass against the per-market glossary, checking character expansion against the tightest layout slot and verifying placeholder integrity before the draft advances. The LQA gate — scored against the ISO 17100-aligned MQM scorecard — runs as a sample on the completed lane before client delivery, not as a final afterthought.

On the product catalog lane, we separate SKU-level attributes from claims-bearing descriptive copy at the export stage. Attributes such as color names, material codes, and size labels are appropriate for AI drafting with post-editing review. Product descriptions that carry benefit language, outcome statements, or comparative claims are flagged and routed to human translators with category expertise. This distinction matters because the majority of consumers will not purchase from a storefront they don't trust — and trust erodes quickly when localized product copy reads as machine output or, worse, misstates a claim in the target market.

We do not translate claims-bearing lanes without a human sign-off. Skincare benefit claims, supplement health statements, medical-device instructions, and food-labeling copy do not move from draft to delivery without a named translator who has category experience taking responsibility for the output. We label drafts on those surfaces clearly as drafts and do not represent them as ready for publication. The regulatory risk belongs to the client; the translator who signs off has to be a person, not a process.

We do not concatenate strings a developer has intentionally split. A storefront that exports {quantity} items in your cart as a single unit stays a single unit. Translating the fragments independently breaks plural logic in a significant share of target locales — particularly those with dual, paucal, or other non-binary plural forms — and produces errors that are invisible in the TM but visible to every user who adds more than one item to their cart.

We do not quote a single blended per-word rate across all three lanes. UI, catalog, and transactional surfaces carry different QA weight, different reviewer requirements, and different risk exposure. Pricing them as one number hides which lane is actually driving cost on a given program and makes it impossible for the client to make informed decisions about where to invest in higher-quality review versus where MTPE is genuinely sufficient.

The questions below cover the differences translators and agency PMs most often raise about e-commerce localization — translation versus localization, AI capability, and a concrete worked example.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between translation and localization?

Translation converts text from one language to another, while localization adapts the entire user experience — including tone, currency, units, imagery, and cultural references — to feel native to a target market. For e-commerce specifically, localization goes beyond product descriptions: it covers checkout flows, payment method names, date and address formats, legal disclaimers, and even color choices that carry different connotations across cultures. A certified translation guarantees linguistic accuracy for regulatory or legal content; localization ensures the surrounding commercial context resonates. Translators and agencies handle both layers on production projects.

Can AI do localization?

AI can produce strong first drafts for localization, but human review remains essential for certified, commercially sensitive, or culturally nuanced content. Modern neural machine translation (NMT) engines handle high-volume, repetitive strings — UI labels, metadata, structured data files — with acceptable quality that a post-editor can refine efficiently. However, AI consistently struggles with idioms, brand voice, legal phrasing that must meet certification standards, and market-specific cultural references. The professional standard for certified e-commerce content is AI-assisted drafting plus human post-editing and sign-off, not fully automated output.

What's the best way to split localization workflows for a D2C store?

The most efficient approach is to tier content by risk and visibility, then assign different workflows to each tier. High-stakes content — legal notices, certified product claims, regulated labeling — requires full human translation and review. Core marketing copy (product descriptions, landing pages, email campaigns) benefits most from AI-drafted first drafts with professional post-editing. Low-risk, high-volume strings (UI labels, error messages, structured files like JSON or YAML) can move through a lighter post-edit cycle. Agencies define these tiers in a style guide and project brief before handoff, which keeps turnaround times and per-word costs predictable across large SKU catalogs.

Can I use AI for storefront localization but something different for other content?

Yes — using different production methods for different content types is standard practice in professional localization workflows. Storefront strings (navigation labels, button text, structured locale files) are ideal candidates for AI-assisted translation because they are short, repetitive, and low-risk. Product marketing copy, customer reviews, and UGC benefit from AI drafting with human post-editing for tone and brand consistency. Certified content — regulated claims, warranties, terms of service — should always follow a full human translation and certification workflow regardless of what is used elsewhere. Mixing methods by content type is not a compromise; it is how agencies control cost without sacrificing quality where it matters.

How do I estimate translation costs for JSON, XML, YAML, Strings, and ARB files?

Cost for structured locale files is calculated on translatable string word count after filtering out keys, markup, and non-translatable placeholders. Professional CAT tools and TMS platforms parse JSON, XML, YAML,.strings, and ARB files to extract only the text segments, then apply a per-word rate — ranging from $0.08 to $0.25 per word for post-edited AI output up to $0.15–$0.35+ for fully human translation, depending on language pair and specialization. Translation memory (TM) matches reduce costs further: 100% matches are often billed at 0–30% of the full rate, and fuzzy matches at 30–70%. Agencies provide a word-count report and TM leverage estimate before quoting.

Should I use AI translation for skincare/beauty product copy or is human review necessary?

Human review is necessary for skincare and beauty product copy, even when AI produces the first draft. Beauty copy relies heavily on sensory language, brand voice, and culturally loaded terms (e.g., words for 'whitening' or 'natural' carry very different implications across markets) that AI handles inconsistently. Regulatory claims — ingredient disclosures, SPF ratings, dermatologist-tested statements — may require certified translation in markets like the EU, South Korea, or Brazil to meet labeling law. The professional workflow is AI-assisted drafting to reduce cost and turnaround time, followed by a human post-editor with subject-matter familiarity and a final review for regulatory compliance before publication.

How do I localize a site for non-English markets without blowing the budget?

The most effective budget control strategy is to prioritize pages by revenue impact and use tiered production methods matched to each content type. Start with AI-assisted translation for high-volume, lower-risk content (category pages, structured files, FAQs) and reserve full human translation for checkout flows, legal pages, and top-converting product pages. Build and maintain a translation memory from day one — TM leverage reduces per-word costs by 20–50% on repeat content across market expansions. Glossary management and a clear style guide also reduce revision cycles, which is often where projects overspend. Agencies working with SaaS-generated first drafts can further compress per-word costs while keeping certified quality on the content that requires it.

  • What goes wrong with expo-localization in production — and what should the agency flag?
  • What does an Expo localization project cost at translator rates?
  • What should translators and agencies ask the Expo dev team before quoting?
  • Frequently asked questions

Expo projects reach a translator's desk as JSON resource bundles, not as native source — and the module deciding which bundle loads at runtime is expo-localization. This guide frames the module from the production desk inside the broader Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide workflow, so agencies can quote, scope, and QA Expo handoffs without surprises.

What is expo-localization and what does it actually do?

expo-localization is an Expo SDK module that exposes the device's locale, region, calendar, timezone, measurement system, and currency to a React Native app, so a paired i18n library — i18n-js, i18next, or Intlayer — can pick the right translated strings. It detects; it does not translate.

The module's scope matters for scoping a quote. These are the surfaces it covers and the surfaces it leaves to someone else:

SurfaceHandled by expo-localizationHandled elsewhere
Device locale detectionYes — languageTag, regionCode—
Calendar, timezone, first day of weekYes—
Measurement system, currency codeYes — reported onlyIntl.NumberFormat for rendering
UI string translationNoi18n-js, i18next, next-intl, Intlayer
App name on home screenNoapp.json locales map
App Store / Play Store listingsNoStore Connect, Play Console
User-chosen language overrideNoAsyncStorage or SecureStore

What does expo-localization return at runtime?

Localization.getLocales() returns an array of locale objects with languageTag (for example, en-US), regionCode, textDirection, measurementSystem, and currencyCode. Localization.getCalendars() returns calendar, timezone, and first-day-of-week values. These feed the i18n library's locale selector.

  • languageTag — the BCP-47 string the i18n library keys on.
  • regionCode — the two-letter country code, useful for en-US vs. en-GB splits.
  • textDirection — "ltr" or "rtl", reported only; mirroring is applied via I18nManager.
  • measurementSystem — "metric", "us", or "uk".
  • currencyCode — ISO 4217 string, consumed by Intl.NumberFormat.

What does expo-localization NOT do?

expo-localization does not translate strings, does not localize the app name, does not translate store listings, and does not persist a user-chosen language override. Each is a separate step the translator or developer must handle.

How is expo-localization installed and configured in an Expo project?

expo-localization is installed with npx expo install expo-localization, added to the plugins array in app.json, and imported as import * as Localization from 'expo-localization'. The config plugin wires native iOS and Android locale permissions at prebuild time, so translators receive a build that resolves device locale correctly.

  1. Run npx expo install expo-localization.
  2. Add "expo-localization" to the plugins array in app.json.
  3. Add a sibling locales map pointing each supported locale to a JSON file.
  4. Import the module: import * as Localization from 'expo-localization'.
  5. Run npx expo prebuild to generate native projects with locale assets in place.

What goes in app.json for expo-localization?

The plugins array takes "expo-localization" as a bare string entry. The locales map, a sibling of ios and android, points each supported locale to a JSON file containing CFBundleDisplayName, usage descriptions, and Android app_name overrides.

Which Expo SDK versions matter for translators?

Expo SDK 49+ ships the config-plugin pattern that most translator-facing documentation predates. Projects on older SDKs typically arrive with hard-coded app names and missing locale descriptions, which is why agencies keep seeing untranslated home-screen labels on test builds. SDK 33's upgrade also removed the legacy Localization.locale property, breaking code that was never migrated.

How does expo-localization fit into the multi-language translation stack?

expo-localization sits at the detection layer: it reports the user's locale. A string catalog library — i18n-js, i18next, next-intl, or Intlayer — sits at the rendering layer and looks up the matching key from a JSON resource file. Translators work exclusively on the JSON files, never on expo-localization itself.

LibraryPairing patternTranslator-side artifact
i18n-jsTranslations object keyed by locale, assigned via i18n.localeOne JSON per locale, flat or shallow-nested
react-i18nextNamespaced JSON files, {{name}} interpolation, Trans componentNamespaced JSON per locale
next-intlShared with Next.js web code, ICU messagesJSON per locale, ICU syntax
IntlayerTyped per-component content with Metro bundlingPer-component content files

expo-localization + i18n-js: the common pairing

Many Expo projects pair expo-localization with i18n-js: expo-localization provides the languageTag, i18n-js loads a translations object keyed by locale, and i18n.locale = Localization.getLocales()[0].languageTag wires them together. The translator receives one JSON file per locale.

expo-localization + react-i18next or next-intl

Projects reusing a React web codebase typically swap i18n-js for react-i18next or next-intl, using JSON namespaces, double-curly interpolation {{name}}, and the Trans component for inline markup. The translator-side difference is segment granularity, not the detection layer. For the full engineering view, see React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline, with cross-framework patterns covered in How to Add i18n to an Astro Site.

How does the agency choose a locale override at runtime?

A user-chosen locale override — the in-app language switcher — is stored in AsyncStorage or SecureStore, read at app launch, and used to seed the i18n library's locale before falling back to Localization.getLocales(). expo-localization has no built-in persistence.

What does the translator actually receive from an Expo project?

A translator working on an Expo app receives a resource bundle — JSON files, one per locale, keyed by string ID — plus a translation memory, a term base, a style guide, and ideally a pseudo-localized staging build. The expo-localization module itself is invisible to the translator; it only shapes which locale the test build loads at runtime. The module's job is device locale detection — surfacing values like languageTag, regionCode, textDirection, measurementSystem, currencyCode, calendar, and timezone — and none of those values are translatable strings. What becomes a translator artifact is the JSON catalog that a pairing library such as i18n-js or react-i18next loads based on the languageTag expo-localization reports.

expo-localization produces (runtime)Translator receives (artifact)
languageTag (en-US, ja-JP)Filename or folder key: en-US.json, ja-JP.json
regionCode (US, JP)Variant notes in style guide
calendar, timezoneNo artifact — rendered by Intl APIs
textDirection (rtl)RTL QA notes, mirrored screenshots
measurementSystem, currencyCodeFormat notes, not strings
— (out of module scope)JSON strings for app_name and CFBundleDisplayName via app.json locales

One coverage gap that frequently surprises agencies is that expo-localization does not localize the app name — neither CFBundleDisplayName on iOS nor app_name on Android — and it does not touch App Store or Play Store listing copy. Those strings live in a separate locales map inside app.json, sibling to the ios and android keys, where each locale maps to a JSON file holding display names and usage descriptions. Translators must confirm this scope is explicitly included or excluded in the handoff package before work begins.

When a project uses a typed, per-component content approach with Metro bundling, the artifacts may be structured differently from a flat JSON catalog — but the translator-facing deliverable is still a set of locale-keyed content files that must be returned in the same structure. Regardless of the underlying library, co-locating content with components is a pattern that facilitates maintenance in large-scale applications, which means translators may receive many smaller files rather than one monolithic catalog. Agencies should confirm file count and directory structure during scope review.

What does a clean i18n handoff for Expo look like?

A clean Expo i18n handoff satisfies 5 conditions, all of which are verifiable before translation begins:

  1. Strings externalized — no literals in source files, all copy in JSON catalogs.
  2. ICU plural and gender rules declared — for every count and gendered noun, so that translators receive the correct message-format variants rather than a flat string.
  3. Localization.getLocales() wired — as the default locale, with a persisted override for testing.
  4. RTL mirroring verified — I18nManager.forceRTL and I18nManager.allowRTL must be wired for Arabic and Hebrew; expo-localization reports textDirection but does not apply the mirroring itself, so this is an engineering responsibility that must be confirmed complete before RTL translation QA begins.
  5. No baked copy in assets — PNGs, SVGs, and canvas elements carry no hard-coded text.

ICU MessageFormat plural and gender rules are part of this checklist because every count-bearing string — item counts, notification badges, quantity pickers — requires a separate plural form per language, and every gendered noun requires a gender variant. Receiving a catalog without these rules forces translators to raise queries that stall delivery.

Where does pseudo-localization fit in the Expo workflow?

Pseudo-localization fits between extraction and translation as a dev-side stress test on the Expo build. It inflates strings by 30–50% and swaps ASCII characters to expose hard-coded text and truncated UI before any human translation budget is spent. A clean upstream pseudo-localization pass delivers resource files with the full user-visible string set, UI containers already sized for 30–50% expansion, and file encoding verified as UTF-8. Agencies that receive a build that has not passed a pseudo-localization gate carry the risk of discovering layout regressions mid-translation — a cost that should be reflected in the quote or contractually placed back on the development team. CJK-specific QA, including Chinese rendering checks, belongs in the same gate as pseudo-localization sign-off.

How is the app name localized in Expo, and why do translators keep seeing it skipped?

The app name is localized in Expo through the locales map in app.json, not through expo-localization. Each supported locale points to a JSON file with CFBundleDisplayName for iOS and app_name for Android. expo-localization does not touch this surface, which is why in-app text translates correctly while the home-screen icon stays in English.

What does the app.json locales entry look like?

The locales entry is a sibling of ios and android:

"locales": { "ja": "./languages/japanese.json", "fr": "./languages/french.json" }

Each referenced JSON file contains native keys the launcher and store listing display:

  • CFBundleDisplayName — iOS home-screen label.
  • NSCameraUsageDescription — iOS permission prompt.
  • NSLocationWhenInUseUsageDescription — iOS permission prompt.
  • app_name — Android launcher label written into strings.xml at prebuild.

Why are most app-name localization tutorials outdated?

Most tutorials predate Expo SDK 49's config-plugin lifecycle and reference pre-prebuild native file edits that no longer apply to managed workflow projects. Translators receiving builds from those docs see the JSON picked up on iOS but silently dropped on Android — the broken handoff pattern agencies now flag on intake.

What goes wrong with expo-localization in production — and what should the agency flag?

Three recurring failures hit production Expo localization: the SDK 33-era Localization.locale is undefined crash after upgrades, a non-exhaustive switch over languageTag that throws for untested locales, and iOS Simulator returning a stale locale after a Settings → General → Language & Region change. Each has a documented fix.

Why is Localization.locale undefined after an SDK upgrade?

Localization.locale was removed from the module API in later Expo SDKs in favor of Localization.getLocales()[0].languageTag. Codebases carried from SDK 33–40 crash with undefined is not an object until the call site is migrated. Translators see this as a test build that never loads any locale.

What triggers the 'switch must be exhaustive' TypeScript error?

TypeScript treats languageTag as a string, so a switch (languageTag) statement with locale cases hits the exhaustiveness check and throws at compile time. The fix is a default branch that falls back to the source language, which also prevents runtime crashes for unshipped locales.

How do you refresh the simulator and emulator after a locale change?

  • iOS Simulator — Settings → General → Language & Region; reload the app to refresh the session before expo-localization picks up the new locale.
  • Android emulator — Settings → System → Languages; pseudo-locales en-XA and ar-XB appear in Developer Options when pseudoLocalesEnabled true is set in build.gradle.

Pricing

What does an Expo localization project cost at translator rates?

An Expo app with 10,000 source strings budgets at

What should translators and agencies ask the Expo dev team before quoting?

Before quoting an Expo project, ask 6 questions whose answers decide whether the handoff is translator-ready or a scope trap. Each question maps to a concrete risk: a wrong or missing answer indicates rework, delayed delivery, or a budget overrun that will fall on the agency unless it is contractually pre-empted.

  1. Which Expo SDK version is in production — 49+ or legacy? SDK 49 introduced the config-plugin prebuild pattern, and most translator-facing setup tutorials predate it. A project running a legacy SDK version may have locale detection wired differently, which affects how the translation catalog is loaded and which file-naming conventions apply. Known regressions have appeared in specific SDK patch releases, and confirming the team is on a stable, up-to-date patch is a prerequisite for reliable locale detection in test builds.
  2. Which i18n library is in use — i18n-js, react-i18next, or another? The library determines catalog format, interpolation syntax, and whether namespace-split JSON files or a single flat file are expected. React-i18next uses {{name}} interpolation and JSON namespaces; i18n-js uses a translations object keyed by locale. Translators must receive format documentation alongside the files.
  3. Is the app.json locales map populated for every target locale? The locales map is the mechanism for localizing the app name (CFBundleDisplayName on iOS and app_name on Android) and usage description strings. Expo-localization does not handle this scope — if the map is absent or incomplete, those strings are untranslated regardless of how thorough the in-app catalog is.
  4. Has pseudo-localization run, and are the expansion limits documented? A pseudo-localization pass inflates strings 30–50% to expose hard-coded text and UI truncation before human translation begins. If it has not run, the agency carries the risk of layout regressions discovered mid-project.
  5. Which locales are in scope, and are RTL locales (ar, he) included? Arabic and Hebrew require I18nManager.forceRTL and I18nManager.allowRTL to be wired on the engineering side — expo-localization reports textDirection but does not apply mirroring. RTL LQA requires a functional mirrored build, not just a string file, so confirming engineering readiness before translation begins avoids a blocked review phase.
  6. Are App Store and Play Store listings in or out of scope? Store listing copy is managed outside expo-localization — through the app.json locales map and external store consoles — and has its own word count, review cycle, and character-limit constraints. It must be explicitly included or excluded in the statement of work.

A development team that can answer all six questions with documented evidence is ready for handoff. A team that cannot answer questions 1, 3, or 4 is presenting a project that will generate translator queries, revision rounds, and timeline risk that the quote does not cover.

Expo projects most often launch with a 5-locale set: English, Spanish, French, German, and Japanese. Right-to-left locales (Arabic, Hebrew) and CJK locales (Chinese, Korean) add QA passes but no module-level change — expo-localization reports them identically.

Frequently asked questions

What does expo-localization actually cover vs. what you still have to handle manually?

expo-localization handles device-level locale detection — reading the user's preferred language, region, currency symbol, decimal separator, and text direction — but it does not translate any strings for you. You still have to supply every translated string yourself, wire up a library like i18n-js or i18next to serve them, handle pluralization rules, format dates and numbers per locale, and manage fallback chains when a language is unsupported. For translators and agencies, this means the actual translation files (typically JSON or PO) remain a fully manual deliverable that no Expo package replaces.

How do I add internationalization to an Expo app using expo-localization and i18n-js?

You install expo-localization to read the device locale, then configure i18n-js to load the correct translation file for that locale. The typical setup is: install both packages, create one JSON translation file per language (e.g., en.json, fr.json, de.json), initialise i18n-js with those files and set its locale from Locale.getLocales()[0].languageTag. From a translation-production standpoint, each JSON file is the deliverable — the strings inside are what translators author, review, and certify before the file ships.

How do I localize the app name (not just in-app text) using expo-localization?

Localizing the app name shown on the device home screen requires platform-specific configuration that expo-localization does not touch. On iOS you add localized InfoPlist.strings files (CFBundleDisplayName per language) inside the native project; on Android you add strings.xml files under res/values-{locale}/ folders. In a managed Expo workflow this means using the expo-build-properties plugin or ejecting to a bare workflow. These localized app-name strings are short but still count as translated content — agencies should include them in scope alongside UI strings.

what is expo localization

expo-localization is an Expo SDK module that exposes the device's locale settings — language tag, region, currency code, decimal/grouping separators, and text direction — to a React Native app at runtime. It does not provide translations or a translation management system; it is purely a locale-detection utility. Developers use it as the input signal for an i18n library (i18n-js, i18next, LinguiJS, etc.) that then selects and renders the correct pre-translated strings. For translation teams, expo-localization defines which locales the app must support, directly driving the list of target languages that need certified translations.

what is product localization

Product localization is the process of adapting a software product — its text, UI layout, date/number formats, images, and cultural conventions — so it functions naturally for users in a specific locale. It goes beyond simple translation: a fully localized product handles right-to-left text, local currency and measurement systems, locale-appropriate imagery, and legal or regulatory copy. For translators and agencies, product localization means delivering not just translated strings but also locale-specific formatting rules, pluralization, and sometimes certified translations of legal notices or terms of service embedded in the product.

How do I implement localization in React Native?

The standard approach is to use expo-localization (or the community react-native-localize package) to detect the device locale, then pair it with an i18n library such as i18next, i18n-js, or LinguiJS to serve the right translated strings. Translation content is stored in resource files — typically JSON or PO — one file per target language, which is the artifact translators produce. Additional steps include handling RTL layout with React Native's I18nManager, formatting dates with a library like date-fns or Intl, and setting up a fallback locale for unsupported languages.
