pages.title: Internationalization Strategies: How Translation Agencies Choose and Operationalize Them
pages.h1: Internationalization Strategies: How Translation Agencies Choose and Operationalize Them
pages.meta_description: Internationalization strategies are the four strategic postures — international, multidomestic, global, transnational — translation agencies pick before
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What are internationalization strategies and why do they matter to a translation agency?
  • What are the four main internationalization strategies?
  • What are the common market entry modes an agency pairs with each strategy?
  • What frameworks and steps structure an internationalization strategy decision?
  • How does each internationalization strategy translate into agency production shape and pricing?
  • What are the common mistakes agencies make when picking an internationalization strategy?
  • How does an agency connect its internationalization strategy to adjacent delivery lanes?
  • Frequently asked questions

Scaling a translation agency across national markets starts with a strategic choice, not a sales tactic. The internationalization strategy an agency picks upstream decides its workflow shape, pricing lanes, quality thresholds, and the i18n handoff it accepts from clients. This page sits above our Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide and our Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs as the strategic decision that feeds both lanes.

What are internationalization strategies and why do they matter to a translation agency?

Internationalization strategies are the four strategic postures — international, multidomestic, global, and transnational — a firm adopts to compete across national markets, balancing global integration against local responsiveness. For a translation agency, the choice dictates production workflow, pricing lanes, and the i18n handoff shape it accepts from clients.

Why the posture matters in operational terms:

  • Workflow shape — one TMS and one QA rubric worldwide, or decentralized per-locale production units.
  • Pricing lanes — flat global rates, or locale-tiered rates reflecting certification cost.
  • Entry mode fit — exports and licensing versus joint ventures and wholly-owned subsidiaries.
  • i18n handoff — what the client ships (externalized strings, ICU plurals) before the agency can quote.
  • Quality threshold — one rubric across all locales, or per-locale rubrics tuned to jurisdictional requirements.

How does internationalization strategy differ from internationalization and localization?

Strategy is the posture; internationalization (i18n) is the engineering readiness that makes the posture executable; localization (L10n) is the per-locale adaptation of each deliverable. Our Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs defines i18n as designing a product or workflow to support multiple locales without structural redesign, and L10n as adapting output for a specific market.

Put another way: strategy answers "how do we compete across borders"; i18n answers "is the source build ready to be localized"; L10n answers "does the Spanish deliverable read right to a Mexican notary". Agencies that conflate the three ship mismatched quotes.

What are the four main internationalization strategies?

The four main internationalization strategies are international (export home-country products with minimal change), multidomestic (customize per country, decentralize decisions), global (standardize worldwide for scale), and transnational (combine global integration with local responsiveness). Each posture carries a distinct trade-off on the integration-responsiveness grid.

StrategyIntegrationResponsivenessCore move
InternationalLowLowExport home offerings with minimal change
MultidomesticLowHighCustomize per country, decentralize decisions
GlobalHighLowStandardize worldwide for scale
TransnationalHighHighStandard backbone, locale-specific deliverables

What does an international strategy look like in practice?

An international strategy exports core products and services from the home market with minimal adaptation, relying on home-country competencies. For a US-based translation agency, this means serving outbound-US clients with a single English-source production line and selling into foreign buyers who accept the agency's native workflow.

Entry modes stay light. Exporting and licensing dominate because the agency reuses one TMS, one translator pool, and one certificate-of-accuracy template. Margin stays intact; addressable market narrows to buyers who accept US-style delivery.

What does a multidomestic strategy look like in practice?

A multidomestic strategy customizes offerings for each national market and decentralizes decision-making to local units. Certified translation production naturally skews multidomestic because jurisdictions impose non-negotiable per-country certification formats — a USCIS certificate of accuracy differs materially from a German sworn translator stamp or a French assermenté seal.

Operational signals of a multidomestic posture:

  • Separate price books per locale, often tiered by regulatory load.
  • Locale-owned QA rubrics instead of a single global checklist.
  • In-market reviewers with jurisdiction-specific credentials.
  • Country-specific intake forms that capture certification requirements upfront.

Markets with deep per-locale rules reinforce this posture. Our Chinese Localization: What Makes It Harder Than Most Projects is one example of a locale that resists flattening into a single global rubric.

What does a global strategy look like in practice?

A global strategy standardizes products, processes, and pricing worldwide to extract economies of scale. An agency pursuing global strategy ships one TMS, one TM, one QA rubric, and one price book across every locale — maximizing margin but accepting weaker fit for jurisdictionally bound deliverables.

The posture pays off in unregulated verticals: marketing content, software UI strings, product descriptions. It breaks down the moment a deliverable carries a legal signature or official seal.

What is a transnational strategy and when do agencies pick it?

A transnational strategy pursues global efficiency and local responsiveness simultaneously, standardizing the production backbone while allowing locale-specific rules to govern each deliverable. This matches the glocalization pattern: standardize intake, first-draft generation, and translator review, while locale rules govern certification format, stamps, and credentials.

Agencies pick transnational when they run both unregulated content (web, marketing) and regulated content (immigration, legal, medical) through the same production spine. The backbone scales; the deliverables stay compliant.

How do the four strategies compare on integration, responsiveness, cost, and agency fit?

The four strategies trade off along two axes — pressure for global integration and pressure for local responsiveness — producing distinct cost structures and agency fits. The table below summarizes each posture's standardization level, decision locus, pricing shape, and ideal translation-agency use case.

StrategyStandardizationDecision locusPricing shapeAgency fit
InternationalHome-country processHeadquartersOne price book, home currencyOutbound-US agencies, English-source lanes
MultidomesticLow — per localeLocal unitsTiered per market, certification add-onsCertified translation, sworn translators, court-filing lanes
GlobalHigh — one worldwideHeadquartersFlat per-word with TM leverageMarketing, UI strings, SaaS copy without legal weight
TransnationalBackbone standard, deliverables localSharedStandard spine + locale premiumsMixed regulated/unregulated portfolios

What are the common market entry modes an agency pairs with each strategy?

The 5 common market entry modes are exporting, licensing, franchising, joint venture, and wholly-owned subsidiary — ordered by rising commitment, risk, and control. Entry mode is the operational tactic; it only works when it inherits the correct internationalization strategy upstream.

  • Exporting — serve foreign buyers from the home production base; lowest commitment.
  • Licensing — license the agency's methodology or brand to a local operator.
  • Franchising — package the full production system for a local franchisee.
  • Joint venture — share equity and control with a local partner for market knowledge.
  • Wholly-owned subsidiary — stand up a local legal entity under full agency control.

Which entry mode fits which strategy?

Export and licensing pair with international strategy because they minimize local investment; joint ventures suit multidomestic firms that need local market knowledge; wholly-owned subsidiaries fit global and transnational players that must control process and quality end-to-end.

StrategyDefault entry modeWhy
InternationalExporting, licensingMinimal local investment; home process stays intact
MultidomesticJoint venture, franchisingLocal partner supplies jurisdiction expertise
GlobalWholly-owned subsidiaryHeadquarters controls the one worldwide process
TransnationalWholly-owned subsidiary + JV mixStandard spine centrally owned; local nodes partner-owned

Why does picking entry mode before strategy backfire for LSPs?

Agencies that open a foreign subsidiary before fixing their integration-responsiveness posture inherit duplicated TMS stacks, mismatched price books, and incompatible QA rubrics. The fix is a 2-step sequence: lock the strategic posture first, then let it dictate which of the 5 entry modes to execute.

The failure mode is predictable. A subsidiary opens in Berlin to chase German sworn-translation demand. Headquarters assumes a global rubric applies. The Berlin office rewrites the rubric for sworn format. Two years in, the agency runs two incompatible production lines under one brand.

How it works

What frameworks and steps structure an internationalization strategy decision?

1

How does the integration-responsiveness grid classify agency programs?

The I-R grid plots pressure for global integration against pressure for local responsiveness, producing the four strategy quadrants. Certified translation sits in the high-responsiveness band because jurisdictional certification cannot be flattened by scale.

Marketing copy sits in the opposite corner — high integration pressure, low responsiveness pressure. Running both through the same agency forces a transnational posture or two separate lanes.

2

What role does Porter's Diamond play in picking a target market?

Porter's Diamond analyzes 4 country-specific competitive advantage factors — factor conditions, demand conditions, related industries, and firm strategy/rivalry — to score each candidate market before an agency commits capital.

  • Factor conditions — pool of qualified translators and sworn credentials in-market.
  • Demand conditions — volume of regulated filings, immigration flows, cross-border legal activity.
  • Related industries — immigration law firms, universities, courts that generate referral volume.
  • Firm strategy and rivalry — density of local LSPs and their pricing floor.

The Uppsala model complements the Diamond. It describes gradual internationalization through increasing market commitment — start with exports, graduate to a subsidiary once learning compounds.

3

What i18n prerequisites must hold before any strategy executes?

Internationalization is complete when 5 engineering conditions hold in the source build: strings are externalized, ICU plural and gender rules are declared, date/number/currency formats resolve from locale IDs, right-to-left mirroring works end-to-end, and no copy is hard-coded in images or canvas. Without these, every strategy stalls at the first handoff.

  • Externalized strings — no literals in source files.
  • ICU plurals and gender — declared for every count and gendered noun.
  • Locale-driven formats — dates, numbers, currency resolve from locale IDs.
  • RTL mirroring — end-to-end for Arabic, Hebrew, Farsi.
  • No baked copy — no text inside images, SVG, or canvas elements.

Depth on these checks lives in i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds. Validation of readiness runs through Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds.

Pricing

How does each internationalization strategy translate into agency production shape and pricing?

Each strategy drives a distinct cost base and quality threshold. The published cost base — translation $0.10–$0.25 per word, review $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA $40–$90 per 1,000 words, PM 10–15%, tooling amortized per project — reshapes margins depending on which posture the agency adopts.

StrategyProduction shapePrice positionMargin driver
InternationalSingle home lineHome-market ratesNo locale overhead
MultidomesticParallel per-locale cellsTop of band + certification premiumPrice captures compliance cost
GlobalOne worldwide processBottom of bandTM reuse, central PM
TransnationalCentral spine + local nodesMid-band with locale premiumsShared tooling, local rubrics

What does a 5-language, 50,000-word program cost under each strategy?

A mid-size multi-locale program covering 5 languages and 50,000 words costs $25,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and certification requirements. A global strategy pulls that figure toward the low end through TM reuse; a multidomestic strategy sits at the high end because each locale re-runs its own LQA cycle.

StrategyLikely totalWhat drives the figure
International$35,000–$55,000Home-market pricing, no per-locale LQA cycles
Multidomestic$55,000–$75,000Per-locale review and certification add-ons
Global$25,000–$40,000Deep TM leverage, one QA pass
Transnational$40,000–$65,000Shared tooling + locale-tuned LQA

What quality threshold does each strategy enforce?

Quality is scored per 1,000 words against a weighted MQM-style rubric at release, with a release threshold under 2 errors per 1,000 words. A transnational strategy enforces that threshold per locale with locally-tuned rubrics; a pure global strategy applies one rubric worldwide and accepts weaker locale fit.

The rubric covers accuracy, terminology, compliance, and readability. Multidomestic programs push the compliance weighting higher per locale; global programs weight terminology and readability more evenly across markets.

How does certified translation production constrain strategy choice?

USCIS-ready certified translation runs $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per page, with a certificate of accuracy signed by a competent translator required on every page. Because USCIS does not maintain a register of approved translators and the certificate format is non-negotiable, agencies serving US immigration work default to a multidomestic or transnational posture — a global strategy that strips locale-specific certification will see rejections and RFEs.

The USCIS case is instructive. The certificate format is a per-jurisdiction artifact that no amount of scale economizes away. An agency that tries to flatten it into one worldwide template loses filings. The posture choice is forced by the deliverable.

Get a quote

What are the common mistakes agencies make when picking an internationalization strategy?

The 4 recurring mistakes are: standardizing before locale rules are mapped, treating entry mode as a substitute for strategy, under-investing in i18n engineering readiness, and copying a global strategy from a non-regulated vertical into a certified-translation program. Each mistake shows up as rejected deliverables, RFE loops, or margin erosion within the first 6 months.

  1. Standardize-first — one rubric is written before anyone maps per-locale certification rules.
  2. Entry-mode substitution — a subsidiary opens before the posture is chosen.
  3. i18n under-investment — strings arrive un-externalized; every project renegotiates scope.
  4. Vertical copy-paste — a marketing-content global playbook is applied to immigration work.

How does an agency connect its internationalization strategy to adjacent delivery lanes?

The strategy sits upstream of 4 delivery lanes the agency already runs — application localization, product localization, website localization, and the i18n engineering readiness check. Each lane inherits the signed strategy; none of them is re-explained inside the strategy document itself.

  • Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide — mobile and desktop app lane.
  • Product Localization: How Translators and Agencies Deliver It — SaaS and product lane inheriting the strategy.
  • React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline — framework-specific handoff shape.
  • i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds — engineering readiness check that gates every lane.

Smaller operators and SMEs typically start on international or multidomestic footing and build toward transnational as volume compounds. Emerging markets with heavy regulatory load reward multidomestic posture over global for regulated deliverables. Competitive advantage flows from matching the posture to industry structure and regulatory load, not from the entry mode alone.

Agencies ask the same 5 questions when they first scope an internationalization strategy: what the term means, how it differs from global strategy, whether transnational is always better, how to score candidate markets, and whether a small LSP needs a formal strategy at all. Short answers follow.

Frequently asked questions

What is the meaning of internationalisation?

Internationalisation (i18n) is the process of designing products, services, or organisations so they can operate effectively across multiple countries, languages, and cultures. For translation agencies and certified translation producers, it refers specifically to the strategic and operational decisions that allow a firm to serve clients in new linguistic markets — such as building multilingual workflows, recruiting specialized translators, and adapting quality-assurance processes to meet the certification standards of different jurisdictions (e.g., USCIS requirements in the US or sworn translation standards in the EU).

What are the four main global strategies?

The four main global strategies are international, multidomestic, global, and transnational — often mapped using the Bartlett & Ghoshal framework. For a translation agency, an international strategy means exporting a core service model with little local adaptation; a multidomestic strategy means tailoring services heavily to each market (e.g., country-specific certification formats); a global strategy means standardising processes and pricing worldwide; and a transnational strategy means balancing global efficiency with local responsiveness — for example, using centralised MT-assisted first-draft production while adapting certification outputs per jurisdiction.

What is a transnational strategy?

A transnational strategy seeks to achieve both global efficiency and local responsiveness simultaneously, rather than sacrificing one for the other. For translation agencies, this means standardising high-volume production workflows — such as using AI-generated first drafts for certified translations — while still adapting deliverables to meet country-specific certification requirements, style conventions, and legal formats. It is considered the most complex strategy to operationalise because it requires tight coordination across geographically distributed teams, shared technology platforms, and localised quality control.

What are the main strategies used in internationalization?

The main internationalisation strategies for translation agencies are market penetration (expanding volume in existing language pairs), market development (adding new language pairs or target countries), service diversification (offering certified, sworn, or notarised translation alongside standard translation), and strategic partnerships or acquisitions (buying or partnering with agencies that hold local certifications or vendor networks). Operationally, agencies also choose between in-house capacity building and outsourced freelance networks, and increasingly adopt technology-first approaches — such as AI-assisted first-draft production — to scale certified translation output without proportional headcount growth.

What are the main strategies used in translation?

The main production strategies in translation are direct transfer (literal/formal equivalence), adaptation (cultural and functional equivalence), and hybrid approaches that combine both depending on text type. In certified translation specifically, formal equivalence is dominant because legal and official documents must reflect the source text structure closely to satisfy certification requirements. Agencies increasingly layer these linguistic strategies onto technology workflows — using MT or AI-generated first drafts for speed, followed by human post-editing and certification sign-off — balancing throughput with the accuracy standards required for immigration, legal, and governmental submissions.

What is a global strategy?

A global strategy is an approach in which a firm standardises its products, processes, and pricing across all markets to maximise efficiency and consistency, treating the world as a single, largely uniform market. For a translation agency, a global strategy might mean uniform pricing per word, standardised project management workflows, and centralised quality assurance regardless of which country the end client is in. The trade-off is reduced local adaptation — which can create friction when dealing with jurisdiction-specific certification requirements that vary significantly between, for example, the US, UK, and EU member states.

What is Peter Newmark's theory of translation?

Peter Newmark proposed a spectrum between 'semantic translation' (staying close to the source text's form and meaning) and 'communicative translation' (prioritising the effect on the target-language reader). For certified translation production, Newmark's semantic approach is most relevant: official documents such as birth certificates, diplomas, and legal contracts require high fidelity to the source structure and terminology, because deviations can invalidate certification. Newmark also introduced the concept of 'transference' for proper nouns and culture-specific terms — directly applicable when certified translators must decide whether to translate or retain names, titles, and institution names in legal documents.
pages.excerpt: Internationalization strategies are the four strategic postures — international, multidomestic, global, transnational — translation agencies pick before scaling.

pages.title: JS Localization: How Translators Fit Into a JavaScript i18n Pipeline
pages.h1: JS Localization: How Translators Fit Into a JavaScript i18n Pipeline
pages.meta_description: JS localization is the translator-facing stage of a JavaScript i18n pipeline — JSON catalogs, Intl API formatting, ICU plurals, and library handoff explained.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is JS localization from the translator's side of the desk?
  • How does the native JavaScript Intl API shape what translators receive?
  • Which JS localization libraries will translators actually meet?
  • What do JS localization resource files look like, and which placeholders must translators preserve?
  • What are the key steps to localize a JavaScript app from the translator's side?
  • How does Next.js App Router change JS localization for translators?
  • Manual JSON, AI-generated translations, or hosted platform — which workflow fits the project?
  • How much does JS localization cost, and how do agencies price it?
  • Frequently asked questions

JavaScript localization is where a translator's work meets the engineer's build pipeline — the stage after internationalization, where JSON catalogs, ICU plural blocks, and Intl API arguments must be adapted per locale without breaking the render. This page reframes the JS i18n stack from the translator's desk inside the broader How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying process, and defers the engineering-side split to i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds.

What is JS localization from the translator's side of the desk?

JS localization is the stage of a JavaScript i18n pipeline where translators adapt externalized strings, ICU plurals, and locale-aware formats inside JSON resource bundles so a JS app renders correctly in each locale, after engineers finish internationalization. The translator never edits the component tree. They edit a mirrored catalog per locale ID.

The deliverable is predictable across projects:

  • One JSON resource bundle per target locale, keys and structure identical to the source.
  • ICU plural and select blocks reauthored to the target language's CLDR categories.
  • Intl API arguments preserved byte-for-byte inside the string.
  • Placeholder parity verified against the English source.

How does JS localization differ from JavaScript internationalization (i18n)?

Internationalization is the one-time engineering work that externalizes strings and wires the Intl API. JS localization is the per-locale linguistic work translators repeat for each language, delivered against the JSON or ICU resource bundles i18n produced. The full engineering-side split sits on i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds.

Who owns which step — engineer, translator, PM?

Three owners split the pipeline cleanly:

  • Engineer — externalizes strings, chooses the i18n library, wires middleware, declares ICU categories.
  • Translator — localizes each JSON catalog, preserves placeholders, reauthors plural blocks per target language.
  • Project manager — runs LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, keeps translation memory in sync across releases, and signs off per-locale delivery.

How does the native JavaScript Intl API shape what translators receive?

The native Intl API formats dates, numbers, currency, plurals, and relative time directly from a locale identifier like en-US or ar-EG, so translators receive source strings with Intl calls already in place. Their job is to preserve the API arguments and translate only the surrounding text.

Which Intl objects appear in source files translators open?

Translators meet six Intl objects most often. Each takes a locale identifier plus an options object the linguist must not alter.

Intl objectWhat it formatsTranslator action
Intl.LocaleLocale identifier parsing (language-script-region)Match filename byte-for-byte
Intl.DateTimeFormatDates and times per calendarPreserve options; translate month/day labels only if explicit
Intl.NumberFormatNumbers, currency, units, percentagesPreserve currency/unit codes; never change style key
Intl.PluralRulesCLDR plural categories per languageAuthor the target language's categories (zero/one/two/few/many/other)
Intl.RelativeTimeFormat"3 days ago", "in 2 hours"Translate output phrase; preserve numeric argument
Intl.ListFormatSerial lists ("A, B, and C")Preserve type and style; translate items only

How does Intl.Locale encode language, region, and script?

Intl.Locale encodes a Unicode BCP 47 locale identifier as language-script-region plus extensions — for example en-Latn-US or zh-Hant-TW. The translator's locale JSON filename must match this identifier byte-for-byte, including hyphen case. A file named es-mx.json will not load against a config expecting es-MX.

Which Intl arguments must the translator preserve verbatim?

Four argument classes survive translation untouched:

  • The locale string itself (en-US, zh-Hant-TW).
  • Options object keys: style, currency, unit, numberingSystem, calendar, notation.
  • Any formatToParts call signature in a template.
  • Named arguments referenced from the string body.

Change any of them and the output format breaks silently per locale.

Which JS localization libraries will translators actually meet?

Translators meet seven JS localization libraries most often: i18next, next-intl, vue-i18n, @angular/localize, Globalize, Polyglot, and Tolgee — each emits a different JSON shape, placeholder syntax, and plural convention the translator must honor.

LibraryResource formatPlaceholderPlural styleCAT risk
i18next / react-i18nextNamespaced JSON{{name}}ICU or suffix keysMedium (Trans tags)
next-intlJSON ICU{name}ICU plural/selectMedium (nested braces)
vue-i18nFlat/nested JSON{count}Pipe-separated formsLow
@angular/localizeXLIFF{$INTERPOLATION}ICU pluralLow
GlobalizeCLDR + message JSON{name}CLDR via Intl.PluralRulesLow
PolyglotFlat JSON%{name}smart_countLow
TolgeeHosted + ICU JSON{name}ICU pluralLow (in-context)

i18next and react-i18next: namespaced JSON and double-curly interpolation

i18next uses namespaced JSON catalogs with double-curly interpolation like {{name}} and a Trans component for inline markup. Translators receive one JSON per namespace per locale and must keep key order and nested structure identical across languages. React-specific pipeline detail sits on React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

next-intl: ICU messages, server components, and middleware-aware catalogs

next-intl ships JSON ICU messages consumed inside Next.js server and client components, with middleware deciding which locale JSON loads per request. Translators keep ICU plural and select blocks structurally identical so the App Router build does not throw at render.

Globalize: CLDR-backed formatting with per-feature translation files

Globalize loads Unicode CLDR data per locale and exposes separate translation files for messages, dates, numbers, and currency. Translators work only on the message JSON. CLDR handles date, number, and currency formatting from the locale identifier.

Polyglot and lightweight message libraries

Polyglot is a minimal interpolation-and-plural helper with a flat phrases object and %{name} placeholders. Translators receive a single JSON per locale, no namespacing, and must respect Polyglot's smart_count pluralization syntax. vue-i18n sits in a similar lightweight bracket with flat or nested JSON, named {count} interpolation, and pipe-separated plural forms.

Tolgee: in-context editing as an alternative to raw JSON handoff

Tolgee is both an i18n library and a hosted platform where translators edit strings directly on the live page instead of in en.json, with machine-translation suggestions wired into the editor as post-editing drafts. This removes the triple string → key → component lookup that slows every raw-JSON project.

Node.js server-side localization: Express, i18n-node, and template engines

Node.js server-side JS localization pairs an i18n library (i18n-node, i18next, or next-intl) with a template engine like Mustache or EJS. Translators receive the same JSON catalogs but must watch for template helpers like {{t 'key'}} that compile at render time. For a sibling pairing pattern in a different JS runtime, see Expo Localization: What Translators and Agencies Need to Know About expo-localization.

What do JS localization resource files look like, and which placeholders must translators preserve?

JS localization resource files are overwhelmingly JSON — flat, nested, or ICU — plus occasional JS modules exporting a messages object. Translators preserve three placeholder families: single-curly ICU like {name}, double-curly like {{name}}, and printf-style like %s or %{name}. The full resource-format table sits on Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.

Flat JSON vs nested JSON vs ICU MessageFormat

Three JSON shapes dominate JS catalogs:

  • Flat JSON — dotted keys like "home.title" at the top level.
  • Nested JSON — actual object hierarchy, read with path syntax.
  • ICU MessageFormat — plural, select, and gender logic wrapped inside the string value itself.

Translators must confirm which pattern the library expects before touching the file.

How ICU plural and select blocks look in a JS catalog

An ICU plural block reads {count, plural, =0 {no items} one {# item} other {# items}}. It must be reproduced structurally in every target locale, using the CLDR plural categories (zero, one, two, few, many, other) that language requires — not a one-to-one copy of English. Arabic needs six categories. Japanese needs one. Russian needs four.

Three placeholder syntaxes break CAT segmentation most often:

  1. ICU select blocks with nested braces.
  2. Trans-component inline tags.
  3. Escaped double-quotes inside JSON values.

Translators tag these as non-translatable or use the CAT tool's placeholder-protection feature before accepting the segment.

How it works

What are the key steps to localize a JavaScript app from the translator's side?

1

Receiving the catalog: en.json, namespaces, and locale IDs

Translators receive one en.json (or a namespaced folder like /locales/en/common.json) as the source. They create a mirror file per locale ID — es-MX.json, ar-EG.json, zh-Hant-TW.json — with identical keys, structure, and Intl options. The locale identifier follows BCP 47: ISO 639-1 language code plus optional ISO 3166-1 country code.

2

Translating strings while preserving keys, placeholders, and comments

Translators change only the value side of each key-value pair. They keep placeholders byte-for-byte and preserve any JSON5 or source-location comments the engineer attached. Those comments resolve the "string → key → component" triple-lookup problem downstream, pointing the linguist to the exact file and line where the string renders.

3

Delivering the file: validation, lint, and build-time checks

Before delivery, four checks run against the per-locale file:

  • JSON lint — valid syntax, no trailing commas, matched braces.
  • ICU compile — every plural and select block parses.
  • Placeholder parity — every {name} and {{name}} in the source exists in the target.
  • Key completeness — no missing keys versus the source.

CI typically fails the PR on any missing key or malformed ICU block. A test build with Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds catches rendering regressions before real locales ship. Before localization starts, five i18n prerequisites must hold in the source build — strings externalized, ICU plurals and gender declared, locale-driven formats, RTL mirroring, and no copy baked into images or canvas — per Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide.

How does Next.js App Router change JS localization for translators?

The Next.js 13+ App Router moves locale handling into middleware and a [locale] route segment, so translators must know which URL serves which JSON catalog, whether the default locale ships with a /en/ prefix, and how server components stream translations differently from client components.

Middleware-driven locale detection and routing

Next.js middleware reads the Accept-Language header, matches an available locale, and rewrites the request to /[locale]/.... Translators inherit the resulting URL inventory as fixed. Any locale not registered in the middleware config will never load its JSON catalog, no matter how complete the translation file is.

Removing the default-locale prefix from URLs

next-intl requires explicit configuration — localePrefix: 'as-needed' — to strip the /en/ prefix from the default locale. This changes hreflang emission and the URL translators record in their delivery sheet; the prefix is not stripped automatically. The hreflang implications sit on Localization SEO: How Translators Make Localized Pages Rank.

App Router file structure translators should expect

App Router projects place catalogs under /messages/{locale}.json or /locales/{locale}/*.json. The [locale] folder under /app contains page.tsx and layout.tsx. Translators receive the /messages folder, not the component tree, and keys resolve by convention — not by import. A missing key in es-MX.json falls back to the source locale silently unless strict mode is on.

How it works

Manual JSON, AI-generated translations, or hosted platform — which workflow fits the project?

1

When manual JSON editing still wins

Manual JSON editing wins on short-string, high-visibility surfaces — marketing hero copy, legal footers, transactional emails — where translation memory leverage is low and brand voice is high. Translators price this at $0.10–$0.25 per source word with review at $0.04–$0.08 per word.

2

When AI-drafted JSON plus human post-edit is defensible

AI-drafted JSON plus human post-edit is defensible when the catalog exceeds roughly 5,000 segments across 10+ locales and the strings are UI-dense but low-nuance. LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words becomes the quality gate that keeps the posture auditable against frameworks like ISO 17100.

3

When Tolgee or a hosted platform earns its subscription

Tolgee and comparable hosted platforms earn their subscription when the DX friction of the triple string → key → component lookup becomes the bottleneck, or when third-party translators must see live context. In-context editing cuts review cycles that would otherwise bounce JSON back through PRs.

4

GraphQL/CMS-driven catalogs for enterprise content

GraphQL and headless CMS integrations manage translation content at scale by storing strings as structured content and querying per locale. This suits marketing-heavy JS apps where editors — not engineers — ship new copy. Translators receive CMS exports rather than git-tracked JSON. Platform-level patterns on How Shopify Localization Works and What It Means for Your Agency and How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know contrast with the file-based model, and How to Add i18n to an Astro Site covers content-collection handoff for an adjacent JS stack.

Pricing

How much does JS localization cost, and how do agencies price it?

US agencies price JS localization in four stacked line items: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and project management at 10–15% of project value, with tooling amortized per project.

Line itemRateScope
Translation$0.10–$0.25 / source wordPer language, per pass
Review$0.04–$0.08 / wordSecond linguist, bilingual check
LQA$40–$90 / 1,000 wordsScorecard against ISO 17100 criteria
Project management10–15% of project valueTM maintenance, release cycles

A 5-language, 50,000-word JS app worked example

A mid-size JS app covering 5 languages and 50,000 words budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end. The spread is driven by three variables:

  • Translation-memory leverage from prior releases.
  • Turnaround speed demanded by the release calendar.
  • Whether ICU plural and select blocks need from-scratch authoring per locale.

Where AI pre-translate shifts the cost mix

AI pre-translate shifts cost away from fresh translation and into review ($0.04–$0.08 per word) and LQA ($40–$90 per 1,000 words). The per-word rate falls but the quality-gate line items rise. The end-to-end number for a JS app moves inside the same $25,000–$75,000 band, not below it.

Get a quote

The questions translators and localization PMs ask most about JS localization cluster around library choice, Next.js App Router behavior, scaling catalogs to many languages, and the DX friction of finding a string in code — answered below from the production side.

Frequently asked questions

What is localization in coding?

In software development, localization (l10n) is the process of adapting an application's UI strings, date formats, number formats, and other content so it works correctly for a specific locale or language. It sits downstream of internationalization (i18n), which is the engineering work that makes an app localization-ready — for example, externalizing strings into JSON or PO files. For translators, localization in code means the source strings they translate are pulled from resource files (like en.json), translated, and loaded at runtime. Understanding this pipeline helps translators deliver files that slot directly into a developer's build.

Do I have to write translations for all languages manually in JSON files?

You don't have to write every translation manually from scratch, but a qualified human translator (or a first-draft tool followed by a translator) must review every string before it ships. Most JS i18n pipelines store translations in per-locale JSON files (e.g., fr.json, de.json), one file per language. Machine translation or AI tools like a first-draft SaaS can populate those files quickly, but certified or professional-grade output still requires a translator to verify accuracy, tone, and completeness. Agencies typically own the QA step that bridges the raw JSON output and the final approved file.

What's the best way to implement localization in Next.js — CMS or ChatGPT?

Neither a headless CMS nor ChatGPT alone is a complete localization solution — the best approach combines a structured i18n library (like next-intl or next-i18next) with professional translator review. A CMS is useful for marketing copy that changes frequently; a code-based JSON workflow is better for UI strings. AI tools, including ChatGPT, can generate fast first drafts that translators then post-edit, which is exactly the model certified translation pipelines are adopting. The critical point for agencies is that no AI output should be delivered as a finished certified translation without a qualified human reviewer signing off.

How do I set up internationalization in Next.js 15 app router?

In Next.js 15 with the App Router, the standard approach is to wrap your app with a locale-aware layout using a [locale] dynamic segment and a middleware file that detects and redirects to the correct locale. Libraries like next-intl provide a useTranslations() hook and a server-side getTranslations() function that load strings from per-locale JSON files at build or request time. You define supported locales in your next.config.js (or next.config.ts), and the middleware handles routing. For translation teams, the output is a set of JSON resource files — one per locale — that translators populate and agencies review before deployment.

Which i18n library works best with Next.js 13+ app router?

next-intl is widely regarded as the best fit for Next.js 13+ App Router because it was purpose-built for React Server Components and supports both server-side and client-side translation loading. next-i18next remains popular for Pages Router projects but requires more configuration to work with App Router. Paraglide JS (by inlang) is a newer, type-safe alternative worth evaluating. For translation teams, the choice of library determines the file format (usually JSON) and the key structure they'll receive — so agencies should confirm the format with the dev team before starting translation work.

How do I find a UI string in code when using a localization file?

Search your codebase for the translation key used in the component, then look up that key in the relevant locale JSON file. For example, if a component calls t('checkout.submitButton'), search for checkout.submitButton in your en.json (or equivalent source-language file) to find the original string. Most editors support global search across files (Ctrl+Shift+F in VS Code). For translators working outside the codebase, a translation management system (TMS) or a shared spreadsheet keyed by the same IDs gives equivalent visibility without needing code access.

How do I format numbers in JavaScript?

Use the built-in Intl.NumberFormat API to format numbers according to a specific locale in JavaScript. For example, new Intl.NumberFormat('de-DE').format(1234567.89) outputs '1.234.567,89' — correct for German locale conventions. This matters directly for translators and localization engineers because numeric formatting (decimal separators, thousands separators, currency symbols) varies by locale and should never be hardcoded. The Intl API covers number, currency, and percentage formatting and is supported in all modern browsers and Node.js without any external library.

pages.title: Localisation Project: How Translators and Agencies Scope, Run, and Deliver One
pages.h1: Localisation Project: How Translators and Agencies Scope, Run, and Deliver One
pages.meta_description: A localisation project is a single multi-locale job that converts source content into reviewed, QA-passed target files on a fixed scope, SLA, and budget.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is a localisation project?
  • What are the key elements of a localisation project?
  • What are the core phases of a localisation project?
  • Who runs a localisation project and what do they each do?
  • How much does a localisation project cost and how is it budgeted?
  • How do you evaluate whether a localisation project is good or janky?
  • How does a translator break into running localisation projects as a PM?
  • Frequently asked questions

Inside a localization program, work ships one job at a time. Each job carries its own scope sheet, its own translator panel, its own SLA clock, and its own certification gate. That job is the localisation project — the atomic unit of delivery a translator or LPM actually runs.

What we offer

What is a localisation project?

A localisation project is a single bounded job inside a localisation program that converts a defined source scope into reviewed, QA-passed target-language files for one or more locales under a fixed SLA, cost base, and acceptance checklist signed off by a localization project manager. The project is the delivery unit; the program is the standing operation above it.

What are the key elements of a localisation project?

A localisation project has five scoping elements the translator inspects before quoting: the extracted resource bundle, the project translation memory, the client term base, the locale style guide, and the pseudo-localisation or staging build used for in-context review.

ArtifactPurposeFormat
Resource bundleSegments, placeholders, limitsXLIFF, JSON, .strings, strings.xml
TM leverage reportVolume by match bandCSV or TMS export
Term baseApproved and forbidden termsTBX
Locale style guideRegister, tone, format rulesPDF or wiki
Pseudo-loc or staging buildIn-context reviewAPK, URL, build link

What goes in the resource bundle and locale pair list?

The resource bundle lists segment count, placeholder density, character limits per key, and context fields across formats such as XLIFF, JSON, .strings, and strings.xml. Locale pairs are declared as BCP 47 tags combining ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1, so es-MX and es-ES generate separate quote lines.

  • es-MX ≠ es-ES — separate TMs, separate term bases.
  • pt-BR ≠ pt-PT — separate reviewers.
  • fr-CA ≠ fr-FR — separate style guides.

JSON and XLIFF handling for front-end frameworks is covered in React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

What TM leverage report does a localisation project need?

The TM report breaks volume into ICE, 100%, 95–99%, 85–94%, and no-match bands, which drive the per-word discount schedule and set realistic throughput for the LPM's schedule.

  1. ICE matches: in-context, zero edit expected.
  2. 100% matches: segment-level identical.
  3. 95–99% fuzzy: light edit.
  4. 85–94% fuzzy: moderate edit.
  5. No match: full translation rate.

What does a usable localisation brief include?

A usable brief lists target locale, tone register, forbidden terms, brand voice reference, staging URL, character limits per key, and milestone deadlines — not just an EN-to-ES language pair. A website brief, for example, names the staging URL and in-page character limits; see Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project for a non-app lane example.

What we offer

What are the core phases of a localisation project?

A localisation project runs through six core phases: scope and kickoff, file preparation and TM leverage, translation, bilingual review, LQA sampling, and delivery with certification sign-off where the lane requires one.

Who runs a localisation project and what do they each do?

A localisation project runs on five roles: the localization project manager coordinates the job, the translator produces target segments, the reviewer checks every segment, the LQA tester samples against a scorecard, and the localization engineer handles file prep and build integration. Each role is a distinct cost line and a distinct quality gate — removing any one of them creates a gap that the others cannot cover.

RoleProducesBilled as
LPMScope, schedule, delivery10–15% of project value
TranslatorTarget segments$0.10–$0.25 per source word
ReviewerEdited segments$0.04–$0.08 per source word
LQA testerScorecard with error typing$40–$90 per 1,000 words
Localization engineerFile prep, pseudo-loc, build integrationHourly or amortized

What does the localization project manager (LPM) own on a single job?

The LPM is the single point of contact for the client across the entire job — clients deal with one coordinator, not thirty linguists or engineers. On any given project, the LPM confirms scope, assigns linguists, dispatches through the TMS, tracks SLA, runs pre-delivery QA, and handles exceptions. A working LPM typically carries 8–15 concurrent projects at once, which means exception-handling speed and clear communication discipline are non-negotiable skills at that desk. The LPM's fee is priced at 10–15% of total project value, reflecting the coordination overhead that makes every other role more efficient.

What do translators, reviewers, and LQA testers each produce?

Translators deliver target-language segments against the active TM and term base; every segment they produce is constrained by pre-approved terminology so that forbidden terms hard-fail at the editor level before review even begins. Reviewers then edit every segment for accuracy and locale fit — not a sample, every segment — producing a corrected file that feeds directly into delivery. LQA testers work last, sampling a defined slice of translated content against an MQM-style scorecard that buckets errors into accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style categories. Each tester's output is a scored artifact, not an opinion, and that scorecard travels with the delivery package as evidence of quality. Being connected across all three of these functions is precisely what gives a strong LPM the visibility to catch problems before they reach the client.

For role depth beyond the project unit, see Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs.

Pricing

How much does a localisation project cost and how is it budgeted?

A localisation project is budgeted on four stacked line items in US dollars: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and project management at 10–15% of project value, plus tooling amortized per project.

Line itemRateBasis
Translation$0.10–$0.25per source word
Review$0.04–$0.08per source word
LQA$40–$90per 1,000 words
Project management10–15%of project value
Certificate of accuracy$25–$150per 250-word page (certified lanes)
Notarization$10–$50per document, optional

What does a mid-size multi-locale localisation project budget look like?

A 5-language, 50,000-word localisation project budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end, depending on TM leverage, turnaround speed, and whether the lane requires a certificate of accuracy. The planning layer above this budget is covered in Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs.

How does AI pre-translation shift the project cost mix?

AI pre-translate drops the translation line and shifts spend into review at $0.04–$0.08 per word and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, which carry more of the quality burden once raw output is machine-generated. The scorecard gate does not move; the sampling density often tightens.

Get a quote

How do you evaluate whether a localisation project is good or janky?

A localisation project is evaluated against an MQM-style LQA scorecard priced at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, covering accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style. A 'janky' output is one that fails locale convention and terminology first — those two categories are the ones end users notice immediately, even when they are comfortable reading the source language alongside the translation. A polished output passes all five categories with zero critical errors and carries a scorecard artifact as proof.

Error categoryJanky signalPolished signal
AccuracyDropped clauses, wrong numbersSegment-level fidelity
FluencySource-language word orderNative reading rhythm
TerminologyTerm base missesZero forbidden-term hits
Locale conventionWrong date, currency, addressLocale-correct formats
StyleRegister driftStyle guide alignment

Which error categories most often make a localisation project feel janky?

Locale convention errors — wrong date format, incorrect currency symbol, misformatted address — and terminology slips against the client term base are the two categories end users notice first, even when they also read source-language content comfortably. Accuracy errors matter enormously for certified or legal content, but for general product copy it is the locale convention failures that break trust fastest, because they signal that the content was never adapted for the target market — only translated. Fluency and style errors read as awkward rather than wrong, so they erode confidence more slowly; terminology and locale convention errors read as factually incorrect, so they erode it immediately.

A project that has been run well leaves a clear audit trail: the LQA scorecard is aligned to ISO 17100 quality standards, every critical error has a resolution note, and the final file matches the locale style guide on date, number, and address formatting. A project that has been run badly lacks that artifact chain — the scorecard is missing, the term base was never loaded, or the locale style guide was never issued at kickoff. Evaluating a project's quality is therefore as much about inspecting the process artifacts as it is about reading the translated text itself.

How does a translator break into running localisation projects as a PM?

A translator moves into localisation project management by stacking three capabilities on top of linguistic skill: CAT tool and TMS fluency, TM and term base governance, and vendor and budget tracking. The transition is achievable because translators already own the quality literacy that makes a strong LPM — they understand what a bad segment looks like, they can read a TM leverage report, and they know why a forbidden-term hit in the editor matters. What they add on the LPM desk is the coordination and commercial layer that sits above the linguistic work.

Which skills transfer from translation to project management?

CAT tool fluency, QA literacy, and style-guide discipline transfer directly from the translation seat to the PM desk — a translator who has worked inside a TMS already understands dispatch, segment status, and pre-delivery QA in a way that a generalist PM has to learn from scratch. Vendor negotiation, PO alignment, concurrent-job scheduling across 8–15 active projects simultaneously, and exception handling are learned on the LPM desk itself, not at the translation seat. The LPM role is defined by its breadth of contact — coordinating across engineering, client, and linguist teams at once — and that cross-team fluency is something translators build naturally by working with reviewers and engineers throughout their linguistic career.

  • Transfers directly: CAT tool fluency, TM leverage reading, term base governance, QA literacy, style guide discipline.
  • Learned on the LPM desk: vendor management, budget tracking, SLA enforcement, concurrent-job scheduling across 8–15 projects, exception handling, scope confirmation, and client-facing communication.

A translator targeting the LPM role should also understand the commercial structure of a project: translation is billed at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per source word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and PM coordination at 10–15% of total project value. Knowing those numbers is essential for confirming scope, assigning work at the right tier, and tracking budget against delivery without surprises.

Common questions cover scope boundaries, SLA numbers, cost ranges, locale coding, and whether AI reduces the need for a human localisation project at all.

Frequently asked questions

How does localisation work?

Localisation works by systematically adapting source content — text, visuals, formats, and functionality — so it feels native to a target locale, not just translated. For a certified translation project specifically, this means the linguist or agency scopes the source document, assigns a qualified translator for the target language pair, produces a draft (increasingly via CAT tools or AI-assisted first-draft platforms), edits and proofreads against quality standards (ISO 17100 is the dominant benchmark), and attaches a signed certificate of accuracy before delivery. Turnaround for a certified document typically runs 24–72 hours depending on volume and language pair.

What does a localization project manager do?

A localisation project manager (LPM) coordinates every moving part of a translation or localisation project from intake to delivery. Day-to-day tasks include scoping source files, calculating word counts, assigning linguists and reviewers, setting deadlines, managing translation memories and termbases, tracking costs against quotes, and performing final quality checks before client handoff. On certified translation projects, the LPM also ensures the correct credentials and certification statements are in place for each target language. They act as the communication bridge between the client, the translator, and any DTP or desktop publishing specialists.

What is the average salary for a localization project manager in the US?

Entry-to-mid-level localisation project managers in the US typically earn between $45,000 and $75,000 per year, while senior or programme-manager roles at larger LSPs or tech companies can reach $90,000–$120,000+. Salary varies significantly by industry vertical (legal and medical tend to pay more), company size, and whether the role is in-house or agency-side. Certified translation agencies often staff LPMs at the lower end of that range, while global SaaS or life-sciences firms sit at the higher end.

What tools or workflows do localization PMs actually use?

Most localisation PMs rely on a combination of a translation management system (TMS), CAT tools, and project tracking software. Common TMS platforms include Phrase, Memsource, and XTM; CAT tools like SDL Trados, memoQ, and Wordfast handle segment-level translation with translation memory leverage. For certified translation workflows, AI-assisted first-draft platforms are increasingly used to accelerate the initial draft before a credentialed translator reviews and certifies. PMs also use standard PM tools — spreadsheets, Trello, Asana, or Jira — for deadline and resource tracking, plus QA tools like Xbench or Verifika for automated checks.

How do you evaluate whether a localization is good or bad?

A good localisation reads as if it were written natively in the target language — terminology is consistent, tone matches the register of the source, and locale-specific formats (dates, currencies, addresses) are correct. For certified translations, evaluators also check that meaning is complete and accurate against the source, with nothing omitted or added. Structured quality frameworks like ISO 17100 or the MQM (Multidimensional Quality Metrics) error taxonomy provide objective scoring across dimensions such as fluency, accuracy, and terminology. Practical red flags include calques (word-for-word constructions), untranslated strings, and mismatched legal terminology.

What makes a localization feel 'janky' vs polished?

A janky localisation feels like it was produced by someone who translated words rather than meaning — the result is awkward phrasing, inconsistent terminology, and cultural references that don't land. Common culprits include literal translation of idioms, failure to adapt number or date formats, ignoring text-expansion (German or Finnish strings can run 30–40% longer than English, breaking UI layouts), and mismatched formality levels. A polished localisation is invisible: the reader never senses a source document existed. On certified translations specifically, jank often shows up as inconsistent legal terms or missing obligatory phrasing required by the target jurisdiction.

How do translation jobs work?

Translation jobs are typically scoped by word count, language pair, subject matter, and required turnaround before being quoted and assigned to a qualified linguist. Agencies or in-house teams intake source files, run them through a CAT tool to calculate leveraged word counts (fuzzy matches and repetitions reduce the billable volume), assign a translator and reviewer, and deliver a final file plus — for certified work — a signed certificate of accuracy. Freelancers may work directly with end clients or through an LSP. Rates for certified translation commonly range from $0.10 to $0.25 per source word depending on language pair and specialisation.

Can you give me an example of localization?

A certified birth certificate translated from Spanish to English for a US immigration application is a clear example of localisation in a translation context. The translator doesn't just convert words — they render official names, dates in MM/DD/YYYY format, and institutional titles in a way that a USCIS officer will recognise, then attach a certification statement attesting to the translation's accuracy and completeness. Another example is adapting a software UI from US English to UK English, adjusting spellings, date formats, and currency symbols so the product feels locally native.

What is localisation in software?

Software localisation is the process of adapting a software product's interface, help content, and supporting documentation so it functions and feels native in a specific locale. This goes beyond translating UI strings — it includes adapting date/time formats, currency symbols, right-to-left text rendering, character encoding, and culturally appropriate imagery. For translation SaaS products in particular, localisation also means ensuring that any auto-generated certified translation output conforms to the legal and stylistic conventions of the target market, not just the source language.
