pages.title: Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs
pages.h1: Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs
pages.meta_description: A localisation strategy defines which locales to launch, what lanes to translate, which quality tier each lane earns, and how the agency bills — scoped for
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is a localisation strategy from the agency's side of the desk?
  • What are the core elements of a localisation strategy an agency must document?
  • How does an agency build a localisation strategy step by step?
  • How do you price a localisation strategy engagement itself?
  • What KPIs does the strategy hold the translator and agency to?
  • What are the common failure modes in a localisation strategy, and how do agencies prevent them?
  • How does a localisation strategy connect to adjacent delivery lanes the agency already runs?
  • Frequently asked questions

Every localisation program needs a planning layer that sits above the individual translation projects — the document that tells a producer which locales, which content lanes, which quality tier, and which workflow apply before a single resource bundle is opened. This page writes that layer from the agency's side of the desk, not the buyer's.

What we offer

What is a localisation strategy from the agency's side of the desk?

A localisation strategy is a written plan the agency and client sign before any string is translated, defining which locales to launch, which content lanes to localise, which quality tier each lane earns, how terminology and style are governed, and how the work is priced and measured. It is the agency's scoping artifact, not a marketing deck.

What are the core elements of a localisation strategy an agency must document?

A complete localisation strategy documents seven elements: target locales and their tier, in-scope content lanes, quality tier per lane, terminology and style governance, workflow and tooling, pricing basis per lane, and measurable KPIs. Missing any one of the seven turns the document into a wishlist rather than a signable SOW schedule.

ElementOwnerOutput in the signed document
Locale tiersAgency strategist + client PMTier matrix (Tier 1–4) with named locales
Lane scopeAgency strategistLane × tier scope sheet
Quality tierAgency locale leadError-per-1000-words threshold per lane
GovernanceAgency + client reviewerTerm base / style guide ownership clauses
WorkflowAgency engineeringTMS integration diagram, pseudo-loc checkpoint
Pricing basisAgency commercialPer-lane rate card with TM leverage schedule
KPIsBoth partiesFour measured dimensions tied to monthly invoice

Which target locales make the first cut, and how are they tiered?

Locales are grouped into four tiers: Tier 1 full localisation across all six lanes, Tier 2 product and support only, Tier 3 machine translation with light post-editing, Tier 4 English retained with locale-aware formats. The tier a locale earns drives every downstream cost.

TierLane coverageQuality tierTypical use
Tier 1 — FullAll six lanesPublication-grade on legal and marketing; functional on productTop-revenue or regulated markets (e.g. Japan, Germany)
Tier 2 — PartialProduct strings + support KBFunctionalSecondary growth markets
Tier 3 — MT + PEMTProduct strings onlyGist with post-editingLong-tail markets validating demand
Tier 4 — English retainedNone localised; locale-safe formats onlyN/AMarkets where English is the de facto business language

Which content lanes belong in scope, and which stay in English?

The six lanes — product strings, website, marketing, support KB, legal/compliance, and in-product video — are each scoped in or out per locale tier. Legal and compliance stays in-scope for regulated markets regardless of tier. The website lane is scoped per our Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project playbook rather than re-explained here.

Scope assignment per lane follows three rules:

  1. Legal and compliance is always in-scope where the locale has regulatory exposure.
  2. Product strings are in-scope wherever a user can select the locale in-app.
  3. Marketing and video are in-scope only when the client funds in-market demand generation.

What quality tier does each lane earn, and who reviews it?

Quality tiers run from publication-grade through functional to gist, each with a named reviewer pool and a per-1000-word scoring rubric at release.

  • Publication-grade — legal filings, marketing hero copy. Reviewer: in-country subject-matter expert. Threshold: under 2 errors per 1000 words.
  • Functional — product strings, support KB top articles. Reviewer: senior in-country linguist. Threshold: under 5 errors per 1000 words.
  • Gist — long-tail KB, user-generated content. Reviewer: post-editor spot-check. Threshold: comprehensibility pass on sampled segments.

Who owns the term base and style guide, and how are changes approved?

Term base ownership belongs to the agency's locale lead. Style guide ownership belongs to the client's in-market reviewer. Changes to either require written sign-off from both before the next sprint pulls the update.

The governance clause set the agency inserts into every strategy document covers five items:

  1. Term base ownership and change-request workflow.
  2. Style guide ownership and sign-off path.
  3. New-locale approval authority and lead time.
  4. TM leverage discount schedule.
  5. Quality-score release gate and its override procedure.

What are the measurable benefits a localisation strategy unlocks for the client?

Documenting the expected gains gives the strategy a business case that survives budget scrutiny. The four benefits the strategy underwrites are:

  • Faster time-to-market per locale — one shared backbone cuts repeat scoping work on each new launch.
  • Reduced rework costs — pseudo-loc and TM leverage surface defects before translator hours are spent.
  • Higher in-country conversion rates — publication-grade marketing on Tier 1 locales outperforms raw translation.
  • Defensible compliance posture — legal lanes carry a quality tier and reviewer sign-off that holds up in audit.

How does an agency build a localisation strategy step by step?

An agency builds the strategy in six steps: audit the source, tier the locales, scope the lanes, set the quality rubric, wire the workflow, and lock the pricing basis. The output is a signed document delivered before any resource bundle is translated.

Step 1 — How do you audit the source for localisation readiness?

Audit the source by checking for externalised strings, locale-safe date and currency handling, Unicode support, and a stable resource bundle format. Anything failing the audit becomes an i18n ticket owned by the client's dev team, not a translation line item. See i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds for the engineering prerequisites.

The audit output is a one-page defect list with four columns: defect, severity, owner, and target fix date. The strategy document cannot be signed until every high-severity defect has a named owner.

Step 2 — How do you tier the target locales?

Tier each locale by three inputs: revenue potential from the client's market research, regulatory requirements, and the agency's existing translator coverage and TM leverage for that language pair. Regulatory exposure forces Tier 1 regardless of revenue.

The tiering output goes into the strategy as a locked matrix. Changing a locale's tier mid-program requires a formal change order.

Step 3 — How do you scope each content lane per locale?

Scope lanes by multiplying the locale tier against the lane matrix:

  • Tier 1 locales take all six lanes.
  • Tier 2 takes product strings plus support KB.
  • Tier 3 takes MT-plus-PEMT on product strings only.
  • Tier 4 keeps English with locale-safe date, number, and currency formats.

Step 4 — How do you set the quality rubric and reviewer pool?

Set the quality rubric by assigning each lane a target error-per-1000-words threshold, a named reviewer pool, and a release gate that blocks publishing if the score falls below the threshold on sample segments. The rubric is carried over from our certified-translation QA model and adapted lane by lane.

Reviewer pools are named individuals, not vendor categories. The strategy lists the primary reviewer and one named backup per locale per lane.

Step 5 — How do you wire the workflow and tooling?

Wire the workflow by connecting the client's repo or CMS to the agency's TMS, defining pseudo-loc and staging checkpoints, and setting TM leverage rules so pre-translated segments route to review rather than full translation. Framework-specific pipelines (React i18n, Shopify, Webflow, Pendo) inherit from this one wiring diagram.

Where does machine translation fit as a production stage, not a finished answer?

Machine translation sits as a pre-translation stage for Tier 3 locales and long-tail KB content. It is always followed by post-editing against the same term base and style guide used elsewhere. Raw MT output is never shipped.

Pseudo-localization sits earlier in the workflow as a checkpoint that surfaces i18n defects before translator time is spent. It is a build-step, not a translation step.

Step 6 — How do you lock pricing and measurement?

Lock pricing by assigning each lane its own basis and tying monthly invoices to the quality score at release. One rate card does not fit six lanes.

LanePricing basisTM leverageReviewer pool
Product app stringsWeighted wordFull schedule appliesSenior in-country linguist
WebsitePer-source-word + engineering hoursFull schedule appliesIn-country marketing reviewer
Marketing contentPer-source-word, transcreation surcharge on hero copyPartial (new assets rarely leverage)In-country marketing reviewer
Support KBWeighted word, MT+PEMT on long-tailFull schedule appliesPost-editor spot-check
Legal / compliancePer-source-word + per-1000-words quality surchargeNone on new regulated textIn-country subject-matter expert
In-product videoPer-minute for subtitles; per-minute higher for dubbingNoneIn-country voice/subtitle reviewer

Pricing

How do you price a localisation strategy engagement itself?

The strategy document is priced as a fixed-fee pre-production engagement — scoped as a 2–4 week consulting block covering source audit, locale tiering, lane scoping, and the signed pricing matrix. It is delivered before any translation PO is cut. Giving the strategy away as pre-sales trains clients to treat planning as free.

Fixed-fee pricing avoids the two failure modes of hourly consulting: scope creep on the agency side and budget anxiety on the client side. The quote covers one audit cycle, one tier matrix, one scope sheet, one rubric, and one 12-month pricing schedule — revisions beyond that are change orders.

What goes into the fixed-fee pre-production deliverable?

The deliverable bundles six artifacts into one signed document:

  1. Locale tier matrix.
  2. Lane scope sheet.
  3. Quality rubric with per-lane thresholds.
  4. Governance clauses.
  5. Workflow diagram with TMS integration points.
  6. 12-month pricing schedule.

The signed document becomes the SOW schedule referenced by every subsequent translation PO. One strategy, many POs.

Where does regulated content (e.g. USCIS filings, EU legal) force a quality tier up?

Regulated content forces publication-grade quality regardless of locale tier. For example, USCIS-ready certified translation runs $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per page, with a certificate of accuracy signed by a competent translator required on every page. The strategy document must budget regulated lanes separately from standard localization lanes, because the TM leverage schedule does not apply to new regulated text.

The same quality-tier uplift applies to EU medical device labeling, financial disclosures, and privacy policies in jurisdictions with named-regulator exposure. The strategy names the regulator the lane is prepared for; the receiving authority confirms acceptance.

Get a quote

What KPIs does the strategy hold the translator and agency to?

The strategy holds the agency to four measurable KPIs per release, each tied to monthly invoicing:

KPIMeasurementTargetInvoice impact
Quality score per 1000 wordsWeighted rubric on sampled segmentsBelow lane thresholdRelease gate; miss blocks publish
TM leverage %Leveraged words / total wordsBaseline set in Step 6Discounts applied against full rate
On-time deliveryDelivered vs sprint cadence95% on-timeService credits below target
In-locale reviewer sign-off rateApproved releases / submitted releases90% first-pass approvalRepeat rework at agency cost

What are the common failure modes in a localisation strategy, and how do agencies prevent them?

Five failure modes recur, each prevented by a specific governance clause in the strategy document:

  • Launching Tier 1 locales without regulated-content budget. Prevented by a legal-lane line item on every Tier 1 locale in the pricing schedule.
  • Treating the term base as a one-time deliverable. Prevented by a term base ownership clause assigning the agency locale lead as permanent owner.
  • Skipping pseudo-loc. Prevented by a workflow clause making pseudo-loc a mandatory sprint-zero checkpoint.
  • Pricing all lanes on raw word count. Prevented by the per-lane pricing basis table in Step 6.
  • Letting the client's PM own the style guide. Prevented by a style guide ownership clause naming the in-market reviewer, not the PM, as owner.

How does a localisation strategy connect to adjacent delivery lanes the agency already runs?

The strategy document references the agency's existing lane playbooks rather than re-explaining them. Each lane inherits a single consistent process from the signed strategy and the published guide.

  • Application lane — follows the Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide.
  • Website lane — follows the Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project playbook.
  • Engineering readiness — follows i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds.

Framework and platform specifics — React i18n pipelines, Shopify and Webflow CMS routing, Pendo in-product content, and locale-specific guides like Chinese localization — carry their own siblings that the strategy document names rather than duplicates.

The questions agencies hear most on strategy engagements cluster around examples, when a localisation strategy fits versus a transnational one, and how it differs from international strategy and from a translation plan.

Frequently asked questions

What is a localization strategy?

A localization strategy is a structured plan for adapting content, products, or services to meet the linguistic, cultural, and regulatory requirements of specific target markets. For translation agencies and LSPs, it defines which locales to support, how workflows are staffed and tooled, how certified translation programs are priced, and what quality standards apply per locale. A mature strategy accounts for volume forecasting, translator specialisation (legal, medical, financial), technology stack, and turnaround SLAs — typically broken down market by market rather than applied globally as a single ruleset.

Can you give me an example of localization?

A practical example for a translation agency is delivering certified legal translations for a client expanding from the US into the EU: the same source contract is adapted into German, French, Polish, and Spanish, each version carrying a sworn or certified translator's stamp valid in that jurisdiction. Beyond language, the process may require adjusting date formats, legal terminology, notarisation conventions, and even document layout to meet country-specific official requirements. Each locale is treated as a distinct deliverable, not a copy-paste variant.

When should a firm follow a localization strategy?

A firm should adopt a formal localization strategy when it is serving — or planning to serve — multiple language markets where compliance, cultural fit, or legal certification requirements differ meaningfully. For translation agencies, this threshold is typically crossed when managing more than two or three active locales simultaneously, when certified output (USCIS, sworn, apostilled) is part of the deliverable mix, or when clients demand consistent turnaround and pricing across markets. Ad-hoc locale management becomes a quality and margin risk beyond that scale.

What is global localization?

Global localization (sometimes called 'glocalization') is the practice of designing a program that scales across many markets while still customising output for each individual locale's linguistic and cultural context. For LSPs running multi-locale certified translation programs, it means standardising the production workflow — intake, first-draft generation, translator review, certification — while allowing locale-specific rules (target language conventions, required credentials, stamp formats) to govern the final deliverable. The goal is operational efficiency at scale without sacrificing jurisdiction-level compliance.

What is internationalization and localization?

Internationalization (i18n) is the process of designing a product or workflow so it can support multiple locales without requiring structural redesign; localization (L10n) is the act of adapting that output for a specific market. In a certified translation production context, internationalization means building a workflow — including first-draft tooling, style guides, and QA checklists — that can accommodate any language pair and certification format, while localization means applying the correct target-language terminology, legal register, and certification conventions for each jurisdiction delivered.

What is internationalization vs localization?

Internationalization is the upfront infrastructure work; localization is the market-specific execution that runs on top of it. A translation agency internationalizes when it configures its TMS, CAT tools, and first-draft pipeline to handle bidirectional scripts, varied certification templates, and multi-currency pricing. It localizes when a translator adapts a birth certificate for the German standesamt versus the Spanish registro civil — applying the exact terminology, format, and credential requirements each authority demands. Both disciplines are necessary; neither replaces the other.

What is L10n?

L10n is the standard industry abbreviation for 'localization,' formed by taking the first letter 'L,' the count of omitted letters (10), and the last letter 'n.' It is widely used in LSP project management, TMS interfaces, and tool documentation to save space. In certified translation production workflows, L10n tasks specifically include adapting linguistic content, legal register, certification wording, and document formatting to meet the requirements of a target jurisdiction — distinguishing this work from the broader i18n (internationalization) setup that enables it.

What are the best localization tools?

The most widely used localization tools in professional translation production are CAT (computer-assisted translation) platforms such as SDL Trados, memoQ, and Phrase, combined with translation memory and terminology management systems. For certified translation programs specifically, agencies also rely on TMS platforms (XTRF, Plunet) for project and vendor management, and increasingly on AI-assisted first-draft generation tools to reduce per-word production costs before a human translator applies certification review. Quality assurance tools like Xbench or Verifika are standard for pre-delivery checks across large multi-locale batches.

What are some tips for becoming a good translator?

The foundation of a good professional translator is near-native command of both source and target language combined with deep subject-matter expertise in at least one specialist domain — legal, medical, or financial. For certified translation work specifically, understanding the certification and notarisation requirements of each target jurisdiction is as important as linguistic accuracy. Productive translators also invest in CAT tool proficiency, maintain curated termbases, and treat post-editing AI first drafts as a distinct skill: knowing when to accept, revise, or override machine output without losing speed gains.

pages.title: Localization Codes: The Standards Translators and Agencies Use
pages.h1: Localization Codes: The Standards Translators and Agencies Use
pages.meta_description: Localization codes are ISO 639 language, ISO 3166 country, ISO 15924 script, and BCP 47 locale tags that identify what to translate for which locale.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What are localization codes and which standards define them?
  • What is the difference between ISO 639-1, ISO 639-2, and ISO 639-3?
  • How does BCP 47 compose a full locale identifier from these codes?
  • Which localization codes appear in the files a translator actually opens?
  • Which localization codes trip up real projects the most?
  • How should localization codes appear in URLs for multilingual SEO?
  • How does a translator deliver endonyms instead of English language names?
  • How should an agency prioritize which localization codes to ship first?
  • What does a localization-code QA checklist look like at handback?
  • Frequently asked questions

Every localized asset — a resource bundle, a URL, an XLIFF segment, a Webflow page — carries an identifier that binds it to one locale. Localization codes are that identifier layer. They sit beneath translation work as part of How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying and every other multi-locale engagement, and most translator rework traces back to a mistagged code rather than a mistranslated word.

What are localization codes and which standards define them?

Localization codes are standardized identifiers that name a target locale for translation tooling. They combine ISO 639 language subtags, ISO 15924 script subtags, and ISO 3166-1 region subtags under the BCP 47 composition rules maintained by IETF.

Four standards do the work:

  • ISO 639 — language identity, in three parts (639-1 2-letter, 639-2 3-letter, 639-3 3-letter extended).
  • ISO 15924 — 4-letter script subtags (Latn, Hant, Hans, Cyrl, Arab).
  • ISO 3166-1 — 2-letter country codes used as BCP 47 region subtags (US, BR, MX, DE).
  • BCP 47 — the IETF rule set that assembles the three above into a single locale tag.
  • UN M.49 — numeric region codes (419 Latin America, 150 Europe, 005 South America) accepted by BCP 47 as region subtags.

How does the 4-layer code stack (language, script, region, extension) fit together?

A BCP 47 locale tag stacks four layers: language, script, region, and private or variant extensions. Translators read the stack left-to-right to know what to translate, in which script, for which market.

LayerStandardExample subtagWhat breaks if dropped
LanguageISO 639-1 / 639-2 / 639-3zh, en, yueNo translation target at all
ScriptISO 15924Hant, Hans, Cyrl, LatnChinese and Serbian ship in the wrong writing system
RegionISO 3166-1 or UN M.49TW, BR, 419Vocabulary, pricing, and reviewer pool get wrong assignment
Variant / extensionBCP 47 extension (u-, x-)u-ca-gregory, x-corpCalendar, collation, and private tags fail silently

Dropping the script subtag is the breakage that costs the most hours. A tag of zh with no Hans or Hant forces the engine to guess, and the guess routes Mainland copy into a Hong Kong reviewer queue.

Who maintains localization code standards and how often do they change?

ISO maintains 639, 3166, and 15924; the Library of Congress serves as the ISO 639-2 registration authority; IETF maintains BCP 47 through the IANA Language Subtag Registry. Updates publish on separate cadences, which is why translators pin a snapshot per project.

  • ISO 639-3 adds and retires codes annually through SIL International.
  • ISO 3166-1 changes when a country, territory, or alpha-2 assignment changes.
  • The IANA Language Subtag Registry is the authoritative source consolidating all three ISO lists for BCP 47.
  • Freeze a registry snapshot at project kickoff and ship it with the TM. Mid-sprint drift breaks acceptance tests.

What is the difference between ISO 639-1, ISO 639-2, and ISO 639-3?

ISO 639-1 is 2-letter (en, de, fr), ISO 639-2 is 3-letter with bibliographic and terminologic variants (fre/fra, ger/deu), and ISO 639-3 is 3-letter codes covering roughly 7,900 individual languages including minority and constructed languages.

PartFormatScopeTypical use
ISO 639-12-letter~184 mainstream languagesWeb, CAT tools, hreflang, BCP 47
ISO 639-23-letter, /B and /T~500 languagesBibliographic archives, MARC records
ISO 639-33-letter~7,900 individual languagesMinority and constructed languages, SIL cataloging

When does a translator use 2-letter versus 3-letter codes?

Use ISO 639-1 2-letter codes for mainstream i18n (web, CAT tools, hreflang, BCP 47). Use ISO 639-2 or 639-3 3-letter codes for archival systems, bibliographic metadata, and any language without a 2-letter code — Cherokee (chr), Cornish (cor, kw), or Esperanto variants.

  • Web, mobile, and CAT tooling: 2-letter.
  • Library and bibliographic systems: 3-letter /B.
  • Linguistic research, long-tail minority locales: ISO 639-3.
  • Cantonese and other spoken varieties with no 2-letter code: ISO 639-3 (yue) or BCP 47 extended (zh-yue).

What is the bibliographic vs terminologic split in ISO 639-2 (fre vs fra)?

ISO 639-2/B is bibliographic, chosen from English-language names (fre French, ger German). ISO 639-2/T is terminologic, chosen from the native name (fra, deu). Translators pick /T for linguistic tooling and /B only when the client's archive demands it.

The pairs that most often collide in client exports:

  • French — fre (/B) vs fra (/T)
  • German — ger (/B) vs deu (/T)
  • Dutch — dut (/B) vs nld (/T)
  • Greek — gre (/B) vs ell (/T)
  • Chinese — chi (/B) vs zho (/T)
  • Icelandic — ice (/B) vs isl (/T)

How do you normalize both 2-letter and 3-letter codes in one system?

Maintain a lookup table that maps every ISO 639-1 code to its ISO 639-2/T and ISO 639-3 equivalents, and canonicalize to one form at ingest. The IANA Language Subtag Registry is the authoritative source; freezing a snapshot per project prevents mid-sprint drift.

How does BCP 47 compose a full locale identifier from these codes?

BCP 47 assembles a locale as language-Script-REGION-variant-extension, with hyphens, specific case rules, and a prescribed order (zh-Hant-TW, sr-Latn-RS, en-Latn-US-u-ca-gregory). Translators who alter case or punctuation break locale resolution.

The assembly steps:

  1. Pick the primary language subtag from ISO 639-1 when it exists; fall back to ISO 639-2/T or 639-3.
  2. Add an ISO 15924 script subtag when the language can appear in more than one script.
  3. Add an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 or UN M.49 numeric region subtag when the market matters.
  4. Append variant and extension subtags last, under the u- (Unicode) or x- (private) prefix.
  5. Join all subtags with single hyphens — no underscores, no spaces.

What are the case conventions for language, script, and region subtags?

Language subtags are lowercase (en, zh), script subtags are Title Case (Latn, Hant, Cyrl), and region subtags are UPPERCASE (US, TW, BR). BCP 47 parsers are case-insensitive, but filenames and build configs are not.

  • Correct: en-Latn-US, zh-Hant-TW, sr-Cyrl-RS.
  • Parses but risks filename mismatch: EN-LATN-US, zh-hant-tw.
  • Fails most i18n configs: en_US, es_mx (underscores belong to POSIX/Android, not BCP 47 JSON keys).

Why do locale filenames have to byte-match the BCP 47 tag?

A file named es-mx.json will not load against an i18n config expecting es-MX; the string compares byte-for-byte including hyphen case. Underscore conventions (en_US) belong to POSIX and Android resource folders — never to BCP 47 JSON keys. The deeper mechanics live on JS Localization: How Translators Fit Into a JavaScript i18n Pipeline and React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

The three byte-match failures that cost translators handback cycles:

  1. Lowercase region in the filename against uppercase region in the config (es-mx.json vs es-MX).
  2. Underscore in a filename intended for a hyphenated BCP 47 key (en_US.json vs en-US).
  3. Missing script subtag when the engine was configured for the scripted form (zh.json vs zh-Hans).

What is a region subtag and how is it different from an ISO 3166 country code?

A BCP 47 region subtag can be either an ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code (US, BR, DE) or a UN M.49 numeric region code (419 for Latin America, 150 for Europe). Region subtags target markets, not countries — es-419 covers all Latin American Spanish.

Which localization codes appear in the files a translator actually opens?

Translators meet locale codes in resource-bundle filenames (en-US.json, fr-CA.po), hreflang attributes in HTML, Intl.Locale strings in JavaScript, Android values-xx-rYY folders, iOS .lproj directories, and XLIFF file target-language headers. The resource bundle and i18n-split details sit on Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.

How do codes differ between web (hreflang), iOS (.lproj), Android (values-), and XLIFF?

Web uses BCP 47 with hyphens (es-MX); iOS .lproj follows BCP 47 too (es-MX.lproj, zh-Hant.lproj); Android uses hyphen-less language with r+region (values-es-rMX); XLIFF 2.x requires BCP 47 in source-language and target-language attributes.

Four conversion rules keep handbacks clean:

  • Web → iOS: identical tag, append .lproj.
  • Web → Android: split es-MX into values-es-rMX.
  • Web → POSIX: replace hyphen with underscore (es_MX), add .UTF-8 if required.
  • XLIFF → Web: copy the target-language attribute verbatim.

What does an hreflang pair look like with correct ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 codes?

Each page references all its alternates — including itself — using ISO 639-1 language codes plus optional ISO 3166-1 country codes, written as hreflang="es-MX", hreflang="pt-BR", hreflang="fr-CA". A missing self-reference drops the whole cluster. The ranking consequences live on Localization SEO: How Translators Make Localized Pages Rank, and the CMS-side configuration sits on How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.

Which localization codes trip up real projects the most?

Five locale pairs cause most rework: Serbian Latin vs Cyrillic (sr-Latn vs sr-Cyrl), Chinese Traditional vs Simplified (zh-Hant vs zh-Hans), Norwegian Bokmål vs Nynorsk (nb/nn/no), Cantonese (yue/zh-yue), and Filipino vs Tagalog (fil/tl). Each triggers LQA rework at $40–$90 per 1,000 words on top of the base $0.10–$0.25 per word rate.

How are regional variants of Spanish, Portuguese, and French encoded?

Spanish variants ship as es-ES (Castilian), es-MX (Mexican), es-AR, es-CO, or the regional macro es-419 for Latin America. Portuguese splits pt-BR and pt-PT; French splits fr-FR, fr-CA, fr-BE, fr-CH. Each is a separate deliverable with its own TM, reviewer pool, and price, as covered on Localization in Marketing: What Translators and Agencies Deliver.

How is Chinese encoded across script and region (zh-Hant-TW, zh-Hans-CN, zh-HK)?

Chinese requires a script subtag because the language alone is ambiguous. Use zh-Hans-CN for Simplified Mainland, zh-Hant-TW for Traditional Taiwan, and zh-Hant-HK for Traditional Hong Kong — the latter two share a script but diverge in vocabulary.

Why is Cantonese hard to represent in standard code systems?

Cantonese has an ISO 639-3 code (yue) and a BCP 47 extended tag (zh-yue), but many legacy systems only accept zh with no spoken-variant subtag. Agencies submit yue, fall back to zh-Hant-HK by convention, or document the mismatch in the handoff.

Which other common codes get mis-tagged (nb vs no, fil vs tl, iw vs he, in vs id)?

Norwegian Bokmål is nb; the macrolanguage no is deprecated for new projects. Filipino is fil, not tl. Hebrew is he (iw is a legacy Java code). Indonesian is id (in is a legacy Java code). Yiddish is yi (ji is legacy). Modern builds reject legacy tags silently.

Legacy tagReplacementLanguage

nonb or nnNorwegian

How should localization codes appear in URLs for multilingual SEO?

The standard pattern is www.example.com/{lang-code}/page, using subdirectories like /en/, /es-MX/, /pt-BR/. Each URL emits an hreflang pair matching its directory, with ISO 639-1 language codes and optional ISO 3166-1 country codes.

When should URLs use /en/ versus /en-US/?

Use /en/ when a single English edition serves every market and /en-US/ only when a separate en-GB or en-AU edition exists on the same site. Adding a region subtag you cannot staff with distinct content fragments ranking signals.

Subdirectory, subdomain, or query parameter — which structure holds hreflang signals best?

Subdirectories (/es-MX/) are easiest for crawlers and simplest for translators to QA. Subdomains (es.example.com) require separate crawl budgets. Query parameters (?lang=es-MX) are discouraged because many crawlers treat them as duplicates.

How does a translator deliver endonyms instead of English language names?

Build a code-to-endonym lookup (en → English, de → Deutsch, ja → 日本語, ru → Русский, zh-Hans → 简体中文) because engines like Godot, older Xcode projects, and legacy Android ship English language names only. Deliver it as a CSV or JSON keyed by BCP 47 tag.

How should an agency prioritize which localization codes to ship first?

Score candidate locales on ISO 639-3 code availability, in-market speaker count, ISO 3166-1 region reach, client revenue coverage, and TM leverage. A mid-size 5-language, 50,000-word program budgets $25,000–$75,000 — code triage decides which five.

A defensible scoring sheet weights:

  1. Code availability — does ISO 639-3 cover the language with a stable tag? (0 or 10)
  2. Speaker count in the target region (0–20).
  3. Region reach — single country or macro region like es-419 (0–10).
  4. Client revenue share tied to that locale (0–30).
  5. TM leverage from prior projects (0–20).
  6. Reviewer pool depth — enough qualified reviewers to run LQA (0–10).

What does a localization-code QA checklist look like at handback?

Verify seven items before handback: BCP 47 tag spelling, filename byte-match, script subtag present where ambiguous, hreflang self-reference, region subtag matches reviewer pool, no deprecated tags (iw, in, no, ji), and endonym map delivered if the engine needs it.

  1. Spell every BCP 47 tag against the frozen IANA Language Subtag Registry snapshot.
  2. Compare each filename byte-for-byte against the config key — hyphen case included.
  3. Confirm a script subtag on every Chinese, Serbian, and Uzbek deliverable.
  4. Audit hreflang blocks for the self-reference line and matching reciprocal pairs.
  5. Match region subtags to the reviewer pool contracted for that market.
  6. Replace any legacy tag (iw, in, ji, no) with its modern replacement.
  7. Attach the endonym CSV when the client's engine ships English-only language names.

Translators and agency PMs most often ask about mixing 2-letter and 3-letter codes, representing dialects, choosing codes vs full names in UI, and why Cantonese and some minority languages remain hard to tag.

Frequently asked questions

What's the difference between ISO 639-1, ISO 639-2, and ISO 639-3?

ISO 639-1 uses 2-letter codes (e.g., 'fr' for French), ISO 639-2 uses 3-letter codes covering ~490 languages, and ISO 639-3 expands to 3-letter codes for over 7,000 living, extinct, and constructed languages. ISO 639-1 is the most widely used in web and software localization (BCP 47 tags, HTTP headers, HTML lang attributes). ISO 639-2 is common in library cataloguing and some government standards. ISO 639-3, maintained by SIL International, is the go-to for linguistic research and for languages that lack an ISO 639-1 code — essential when certifying translations for less-resourced languages.

How do I support both 2-letter (ISO 639-1) and 3-letter (ISO 639-2) language codes in the same system?

The standard approach is to store codes internally in one canonical format — typically ISO 639-1 where available — and maintain a lookup table that maps 3-letter ISO 639-2/639-3 codes to their 2-letter equivalents. SIL's public ISO 639-3 tables include a column explicitly linking each 3-letter code to its ISO 639-1 counterpart when one exists. For languages with no ISO 639-1 code (e.g., 'haw' for Hawaiian), fall back to the 3-letter form. This hybrid approach is used by major localization platforms and keeps BCP 47 language tags valid across both translation management systems and certified document metadata.

How do I represent Spanish dialects or regional variants in ISO 639-3?

ISO 639-3 treats Spanish as a single macro-language ('spa'), so regional variants are represented using BCP 47 language tags that combine the ISO 639-1 code with an ISO 3166-1 region subtag — for example, 'es-MX' for Mexican Spanish or 'es-419' for Latin American Spanish broadly. ISO 639-3 does not assign separate codes to dialect-level variants of major world languages like Spanish. For certified translation workflows, the region subtag is the practical mechanism agencies use to specify target locale, since a certificate for 'es-MX' and 'es-ES' may carry different legal standing depending on the target jurisdiction.

What are region subtags and how are they different from country codes in language tags?

Region subtags in BCP 47 language tags are drawn from ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country codes (e.g., 'US', 'BR') or UN M.49 numeric codes (e.g., '419' for Latin America), and they specify the regional variety of a language rather than identifying a country per se. The distinction matters because a region subtag describes linguistic conventions — spelling, date formats, legal terminology — not citizenship or geography. For example, 'fr-CA' signals Canadian French conventions (distinct vocabulary, some legal terms) versus 'fr-FR'. In certified translation production, using the correct region subtag ensures the right locale-specific glossaries, style guides, and legal terminology are applied.

Why is Cantonese hard to represent in standard language code systems?

Cantonese lacks its own ISO 639-1 code and sits under the Chinese macro-language umbrella in many systems, making unambiguous tagging difficult. ISO 639-3 does assign it the code 'yue', which is the most precise identifier available. In BCP 47, Cantonese is best tagged as 'zh-yue' or simply 'yue', but many platforms still collapse it under 'zh' (Chinese), causing it to be treated as interchangeable with Mandarin. For certified translation agencies handling Hong Kong or Macau documents, this ambiguity is significant — a document certified in Cantonese written form (Traditional script, 'zh-Hant-HK') is legally distinct from Simplified Chinese Mandarin.

Should I use language codes (EN/DE/ES) or full language names in my UI/localization files?

Use language codes (BCP 47 tags like 'en', 'de', 'es-MX') internally in localization files and configuration, and display full language names — ideally endonyms — to end users. Codes are machine-readable, collision-free, and standard across translation management systems, CAT tools, and certified document metadata. Full names are human-readable but ambiguous (is 'Chinese' Simplified or Traditional? Mandarin or Cantonese?). The industry best practice is to store the BCP 47 tag as the canonical key and derive the display name from it programmatically, using a library like ICU or the Unicode CLDR data set.

What are language codes?

Language codes are standardized short identifiers assigned to human languages so that software, databases, and documents can reference a language unambiguously. The most widely used standards are ISO 639-1 (2-letter, e.g., 'en' for English), ISO 639-3 (3-letter, covering 7,000+ languages), and BCP 47 tags that combine a language code with optional script and region subtags (e.g., 'zh-Hant-TW'). In certified translation workflows, language codes appear in document metadata, translation memory systems, CAT tool project settings, and on certificates of accuracy to identify the source and target languages precisely.

What is an example of localization?

A clear example of localization is adapting a certified immigration document translation not just linguistically but also for the conventions of the target country — converting dates from MM/DD/YYYY to DD/MM/YYYY, replacing US state abbreviations with the target country's administrative divisions, and adjusting legal terminology to match the receiving jurisdiction's official usage. Localization goes beyond word-for-word translation to ensure the document is functionally and legally appropriate in its destination context. For translation agencies, this distinction between translation and localization directly affects which style guides, glossaries, and region subtags (e.g., 'pt-BR' vs. 'pt-PT') are applied to a project.

Can I certify my own translation?

In most jurisdictions, you cannot certify your own translation if you are the person who needs the document — but a bilingual individual who is not the document's subject can self-certify in some countries, including the United States. In the US, USCIS accepts a signed statement from the translator attesting to their competence and the accuracy of the translation, with no requirement for a notary or third-party credential. However, countries like Germany, France, and many others require a sworn or court-certified translator (Beeidigter Übersetzer). Agencies producing certified translations should verify the destination jurisdiction's requirements before issuing any certificate.
pages.excerpt: Localization codes are ISO 639 language, ISO 3166 country, ISO 15924 script, and BCP 47 locale tags that identify what to translate for which locale.

pages.title: Localization Coding: How Translators and Developers Share the Resource File
pages.h1: Localization Coding: How Translators and Developers Share the Resource File
pages.meta_description: Localization coding externalizes UI strings into resource files, uses format placeholders over concatenation, and routes ICU plurals, BCP 47 locales, and
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is localization coding, and why does it decide whether translators can deliver clean files?
  • How does localization coding differ from internationalization (i18n), and where does each stop?
  • What are the common technical approaches to localization coding across modern stacks?
  • How should dynamic strings with variables be structured so translators can keep grammar intact?
  • What locale and language codes should the resource files carry?
  • Can AI tools like ChatGPT and Copilot write or audit localization code reliably?
  • How does the certified translation lane fit the same localization coding substrate?
  • What are the common pitfalls when building a localization system from scratch?
  • Frequently asked questions

Localization coding sits inside a broader app localization pipeline — the engineering substrate that lets translators deliver clean resource files into a developer's build without touching source code. For the pipeline framing, see Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide. This page covers the substrate itself: resource files, placeholders, ICU plurals, BCP 47 tags, and the certified lane that reuses the same files.

What is localization coding, and why does it decide whether translators can deliver clean files?

Localization coding is the engineering practice of externalizing UI text into resource files, parameterizing variables with placeholders, declaring plural and locale rules, and tagging locales with BCP 47 identifiers so translators produce locale builds without touching source code. It is the shared contract between the developer who structures the file and the translator who fills it — and when that contract is broken on the engineering side, no amount of linguistic skill at the translator's desk can produce a clean build. The practice decides handoff quality because every rework cycle traces back to one of six root causes.

  • Hardcoded strings never reach the resource file and are invisible to the TMS.
  • Concatenated sentences force English word order on inflected languages such as German, Japanese, and Arabic.
  • Missing plural declarations collapse three to six grammatically required forms into one.
  • Free-text locale names break TMS routing that depends on BCP 47 tags.
  • Placeholder drift between source and target files breaks the build at compile time.
  • No screenshots or pseudo-localization leaves translators guessing at character limits and UI context.

Pseudo-localization is a test build that expands and accents source strings to surface truncation, hardcoded strings, and encoding bugs before a single segment reaches a human translator. Running it early is the single highest-leverage quality gate in the pipeline, because defects caught there cost a fraction of what they cost when they surface at the LQA stage. The LQA gate prices at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated and runs an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. Catching a hardcoded string at that stage costs roughly ten times what catching it at pseudo-loc costs — making localization coding decisions directly responsible for program economics, not just technical correctness.

How does localization coding differ from internationalization (i18n), and where does each stop?

Internationalization is the upfront engineering that makes a codebase locale-ready — externalized strings, Unicode encoding, locale-aware formatting APIs, and bidirectional layout support — while localization coding is the per-locale execution that fills those resource files with translated strings, plural rules, and BCP 47 tags. Internationalization is the critical engineering practice of preparing a software application so that it can be adapted to various languages and regions without requiring code changes at the time of each new locale launch. The i18n layer ships once. The l10n layer ships every time a new locale lands, and it operates entirely within the structure the i18n layer created.

DimensionInternationalization (i18n)Localization (l10n)
ScopeUpfront engineeringPer-locale execution
OwnerDeveloperTranslator + localization engineer
ArtifactsExternalized strings, Unicode encoding, locale-aware APIs, bidirectional supportTranslated strings, plural rules, date/number formats, locale-specific legal copy
ShippedOnceEvery new locale
Failure modeHardcoded strings, broken encoding, layout that clips RTL textWrong plural form, mis-routed BCP 47 tag, placeholder mismatch

Key i18n practices include externalizing all user-facing strings from the codebase, using a library that supports pluralization and locale-specific formatting for dates and numbers, and designing user interfaces that can accommodate text expansion and right-to-left languages. Each of those practices creates a specific hook that the l10n layer depends on: the externalized string file is where translators work, the pluralization library is what reads their plural-branch entries, and the RTL-capable UI is what renders their Arabic or Hebrew output without clipping.

For the program-planning view that sits above both layers, see Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs.

What does the handoff from i18n to l10n look like in a real repository?

The developer externalizes every user-facing string into resource files — en.json, strings.xml, Messages.resx — wires ICU MessageFormat or gettext for plurals, and commits a locale-neutral build. A Translation Memory stores all previously translated source-and-target language pairs, so segments that reappear across locale cycles return at full leverage rather than being re-translated from scratch. The translator then receives the resource files via TMS or Git and returns locale-stamped copies keyed to the correct BCP 47 tag.

  1. Developer extracts strings into the source resource file.
  2. CI pipeline pushes the file to the TMS, keyed by BCP 47 locale tag.
  3. Translator opens segments in the CAT tool, with TM and term base pre-loaded.
  4. Reviewer passes at $0.04–$0.08 per source word, checking every segment pre-LQA.
  5. LQA scorecard runs at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style framework.
  6. Signed-off file commits back to the repository as es-MX.json or de-DE.json.

What are the common technical approaches to localization coding across modern stacks?

The three common approaches are resource-file externalization with key-value lookups, inline ICU MessageFormat for complex plural and gender rules, and gettext-style .po files with msgid/msgstr pairs — each paired with a BCP 47 locale tag and loaded at runtime by the i18n library. The approach is set by the stack, not by preference.

Which string resource file format fits which stack?

Translators receive .po on PHP and Python projects, .resx on .NET, strings.xml on Android, .strings on iOS, .json on JavaScript and React, and XLIFF as the interchange format CAT tools consume. Each format carries different placeholder syntax and plural handling.

FormatStackPlaceholder syntaxPlural handlingCAT support
.po (gettext)PHP, Python, GNU%(name)s, %s, %dnplurals + Plural-Forms headerNative in most CAT tools
.resx.NET{0}, {1}External library (e.g., Humanizer)Via XLIFF export
strings.xmlAndroid%1$s, %2$d<plurals> element, CLDR categoriesNative in most CAT tools
.strings / .stringsdictiOS%1$@, %2$d.stringsdict with NSStringLocalizedFormatKeyNative in most CAT tools
.jsonJavaScript, React, Node{name}, {count}ICU MessageFormatVia plugins or XLIFF conversion
XLIFF (1.2 / 2.0)InterchangePreserves source placeholdersCarries ICU or nativeNative — the lingua franca

For JSON stacks specifically, see JS Localization: How Translators Fit Into a JavaScript i18n Pipeline and React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline. React Native programs follow Expo Localization: What Translators and Agencies Need to Know About expo-localization. Static-site stacks using JSON namespaces track with How to Add i18n to an Astro Site.

Why do format placeholders beat string concatenation in every target language?

Format placeholders like %1$s, {name}, or {0} let translators reorder arguments inside a single resource entry, while concatenation forces English word order on languages like German, Japanese, Arabic, and Russian — producing ungrammatical output no reviewer can rescue. Concatenation is the single most common cause of broken grammar in Slavic, Semitic, and East Asian locales.

Consider "You have {count} messages from {name}". A translator working in German needs the verb at the end. A translator working in Japanese reorders subject, object, and verb entirely. A translator working in Arabic flips reading direction and inflects {name} for case. All three fit inside one placeholder-based entry. None of them survive concatenation like "You have " + count + " messages from " + name, because the fragments cannot be reassembled.

  • Android/Java: %1$s, %2$d (positional, so translators reorder).
  • ICU / react-intl: {name}, {count} (named, so translators reorder by name).
  • .NET: {0}, {1} (positional index).
  • Python gettext: %(name)s (named, dictionary-style).

How do ICU MessageFormat and gettext handle plural rules translators actually see?

ICU MessageFormat exposes CLDR plural categories (zero, one, two, few, many, other) inside a single message; gettext uses nplurals and a Plural-Forms header per .po file — Russian declares 3 forms, Arabic 6, Welsh 6, Japanese 1, and the translator fills each category key.

LanguagePlural formsCLDR categories usedgettext nplurals
English2one, other2
Russian3one, few, many3
Arabic6zero, one, two, few, many, other6
Welsh6zero, one, two, few, many, other6
Polish3one, few, many3
Japanese1other1
Chinese1other1
French2one, other2

CJK languages carrying one plural form are a frequent source of over-engineered keys. For CJK specifics on top of the plural rule, see Chinese Localization: What Makes It Harder Than Most Projects.

How should dynamic strings with variables be structured so translators can keep grammar intact?

Dynamic strings must keep the full sentence in one resource entry with named or positional placeholders — never split across multiple keys — because word order, gender agreement, and clitic placement differ by locale and cannot be reassembled correctly from fragments at runtime. String concatenation is an anti-pattern: it breaks word order in German, Japanese, Arabic, and Russian, and it is structurally impossible to fix at translation time without changing the code. One sentence equals one key — that rule is the foundation of every platform's resource-file convention.

What does a correctly structured ICU message look like for a count-plus-name sentence?

Placeholder syntax varies by platform and must be preserved exactly as received. Android and Java use positional specifiers such as %1$s and %2$d. ICU MessageFormat and React-intl use named tokens such as {name} and {count}. .NET resource files use indexed tokens such as {0} and {1}. Python gettext uses named mapping syntax such as %(name)s. Translators must carry every placeholder through to the target segment without altering its syntax, because the runtime substitution engine matches the token literally.

A single ICU entry such as {count, plural, one {# message from {name}} other {# messages from {name}}} lets translators choose the correct plural form and reposition {name} according to target-language grammar. The equivalent concatenation — count + ' messages from ' + name — breaks the moment the target language inflects the noun or moves the verb. ICU plural categories are drawn from CLDR: the available categories are zero, one, two, few, many, and other. Russian requires three active categories. Arabic requires all six. Welsh also requires six. Japanese requires only one — other — because the language has no grammatical plural distinction. French requires two. Each branch keeps {name} and the # count token intact and reorders them per locale grammar.

How do gender and case agreement get represented in the resource file?

ICU select clauses — {gender, select, female {her message} male {his message} other {their message}} — represent gender agreement inside a single string entry, keeping the logic in the resource file rather than in conditional code. Case agreement in Slavic and Finnic languages requires either declined variants per form or a developer comment on the key specifying the grammatical context so the translator supplies the correctly inflected form.

  • Gender: ICU select with female / male / other branches; translator fills each branch independently.
  • Case: pass the inflected noun as a separate variable, or add a developer comment specifying nominative, genitive, or accusative context.
  • Formality: ICU select with formal / informal branches for German Sie/du, French vous/tu, and Japanese keigo registers.
  • Positional placeholders: keep platform syntax intact — %1$s, {name}, {0}, or %(name)s — and never reorder without confirming the runtime supports reordering.

What we offer

What locale and language codes should the resource files carry?

Resource files are tagged with BCP 47 identifiers that combine an ISO 639-1 two-letter language code with an optional ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 country code — es-MX for Mexican Spanish, fr-FR for metropolitan French, pt-BR for Brazilian Portuguese — and the TMS stores every translated segment against the BCP 47 tag, not a free-text locale name. Storing segments against a structured tag rather than a display name is what allows the TMS to route content correctly, apply the right term base, and surface TM leverage across locale variants that share a root language. A client adding es-AR to an existing es-ES program inherits the shared term base through the BCP 47 language-subtag structure, reducing net-new word volume from the first segment.

Can AI tools like ChatGPT and Copilot write or audit localization code reliably?

AI tools reliably scaffold ICU MessageFormat skeletons, generate boilerplate key structures, and audit placeholder parity between source and target files, but AI-generated translations still require human review before the LQA gate at $40–$90 per 1,000 words. The scaffolding use is sound. The finished-translation use is not.

What should an agency let AI do, and what stays with a human reviewer?

AI handles key-naming conventions, placeholder-parity checks, pseudo-translation stubs, and plural-category skeletons. A human reviewer owns terminology, locale convention, tone, and the certificate-of-accuracy wording on certified lanes — because those decisions are legally or contractually operative.

TaskAI (ChatGPT, Copilot)Human reviewer
ICU MessageFormat skeletonYesSign-off
Key naming conventionsYesSign-off
Placeholder parity audit (source vs target)YesSpot-check
Pseudo-translation stubsYesSpot-check
Plural-category skeleton (CLDR branches)YesFill content
Finished translationDraft onlyOwns
Terminology, tone, locale conventionNoOwns
Certificate of accuracy wordingNoOwns

Who runs this inside the agency is the localization engineer. For scope, pay, and reporting line, see Localization Engineer Job: What the Role Does, Pays, and Requires. Senior engineers at major tech firms earn total compensation of $150,000–$200,000.

Pricing

How does the certified translation lane fit the same localization coding substrate?

Certified translation runs as a regulated lane on the same resource-file substrate: locked boilerplate for the certificate of accuracy and named-translator attestation fields sit in domain logic rather than the presentation layer, and USCIS filings price at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or

Certified translation runs as a seventh regulated lane on the same resource-file substrate: locked boilerplate for the certificate of accuracy and named-translator attestation sit in domain logic rather than presentation, and USCIS filings price at $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard page with optional notarization at $10–$50. The lane shares term base and style guide with the other six delivery lanes — product app, website, marketing, support KB, legal/compliance, in-product video.

For the full lane framing inside multi-locale programs, see Localization Management: How Translators and Agencies Run Multi-Locale Programs. For how it scopes against enterprise programs, see How Enterprise Localization Programs Are Structured and Run.

Where should localization data live — presentation layer or domain logic?

Display strings and format masks live in the presentation layer. Currency math, tax rules, legal clauses, and certified-document attestation fields live in domain logic — because those values change the result of the computation, not just how it renders, and a mis-rendered attestation can invalidate the certification.

  • Presentation layer: UI labels, button text, date format masks, currency symbol, number separators.
  • Domain logic: VAT rate, tax jurisdiction rules, currency conversion math, legal clause bodies, certificate of accuracy boilerplate, per-page attestation field.

A currency symbol belongs in presentation. A VAT rate belongs in domain logic. A certified-document attestation field belongs in domain logic, because its wording is legally operative. For the same rule applied to corporate programs, see Business Localization: How Agencies Deliver Multi-Locale Programs for Corporate Clients.

5–

Get a quote

Pricing

What are the common pitfalls when building a localization system from scratch?

The repeating pitfalls are hardcoded strings, concatenated sentences, missing plural declarations, free-text locale names instead of BCP 47 tags, placeholder drift between source and target files, and no screenshots or pseudo-loc for translator context — each one causes rework the LQA pass surfaces too late. Rework cost compounds. For how to present rework savings to a client, see How to Measure and Present the ROI of Localization Work.

What should the translator receive before any strings are translated?

The pre-handoff bundle contains externalized resource files tagged with BCP 47, an ICU or gettext plural declaration per locale, screenshots or a pseudo-loc build for context, a term base and style guide, and placeholder documentation listing every {variable} and %s token.

  1. Externalized resource files — no hardcoded strings in source.
  2. BCP 47 tag on each file (en.json, es-MX.json, fr-FR.json).
  3. ICU MessageFormat or gettext Plural-Forms declaration per locale.
  4. Screenshots or a pseudo-loc build — see Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds.
  5. Term base and style guide shared across all seven delivery lanes.
  6. Placeholder documentation: every {variable}, %s, %1$s, and {0} listed with its runtime value type.
  7. Developer comments on gender, case, and formality context for ambiguous keys.

Short answers to the questions translators and agency PMs ask when they first open a developer's resource file.

Frequently asked questions

What is localisation in software?

In software, localisation (l10n) is the process of adapting a product's interface, content, and behaviour for a specific locale — covering language, date formats, currency, pluralisation rules, and more. It goes beyond swapping text strings: developers store translatable content in resource files (JSON, XLIFF, .strings, .resx, etc.) that translators fill in for each target language. A well-structured resource file separates code from content, letting translators work without touching the codebase and enabling the app to load the correct strings at runtime.

What is the difference between translation and localization?

Translation converts text from one language to another, while localization adapts the entire user experience for a target market. Translation is one component inside localization: a localized product also adjusts number formats, currency symbols, date order, images, right-to-left layout, pluralisation logic, and cultural references. For translators working with resource files, this distinction matters because some strings carry placeholders, gender agreements, or plural forms that require locale-specific handling beyond word-for-word rendering.

What's the difference between translation and localization?

Translation converts text from one language to another, while localization adapts the entire user experience for a target market. Translation is one component inside localization: a localized product also adjusts number formats, currency symbols, date order, images, right-to-left layout, pluralisation logic, and cultural references. For translators working with resource files, this distinction matters because some strings carry placeholders, gender agreements, or plural forms that require locale-specific handling beyond word-for-word rendering.

Is it localization or localisation?

Both spellings are correct — "localization" follows American English conventions and "localisation" follows British English. The industry uses both interchangeably, and you'll see each in major style guides, tool documentation, and standards bodies such as LISA and W3C. The shorthand "l10n" (the letter L, ten characters, then N) is the universally accepted abbreviation in technical contexts and avoids the spelling debate entirely.

What is an example of localization?

A classic example is an app that displays dates as MM/DD/YYYY in the United States but switches to DD/MM/YYYY for the United Kingdom and YYYY-MM-DD for ISO-standard markets. At the string-resource level, this means the developer stores a date-format pattern as a translatable key, and the translator (or locale configuration) supplies the correct pattern for each region. Other examples include adapting currency symbols, swapping metric and imperial units, adjusting plural forms in Slavic languages, and mirroring UI layout for Arabic or Hebrew.

How do I handle sentence building across different languages in a string resource file?

Use named placeholders and keep full sentences as single string keys rather than concatenating fragments. Splitting a sentence into pieces (e.g., "You have" + count + "messages") forces a fixed word order that breaks in languages where the verb or noun comes first. Instead, store the whole sentence as one key — "You have {count} messages" — and let the ICU MessageFormat or similar standard handle pluralisation and gender agreement per locale. This gives translators full sentence context and the freedom to reorder elements naturally.

What's the best way to structure localization strings to avoid broken grammar in other languages?

Store complete sentences as single resource keys and use a message-formatting standard such as ICU MessageFormat or GNU gettext for plurals, gender, and select cases. Never split sentences across multiple keys or hard-code conjunctions in code — what reads naturally in English often produces ungrammatical output in German, Japanese, or Arabic when reassembled. Add context comments (developer notes) to every key so translators know the UI location, the gender of any referenced noun, and the possible values of each placeholder. Consistent key naming and a glossary of product terms reduce inconsistency across large files.

How do I deal with word order differences when localizing dynamic strings?

Use named, reorderable placeholders rather than positional ones so translators can place variables wherever grammar demands. For example, "{user} sent {count} files" allows a German translator to write "{count} Dateien wurden von {user} gesendet" without touching the code. Positional placeholders like %1$s and %2$s exist in some frameworks for the same reason — they let translators swap order freely. Avoid constructing sentences by concatenating separate strings in code, as this locks word order to the source language structure.

What are common pitfalls when building a localization system from scratch?

The most common pitfalls are string concatenation (forcing source-language word order), missing plural forms, hard-coded punctuation and spacing in code, and neglecting context metadata for translators. Developers often underestimate string expansion: translated text can be 30–100% longer than English, breaking fixed-width UI elements. Other frequent issues include not supporting right-to-left scripts, ignoring locale-specific number and date formats, and treating the source-language file as a living document without a change-tracking workflow — which causes translators to miss updates and ship stale strings.

What does "localization" mean?

Localization means adapting a product, document, or piece of content so it feels native to a specific locale — not just translated, but culturally and technically appropriate. In software, this covers UI strings, date and number formats, currency, images, and legally required terminology. In document translation (including certified translation), localization means ensuring the target text conforms to the conventions, register, and regulatory language of the destination country, not merely rendering words from one language into another.

What is another term for localization?

The most common alternative term is "l10n," the numeronym used in technical documentation. In a broader sense, "adaptation" or "transcreation" are used when cultural rewriting goes beyond linguistic conversion, while "internationalisation" (i18n) refers to the engineering work that makes a product ready for localization. In the certified translation industry, terms like "target-market adaptation" or simply "adaptation" appear when translators must align a document with local legal or regulatory conventions.

What is sl and tl in translation?

SL stands for source language — the language the original document is written in — and TL stands for target language — the language it is being translated into. These abbreviations are standard shorthand across translation studies, CAT tools, and resource file workflows. In a bilingual resource file or XLIFF segment, you will typically see a source element (SL string) paired with a target element (TL string) for each translatable unit, which is exactly the structure translators and developers share when collaborating on localization.
