  • Phrase TMS sits above the CAT editor layer and handles project routing, vendor assignment, and analytics, while multi-translator teams share a single TM in real time through role-based access controls.

What is Phrase CAT?

Phrase CAT is the browser-based segment editor inside the Phrase Language Intelligence Platform, formerly Memsource, where translators edit each source segment against translation memory, term-base hits, inline QA warnings, and Phrase AI pre-translate scores. A downloadable desktop editor exists for Windows and macOS, but the defaults are cloud-first. For the shared vocabulary — TM, term base, QA — see CAT Tool: What It Is, What It Does Inside a Translator's Workflow.

Buyers confuse Phrase with three adjacent things. The table below separates them in one glance.

TermWhat it isWhen you need it
Phrase CAT editorThe segment-level bilingual grid where translation actually happens.Any translator editing segments against TM and term base.
Phrase TMSProject routing, vendor assignment, deadlines, analytics above the editor.Agencies and localization managers running multi-vendor jobs.
MemsourceLegacy name for the same product before the 2021 rebrand.Reading old contracts, CVs, or documentation.
Phrase AIMT engine plus per-segment scoring layer feeding pre-translate.Routing high-confidence segments to lighter post-edit.

Is 'phrase cat' the editor or a cat idiom?

'Phrase cat' resolves to two unrelated queries: the Phrase CAT editor used by professional translators, and 'cat phrases' meaning idioms about cats. This page covers the editor only. The pet-vocabulary meaning is not addressed below.

Why is Phrase CAT sometimes called Memsource?

Memsource rebranded to Phrase in 2021 after acquiring Phrase GmbH, so legacy documentation, agency contracts, and translator CVs still refer to the same editor as Memsource. Vendor onboarding packs, PO templates, and job tickets issued before the rebrand use the Memsource name. The product and the file formats did not change.

What does the Phrase CAT editor actually do segment by segment?

The Phrase CAT editor splits a source document into segments and shows, for each one, the translation-memory match band, term-base hit, Phrase AI pre-translate score, and inline QA warnings in a single bilingual grid. The translator edits in that grid and the system writes the confirmed result back to the shared TM in real time, so every confirmed segment immediately benefits any other translator working on the same project or language pair.

A simplified pass through one segment looks like this.

Each segment routes through 5 decision bands: 101% in-context matches lock or confirm automatically; 95–99% matches go to light edit; 75–94% matches go to full post-edit; below-75% segments route to Phrase AI scoring, then either light MTPE (high confidence) or full human translation (low confidence). Every path ends with an inline QA check before the segment is confirmed and written to TM.[Light edit]

 B -- Below 75% --> F{Phrase AI score?}
 F -- High confidence --> G[Light MTPE]
 F -- Low confidence --> H[Human translate]

How does Phrase handle translation memory match bands?

Phrase surfaces TM matches against the industry-standard 75% fuzzy floor, with bands at 75–84%, 85–94%, 95–99%, 100% exact, and 101% in-context, each discounting the $0.10–$0.25 per-source-word base rate. The band drives the per-word payout the translator sees on the job sheet. A 101% in-context match is the highest confidence tier — it signals that both the segment string and its surrounding context are identical to a previously confirmed translation, so the segment is pre-confirmed or locked and billed at 0–25% of the base rate. A no-match or below-75% segment carries the full base rate because it requires original translation effort with no TM leverage.

Match bandWhat it meansTypical rate treatment

100% exactExact string match, context not confirmed.Often 25–40% of base rate.
95–99%Near-exact fuzzy; small edits expected.Often 40–60% of base rate.
85–94%Fuzzy; moderate edit effort.Often 60–75% of base rate.
75–84%Low fuzzy at the floor.Often 75–100% of base rate.
Below 75% / no matchTreated as new translation.Full base rate, $0.10–$0.25 per source word.

For a buyer-side comparison of translation memory software, see Choosing Translation Memory Software: What to Compare Before Buying.

What does the Phrase AI pre-translate layer score?

Phrase AI pre-translate runs the segment through an MT engine, scores the output per segment for confidence, and routes high-confidence segments to lighter post-edit while flagging low-confidence ones for full human translation. The score is not a surface-level estimate — it reflects the engine's internal confidence in the specific target output for that segment, accounting for domain, register, and term-base alignment. That score becomes the pricing lever in an MTPE job: lighter effort on scored-high segments bills at reduced MTPE rates, while scored-low segments carry full post-edit or human-translation rates. Phrase TMS records the pre-translate scores at the project level, giving project managers an analytics layer to audit routing decisions and refine thresholds over time. For deeper detail, see What Phrase AI Does and Whether It Fits Your Workflow.

How do term bases and inline QA show up in the editor?

Term-base matches highlight in the source segment and auto-insert on target focus, enforcing approved terminology without requiring the translator to search a separate glossary. Inline QA checks run continuously as the translator types, surfacing issues at the moment they occur rather than deferring them to a batch QA step. This means error correction happens at zero marginal cost — fixing a tag error mid-segment is a keypress, whereas catching the same error at final review requires reopening, re-confirming, and re-exporting the file. The inline warnings cover a comprehensive set of failure modes:

  • Missing or reordered inline tags.
  • Number and date mismatches between source and target.
  • Segment length violations against UI character limits.
  • Term-base divergence where an approved term was not used.
  • Double spaces, trailing punctuation, and placeholder damage.
  • Untranslated segments and copied-source warnings.

Comments and in-editor notifications complete the collaboration surface: translators, reviewers, and project managers can thread discussions on any segment without leaving the editor, and role-based access enforced through Phrase TMS determines which users can confirm, lock, or reject segments. The result is a single interface that handles translation, review, QA, and team communication in one place.

How it works

How does Phrase CAT fit inside a professional translation workflow?

1

How does Phrase CAT differ from Phrase TMS?

Phrase TMS owns project routing, vendor assignment, deadlines, and analytics across jobs, while the Phrase CAT editor owns segment-level translation inside each job — same platform, different layers.

LayerOwnsPrimary user
Phrase TMSProjects, vendor assignment, deadlines, analytics, role-based access.Project manager, localization lead.
Phrase CAT editorSegments, TM, term base, inline QA, Phrase AI pre-translate, comments.Translator, reviewer, LQA reviewer.

2

Which workloads does Phrase CAT fit best?

Phrase CAT fits continuous software-string localization, SaaS UI, help-center and documentation work, and repository-connected content — anywhere source files update constantly and multiple translators need shared live TM. Typical fits include:

  • SaaS UI strings pulled from GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket connectors.
  • Help-center and knowledge-base articles syncing from Zendesk or Intercom.
  • Marketing site pages pushed from a headless CMS.
  • Mobile app resource files on continuous release cycles.
  • Product documentation stored as Markdown in a repo.

3

Where does Phrase CAT struggle on certified-translation lanes?

Phrase CAT's browser-first editing weakens offline control for certified lanes, where USCIS filings run $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per 250-word page and the certificate of accuracy is mandatory on every page. A downloadable desktop editor exists, but the defaults are cloud, and the certified-lane workflow needs tighter page-image control, signed PDF output, and offline archive copies.

Pricing

How is Phrase CAT priced for translators and agencies?

Phrase is priced at

Phrase is priced at $27–$55 per user per month on professional tiers, billed per seat, with the CAT editor bundled into Phrase TMS plans rather than sold as a standalone editor. The tier picks what sits above the editor: connectors, analytics depth, API quotas, and SSO.

The tier determines what capabilities sit above the editor itself — connectors to content sources, analytics depth, API call quotas, SSO, and the breadth of the shared vendor pool. The platform's compliance posture is part of what justifies the per-seat cost for regulated buyers: the infrastructure is built to meet ISO 27001, GDPR, CCPA, and PCI DSS requirements, and operates at 99.9% uptime with zero-downtime deployments — a meaningful guarantee for agencies running continuous-localization pipelines where downtime translates directly to missed SLAs. For certified translation production work, the per-seat platform cost sits alongside the $0.10–$0.25 per-source-word translation rate and the $40–$90 per 1,000-word LQA gate, so buyers should model total cost of production across all three layers rather than evaluating the CAT seat price in isolation.

Computer-Assisted Translation Tools: The Working Translator's Field Guide

How does Phrase CAT compare to other professional CAT tools?

Professional translators cluster around 7 CAT tools in 2025 — SDL Trados Studio, memoQ, Phrase, Smartcat, Smartling, OmegaT, and Wordfast — and Phrase sits in the cloud-first, SaaS-string-heavy lane alongside Smartcat and memoQ cloud. The cluster is mapped in full Computer-Assisted Translation Tools: The Working Translator's Field Guide.

Phrase vs Trados: which fits regulated or certified work?

Trados Studio stays stronger on desktop control and offline certified lanes, while Phrase wins on continuous cloud workflows, shared live TM across vendors, and tighter repository-connector coverage. Trados Studio defaults to a Windows desktop install with local project packages; Phrase defaults to a browser session with cloud-stored TM. Side-by-side detail lives in Trados as a CAT Tool: Features, Costs, and Honest Trade-offs.

Phrase vs OmegaT: cloud SaaS or free desktop?

OmegaT is a free open-source desktop CAT that lacks live cloud collaboration, while Phrase charges $27–$55 per user per month for cloud TM sharing, Phrase AI pre-translate, and connector-driven continuous localization. OmegaT fits solo translators comfortable with manual TM and glossary files; Phrase fits teams needing shared state. The deeper read is OmegaT for Professional Translators: What It Does and What It Lacks.

How does Phrase CAT output pass certified-lane quality gates?

Phrase CAT output still has to pass the LQA gate priced at $40–$90 per 1,000 words translated, scored against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 covering accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style — the editor does not replace the gate. The LQA pass runs after the segment-level translation closes.

  1. Translator confirms all segments in the Phrase CAT editor, resolving inline QA warnings.
  2. Reviewer runs a second pass against TM and term-base enforcement.
  3. LQA reviewer scores a sample against the MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100.
  4. Error categories recorded under accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, style.
  5. Score crosses the pass threshold or the job returns to the translator for rework.
  6. Signed certificate of accuracy issued per page for certified-lane deliveries.

A typical certificate of accuracy page, which Phrase itself does not generate, carries this shape:

ElementWhat it saysWhy it is there
Statement of competence"I, [Translator name], certify that I am competent to translate from [source] into [target]."Establishes translator standing for the receiving authority.
Statement of accuracy"The attached is a true and accurate translation of the original [Document type]."USCIS and similar bodies require this exact assertion.
Date and signature". Signed, [Translator name]."Ties the certification to a dated act.
Contact block"[Translator name], [Address],,."Lets the receiving authority verify.

Who should and should not pick the Phrase CAT editor?

Phrase CAT fits translators and agencies running cloud SaaS-string, help-center, and continuous-localization work with shared TM across distributed vendor pools; it fits less well for solo translators on offline certified lanes who need desktop-only control or who cannot sustain a per-seat subscription. The decision is not purely about features — it is about whether the surrounding workflow architecture matches what Phrase TMS provides above the editor layer.

  • Pick Phrase CAT if the content stream is continuous and connectors to source repositories, CMS platforms, or support-desk systems are a hard requirement — Phrase TMS manages those integrations natively above the editor layer.
  • Pick Phrase CAT if Phrase AI pre-translate scoring will drive an MTPE pricing model, routing high-confidence segments to light review and low-confidence segments to full human translation at differentiated rates.
  • Pick Phrase CAT if the agency runs multi-translator projects where a shared, real-time TM and role-based access controls are necessary to prevent segment collision and enforce review hierarchies.
  • Pick Phrase CAT if data security and compliance are buying criteria — the platform operates under ISO 27001, GDPR, CCPA, and PCI DSS controls, which matters for agencies handling regulated or personally identifiable content.
    • Phrase CAT is a poor fit for predominantly offline certified filings — USCIS-style certified translations require tighter page-image control, signed PDF output, and offline archive copies that Phrase's cloud-first defaults do not provide. CAT fits translators and agencies running cloud SaaS-string, help-center, and continuous-localization work with shared TM across vendors; it fits less well for solo translators on offline certified lanes who need desktop-only control.
    • Pick Phrase CAT if the content stream is continuous, vendors are distributed, and connectors to GitHub, Zendesk, or a headless CMS matter.
    • Pick Phrase CAT if Phrase AI pre-translate scoring will drive an MTPE pricing model.
    • Skip Phrase CAT if work is predominantly offline certified filings priced $25–$150 per 250-word page with signed-PDF handoffs.
    • Skip Phrase CAT if the budget cannot sustain $27–$55 per user per month per seat.

    For an alternatives shortlist shaped around these verdicts, see Phrase Alternatives Worth Considering for Your CAT Workflow.

    5–

    How we work with Phrase CAT inside our certified-translation pipeline

    We treat Phrase CAT as one segment surface among several, not as the gate. Our pipeline produces first drafts of certified translations, routes them to a human translator for post-edit against TM and term base, and then runs an LQA pass against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 before issuing the certificate of accuracy. The editor choice follows the lane, not the other way round.

    On cloud SaaS-string and continuous-localization work, Phrase CAT earns its seat on live TM sharing and connector coverage. On certified filings bound for USCIS or a court, we keep the signed-PDF and page-image control inside a desktop surface and use Phrase for the segment pass only.

    We will not route a certified-lane job through a browser-only workflow and call the Phrase AI pre-translate score the quality gate. The score is a routing signal for post-edit effort, not a substitute for the LQA pass priced at $40–$90 per 1,000 words. We will not issue a certificate of accuracy unless a human reviewer has confirmed every segment against the source.

    We also decline to re-price certified-lane work at MTPE rates on the basis of high Phrase AI scores. The $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per 250-word page floor exists because the receiving authority holds the translator accountable, not the engine.

    Phrase CAT is the browser-based segment editor inside the Phrase Language Intelligence Platform, formerly Memsource, bundled with Phrase TMS on seats priced $27–$55 per user per month.

    Frequently asked questions

    What is the cat phrase?

    In translation technology, "Phrase CAT" refers to Phrase's computer-assisted translation (CAT) tool — a professional editor environment where translators work through segments, apply translation memories, and manage terminology. "CAT" stands for Computer-Assisted Translation, a category of software that accelerates human translation rather than replacing it. Phrase is one of the leading platforms in this space, offering a segmented editing interface, glossary integration, and quality-assurance checks. For certified translation workflows, the CAT editor is where linguists review, edit, and finalize source-matched segments before certification.

pages.title: Product Localization: How Translators and Agencies Deliver It
pages.h1: Product Localization: How Translators and Agencies Deliver It
pages.meta_description: Product localization is how translators and agencies adapt an app or SaaS product — strings, UI, formats, cultural references — into a release-ready build per
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is product localization from the translator's side of the desk?
  • Where does product localization sit inside a broader localization program?
  • What are the core benefits of product localization an agency can promise a client?
  • How does the product localization process run from brief to release?
  • How do agencies price product localization?
  • What breaks a localized product after release and how do production teams respond?
  • What examples show product localization working at scale?

Product localization sits inside a six-lane localization program as the production discipline that ships the adapted build itself. This page is written for the translators, project managers, and agency leads who scope, price, and QA that lane — not for buyers of translation services. It pairs with our parent cluster, How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying, which frames the client-facing conversation this guide produces against.

What is product localization from the translator's side of the desk?

Product localization is the end-to-end adaptation of a software product's strings, UI, formats, imagery, and regulatory text for a target locale, delivered by translators and agencies against a term base, locale style guide, translation memory, and an in-context review build the client ships. The translator does not touch marketing copy, support articles, or the website in this lane. Those are separate lanes with separate SLAs. The deliverable is a locale build that passes LQA and ships.

What are the key elements translators adapt in a product?

There are 6 elements translators adapt during product localization: UI strings, in-product copy, number and date formats, imagery and iconography, legal and regulatory boilerplate, and voice or audio assets where present.

  • UI strings — menu labels, buttons, tooltips, error messages.
  • In-product copy — onboarding, empty states, email templates triggered by the app.
  • Number, date, currency, phone, and address formats — resolved from locale IDs, not hard-coded.
  • Imagery and iconography — screenshots, flags, gestures, color-coded status indicators.
  • Legal and regulatory boilerplate — consent dialogs, data-processing notices, age gates per market.
  • Voice and audio assets — recorded VO, in-game dialog, synthesized prompts.

How is product localization different from translation, internationalization, and content localization?

Translation converts text; internationalization (i18n) prepares code to accept locales; product localization (l10n) ships the adapted build; content localization adapts the surrounding editorial, marketing, and support assets. The four are sequential and overlapping, not interchangeable. The foundational definition of localization versus translation is covered on Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds, so this page does not re-explain it.

  • Translation — converts source text to target text, no code or build involved.
  • Internationalization (i18n) — refactors code so the product can accept any locale.
  • Product localization (l10n) — adapts and ships the actual locale build.
  • Content localization — adapts marketing pages, support KB, and campaign assets; detailed in Content Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce It.

Where does product localization sit inside a broader localization program?

Product localization is one of 6 delivery lanes inside a broader localization program: product app, website, marketing content, support knowledge base, legal and compliance documents, and in-product video. Each lane carries its own SLA and reviewer pool. All six share one term base and one style guide per locale.

LanePrimary assetsShared with product lane
Product appUI strings, in-product copy, formats—
WebsitePages, nav, SEO metadataTerm base, style guide, TM
Marketing contentCampaigns, landing pages, adsTerm base, style guide, TM
Support KBHelp articles, release notesTerm base, style guide, TM
Legal and complianceToS, privacy, consent copyTerm base, locked segments inherited by product
In-product videoVO, captions, dubsTerm base, style guide

Related sibling lanes have their own canonical guides: Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide, Content Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce It, How Shopify Localization Works and What It Means for Your Agency, and How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.

Which artifacts does the product lane share with other lanes?

The product lane shares the term base and locale style guide with all five other lanes, and shares the translation memory with the website, support KB, and marketing content lanes. Legal and compliance keeps locked segments the product lane inherits unchanged.

  • Term base — one per locale, owned jointly by client PM and agency terminologist, shared across all six lanes.
  • Locale style guide — tone, register, formatting, forbidden phrasings, voice-of-brand examples per locale.
  • Translation memory (TM) — shared across product, website, support KB, and marketing lanes; drives repetition discounts.
  • Locked segments — regulated legal strings pass through from the compliance lane without edits.

Why us

How does product localization shorten time to market?

Product localization shortens time to market when the client ships continuously: strings land in the TMS the moment they are merged, translators work in-sprint against the review build, and the locale release trails the source release by hours rather than quarters. The pre-requisite is a translation management system wired to the source repo and a reviewer pool on standby per locale.

How does localized product QA reduce support ticket volume?

Localized product QA reduces support ticket volume by catching the two highest-ticket error classes before release: untranslated or truncated UI strings, and locale-wrong formats on dates, currency, phone, and address fields. Both are LQA fail categories at under 5 errors per 1,000 words.

  • Untranslated strings surfacing in a translated screen.
  • Truncated labels where German or Finnish expansion blows out a button.
  • Date formats showing MM/DD/YYYY to a DD/MM/YYYY market.
  • Currency defaulting to USD when the account is set to a non-US locale.
  • Phone and address fields that reject valid local formats.

How it works

How does the product localization process run from brief to release?

1

What internationalization prerequisites must be true before localization starts?

Internationalization is complete when 5 conditions hold in the source build: strings are externalized out of code, ICU plural and gender rules are declared, date, number, and currency formats resolve from locale IDs, right-to-left mirroring works end-to-end, and no copy is hard-coded in images or canvas.

  • Externalized strings — no literals in source files.
  • ICU plurals and gender — declared for every count and gendered noun.
  • Locale-driven formats — dates, numbers, currency, phone, address resolve from locale IDs.
  • RTL mirroring — layout, icons, and progress indicators flip for Arabic and Hebrew.
  • No baked copy — nothing rendered inside PNGs, SVGs, or canvas elements.

Common client stacks each need their own i18n pattern. See React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline and How to Add i18n to an Astro Site for two of the most common.

2

Which 5 kickoff artifacts does the translator receive on day one?

The translator receives 5 kickoff artifacts on day one: externalized source as XLIFF, JSON, or .strings; the translation memory for the language pair; the client term base for product names and regulated terminology; the locale style guide for tone, register, and formatting; and the in-context review build the client publishes.

ArtifactFormatOwnerPurpose
Externalized sourceXLIFF, JSON, .strings, .resx, .po, Android XML, iOS stringsdictClient engineeringTranslatable units flow into the TMS.
Translation memoryTMXAgencyPrior approved segments reused per language pair.
Term baseTBX or glossary CSVClient PM + agency terminologistProduct names and regulated terminology stay stable.
Locale style guidePDF or wikiAgency, approved by clientTone, register, forbidden phrasings per locale.
In-context review buildStaging URL, APK, or in-product overlayClient engineeringTranslator sees each string in-place.

The in-context review build is the single highest-ROI tool for the product lane — without it, truncation, context errors, and discoverability gaps slip past LQA. Pendo-style in-app overlays are one common review surface; see How Pendo Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.

3

How does in-sprint translation differ from waterfall handoff?

In-sprint translation pulls new and changed strings into the TMS on every merge, with target locales released hours behind source. Waterfall handoff batches all strings into a single export, translates offline, re-imports, and releases locales weeks or months after source.

  • In-sprint (continuous localization) — TMS webhook on merge, reviewer pool on standby, release trailing by hours.
  • Waterfall — single export per release cycle, offline translation, re-import, locales trail by weeks.

4

What does LQA look like at release and what are the pass thresholds?

LQA at release scores each locale per 1,000 words against a weighted MQM-style rubric covering accuracy, terminology, regulatory compliance, and readability, plus pass/fail checks on regulatory boilerplate and locked brand terms. Critical content passes under 2 errors per 1,000 words; standard content passes under 5.

  • Accuracy — mistranslation, omission, addition.
  • Terminology — term-base adherence.
  • Regulatory — locked segments present and unchanged.
  • Readability — grammar, register, locale conventions.
  • Usability (discoverability) — a translated feature must be reachable in-language.

Pricing

How do agencies price product localization?

Agencies price product localization in three per-word bands referenced from our Application Localization: The Translator's and Agency's Guide: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words. Engineering, in-context build hosting, and term-base governance are billed separately per locale.

ServiceDetails
Casual mobile title10,000 words, $1,500–$5,000 per language.
Mid-market SaaS50,000–150,000 words, mid-five figures per language.
AAA RPG with voice500,000+ words, seven figures across all locales.
Get a quote

What breaks a localized product after release and how do production teams respond?

Three failure classes break localized products after release: platform-update regressions, in-UI discoverability gaps, and region-specific feature rollouts that leave documentation lagging. Each class routes to a different owner on the production team.

How do platform updates break localized builds?

Platform updates break localized builds when a cumulative OS patch changes a dependency the localized binary relies on and the patch is not exposed in the standard uninstall UI. One field-reported case: a Windows KB-series cumulative update blocked a localized game launch and did not appear in Settings > Uninstall Updates, forcing teams to roll back through recovery tooling. The owner is the client's platform engineering team; the agency's role is to triage whether the regression is localization-related before escalation.

How do in-UI discoverability gaps surface in LQA?

In-UI discoverability gaps surface in LQA when a feature ships fully translated but is only findable via unlabeled tab positions or icon-only controls. One example: a Korean-language app whose character-appearance flow lives on the third (rightmost) tab inside a nested management panel, documented only in the source locale. The LQA report logs this as a usability error, not a translation error, and routes a UX fix back to the client.

How are region-specific rollouts handled when documentation lags?

Region-specific rollouts are handled by versioning the term base and release notes per market and feature-flagging strings in the TMS. A feature live in one region (for example a staking reward on a specific trading platform) is gated so untouched locales never display dangling or half-translated UI.

What examples show product localization working at scale?

Three product categories show localization at scale: streaming platforms, global SaaS, and games. Streaming platforms localize UI, metadata, subtitles, and dubs across 30+ locales. Global SaaS runs continuous localization against daily merges. Games pair in-sprint UI localization with batched voice recording per locale. Each pattern pairs a specific cadence to a specific LQA threshold.

  • Streaming — 30+ locales, continuous metadata, batched dub cycles, standard LQA threshold under 5 errors per 1,000 words.
  • Global SaaS — daily merges, in-sprint TMS pulls, release trailing by hours.
  • Games — in-sprint UI, batched VO per locale, critical content under 2 errors per 1,000 words for regulated markets.

High-filtering markets add their own constraints — see Chinese Localization: What Makes It Harder Than Most Projects.

pages.title: Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds
pages.h1: Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds
pages.meta_description: Pseudo localization replaces source strings with accented, expanded characters so engineers can catch i18n bugs before translators receive the files.
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is pseudo localization?
  • How does pseudo localization work on a source string?
  • What issues does pseudo localization catch before translation starts?
  • Which frameworks and engines support pseudo localization natively?
  • What does a pseudo-localized string actually look like?
  • Why do end users sometimes see pseudo-localized text on Xbox or Windows?
  • How does pseudo localization affect what translators and agencies receive?
  • Frequently asked questions

Pseudo localization sits inside the software internationalization pipeline as the engineering quality step that runs before any translator opens the source file. For translators and agencies working downstream, understanding this pass explains why some XLIFF handoffs arrive clean while others drag mid-sprint source edits across the project. This article reframes pseudo-loc for the people who receive the files, not the engineers who configure it, as one upstream stage inside How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying.

What is pseudo localization?

Pseudo localization is a software testing method that replaces source-language strings with accented, expanded, bracketed versions of the same text so engineers catch internationalization defects — hardcoded strings, truncated UI, broken encoding — before real translators receive the files. The transformation is mechanical, not linguistic. Every string is still semantically English after the pass.

The pass produces three visible effects on every resource string:

  • Character substitution: Latin letters swap for accented look-alikes (a→à, e→é).
  • Length padding: strings grow 30–50% longer than the source.
  • Bracket wrapping: markers such as [! … !] frame every translated key.

Why is pseudo localization not a real translation?

Pseudo localization is not a translation because no target language is involved. Every string stays semantically English and is only transformed visually. That is what lets engineers test the UI without waiting on a translator's turnaround, and it is why the pass costs nothing in translation hours.

How does pseudo localization relate to i18n and l10n?

Pseudo localization is the QA bridge between internationalization (i18n) and localization (l10n). Internationalization prepares the code to accept any locale. Localization produces the translated strings. Pseudo-loc verifies i18n readiness so l10n work is not wasted on broken resources. For a worked example of the i18n setup that pseudo-loc then validates, see How to Add i18n to an Astro Site.

How does pseudo localization work on a source string?

Pseudo localization works by running every source string through three transformations in sequence: character substitution, length padding, and bracket wrapping. Each transformation targets a specific defect class. The three together give engineers a single build they can inspect visually.

  1. Substitute each Latin character with an accented Unicode equivalent.
  2. Pad the string by 30–50% to simulate text expansion in target languages.
  3. Wrap the result in bracket markers so untouched text stands out.

How are characters substituted in pseudo localization?

Characters are substituted one-for-one with accented or decorated Unicode equivalents — 'Hello' becomes 'Ĥéļļö'. Readability is preserved for English-speaking testers. The renderer, font stack, and encoding path are forced to handle non-ASCII code points. Any pipeline that assumed ASCII breaks visibly during this pass.

How much are strings padded in pseudo localization, and why?

Strings are padded 30–50% longer than the source to simulate expansion in German, Finnish, and Russian translations. Those three languages routinely take significantly more characters to carry the same meaning. The padding blows out buttons, labels, and fixed-width columns in the test build, where a layout fix is cheap. A fix after translation is not.

What do the brackets and markers do in pseudo localization?

Each pseudo-localized string is wrapped in markers such as [! … !] or ⟦ … ⟧. Any text still appearing in plain English on screen is visibly a hardcoded string that bypassed the resource file. The marker turns a subtle bug into a flare the tester cannot miss.

What issues does pseudo localization catch before translation starts?

Pseudo localization catches four issue classes before translation starts: hardcoded strings that never reached the resource file, UI truncation from text expansion, broken character encoding, and concatenated strings that will not grammatically survive translation.

Issue classHow pseudo-loc exposes itWho fixes it
Hardcoded stringsText remains in plain English against bracketed accented textEngineering
UI truncationButtons, menus, tooltips clip under 30–50% paddingEngineering (layout)
Encoding failuresTofu boxes (□), mojibake, or missing glyphs appearEngineering (font / encoding)
Concatenation bugsTwo bracket pairs appear mid-sentenceEngineering (source rewrite)

How does pseudo-loc expose hardcoded strings?

Hardcoded strings are exposed because they remain in plain English while every resource-file string is visibly accented and bracketed. The untouched text is a visual flare for the engineer. For the translator downstream, the same bug means strings that would never have appeared in the XLIFF are now caught and routed to the resource file before handoff.

How does pseudo localization stress-test text expansion?

Pseudo-loc stress-tests expansion by inflating every string 30–50%. Truncated buttons, overflowed menus, and clipped tooltips surface in the test build. Layout fixes happen in code. They do not come back to the translator as late-stage reduction requests asking for a six-character German label.

What encoding and font failures does pseudo localization reveal?

Encoding and font failures surface as tofu boxes (□), mojibake, or missing glyphs. These appear wherever the UI's font or character pipeline cannot render accented and extended Latin characters. A font that lacks Cyrillic or diacritic coverage fails here, long before a real Russian or Polish translation lands in the build.

Why does pseudo localization flag concatenated strings?

Concatenated strings get flagged because pseudo-loc wraps each resource key independently. A sentence stitched from two keys shows two bracket pairs mid-sentence. That is a structural problem translators cannot fix inside a single segment — the source needs a rewrite into one key with a placeholder.

Which frameworks and engines support pseudo localization natively?

Pseudo localization is natively supported by Android, Unity3D, Symfony 5.2 and later, and Windows. Each framework exposes the pass differently, but the goal is identical: generate a build with accented, expanded, bracketed strings without producing a real translation. Web frameworks with similar i18n hooks follow the same downstream handoff pattern — see React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

FrameworkHow to enablePseudo-locale identifierNotes
AndroidpseudoLocalesEnabled true in build.gradle defaultConfigEnglish (XA), Arabic (XB)XB tests bidirectional (RTL) layout
Unity3DLocalization package, PseudoLocale classDerived from any source localeCreatePseudoLocale() and GetPseudoString() methods
Symfony 5.2+Built-in Pseudo-localization translator serviceRuntime wrapperApplies at runtime, source XLIFF untouched
Windowsqps-ploc / qps-plocm pseudo-localesqps-Ploc, qps-PlocmAvailable from Windows 8 build 7973 onward

How is pseudo localization enabled on Android?

On Android, pseudo localization is enabled by setting pseudoLocalesEnabled true in the defaultConfig block of build.gradle. The build generates two pseudo-locales: English (XA) for accented expansion and Arabic (XB) for bidirectional testing. Both appear in device Developer Options for selection.

How does Unity3D expose pseudo localization?

Unity3D exposes pseudo localization through the Localization package's PseudoLocale class. Engineers generate a pseudo-locale from any existing source locale and apply transformation rules without authoring a separate asset. The CreatePseudoLocale() and GetPseudoString() methods carry the configuration.

How does Symfony 5.2+ handle pseudo localization?

Symfony 5.2 introduced a built-in pseudo-localization translator. The translator wraps the standard service and applies accenting, expansion, and bracketing rules at runtime. The underlying XLIFF resources stay untouched, which keeps the source file clean for the translator who inherits it later.

What does pseudo localization look like on Windows (qps-ploc)?

On Windows, pseudo localization ships as the qps-ploc and qps-plocm pseudo-locales, supported from Windows 8 build 7973 onward. Build 7973 is the earliest OS-level pseudo-locale build on record. ASP.NET Core projects typically consume qps-ploc via the xliff-tasks package, which generates a qps-Ploc satellite resource assembly at build time.

What does a pseudo-localized string actually look like?

A pseudo-localized string takes the source — for example 'Save changes' — and renders it as '[!! Šàvé çĥåñĝéš !!]' with roughly 40% added padding. The three target behaviors are visible at a glance: character substitution in the letters, expansion in the padding exclamation marks, and bracketing in the outer frame.

More examples from a typical UI:

  • 'OK' → '[!! Öķ ķķ !!]'
  • 'Settings' → '[!! Šéţţîñĝš ššš !!]'
  • 'Log in' → '[!! Ļöĝ îñ îîñ !!]'
  • 'Delete account' → '[!! Ðéļéţé àççöûñţ ààç !!]'

How are source English characters mapped to pseudo characters?

Source English characters are mapped to pseudo characters through a fixed substitution table. Typical mappings include a→à, e→é, i→î, o→ö, u→ü, A→Å, E→Ë, I→Ï, O→Ø, U→Ú. Each glyph stays readable to an English-speaking tester. Non-ASCII code points are forced through the rendering stack on every character.

Why do end users sometimes see pseudo-localized text on Xbox or Windows?

End users occasionally see pseudo-localized text on Xbox or Windows because a preview or beta build shipped with the pseudo-locale accidentally enabled. The device is not hacked, infected, or corrupted. It is running a build that Microsoft or a game studio uses for internal i18n QA, and the locale selector landed on qps-ploc instead of a shipping language.

Is pseudo-loc text a sign the device is hacked?

Pseudo-loc text is not a sign the device is hacked. It is a deliberate test transformation that occasionally leaks into preview channels. The symptoms resolve when the build switches the locale back to a shipping language, or when the next preview update ships. For translators and agencies, the practical read is that pseudo-loc has entered mainstream consumer awareness — expect occasional client questions about it.

How does pseudo localization affect what translators and agencies receive?

Pseudo localization affects translators and agencies by shaping the quality of the XLIFF they receive. A project that ran pseudo-loc arrives with fewer hardcoded strings, pre-sized UI containers, and documented expansion limits. A project that skipped it typically returns to the translator with mid-sprint truncation fixes and late-stage source edits.

What a clean upstream pseudo-loc pass delivers to the translator:

  • Resource files that contain the full user-visible string set, with hardcoded strings already pulled into keys.
  • UI containers already sized for 30–50% expansion, so no reduction requests mid-project.
  • Encoding and font coverage already verified for the target scripts.
  • Concatenated sentences already rewritten into single keys with placeholders.

Reddit Engineering, among others, uses pseudo-localization in its localization pipeline to preemptively verify UI comfort across target languages before translators engage. The practice is standard across teams with mature i18n discipline.

How should a translator read a pseudo-loc QA report?

A translator reads a pseudo-loc QA report by sorting findings into three buckets: hardcoded-string tickets, expansion/truncation tickets, and concatenation tickets. Each bucket needs a different response.

  1. Hardcoded-string tickets: engineering fix only. No translation work needed until the string is extracted into the resource file. Flag back to the project manager and move on.
  2. Expansion/truncation tickets: UI fix on the engineering side, sometimes paired with a shorter target request. Confirm the character budget before shortening.
  3. Concatenation tickets: source rewrite needed before translation proceeds. Do not attempt to translate a fragment that will be stitched to another fragment at runtime.

What should agencies ask the client before kickoff?

Agencies ask three questions that preempt the majority of mid-project source churn:

  • Has a pseudo-localization pass run against the current source?
  • Are the resulting defects closed in the build the XLIFF came from?
  • Does the XLIFF handoff reflect the post-fix source, or an earlier snapshot?

A client that answers yes, yes, yes delivers a project that runs on the quoted timeline. A client that cannot answer the questions is a client whose translators will absorb the i18n debt mid-sprint. Price the project accordingly.

Pseudo localization is a software testing pass that transforms source strings into accented, 30–50% longer, bracketed versions to expose hardcoded strings, truncation, and encoding bugs before real translation begins.

Frequently asked questions

What does "i18n" mean?

"i18n" is a numeronym for "internationalization" — the 18 stands for the 18 letters between the first "i" and the last "n." In software development, internationalization means engineering a product so it can be adapted to any locale without code changes — handling variable text expansion, right-to-left scripts, Unicode character sets, date/number formats, and more. It is the technical foundation that makes localization (l10n) possible. Translators encounter it because i18n quality directly affects how cleanly strings can be extracted, translated, and re-integrated.

What is 18 in i18n?

The 18 in i18n represents the 18 letters between the "i" and the "n" in the word "internationalization." This shorthand — called a numeronym — follows the same pattern as "l10n" for localization and "a11y" for accessibility. It originated in engineering communities as a compact way to write long technical terms in tickets, configs, and code comments. Translators working on software projects will see it in build notes, style guides, and pseudo-localization documentation.

What is pseudo-localization and why is it showing up in my app/game/OS?

Pseudo-localization is a software testing technique that automatically replaces source-language strings with accented or extended characters (e.g., "Hello" → "Ħēļļö") to simulate a translated build without real translations. Developers use it to expose UI bugs — truncated text, hardcoded strings, layout breaks — before actual localization begins. If you see strange-looking but still readable text in an app, game, or OS, you are almost certainly running a developer or pre-release build that has pseudo-loc enabled. It is not a sign of a virus or hack; it is an intentional engineering tool.

Why is unlocalized text highlighted in pseudo-loc builds?

Unlocalized (hardcoded) strings appear unhighlighted or unchanged in pseudo-loc builds precisely so developers can spot them instantly. Pseudo-localization transforms every string that flows through the proper localization pipeline, so any text that remains in plain source-language characters has bypassed that pipeline and is hardcoded — a bug. This visual contrast is the core value of the technique: testers can scan a screen and flag unhardcoded strings in minutes rather than combing through source code manually. For translators, it explains why clients sometimes share pseudo-loc screenshots when reporting untranslatable strings.

Is pseudo-loc text a sign my device is hacked or infected?

No — pseudo-localized text is a deliberate developer testing feature, not malware. It appears when a device runs a pre-release, beta, or developer-mode build that has the pseudo-localization flag enabled. The accented and extended characters are generated by the OS or app framework itself (Android, Unity, Windows, etc.) as part of the localization QA process. If you see it on a consumer device, you most likely enrolled in a beta program or sideloaded a test build. A standard factory reset or leaving the beta channel will restore normal text.

What's the difference between translation and localization?

Translation converts text from one language to another, while localization adapts an entire product — content, UI, formats, imagery, and cultural references — so it feels native to a target market. A translation of a date might render "March 5, 2025" in Spanish; localization also changes the format to "5 de marzo de 2025" and adjusts currency symbols, measurement units, and legal disclaimers. In certified translation production, localization considerations matter because the same document may need culturally adapted formatting alongside linguistically accurate rendering to be accepted by target-country authorities.

What does localization mean in translation?

In translation, localization means adapting a translated text so it conforms to the linguistic conventions, cultural norms, and regulatory expectations of the target locale — not just converting words. This includes adjusting idioms, honorifics, number formats, legal terminology, and even document layout. For certified translations specifically, localization ensures that rendered dates, addresses, titles, and official terms match the format a receiving institution (court, embassy, university) expects, which is critical for acceptance. It goes beyond word-for-word accuracy to functional equivalence in context.

What does "localization" mean?

Localization (abbreviated l10n) is the process of adapting a product, document, or service to meet the language, cultural, and regulatory requirements of a specific target locale. It covers everything from translating text and adjusting date/currency formats to redesigning layouts for right-to-left scripts and ensuring legal compliance in the target market. In the translation industry, localization applies both to software (apps, websites) and to documents — including certified translations that must reflect the conventions of the issuing and receiving countries.

What is another term for localization?

"L10n" is the standard industry abbreviation, and "adaptation" or "transcreation" are terms used for creative or marketing content where cultural reinterpretation goes beyond linguistic conversion. In software contexts, localization is sometimes called "language support" or "regional adaptation." In the translation industry, the closest formal equivalent is "locale-specific translation," though most style guides and ISO standards (such as ISO 9001 for translation services) simply use "localization" as the accepted term.

What does software localization mean?

Software localization means adapting a software product — its UI strings, help content, error messages, date/time formats, and layout — so it functions correctly and naturally for users in a specific locale. It follows internationalization (i18n), which prepares the codebase to accept locale-specific assets. For translators, software localization projects involve working inside CAT tools or translation management systems with string files (e.g., .po, .xliff, .resx), respecting character limits, and understanding context provided by screenshots or pseudo-loc builds — which is directly relevant to understanding i18n test artifacts.
