pages.title: Squarespace Localization: How Translators Deliver Multilingual Squarespace Sites
pages.h1: Squarespace Localization: How Translators Deliver Multilingual Squarespace Sites
pages.meta_description: Squarespace localization is the translator's workflow for producing multilingual Squarespace sites: scope the gap, route via Weglot or duplicate-page builds
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is Squarespace localization from the translator's side of the desk?
  • Can Squarespace handle multilingual sites natively?
  • Which production lanes do translators use to localize a Squarespace site?
  • How does the translator handle URLs, hreflang, and the language switcher on Squarespace?
  • What does the translator actually localize on a Squarespace page?
  • How does the translator price a Squarespace localization project?
  • How does the translator QA a Squarespace localized site before release?
  • How does Squarespace localization compare to Webflow for the same client?
  • Frequently asked questions

Squarespace has no native multilingual mode, so every translator project runs on one of three production lanes: a Weglot-routed build, a duplicate-page build, or a headless-export workflow. This guide covers the decision matrix, the hreflang rules, the priced quoting model, and the LQA gates — scoped to American English production practice and ISO 17100-aligned release criteria.

What is Squarespace localization from the translator's side of the desk?

Squarespace localization is the translator's end-to-end workflow for producing a fully functional multilingual Squarespace site — routing content through Weglot or a duplicate-page build because Squarespace ships with no native multilingual mode, then applying hreflang, per-locale metadata, and structured QA gates before go-live. The scope sits inside the broader program covered in Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.

From the translator's chair, Squarespace localization is a platform-constraint problem as much as a language problem. Because the platform provides no built-in locale switcher, no per-locale field, and no automatic hreflang emission, the translator is responsible for every layer of locale structure that a more capable CMS would handle invisibly. That responsibility has real scope: a five-language site at 50,000 source words is a mid-size program that runs

Squarespace localization is the translator's workflow for producing a multilingual Squarespace site, routing content through Weglot or a duplicate-page build because Squarespace has no native multilingual mode, then applying hreflang, locale metadata, and QA gates. The scope sits inside the broader program covered in Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project.

On the production side, the translator owns six deliverables on every Squarespace project:

  • Translated body copy, headings, and button labels across every page.
  • Per-locale metadata — title tag, meta description, Open Graph image.
  • Per-locale image alt text and, where needed, swapped image assets.
  • URL slugs that read natively in the target locale.
  • Hreflang pairs using ISO 639-1 and optional ISO 3166-1 codes.
  • A language switcher wired into the header navigation.

5,000–$75,000 end-to-end once translation, review, LQA, and project management are priced in.

On the production side, the translator owns six concrete deliverables on every Squarespace project:

  • Translated body copy, headings, and button labels across every page.
  • Per-locale metadata — title tag, meta description, Open Graph fields.
  • Per-locale image alt text and, where needed, swapped image assets.
  • URL slugs that read natively in the target locale (e.g., /es/nosotros/ rather than /es/about/).
  • Hreflang pairs written with ISO 639-1 language codes and optional ISO 3166-1 country codes — es-MX, pt-BR, fr-CA — including a self-referential alternate on every page.
  • A language switcher wired into the header navigation, labeled in native script, with no flag icons.

Each deliverable maps to a specific platform touchpoint — a Weglot segment, a Code Injection block, a page's SEO panel — and every one of them requires the translator to act as both linguist and platform operator. The translator who understands which deliverables live where ships cleaner work and avoids the QA defects that most commonly plague Squarespace localization projects.

Can Squarespace handle multilingual sites natively?

Squarespace does not handle multilingual sites natively: there is no built-in locale switcher, no per-locale content field, and no automatic hreflang emission anywhere in the platform. Every translator project — regardless of size — runs on a third-party integration or a manual duplicate-page build to fill that structural gap.

This is a meaningful constraint that shapes every scoping conversation. The platform does localize a small set of commerce and formatting settings by default, but the assets that actually make a site multilingual — page content, URL slugs, metadata, image alt text, and hreflang — are entirely outside native support. Translators who scope a Squarespace project without accounting for this gap routinely under-quote the PM effort required to wire locale structure together by hand.

What does Squarespace localize natively, and what does it miss?

Squarespace natively localizes the site language setting, date formats, and currency on Commerce; it misses per-locale pages, slugs, image alt text, CMS collection fields, metadata, and hreflang emission entirely. The table below is the translator's checklist of what the platform does not localize and the recommended workaround per field.

AssetNative per-locale supportTranslator workaround
Site language settingYesSet at install; no production work required.
Date and currency formatYes (Commerce)Verify correctness per locale during QA.
Page body copyNoWeglot segment editor or duplicate page.
URL slugsNoWeglot slug override or manual slug on duplicate.
Metadata (title, description, OG)NoPer-page SEO panel override via Weglot or duplicate.
Image alt textNoWeglot alt override or duplicate image block edit.
CMS collection fieldsNoWeglot collection sync or duplicate collection.
Product title, description, variantsNoWeglot product sync or duplicate store.
Hreflang emissionNoWeglot automatic or Code Injection on duplicate-page lane.
Language switcherNoWeglot widget or manual header link in native script.

Why does the native gap matter even for a 4-page family business site?

The native gap matters on a 4-page family business site because even the simplest bilingual build needs a language switcher, two distinct URL paths, two complete sets of metadata, and correctly formed hreflang pairs — none of which Squarespace ships out of the box. Hreflang pairs must be written using ISO 639-1 language codes combined with optional ISO 3166-1 country codes — formats such as es-MX, pt-BR, and fr-CA — and each page must carry a self-referential alternate alongside the cross-locale alternates. The translator owns that full locale structure on a 4-page site exactly as they own it on a 400-page site; only the volume changes, never the structural obligation.

Practically, this means the project kick-off for any Squarespace localization engagement — however small — must confirm which production lane handles hreflang injection, who owns the language switcher placement, and how per-locale slugs will be maintained as the client updates content over time. Getting those decisions on paper before translation begins prevents rework that is expensive to fix once a site is live.

Which production lanes do translators use to localize a Squarespace site?

Translators use three production lanes on Squarespace: the Weglot-routed lane for most multilingual builds, the duplicate-page lane for small bilingual sites with manual translation, and a headless-export lane for agencies that need TM leverage and CAT-tool integration. The cross-platform context sits in CMS Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce Multilingual Content Across Platforms.

The choice of lane is a consequential scoping decision because it determines SEO architecture, ongoing maintenance burden, client subscription costs, and the translator's own toolchain. Picking the wrong lane — most often choosing duplicate-page on a 25-page site — is the single largest source of budget overruns on Squarespace localization projects.

The decision matrix below scores each lane against the variables that matter most at scoping time:

VariableWeglot-routedDuplicate-pageHeadless export
Word count sweet spot1,500–50,000+Under 2,50015,000+
Page count sweet spot10+Up to ~10Any
Template complexityAnySimple layoutsAny
SEO ambitionHigh — automatic hreflang and subdirectory URLsLow to mediumHigh
Client budget profileSaaS subscription fee plus production costLowest total cash outlayHighest setup cost; best TM leverage over time
Maintenance as content growsAutomatic string detectionManual on every editPipeline re-run required

How does the Weglot-routed lane work inside the Squarespace dashboard?

The Weglot-routed lane installs the official Squarespace extension directly from the Squarespace dashboard, scans the site for translatable strings, auto-generates subdirectory URLs per locale — /fr/, /es/, /de/ — injects an automatic hreflang block on every page, and exposes a segment-level translation editor where translators post-edit AI output or translate from source. Subdirectory routing is the preferred URL structure for Squarespace multilingual sites because it keeps the root domain's authority intact and is more reliably indexed than subdomain alternatives. The production steps are deterministic:

  1. Client installs the extension from the Squarespace dashboard Extensions panel and connects a Weglot account; the client owns and pays the subscription.
  2. Weglot scans every published page and extracts source strings into a segment editor, organized by page URL.
  3. The translator post-edits machine-translated drafts or clears segments and translates from source against glossary and style guide.
  4. Metadata, URL slugs, and image alt text are localized in dedicated tabs within the same editor — no separate platform panel required.
  5. Weglot emits hreflang pairs using the correct ISO 639-1 and ISO 3166-1 code format on every page automatically, including the self-referential alternate.
  6. The language switcher is placed in the header navigation via Weglot's widget settings, labeled in native script with no flag icons.

How does the duplicate-page lane work for a manual bilingual build?

The duplicate-page lane copies each Squarespace page into a second-language version organized under a /fr/ or /es/ folder, then swaps the body copy, metadata, and image alt text manually — a method that is viable up to roughly 10 pages before maintenance overhead makes it impractical. Beyond that page threshold, every client content edit must be replicated by hand across every locale, and the probability of desynchronized pages climbs rapidly. Production steps for the duplicate-page lane are:

  1. Duplicate each primary-locale page in the Squarespace Pages panel.
  2. Move the duplicates into a new folder named with the target language's ISO 639-1 code (/fr/, /es/).
  3. Translate body copy, button labels, form field labels, metadata, and image alt text in each duplicate page.
  4. Rewrite URL slugs in the target locale so they read natively — /es/nosotros/, not /es/about/.
  5. Add header navigation links pairing each source page with its locale sibling so users can switch between versions.
  6. Inject hreflang alternates via Code Injection in Settings → Advanced, covering every locale pair and the self-referential alternate.

Template selection affects how smoothly this lane runs. Layouts with clean structural separation between content blocks — such as Forte, Impact, and Brine — make duplicate-page edits more predictable, because body copy is visually isolated from design chrome and less likely to produce formatting breakage when swapped.

When does the headless-export lane make sense for an agency?

The headless-export lane is the right choice when an agency runs volumes above 15,000 words, holds an existing translation memory for the client, or needs repeatable pipeline leverage across multiple Squarespace builds. In this lane, translators export page HTML and metadata, process segments in a CAT tool against the TM and terminology base, and push results back as duplicate pages or via the integration API. The upfront setup cost is higher than either alternative lane, but TM reuse on large or recurring programs reduces per-word cost substantially over the project lifetime. Agencies whose Squarespace clients also run React or Next.js front ends can mirror this pipeline architecture per React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

How do these three lanes compare on cost, scale, and SEO?

The three lanes split cleanly along the dimensions of scale, SEO automation, and cost structure: the Weglot-routed lane wins on SEO automation and scale above 10 pages, the duplicate-page lane wins on total cash outlay under 10 pages with no SaaS subscription, and the headless-export lane wins on TM leverage and CAT-tool integration above 15,000 words. Translation rates for Squarespace projects run $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review runs $0.04–$0.08 per source word, and project management typically adds 10–15% of total project value — costs that apply across all three lanes and must be quoted before lane selection, not after.

What we offer

How does the translator handle URLs, hreflang, and the language switcher on Squarespace?

On Squarespace, the translator routes locales as subdirectories (via Weglot) or as duplicate URL trees, emits hreflang pairs using ISO 639-1 language codes plus optional ISO 3166-1 country codes written as es-MX, pt-BR, fr-CA, and places the language switcher in the header navigation. The ranking mechanics are covered in Localization SEO: How Translators Make Localized Pages Rank.

What does the translator actually localize on a Squarespace page?

On a Squarespace page the translator localizes seven asset types: body copy in text blocks, headings and buttons, metadata (title, description, Open Graph), image alt text, product and blog fields, URL slugs, and template-level labels baked into the chosen Squarespace template.

How does the translator handle Squarespace templates and typography across locales?

Squarespace templates like Forte, Impact, and Brine ship Latin-script typography that breaks under German string expansion, Arabic right-to-left flow, and CJK line-height, so the translator flags font swaps, image-text separation, and parallax reflows during the design-QA pass. Template-level notes:

  • Forte — high-contrast serif headings crack under German expansion of 25–35%; nav items wrap to two lines. Fix: tighten letter-spacing and shorten source copy before translation.
  • Impact — clean sans headings handle Arabic once the site language flips to RTL in Design settings; buttons with icons need mirrored padding.
  • Brine — parallax hero sections hard-code image heights; CJK line-height pushes copy below the fold and clips the background image. Fix: swap parallax for a static hero on CJK locales.

What does the translator do with images that contain embedded text?

Images containing embedded text get flagged as a locale blocker. The translator either requests a layered source file from the designer to re-export per locale, or recommends swapping the image for a text block over a plain background. The second path is the Squarespace best practice because it lets Weglot or the duplicate-page method localize the string natively.

How are product fields and blog posts localized on Squarespace Commerce?

On Squarespace Commerce the translator localizes product title, description, variant labels, and category pages one by one — Commerce has no bulk per-locale field editor, so Weglot's product sync or a duplicate-store build are the only two production routes. CMS collections (blog posts, portfolio entries) follow the same rule: no native per-locale CMS editor, routed through Weglot or duplicate collections.

Pricing

How does the translator price a Squarespace localization project?

A Squarespace localization project is priced in four line items the agency already uses on other lanes: translation at $0.10–$0.25 per source word, review at $0.04–$0.08 per word, LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and project management at 10–15% of project value. The Weglot subscription stays on the client's billing to avoid resale markup.

Line itemUnitUS band
Translationper source word$0.10–$0.25
Reviewper source word$0.04–$0.08
LQAper 1,000 words$40–$90
Project managementshare of project value10–15%

What does a 4-page family-business bilingual Squarespace build cost?

A 4-page family-business bilingual build with roughly 1,200 source words prices at $120–$300 for translation, $48–$96 for review, $48–$108 for LQA, and $30–$75 PM — a total envelope of $246–$579 before any Weglot subscription fee the client pays separately. The worked example assumes one target locale, no CMS collections, and the duplicate-page lane.

What does a 50,000-word, 5-locale Squarespace program cost?

A 50,000-word Squarespace program across 5 locales budgets at $25,000–$75,000 end to end depending on TM leverage, turnaround, and whether certified sign-off is in scope. AI pre-translate shifts the mix toward review at $0.04–$0.08 per word and LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words rather than raw translation.

Get a quote

How does the translator QA a Squarespace localized site before release?

Squarespace QA is a two-gate process: a linguistic review pass followed by a structured LQA sample, with a separate round of template-layer checks that are specific to how Squarespace renders translated content across its block-based layouts.

The review gate runs at $0.04–$0.08 per source word and checks every translated segment against the source string, the approved glossary, and the client style guide. A reviewer on a Squarespace project is not simply reading for fluency — they are also confirming that button labels, form placeholders, navigation items, and footer strings have all been captured, because Squarespace surfaces these strings in separate locations from body copy and they are routinely missed on a first translation pass.

The LQA gate samples the translated output at $40–$90 per 1,000 words and scores defects against an MQM-style typology aligned to ISO 17100 — covering accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style. The sample size is set by word volume and risk tier; a Commerce site with localized product pages warrants a larger LQA sample than a brochure site because pricing, legal disclaimers, and call-to-action copy carry higher defect cost.

Which Squarespace-specific defects does LQA catch most often?

LQA on Squarespace most often catches five template-layer failures that linguistic review alone does not reliably surface, because they require rendering the page in a browser rather than reading segments in an editor:

  1. String overflow in header navigation on German, Finnish, and other morphologically rich locales — languages that expand significantly from an English source string can break the navigation bar layout entirely.
  2. Untranslated button labels inherited from the template's hard-coded strings, which Weglot's scanner may not detect if they are rendered via JavaScript after initial page load.
  3. Missing hreflang self-references on duplicate-page builds, where the Code Injection block was added to source pages but not propagated to every locale folder page.
  4. Broken or English URL slugs on duplicate pages — for example, /es/about/ surviving instead of being rewritten to /es/nosotros/ — which degrades both user experience and search indexing.
  5. English alt text left on hero images because the translator worked only in the segment editor and did not open the Image Block settings panel where Squarespace stores alt text separately from the main string inventory.

Each of these defects is detectable with a structured browser-based walkthrough checklist that the QA reviewer runs against every locale before sign-off. Building that checklist into the standard QA workflow — rather than treating it as optional — is what separates professional Squarespace localization delivery from amateur builds that go live with visible errors.

How does Squarespace localization compare to Webflow for the same client?

Squarespace localization and Webflow localization solve the same multilingual problem through fundamentally different platform architectures, and that architectural difference has direct consequences for how a translator scopes, prices, and executes the same client's multilingual program depending on which platform they are working in.

Squarespace localization relies entirely on third-party routing — primarily through an officially installed extension or a manual duplicate-page build — because the platform ships with no native per-locale fields, no locale switcher in the editor canvas, and no automatic hreflang emission. Webflow Localization, by contrast, exposes a locale switcher directly in the editor, per-locale text fields on both static and CMS content, per-locale assets, slugs, SEO metadata, alt text, and visibility toggles as native platform features. A translator producing multilingual output on Webflow is operating inside the platform's designed localization system; a translator producing multilingual output on Squarespace is engineering around a gap that the platform's designers never filled.

The practical effect on quoting is that Webflow projects carry lower project management overhead — the locale structure the translator would otherwise build by hand is already present — while Squarespace projects require PM budget for lane setup, hreflang injection, switcher configuration, and ongoing content synchronization. Project management on a localization program typically runs 10–15% of total project value, and on a Squarespace engagement that percentage is more likely to reach the top of that band than on a Webflow engagement of equivalent word volume.

SurfaceSquarespaceWebflow Localization
Locale switcher in editorNo — third-party extension onlyNative, top of canvas
Per-locale text fieldsNoNative on static and CMS content
Per-locale assetsNoNative
Per-locale slugsNoNative
Per-locale SEO fieldsNoNative — title, description, Open Graph
Per-locale alt textNoNative
Per-locale visibility toggleNoNative
Automatic hreflang emissionVia extension onlyNative
CMS per-locale editorNoNative via Localization panel
Language switcherExtension widget or manual header linkNative component

For a translator advising a client who has not yet committed to a platform, this comparison is a legitimate part of the professional conversation. A client whose site has more than 10 pages, targets three or more locales, and has high SEO ambition is likely to get better long-term value — and lower total localization cost across repeated content cycles — from the platform with native locale architecture built in. The deep dive on the Webflow side sits in How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.

The questions below cover the four scenarios translators and small-business owners hit most often when adding a second language to a Squarespace site: native capability, bilingual family-business setup, managing multiple language pages, and the Weglot-free workaround.

Frequently asked questions

Can Squarespace handle multilingual sites natively?

Squarespace does not have a built-in multilingual CMS in the way that WordPress or Webflow do. It has no native language-switcher or translation management system. Translators and agencies working on Squarespace localization projects must therefore replicate content manually — typically by duplicating pages or entire sections for each target language, then translating and adapting them. Some teams layer in third-party tools such as Weglot or Bablic to automate string detection, but those add cost and introduce a separate workflow to manage alongside the translation itself.

How do I add a second language to my Squarespace website?

The standard approach is to duplicate existing pages and replace the content with translated text for each target language. Because Squarespace lacks a native translation layer, translators typically export text strings manually, translate them (using CAT tools or a first-draft SaaS to speed up certified or professional translation), then paste the translated copy back into the duplicated pages. A language-selector folder in the navigation bar is then used to let visitors switch between language versions. For sites needing certified accuracy — such as legal or medical content — all translated pages should go through a qualified reviewer before publishing.

What's the best way to manage multiple language pages in Squarespace?

The most reliable workflow for translators and agencies is a structured folder-and-page system combined with a rigorous file-naming convention. Create a top-level navigation folder per language (e.g., /en/, /fr/, /de/), duplicate source pages into the appropriate folder, and translate the content using your standard CAT or TMS pipeline before importing it back. Keep a translation memory and glossary active throughout so terminology stays consistent across all language versions. For certified translation projects, version-control your source and target files externally, since Squarespace itself offers no revision history for page content.

Does Squarespace support multilingual?

Squarespace supports multilingual sites only through manual workarounds, not through a dedicated multilingual feature. There is no built-in locale setting, hreflang tag generator, or language-switcher component in the core platform. Translators delivering multilingual Squarespace builds must manually add hreflang tags via custom code injection and build language navigation by hand. Third-party plugins like Weglot can automate some of this, but they sit outside Squarespace's editor, creating a split between what the client sees in the CMS and what appears on the live site.

How do I make my website multilingual?

Making a Squarespace site multilingual requires three parallel workstreams: content translation, structural duplication, and technical SEO setup. First, a professional translator (or a SaaS that generates certified first drafts) produces accurate target-language content. Second, that content is placed into duplicated pages organized under language-specific navigation folders. Third, hreflang attributes are injected via Squarespace's custom code blocks so search engines serve the correct language version by region. For certified document pages — such as legal disclaimers or compliance content — ensure the translator's credentials and certification statement are reflected in the site copy.

Why is a website defaulting to a different language?

A Squarespace site defaults to an unintended language most often because hreflang tags are missing, misconfigured, or absent entirely. Without correct hreflang annotations, search engines guess the target locale from IP address and browser language headers, which can surface the wrong language version to users. On Squarespace, where hreflang must be added manually through code injection rather than a CMS setting, it is easy to miss tags when new pages are added. Translators handing off multilingual Squarespace projects should include a technical checklist confirming that every translated page has a corresponding hreflang tag pointing back to all other language variants.

What is the downside to Squarespace?

For translation and localization work specifically, Squarespace's biggest downside is its lack of a content API or native TMS integration, which forces manual copy-paste workflows. Unlike headless CMS platforms that expose content via API for easy extraction into CAT tools, Squarespace requires translators to scrape or manually extract source text, translate it, and re-enter it page by page. This increases turnaround time and the risk of omissions. For agencies delivering certified translations at scale, this manual overhead is significant and should be factored into project scoping and pricing.

Is Squarespace a no-code platform?

Squarespace is primarily a no-code website builder, but multilingual localization almost always requires at least some custom code. Basic site building — adding pages, images, and text blocks — requires no coding knowledge. However, implementing hreflang tags, language switchers, and locale-aware redirects on Squarespace requires injecting HTML or JavaScript into the platform's code blocks. Translators and agencies delivering fully localized Squarespace sites should either include a developer in the project team or clearly scope which technical elements fall outside the translation deliverable.
pages.excerpt: Squarespace localization is the translator's workflow for producing multilingual Squarespace sites: scope the gap, route via Weglot or duplicate-page builds, and ship hreflang-correct locales.

pages.title: Storyblok Localization: How Translators Produce Field-Level Multilingual Content
pages.h1: Storyblok Localization: How Translators Produce Field-Level Multilingual Content
pages.meta_description: Storyblok localization uses field-level or folder-level translation exposed via the Content Delivery API. Translators receive JSON exports or TMS connector jobs
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • Key points
  • What is Storyblok localization from the translator's side of the desk?
  • Field-level or folder-level — which Storyblok localization model is the project using?
  • What does a translator receive at the start of a Storyblok localization project?
  • How does Storyblok's Content Delivery API serve localized content to the front-end?
  • Which Storyblok fields are translatable and which trip translators up?
  • How do translators price and quote a Storyblok localization project?
  • Native Storyblok translation vs the Translate Fields app vs third-party TMS connectors — which workflow fits?
  • What does the translator hand back, and how is it reviewed in Storyblok?
  • How does Storyblok localization compare to other headless CMS and page-builder platforms?
  • How we work on Storyblok projects
  • Frequently asked questions

Storyblok sits inside the broader headless-CMS localization pattern covered How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying, but its field-level and folder-level split changes what lands on the translator's desk. This page explains the model from the production side: what the deliverable looks like, how to price it, and where the LQA gate blocks publish.

Key points

  • Storyblok is a Headless CMS with Visual Editor, built on Bloks (components) composed into Stories inside Spaces — a structure that directly shapes how translatable content is packaged and delivered to localization teams.
  • Storyblok offers two localization models: field-level translation (per-locale values stored on a single Story using Dimensions) and folder-level translation (a parallel Story tree per locale folder). The content architect's choice determines whether the translator receives per-field JSON or a mirrored folder hierarchy.
  • The five required translator intake artifacts are: the source content export, a translation memory (TM) for the language pair, the client term base, a locale style guide, and staging Space access via a Preview token.
  • Translation is priced at $0.10–$0.25 per source word; review runs $0.04–$0.08 per source word. A mid-size program spanning five languages and 50,000 words costs Storyblok offers two localization models — field-level (Dimensions) and folder-level — and the content architect's choice decides whether the translator receives per-field JSON or a parallel Story tree.
  • The translator intake maps to five artifacts: Space access, Dimensions config, Blok schema, Preview token, and Visual Editor review URL.
  • Storyblok jobs are quoted by translatable-field count × Blok instances × target locales, not by page count or Story count.
  • LQA runs at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 and blocks publish on certified lanes.
  • Un-translated slugs produce /es/english-slug URLs that split SEO signal — a defect LQA must catch before the locale goes live.

5,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage, turnaround, and certification requirements.

  • LQA runs at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 and blocks publish on certified lanes.
  • Native Translation Jobs export as XLIFF or JSON for round-trip handoff; TMS connectors for platforms such as Smartling, Lokalise, Phrase, and Crowdin support continuous localization at scale.
  • Un-translated slugs produce locale-prefixed URLs that carry the source-language slug — a defect that splits SEO signal and must be caught by LQA before the locale goes live.

    • What is Storyblok localization from the translator's side of the desk?

    Storyblok localization is the field-level or folder-level translation of Blok content inside a Storyblok Space, where translatable fields are exposed per locale through the Content Delivery API's language parameter and delivered to translators as JSON exports, Translation Jobs, or TMS connector tickets rather than visual-editor edits. Translators work on externalized content, not inside the editor.

    Storyblok is a headless CMS with a Visual Editor, built on Bloks (components) composed into Stories inside Spaces. The translator never authors in the Visual Editor; the editor is a review surface reached through the staging Preview token.

    Three terms disambiguate the model buyers confuse most often:

    TermWhat it isWhen the translator meets it
    DimensionsField-level locale mechanism on one StoryFlat per-field JSON deliverable
    Folder-levelParallel Story tree per locale (/es/, /de/)Full Story-by-Story deliverable
    Translate Fields appIn-editor MT seeding for post-editingMTPE rates plus LQA still apply
    TMS connectorAutomated sync to Smartling, Lokalise, Phrase, CrowdinJobs appear in the agency's existing CAT environment

    Field-level or folder-level — which Storyblok localization model is the project using?

    Storyblok offers two localization models — field-level and folder-level — and the content architect, not the translator, picks one. Field-level stores per-locale values on a single Story; folder-level duplicates the Story tree inside a locale folder. The choice decides the deliverable shape before the first word is translated.

    flowchart TD
 A[Client content architect decides] --> B{Field-level or folder-level?}
 B -- Field-level --> C[Dimensions on one Story]
 B -- Folder-level --> D[Parallel Story tree per locale]
 C --> E[Translator receives per-field JSON diff]
 D --> F[Translator receives parallel Stories]
 E --> G[LQA $40–$90 per 1,000 words]
 F --> G
 G --> H[Publish to live locale]

    The decision matrix below maps each architecture to the translator's deliverable shape and the risk class the agency must scope for:

    SetupDeliverable shapeRisk to flag
    Field-level (Dimensions)Per-field JSON diff keyed by language codeNested Bloks in richtext silently fall back
    Folder-levelParallel Story tree per locale folderBlok UUID drift breaks references
    Mixed (field-level with structural variants)Per-field JSON plus locale-only StoriesScope creep from un-flagged structural fields

    How does field-level translation shape the translator's deliverable?

    Field-level translation stores every localizable field with per-language values on the same Story. Translators receive a JSON export or TMS job containing only the translatable fields keyed by language code (en, es, de). The Content Delivery API returns the correct value when queried with the language parameter.

    The deliverable is compact. A 50-field Story in 4 locales produces 150 cells to translate (50 fields × 3 non-source locales), not 200 Stories.

    How does folder-level translation shape the translator's deliverable?

    Folder-level translation duplicates the Story tree inside a locale folder (/es/, /de/). Translators receive a parallel set of Stories to translate end-to-end, including Blok structure where the client has permitted structural divergence. Translators must preserve Blok UUIDs so references do not break.

    This shape suits markets where the ES site diverges structurally from EN — a legal disclaimer section only shown in Germany, for example.

    Which setup does Storyblok's Dimensions feature produce?

    Dimensions is Storyblok's field-level mechanism, exposing locale variants on a single Story. When the Space uses Dimensions, translators work against a flat field map. When the Space uses folder-level, Dimensions is off and locale divergence is handled through folder duplication.

    What does a translator receive at the start of a Storyblok localization project?

    A Storyblok translator receives five artifacts mapped to the site's standard intake: the source content as a JSON export or TMS connector job, the TM for the language pair, the client's term base, the locale style guide, and Visual Editor review access via a Preview token to the staging Space. The canonical intake is explained in full Content Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce It; the Storyblok-specific mapping is below.

    Canonical artifactStoryblok equivalentHow it arrives
    Source contentSpace export (XLIFF, JSON) or CDN API pullTranslation Job or TMS connector
    Translation memoryTM for the language pairTMX file or TMS repository
    Term baseClient glossary with Blok-field notesTBX, CSV, or TMS term base
    Style guideLocale style guide plus Blok tone rulesPDF or linked doc
    Staging accessPreview token to Visual Editor on staging SpaceURL plus token header

    Missing any one of the five stalls kickoff. The Preview token is the one Storyblok-specific artifact most often forgotten; without it, LQA cannot review in context.

    How is the source content exported from Storyblok?

    Source content leaves Storyblok through one of three paths:

    1. A native Translation Job in XLIFF or JSON, created inside the Space.
    2. A TMS connector push to Smartling, Lokalise, Phrase, or Crowdin.
    3. A direct Content Delivery API pull using the language parameter against the draft version.

    XLIFF and JSON file semantics are not re-explained here — see Localization Files: What Translators Receive, Parse, and Return.

    What does the Blok schema tell the translator?

    The Blok schema lists every component type and marks which fields are translatable. Translators consult it to confirm scope on seven field classes:

    • Plain text fields
    • Textarea fields
    • Markdown fields
    • Richtext fields (including nested Bloks)
    • SEO title and SEO description
    • Asset alt text
    • The Story slug

    Any field the client forgot to flag as translatable is a defect to raise at kickoff, not at delivery.

    How does Storyblok's Content Delivery API serve localized content to the front-end?

    The Content Delivery API returns a Story in the requested locale when the client passes the language parameter (?language=es) on the request, resolving to either the field-level value stored in that locale's Dimension or the folder-level Story that lives inside the matching locale folder. Translators do not call the API directly, but understanding this contract explains why the slug, SEO fields, and rich-text markdown versions must all be translated in sync — because the API assembles the response from those exact fields at request time.

    What role does the language parameter play?

    The language parameter on each API request selects which locale the API resolves. The language code itself is the first part of the full_slug of each language-specific Story version, and the Visual Editor requests that same path when rendering a preview — meaning the slug structure is load-bearing for both editorial review and live delivery. A missing or mismatched language parameter returns the default-language value. Untranslated fields silently fall back to the source locale — a defect the LQA gate must catch and log before publish, because it is invisible to authors working only in the default-language editor view.

    Does Storyblok's GraphQL Content API change the translator's job?

    The GraphQL Content API exposes the same localized fields through typed queries, so the translator's deliverables remain identical regardless of which API surface the front-end consumes. Typed GraphQL queries return the same localized fields as the REST endpoint; the practical advantage for LQA teams is that front-end engineers request only the translatable fields that are actually rendered, which narrows the LQA sample to the content that ships to end users. This reduces the volume of strings that must be scored without reducing quality coverage on the fields that matter.

    Which Storyblok fields are translatable and which trip translators up?

    Storyblok marks text, textarea, markdown, richtext, SEO metadata, and asset alt text as translatable when the schema flag is set. The three fields that trip translators up are the Story slug, nested Bloks inside richtext, and asset filenames referenced in markdown — each silently falls back to the default locale if missed.

    Field typeTranslatable?Common defect
    Text / TextareaYes, when flaggedFlag off by default on legacy Bloks
    MarkdownYesInline asset filenames stay in source language
    RichtextYes, top level onlyNested Blok fields need independent flags
    SEO title / descriptionYesLength limits differ per locale
    Asset alt textYesOften omitted from Translation Job scope
    SlugYesUn-translated — see SEO risk below

    How should the localized slug be handled?

    The slug is a localizable field in both field-level and folder-level setups. Translators localize the slug to the target language's SEO-preferred form (/es/acerca instead of /es/about), confirm the client's URL strategy, and flag any collision with existing routes. Un-translated slugs create /es/english-slug URLs that split SEO signal and confuse locale routing — the multilingual URL strategy Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project applies directly.

    What happens to nested Bloks inside a richtext field?

    Richtext fields can contain nested Bloks — callouts, embeds, CTAs. Each nested Blok's text fields need the translatable flag independently. Translators returning only the top-level richtext string leave nested Blok copy in English even when the parent Story reads as fully translated.

    Pricing

    How do translators price and quote a Storyblok localization project?

    Translators quote Storyblok work by translatable-field count × Blok instances × target locales, not by Story count. US per-word pricing applies at $0.10–$0.25 for translation and $0.04–$0.08 for review, with LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words as the blocking gate. A mid-size five-locale, 50,000-word Storyblok program lands at $25,000–$75,000 depending on TM leverage and certification requirements.

    Cost lineUS rateUnit
    Translation$0.10–$0.25Per source word
    Review$0.04–$0.08Per source word
    LQA gate$40–$90Per 1,000 words translated
    5 locales × 50,000 words$25,000–$75,000Program total
    Certified lane (e.g. USCIS)$0.10–$0.25 per word or $25–$150 per pageCertificate of accuracy mandatory; notarization $10–$50 optional

    Why does field count beat page count for Storyblok quoting?

    A Storyblok Story is composed of many Bloks, each with multiple translatable fields. A 200-Story marketing site with an average of 6 translatable fields per Story and 4 locales produces 4,800 field edits — far more than a page-count estimate implies.

    The arithmetic matters because:

    • Short fields (SEO title, button label) carry high per-word effort relative to length.
    • Repeated Blok instances (hero, CTA) leverage TM aggressively; field count alone over-prices.
    • Richtext fields with nested Bloks need per-nested-field counting to avoid under-quoting.

    Where does the LQA gate sit in a Storyblok project?

    LQA samples translated output at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. It scores five dimensions:

    1. Accuracy
    2. Fluency
    3. Terminology
    4. Locale convention
    5. Style

    LQA runs before the Story is published to the live locale in the Space. Failing it blocks publish, not just delivery.

    Computer-Assisted Translation Tools: The Working Translator's Field Guide

    How it works

    Native Storyblok translation vs the Translate Fields app vs third-party TMS connectors — which workflow fits?

    1

    When does native Storyblok translation suffice?

    Native translation suffices when volume is low, locales number two to three, and the agency can live with XLIFF or JSON email handoff. Beyond that threshold the manual round-trip starts dropping fields and losing version alignment.

    2

    What does the Translate Fields app change?

    The Translate Fields app surfaces machine-translation suggestions inside the Storyblok editor for post-editing. Translators treat MT output as a draft stage — MTPE rates apply, and the LQA gate still runs at $40–$90 per 1,000 words regardless of whether MT seeded the first pass.

    3

    When should the project use a TMS connector?

    A TMS connector suits continuous localization at scale. Storyblok pushes changed Stories to the TMS automatically. Translators work in their existing CAT environment with full TM leverage. Translated content syncs back to the correct locale on approval.

    Supported connectors include:

    • Smartling
    • Lokalise
    • Phrase
    • Crowdin

    What does the translator hand back, and how is it reviewed in Storyblok?

    Translators hand back either the translated XLIFF or JSON file for import into the Space, or — via a TMS connector — synced field values that land directly on the target locale Dimension without a manual upload step. Native Translation Jobs support both XLIFF and JSON as round-trip export formats, giving agencies the flexibility to process files in any standards-compliant CAT tool. Review happens in Storyblok's Visual Editor using the Preview token on the staging URL, where the LQA sampler loads the content exactly as a live user would see it and scores defects against the MQM-aligned scorecard before any publish action is permitted on certified lanes.

    The handback sequence runs in five steps:

    1. Translator uploads the translated XLIFF or JSON, or the TMS connector marks the job approved and pushes field values automatically.
    2. The locale fields populate on the target Story (field-level Dimension) or on the parallel folder Story (folder-level model), depending on the Space's localization architecture.
    3. The LQA sampler loads the Preview URL with ?language= set to the target locale, rendering the content through the same Visual Editor path that authors and developers use.
    4. Defects — including untranslated slugs, missing SEO meta fields, and malformed rich-text — are logged against the MQM-aligned scorecard at a rate of $40–$90 per 1,000 words; failing scores block publish.
    5. After a passing LQA score is recorded, the Story is published to the live locale in the Space, making the translated content available through the Content Delivery API.

    The Translate Fields app provides in-editor machine translation seeding for post-editing (MTPE) workflows, allowing editors to pre-populate target fields before the translator refines them — but it does not replace the LQA gate on certified lanes.

    How does Storyblok localization compare to other headless CMS and page-builder platforms?

    Storyblok occupies a distinct position between the pure headless CMS model and visual page builders. Like headless peers, it exposes locale-keyed content over a REST and GraphQL API, meaning the translator deliverable is structured JSON or XLIFF rather than a form-field overwrite inside a monolithic editor. Like page builders, it provides a Visual Editor that renders the assembled Blok tree in context, so reviewers can evaluate translated copy inside the actual layout rather than in an isolated string list. No other common category combines both properties in the same localization workflow.

    The key structural difference for translators is that Storyblok's Blok-and-Story architecture means translatable content is scoped at the component level. A single Story can contain dozens of Blok instances, each with its own set of translatable fields — text, textarea, markdown, richtext, SEO title, SEO description, asset alt text, and localized slug — all flagged individually in the Blok schema. This per-field granularity is more surgical than a page-level export and more structured than a flat key-value JSON file, which affects both TM leverage and LQA sampling strategy.

    Translation pricing reflects this complexity: at $0.10–$0.25 per source word for translation and $0.04–$0.08 per source word for review, a program spanning five languages and 50,000 words lands in the

    Storyblok sits between the pure headless model and visual page builders. Like headless peers, it exposes locale-keyed content over an API; like page builders, it offers Visual Editor review. The translator deliverable is closer to locale-keyed JSON than to a per-field CMS-item overwrite. The generic headless pattern across Contentful, Strapi, and Sanity is covered CMS Localization: How Translators and Agencies Produce Multilingual Content Across Platforms and the page-builder contrast is How Webflow Localization Works and What Translators Need to Know.

    5,000–$75,000 range — a figure that shifts significantly based on TM leverage, turnaround requirements, and whether the lane requires ISO 17100–aligned certification. Teams planning budgets account for LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words on top of translation and review costs.

    How we work on Storyblok projects

    We treat the architecture choice as the client's decision and the deliverable shape as a consequence of it. Before kickoff, we confirm which model the Space uses, pull the Blok schema, and quote by translatable-field count × Blok instances × target locales rather than by Story count. The intake only closes when all five artifacts are in hand — including the Preview token.

    We refuse to publish a locale that has not passed LQA against the MQM-aligned scorecard. "The Translate Fields app ran MT on it" is not a substitute for the gate — MT output is a draft stage, and the $40–$90 per 1,000 words still applies on every lane, including AI-seeded ones.

    We do not quietly leave the slug in English because the schema allowed it. Un-translated slugs are a defect we log and return to the client, not a cost-saving we silently ship. On certified lanes, we do not sign a certificate of accuracy on AI output; the certificate requires a human translator's sign-off, and that signature is the point of the lane.

    We decline to quote a Storyblok program on page count. The arithmetic that produces 4,800 field edits from a 200-Story site is the arithmetic that keeps the budget honest, and a per-page quote hides the overage until mid-project.

    Common Storyblok localization questions cover the API language parameter, slug handling, Dimensions configuration, TMS connector choice, and whether MT inside the Translate Fields app replaces LQA. The short answer on the last: it does not — LQA at $40–$90 per 1,000 words runs on every lane.
