pages.title: i18n Translation: How Translators Produce Localized Builds from JSON, YAML, and XLIFF
pages.h1: i18n Translation: How Translators Produce Localized Builds from JSON, YAML, and XLIFF
pages.meta_description: i18n translation is the production step where translators convert externalized source strings into locale resource files — JSON, YAML, PO, XLIFF — ready for
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • Key points
  • What is i18n translation, and how does it differ from 'using an i18n library'?
  • What files arrive at a translator's desk for an i18n translation job?
  • How does i18n translation work step by step for a web development project?
  • Which tools do translators use for i18n translation in 2025?
  • What quality gate does i18n translation have to pass before a build ships?
  • How does i18n translation fit a certified translation production workflow?
  • How we run i18n translation jobs
  • Frequently asked questions

i18n translation is one stage of How App Localization Works and What Clients Are Buying — the production step where a translator receives externalized source strings from an internationalized codebase and ships back locale resource files the build system uses without further engineering.

Key points

  • i18n translation is the production step that converts externalized source strings into target-locale resource files — JSON, YAML, PO, or XLIFF — while preserving every placeholder and ICU rule exactly as authored. Internationalization itself means developing software adaptable to different languages and regions without requiring code changes; translation is where that adaptability becomes real output.
  • Every handoff bundles four input artifacts together: a resource file, a placeholder spec, an ICU plural and gender table, and screenshot or Storybook context for each ambiguous key. Sending fewer than all four forces the translator to guess at meaning, which introduces errors that survive into production builds.
  • Translators must protect five placeholder classes verbatim before committing a translated file: {{name}}, {0}, %s, <Trans> inline React components, and ICU {count, plural, …} blocks. Altering any of these syntactically breaks the runtime, regardless of whether the surrounding translation is linguistically perfect.
  • Every certified-lane job passes an LQA gate priced at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, scored against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. That gate applies whether the draft was produced by a human translator, a CAT tool, or an AI engine.
  • A standalone i18n-editor stops scaling at roughly 5,000 translation keys, four or more target locales, or any weekly-commit continuous-localization cadence — at which point a connected Translation Management System with Git and CI/CD hooks becomes necessary.
  • CLDR plural categories differ substantially by locale: English uses one and other; French adds many; Russian and Polish require one, few, many, and other; Arabic demands all six — zero, one, two, few, many, and other. Locale codes also carry additional parameters such as date formats, currency symbols, and measurement units that shape how strings must be composed.

What is i18n translation, and how does it differ from 'using an i18n library'?

i18n translation is the production step where a translator converts externalized source strings from an internationalized codebase into target-locale resource files — JSON, YAML, PO, or XLIFF — preserving placeholders, ICU plural rules, and locale formatting without touching application code. It is not the same job as wiring an i18n library into source. The engineering layer is one-off; the translation step repeats every release.

Four artifacts must arrive together or the job is incomplete:

  1. A resource file in a supported format (JSON, YAML, PO, or XLIFF).
  2. A placeholder spec documenting {{name}}, {0}, and %s syntax.
  3. An ICU plural and gender table listing categories per target locale.
  4. Screenshot or Storybook context for every ambiguous key.

The engineering layer that produces those strings is covered on i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds. That page defines the scope — string externalization, Unicode, locale-aware formats, ICU plural and gender, RTL layout, fallback chains, and expansion-tolerant UI — so this page stays on the production step.

Disambiguation: i18n vs i18n translation vs l10n

TermWhat it isWhen you need it
i18n (internationalization)Engineering layer: strings externalized, Unicode, ICU, RTL, fallbacks, expansion-tolerant UI.Once per codebase, before any locale ships.
i18n translationLinguistic conversion of i18n resource files into a target locale, placeholder- and ICU-safe.Every release that adds or edits strings.
l10n (localization)Full per-locale adaptation: translation plus currency, date, legal, imagery, and QA.Per locale, per market launch.
i18n-editorStandalone desktop or web app that opens JSON, YAML, PO, and XLIFF key-by-key.Small projects under the TMS threshold.
TMSServer platform with TM, reviewer gates, connectors, and LQA sampling.Above 5,000 keys, four locales, or weekly commits.

What does the '18' in i18n stand for in translation briefs?

The 18 in i18n is a numeronym for the 18 letters between the first 'i' and the last 'n' in 'internationalization'. Translators meet the term the moment a client ships a resource file instead of a Word document. The same convention produces l10n for localization and a11y for accessibility.

How does i18n translation sit between i18n and l10n in production?

i18n is the one-off engineering layer, l10n is the per-locale cultural adaptation, and i18n translation is the specific linguistic conversion of i18n resource files into each target locale — the handoff artifact between the two.

flowchart TD
 A[i18n engineering: strings externalized] --> B[i18n translation: JSON/YAML/PO/XLIFF per locale]
 B --> C[l10n: currency, date, legal, imagery, QA]
 C --> D[Localized build ships]

What files arrive at a translator's desk for an i18n translation job?

Four artifact classes arrive: a resource file (JSON, YAML, PO, or XLIFF), a placeholder spec documenting {{name}} and {0} syntax, an ICU plural/gender table, and screenshot or Storybook context for every ambiguous key. A handoff missing any one of them produces either guesswork or a broken build.

Which resource-file formats do i18n translators actually open?

Translators open five formats regularly: flat JSON, namespaced JSON, YAML, PO/POT, and XLIFF 1.2 or 2.0 — each with its own placeholder syntax, comment convention, and preferred editor.

FormatTypical ownerCommon failure modeEditor translators open it in
Flat JSONFront-end dev shipping a single-file bundleKey collisions when strings reused across screensi18n-editor or TMS
Namespaced JSONReact / Next.js team using react-i18nextTranslator edits one namespace, misses the fallback in anotheri18n-editor or TMS
YAMLRails and static-site generatorsIndentation errors break the file silentlyi18n-editor with YAML lint
PO / POTWordPress, Django, GNU gettext projectsFuzzy flags left in, plural forms header missingPoedit, OmegaT, memoQ
XLIFF 1.2 / 2.0TMS connector export (Phrase, Lokalise, Crowdin, Transifex, memoQ)Inline tag drift, trans-unit state not updatedCAT tool: Trados, memoQ, OmegaT

For deeper detail on the editor class, see i18n-editor: What Translators Use to Edit JSON Translation Files.

What does a React/Next.js i18n handoff look like in practice?

A React handoff is almost always a /public/locales/{lang}/{namespace}.json tree with {{name}} placeholders and <Trans> inline components, delivered through react-i18next or next-i18next and consumed via the useTranslation hook. Next.js App Router projects add a locales array in config and an appWithTranslation wrapper with a server/client component split.

A specimen handoff:

/public/locales/
├── en/
│ ├── common.json
│ └── auth.json
├── fr/
│ ├── common.json
│ └── auth.json
└── ar/
 ├── common.json
 └── auth.json

Framework-specific pipeline detail is on React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline.

What signals that the i18n layer is 'not ready' and the handoff must be rejected?

Reject the handoff when hardcoded strings remain in source, placeholders use mixed syntaxes, ICU plural categories are missing for languages like Arabic or Russian, or screenshots are absent for keys like 'Submit' that collapse into one key for three UI states. Internationalization is complete only when five conditions hold in the source build:

  • Strings externalized — no literals in source files.
  • ICU plural and gender rules declared for every count and gendered noun.
  • Date, number, currency, phone, and address formats resolve from locale IDs.
  • Right-to-left mirroring works end-to-end.
  • No copy baked into images or canvas.

A readiness defect list is a single-page audit artifact; see Localisation Strategy: How Agencies Plan, Price, and Deliver Multi-Locale Programs for how agencies hand that back to engineering.

How does i18n translation work step by step for a web development project?

i18n translation runs in six steps: receive the resource bundle, lock placeholder parity, draft target strings in an i18n-editor or TMS, validate ICU plurals, run LQA against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100, and commit the per-locale file back to the repo or TMS connector.

Three real handoff shapes recur in web-dev projects:

  1. A public/locales JSON tree pulled from a Git repo.
  2. An XLIFF export produced by a TMS connector (Phrase, Lokalise, Crowdin, Transifex, memoQ).
  3. PO files from a Git-tracked WordPress, Django, or gettext project.
flowchart LR
 A[Intake bundle] --> B[Lock placeholder parity]
 B --> C[Draft in editor/TMS]
 C --> D[Validate ICU plurals]
 D --> E[LQA against MQM scorecard]
 E --> F[Commit per-locale file]

Step 1 — How do you intake a JSON or XLIFF bundle without breaking the keys?

Clone or download the resource bundle read-only, diff it against the previous version to identify changed keys, and open it in an i18n-editor that locks the key column so only values are editable. Preserve the key order the source ships with. Run pseudo-localization on the source before translating so overflow and hardcoded strings surface before words are spent — covered on Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds.

Step 2 — How do you preserve placeholders, ICU plurals, and inline tags?

Preserve five placeholder classes verbatim: {{name}} double-brace, {0} positional, %s printf, <Trans> inline React components, and ICU {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}} blocks — any drift breaks the production build.

Run a placeholder-parity checklist before saving every JSON handoff:

  • Every {{variable}} in source appears identically in target.
  • Every {0}, {1} positional index is retained — reorder in text, never in syntax.
  • Every %s and %d printf token is kept in the same order the source uses it.
  • Every <Trans> or <0>…</0> inline tag is closed and nested the same way.
  • Every ICU select and plural block retains its categories and # placeholder.

Step 3 — How do you handle plural, gender, and select rules per locale?

Declare every CLDR plural category the target language requires — English has one and other, French adds many, Russian uses one/few/many/other, Polish uses one/few/many/other, and Arabic uses zero/one/two/few/many/other.

LocaleCLDR plural categories
English (en)one, other
French (fr)one, many, other
Russian (ru)one, few, many, other
Polish (pl)one, few, many, other
Arabic (ar)zero, one, two, few, many, other

A sample ICU block translators receive:

{itemCount, plural,
 one {# item in your cart}
 other {# items in your cart}
}

For Arabic, the same key expands to six categories; omitting zero or two ships a broken plural at runtime.

Step 4 — How do you commit translations back without triggering a merge conflict?

Commit per-locale files on a branch named locale/{lang}, run the i18n linter the client ships, and open a pull request so the CI pipeline can rebuild the bundle, run pseudo-localization, and surface overflow before merge. Keep the key order the source file uses. Namespaces exist so bundles load on demand — split by feature (common.json, auth.json) and never merge two namespaces into one commit.

A locale fallback chain resolves missing keys at runtime without breaking the UI: fr-CA → fr → en. A translator who leaves a key untranslated as an empty string disables that chain for that key.

Which tools do translators use for i18n translation in 2025?

Translators use three tool classes: standalone i18n-editors for JSON/YAML/PO/XLIFF, TMS platforms like Phrase, Lokalise, Crowdin, Transifex, or memoQ for larger programs, and Git-connected CAT tools when the client prefers pull-request-based delivery.

Tool classBest fitFormatsDelivery model
i18n-editor (standalone)Under 5,000 keys, 3 or fewer locales, release-basedJSON, YAML, PO, XLIFFFile in / file out
TMS (Phrase, Lokalise, Crowdin, Transifex, memoQ)5,000+ keys, 4+ locales, weekly cadenceAll, via connectorGit / CI/CD connector
CAT tool (Trados, memoQ, OmegaT)XLIFF from TMS export, agency-side reviewer workflowXLIFF 1.2 / 2.0, TMXPackage in / package out

When is a standalone i18n-editor enough?

A standalone i18n-editor handles projects under roughly 5,000 translation keys, three or fewer target locales, and release-based delivery — above that threshold translation memory leverage, reviewer gates, and LQA sampling demand a TMS. Full detail on scope, placeholder parity, and ICU validation is on i18n-editor: What Translators Use to Edit JSON Translation Files.

When does the project need a Translation Management System on top?

The project needs a TMS when the key count passes 5,000, four or more locales ship in parallel, or commits land weekly on a continuous-localization cadence. File-based editing loses TM leverage, has no reviewer gate, and cannot run the LQA sampling that certified lanes require. The same thresholds published on our continuous-localization guide apply here — see Continuous Localization: How Translators and Agencies Run the Delivery Model.

How does machine translation fit into i18n translation production?

Machine translation enters as a pre-translate stage on repetitive UI strings, with human post-editing (MTPE) priced per word and a mandatory LQA gate at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 before the locale ships. MT without the LQA gate is not an i18n translation deliverable on a certified lane.

What quality gate does i18n translation have to pass before a build ships?

Every i18n translation job on a certified lane passes an LQA gate at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, scored against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100 covering accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style — regardless of whether a translator, CAT tool, or AI produced the draft. The gate is not optional: it is the mechanism that separates a certified deliverable from an unreviewed string dump, and it applies equally to flat JSON files and to complex XLIFF 2.0 bilingual packages.

What does the MQM-style scorecard measure on a JSON locale file?

The scorecard samples strings for five error categories — accuracy, fluency, terminology, locale convention, and style — then weights each by severity to produce a pass/fail against a job-specific threshold. Accuracy errors are the most severe class: a string that conveys the wrong meaning in the target locale is a critical failure even if it is grammatically flawless. Locale convention errors cover the parameters each locale carries beyond raw language — date formats, currency symbols, and measurement units must all conform to the conventions of the target region, not simply be transliterated from the source. Style errors are weighted at minor or major depending on the style guide in force for the product.

What breaks i18n translation builds and never shows up in a word count?

Six silent failures break builds: dropped placeholders, mojibake from the wrong encoding, missing ICU plural categories, overlong strings that overflow fixed widths, untranslated keys committed as empty strings, and markup drift <Trans> components. None of these failures appear in a word count or a simple diff — they require a dedicated pre-commit check or a pseudo-localization pass to catch before the build pipeline runs. Framework-specific failures compound the risk. When ICU message formatting runs inside a server/client component architecture, a plugin class cannot pass directly from a Server Component to a Client Component — the ICU provider requires a deliberate 'use client' wrapper that word-count tooling and standard LQA sampling will not surface.itecture, a plugin class cannot be passed directly from a Server Component to a Client Component, so the ICU provider itself requires a deliberate 'use client' wrapper — an integration detail that neither word-count tooling nor standard LQA sampling will surface on its own.

  • Dropped placeholders — {{name}} deleted during translation.
  • Mojibake — file saved as Windows-1252 instead of UTF-8.
  • Missing ICU categories — zero or two omitted for Arabic.
  • Overflow — German string 40% longer than the English source blows the button width.
  • Empty strings — fallback chain disabled for that key.
  • Markup drift — <0>…</0> left unclosed, React render fails.

How does i18n translation fit a certified translation production workflow?

On certified lanes, i18n translation runs the same gates as document work: a translator plus an independent reviewer per ISO 17100, LQA against an MQM-style scorecard at $40–$90 per 1,000 words, and — when the locale bundle feeds an immigration or legal UI — a signed certificate of accuracy on every page of printed evidence. The deliverable is a locale bundle plus the LQA report and, where printed evidence is required, a certification statement bound to the strings that render on the user's screen.

Internationalization is the engineering discipline that makes software adaptable to different languages and regions without requiring code changes; localization is the subsequent process of adapting that software to the linguistic, cultural, and technical requirements of a specific locale. i18n translation sits at the intersection of both — it is the step that takes the engineer's externalized strings and produces a fully adapted, reviewable resource file for each target locale. This means the translator is not just swapping words: they are responsible for preserving the technical structure (placeholders, ICU rules, encoding) that the internationalization layer depends on, while also satisfying the cultural and terminological expectations that localization demands.

A certified workflow treats each resource file format as a distinct document type with its own structural rules. A flat JSON file, a namespaced JSON bundle, a YAML file, a PO/POT catalog, or an XLIFF 1.2 or 2.0 package each imposes different constraints on how segments are delimited, how metadata is stored, and how the translation memory system reads and writes units. Translators working under ISO 17100 must demonstrate competence in whichever format the handoff uses — not merely language competence. The LQA reviewer then validates the file structurally as well as linguistically, confirming that the target-locale resource file is ready to drop into the build pipeline without modification.

When a locale bundle feeds a user-facing legal or government-adjacent interface, the certification statement is not a courtesy — it is a required artifact that attests to the completeness and accuracy of every string the end user sees. In those contexts, the workflow also mandates that the CAT environment or Translation Management System produce an auditable record linking each source segment to its reviewed translation, so the certifying translator signs against a traceable output rather than a reconstructed export.

How we run i18n translation jobs

We take an i18n translation job only when the four input artifacts arrive together: resource file, placeholder spec, ICU plural table, and screenshot or Storybook context for every ambiguous key. A handoff missing any of them comes back as a one-page defect list, not a quote. That refusal is the single biggest driver of a clean build at merge.

We will not translate directly in a copy of the source file. Keys get locked in an i18n-editor or TMS so only values are editable, and every placeholder class is validated before save. We decline the shortcut of pasting JSON into a general-purpose chatbot — placeholder parity, ICU category completeness, and encoding integrity are not probabilistic deliverables.

We will not sign a certification statement for a locale bundle that has not passed the LQA gate at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. MT output ships only after human post-editing and that same gate — the price does not change because the first draft came from an engine.

Above 5,000 translation keys, four locales, or a weekly commit cadence, we move the program to a TMS connector. File-based editing stops producing the TM leverage and reviewer trail certified work needs; carrying on in an i18n-editor past that point is a defect waiting to be billed.

Six questions recur on every i18n translation brief: what the tool is for, whether it handles JSON, how blog-post localization fits, how web-dev projects actually run it, what i18n means in one line, and how it differs from l10n.

Frequently asked questions

What is the i18n Translation Tool used for?

The i18n Translation Tool is used to extract, translate, and repackage localizable strings stored in developer resource files — primarily JSON, YAML, and XLIFF — so that software interfaces can be shipped in multiple languages. Working translators and agencies use it to receive structured string files from dev teams, produce accurate first-draft or certified translations for each locale, and return locale-ready builds without breaking file syntax. It bridges the gap between a developer's codebase and a translator's workflow, cutting manual reformatting time significantly.

Can the i18n Translation Tool handle JSON files?

Yes, the i18n Translation Tool natively handles JSON files, which are the most common format for storing UI strings in modern web and mobile apps. It parses nested key-value structures, preserves interpolation placeholders (e.g., {{username}} or %s), and returns a locale-specific JSON file that drops straight back into the project. This means translators work only on the string values, never touching keys or code logic, which dramatically reduces the risk of introducing syntax errors into a production build.

How does i18n translation work for web development projects?

In web development, i18n translation works by externalizing all user-facing strings into resource files (JSON, YAML, or XLIFF), then loading the correct locale file at runtime based on the user's language setting. Developers tag strings with keys rather than hardcoding text, an i18n library (such as i18next, react-intl, or Vue I18n) fetches the matching translations, and the UI renders in the target language without a code change. Translators produce the locale files; the tool ensures formatting, pluralization rules, and placeholders remain intact across every language.

What does localization mean?

Localization (L10n) means adapting a product — its text, formats, imagery, and cultural references — so it feels native to a specific locale, not merely translated word-for-word. Beyond language, it covers date and number formats, currency symbols, right-to-left text direction, legal disclaimers, and culturally appropriate examples. For software, localization starts with i18n-ready code and ends with certified, locale-specific resource files delivered by professional translators. A fully localized product in, say, Brazilian Portuguese differs from European Portuguese not just in spelling but in tone, units, and regulatory language.

What is localisation in translation?

Localisation in translation refers to the process of adapting translated content to the cultural, legal, and technical norms of a specific target market — going beyond literal word substitution. A translator localising a SaaS product for the German market, for example, must handle formal address conventions (Sie vs. du), EU-specific GDPR language, decimal comma notation, and locale-coded date formats (DD.MM.YYYY). Localisation is considered a higher-skill deliverable than straight translation and is what agencies certify when signing off on a localized build.

What is 18 in i18n?

The 18 in i18n stands for the 18 letters between the first letter 'i' and the last letter 'n' in the word 'internationalization.' This style of abbreviation — called a numeronym — shortens long technical terms for convenience; 'localization' is similarly shortened to L10n (10 letters between L and n). The convention became common in software engineering during the 1980s and is now the industry-standard shorthand used in framework names, configuration keys, and file-format specifications across the entire software localization industry.

Why is localization called L10n?

Localization is called L10n for the same reason internationalization is called i18n: it is a numeronym where the number replaces the letters between the first and last character of the word (L + 10 letters + n). The convention keeps long compound terms manageable in code comments, CLI flags, and documentation. Both numeronyms originated in engineering communities — reportedly at DEC and later at Sun Microsystems in the 1980s — and have since been adopted universally across the software translation and SaaS industry.

Why use i18n?

Teams use i18n so that adding a new language requires only a new resource file, not a rewrite of application code. By externalizing strings into JSON, YAML, or XLIFF from the start, a single codebase can serve dozens of locales simultaneously — a critical commercial advantage when expanding into new markets. For translators and agencies, an i18n-structured project means clearly scoped work (a finite list of keys), consistent context, and the ability to produce and certify localized builds systematically rather than hunting for translatable text scattered through source code.

Where did the I18n come from?

The numeronym i18n is widely attributed to Digital Equipment Corporation (DEC) engineers in the early 1980s, who needed a compact way to reference 'internationalization' in internal documentation and memos. It gained broader adoption through UNIX and X Window System internationalization efforts, and by the 1990s it appeared in W3C standards documentation. Today it is embedded in the names of major frameworks and libraries — i18next, Rails I18n, Angular i18n — making it one of the most enduring pieces of software engineering shorthand in the industry.

Does it support blog post localization?

The i18n Translation Tool is optimized for structured developer resource files (JSON, YAML, XLIFF) rather than free-form content like blog posts, which are handled through CMS-based localization workflows. That said, if a blog or documentation site exports content to XLIFF or structured Markdown with YAML front matter, those files can move through the same i18n pipeline. Agencies producing certified translations of technical documentation — API guides, release notes, help-center articles — use XLIFF exports from platforms like Contentful or Phrase to keep content localization inside a single certified workflow.

pages.title: i18n-editor: What Translators Use to Edit JSON Translation Files
pages.h1: i18n-editor: What Translators Use to Edit JSON Translation Files
pages.meta_description: An i18n-editor is a desktop or web tool translators use to edit JSON, YAML and XLIFF translation files directly, with placeholder parity checks and ICU plural
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What is an i18n-editor and what does it actually do for translators?
  • Which i18n-editors do translators actually meet in 2025?
  • How does a translator open a JSON handoff in an i18n-editor without breaking it?
  • When does an i18n-editor stop scaling and the project need a TMS?
  • How does an i18n-editor fit into a certified translation production workflow?

Translators receive JSON handoffs faster than any other format, and a standalone i18n-editor is the surface where those files get edited without the overhead of a full TMS login or a developer's IDE.

What is an i18n-editor and what does it actually do for translators?

An i18n-editor is a desktop or browser tool that opens JSON, YAML, PO, or XLIFF translation files in a key-by-key grid, so translators edit per-locale strings side-by-side, preserve {{name}} and ICU placeholders, and save back to the same files without opening the source code or a full TMS. The editor sits on top of the engineering layer described in i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds and consumes what that layer emits. Its primary function is to present every translation key as an editable row in a locale-aware grid so the translator never has to parse raw JSON syntax or touch the surrounding application code.

Translation keys are the backbone of every i18n project. A well-structured i18n-editor exposes those keys alongside their source-language values and lets the translator work one cell at a time, which eliminates the most common class of handoff errors — stray commas, mismatched braces, and accidental key deletions that break a JSON parser at runtime. The editor is responsible for reading the file in, showing a structured interface, and writing the file back out in exactly the encoding and indentation the build pipeline expects.

The editor does four jobs:

  • Loads a /locales folder and parses each language file into rows.
  • Shows source and target columns side-by-side with the key locked.
  • Validates placeholder parity and ICU plural blocks on save.
  • Writes files back to disk in the same encoding, indentation, and key order.

Some editors, such as the open-source Java desktop application distributed on GitHub, target flat and nested JSON only, keeping the tool lightweight and focused. Others cover a much wider surface: nested JSON, Vue single-file components, Angular XLIFF, Android strings.xml, iOS .strings files, and ICU plural blocks — all editable in a single visual interface. IDE extensions take a third approach, resolving translation keys inline inside the component tree and flagging missing translations directly in the gutter so the developer or bilingual engineer never has to leave the editor. Finally, in-context web editors render strings on the live page itself, giving translators a character-budget view that no file-based tool can match.

Which file formats does an i18n-editor open?

An i18n-editor opens the resource bundle formats that react-i18next, vue-i18n, next-intl, @angular/localize, and golang.org/x/text emit on handoff. Format coverage varies significantly by tool: some handle only flat JSON, while others extend to XLIFF 2.0, Android XML, and iOS property lists. The table below maps format to framework and to editor coverage.

FormatFrameworkOpened by
Flat JSONreact-i18next, golang.org/x/textAll major editors
Nested JSONvue-i18n, next-intlVisual editors, IDE extensions, TMS-connected tools
YAMLRails, JekyllIDE extensions, advanced visual editors
Java .propertiesSpring, StrutsDesktop editors, advanced visual editors
gettext .poDjango, WordPressVisual editors, IDE extensions
Android strings.xmlAndroid nativeVisual editors, TMS-connected tools
iOS .strings / .stringsdictiOS nativeVisual editors, TMS-connected tools
XLIFF 1.2 / 2.0@angular/localizeVisual editors, TMS-connected tools

How is an i18n-editor different from a TMS or an in-context platform?

An i18n-editor edits files directly on disk with no server, no translation memory, and no team workflow. A TMS stores segments in a database with TM leverage, glossary enforcement, and reviewer gates. An in-context platform renders strings on the live page for post-editing, which is useful when character budgets and typographic fit matter more than raw throughput.

  • i18n-editor: file in, file out, local only, zero infrastructure.
  • TMS: segment database, TM, QA profiles, reviewer roles, audit log.
  • In-context platform: live-page overlay, character budgets visible, SDK required.

Centralizing translation management adds features like bulk-edit, cross-language search, namespace filtering, and tag-based categorization that no standalone file editor offers. Namespaces let teams group keys by feature, module, or release to match codebase structure, while tags slice the translation set in any direction needed for QA or release gating. The choice of surface depends on team size, pipeline complexity, and whether CI automation or live-page verification matters more to the project.

Which i18n-editors do translators actually meet in 2025?

Translators meet five i18n-editors in production: i18n-editor by jcbvm, BabelEdit, VS Code i18n Ally, Tolgee, and the Lokalise desktop export app. Each matches a different project shape. The matrix below scores them on JSON nesting depth, ICU plural handling, placeholder validation, and git workflow fit.

EditorNested JSONICU pluralsPlaceholder validationGit workflow fit
i18n-editor by jcbvmFlat onlyNoBasicManual
BabelEditFullVisual plural editorStrongGood
VS Code i18n AllyFullPartialInline gutter warningsNative
TolgeeFullFull ICUServer-sideVia CLI
Lokalise desktopFullFullSyncs to TMS QAVia TMS

What is the i18n-editor by jcbvm and when is it still the right pick?

The i18n-editor by jcbvm is an open-source Java desktop app distributed on GitHub that opens a folder of flat JSON locale files in a side-by-side grid. It remains the right pick for small i18next projects under about 1,500 keys that ship no continuous-localization pipeline. The app flattens nested keys and ignores ICU plural blocks, so projects that use either should pick a different editor.

What does BabelEdit do that jcbvm's editor does not?

BabelEdit handles deeply nested JSON, Vue single-file components, Angular XLIFF, and ICU plurals with a visual plural editor, where jcbvm's i18n-editor flattens nested keys and ignores ICU. BabelEdit is the default when a React, Vue, or Angular project uses nested namespaces. It also opens Android strings.xml and iOS .strings natively, which jcbvm does not.

When does an in-IDE editor like i18n Ally replace a standalone app?

VS Code i18n Ally replaces a standalone i18n-editor when the translator is also the developer. Keys resolve inline in the component tree, missing-translation warnings surface in the editor gutter, and git diffs stay inside the same window. The tab-switch between editor and codebase disappears. For dedicated linguists without IDE fluency, a standalone app stays easier.

How does Tolgee's in-context editor compare to a file-based i18n-editor?

Tolgee renders the live app around each string, so a translator sees context — character budget, surrounding UI, RTL mirroring — that a file-based i18n-editor hides. The tradeoff is that Tolgee requires a running build and a Tolgee SDK integration, which many client handoffs do not include. For JavaScript projects, the broader pipeline shape sits in JS Localization: How Translators Fit Into a JavaScript i18n Pipeline.

How does a translator open a JSON handoff in an i18n-editor without breaking it?

A translator opens a JSON handoff by cloning the branch, pointing the i18n-editor at the /locales folder, locking the key column, and running a placeholder-parity check before saving. The goal is to keep {{name}}, ICU {count, plural, …}, and <Trans> tag indices byte-identical to source. A single misplaced brace or a dropped double-curly delimiter is enough to throw a runtime interpolation error in production, so the editor's validation layer is not optional — it is the primary safety mechanism between the translator's output and the deployed build.

JSON resource bundles carry strict formatting requirements that the editor must honor on every save: stable key order, UTF-8 encoding without a byte-order mark, LF line endings, and 2-space indentation must all match the source file exactly. Placeholder parity with the source string is equally mandatory — every interpolation token present in English must appear in the target locale string, even if its position changes to match target-language word order. Editors that enforce these constraints at save time eliminate an entire category of CI failures before the pull request is even opened.

  1. Clone the repository and check out the locale branch.
  2. Open the i18n-editor and point it at /locales or /i18n.
  3. Set the source language to the English file.
  4. Lock the key column against accidental edits.
  5. Translate row by row, keeping placeholders untouched.
  6. Run the placeholder-parity check on the editor's QA panel.
  7. Save with stable key order, UTF-8 no BOM, LF line endings, 2-space indent.
  8. Commit, push, and open a pull request against the main branch.

An i18n-editor must preserve four placeholder syntaxes untouched. Each syntax is framework-specific, and confusing them — for example, collapsing double-curly braces to single-curly — silently breaks runtime interpolation without throwing a JSON parse error, making the bug invisible until the UI renders.

  • react-i18next double-curly: {{name}}, {{count}}, {{user.firstName}} — the double-curly delimiter must be preserved byte-for-byte.
  • next-intl single-curly with ICU: {name}, {count} with optional ICU formatters — the single-curly syntax follows ICU MessageFormat conventions.
  • ICU MessageFormat plural blocks: {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}} — the entire block must be reauthored to the target language's CLDR plural categories, not just the inner strings.
  • Indexed JSX tags from the React Trans component: <0></0>, <1></1>, <2/> — index order must be preserved even when target-language syntax reorders surrounding words.

The Trans component collapses JSX markup into segments that break CAT tools expecting discrete atomic segments, so segment-merging falls to the translator or the LSP. The React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline page covers that pattern end-to-end.

How does an i18n-editor handle ICU plural keys for Arabic, Russian, and Polish?

An i18n-editor exposes CLDR plural categories as sibling keys so that each source string expands into as many target rows as the target language requires. ICU MessageFormat plural and select blocks must be reauthored to the target language's CLDR categories inside the editor — simply copying the English two-category structure to a six-category language like Arabic produces a broken plural at runtime. The table below shows what the grid looks like per source string.

LanguagePlural keys per stringCategory names
English2_one, _other
Polish4_one, _few, _many, _other
Russian4_one, _few, _many, _other
Arabic6_zero, _one, _two, _few, _many, _other

Arabic requires six plural keys per string under react-i18next — _zero, _one, _two, _few, _many, and _other — which raises per-key TMS licensing costs without raising the billable source-word count. An editor that does not surface all six categories forces the translator to add the missing keys by hand in raw JSON, reintroducing the exact file-corruption risk the editor is supposed to prevent. The React i18n: How Translators Fit Into a React Localization Pipeline page explains the pricing impact in more detail.

What does a safe save-and-commit look like from an i18n-editor?

A safe save writes stable key order, UTF-8 without BOM, LF line endings, and 2-space indentation to match the source JSON exactly. Deviating from any one of these four constraints — for instance, writing CRLF line endings on a Windows machine or reordering keys alphabetically — produces a noisy diff that buries the actual translation changes and can fail the project's JSON-schema lint step. The translator then runs the project's lint script, opens a pull request from a locale branch, and waits for CI placeholder-parity and JSON-schema checks before requesting review.

  • Diff only the target locale file, not the source English file.
  • Keep the key order byte-identical to source for clean diffs.
  • Push to a per-locale branch, not to main.
  • Wait for CI to clear placeholder-parity and JSON-schema checks before requesting a code review.

When does an i18n-editor stop scaling and the project need a TMS?

An i18n-editor stops scaling at roughly 5,000 translation keys, four or more target locales, or any continuous-localization cadence that commits weekly. File-based editing loses translation memory leverage, has no reviewer gate, and cannot run the LQA sampling that certified lanes require under an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100.

What quality gates does a file-based i18n-editor skip?

A standalone i18n-editor skips three gates a TMS enforces:

  1. Segment-level review at $0.04–$0.08 per source word, with reviewer sign-off tracked per segment.
  2. LQA sampling at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100.
  3. Mandatory sign-off on the certificate of accuracy for certified lanes.

Which signals say it is time to graduate from an i18n-editor?

Four signals say the project has outgrown an i18n-editor:

  • Key count above ~5,000.
  • More than four active locales.
  • Pull-request-driven weekly releases.
  • A client who requires per-segment review history for audit.

Any one of them makes a hosted TMS the lower-friction option. The decision tree below maps project shape to the correct editor class.

Project shapeRight editor class
<500 keys, 1–2 locales, one-offRaw IDE or VS Code i18n Ally
500–5,000 keys, 2–4 locales, quarterlyStandalone i18n-editor desktop app
Any key count, visual context requiredIn-context platform (Tolgee)
>5,000 keys, 4+ locales, weekly commitsFull TMS with connector

How it works

How does an i18n-editor fit into a certified translation production workflow?

1

Translator edits JSON in the i18n-editor on a locale branch.

2

CI runs placeholder-parity and JSON-schema checks on the pull request.

3

Reviewer scores segments in the TMS at $0.04–$0.08 per source word.

4

LQA samples roughly 10% of volume at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against the MQM-aligned scorecard.

pages.title: i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds
pages.h1: i18n: What Internationalization Means for Translators Producing Localized Builds
pages.meta_description: i18n is the engineering layer that lets one codebase accept any locale. For translators, it determines how clean the strings, placeholders, and plural rules
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • What does i18n mean, and why do engineers write it that way?
  • What does i18n actually cover inside a codebase?
  • How is i18n different from l10n, and where does the handoff happen?
  • What should a translator check to know an i18n layer is actually ready?
  • How does i18n look in the frameworks translators meet most often?
  • How does translation keep syncing with a live i18n codebase?
  • What are the i18n pitfalls that cost translators the most time?

Internationalization reaches a translator through the shape of the files that land in the queue. The engineering choices made weeks earlier decide whether strings arrive with context, whether plural forms are addressable, and whether the next sync will overwrite yesterday's work.

What does i18n mean, and why do engineers write it that way?

i18n is a numeronym for internationalization — the 18 counts the letters between the first 'i' and the last 'n'. Engineers use it to keep tickets short and to sidestep the American/British spelling split in commit messages, config keys, and style guides.

  • i18n — internationalization (18 letters between i…n)
  • l10n — localization (10 letters between l…n)
  • a11y — accessibility (11 letters between a…y)
  • k8s — Kubernetes (8 letters between k…s)
  • g11n — globalization (11 letters between g…n)

Is it 'internationalization' or 'internationalisation' — and does i18n settle it?

Both spellings are correct. American English uses -ization; British English uses -isation. The numeronym i18n is spelling-neutral, which is the practical reason it stuck across codebases shared by international teams. A repo adopts i18n in config keys, folder names (/i18n/), and ticket titles, and the ize-vs-ise argument never reaches the pull request.

How does i18n fit the numeronym family (l10n, a11y, k8s, g11n)?

Numeronyms compress long technical terms by replacing the middle letters with their count. Translators meet all five in engineering tickets and build logs. The convention is read once and applied forever: first letter, count of middle letters, last letter. A ticket titled "i18n: fix a11y labels in k8s dashboard" is parsed by a project manager without a second glance.

What we offer

What does i18n actually cover inside a codebase?

i18n covers string externalization, Unicode encoding, locale-aware date, number and currency formatting, ICU plural and gender rules, bidirectional (RTL) layout, locale fallback chains, and text-expansion-tolerant UI. It is the engineering layer that makes per-locale translation possible without further code changes. Our page on Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project covers the parent cluster this scope belongs to.

How is i18n different from l10n, and where does the handoff happen?

i18n is the one-time engineering work that prepares code for any locale; l10n is the per-locale work of translating, adapting, and testing. The handoff artifact is the resource bundle — JSON, XLIFF, PO, YAML, .strings, or .resx — which is where the translator picks up. Our guide on Website Localization: What Translators and Agencies Actually Do on the Project walks the downstream side of the same split.

The i18n vs l10n split in one table

Dimensioni18n (internationalization)l10n (localization)
Who owns itEngineeringTranslation production, LSP
How oftenOnce, up frontRepeats per locale, continuously
DeliverableCode that externalizes strings and formatsTranslated resource bundle per locale
Primary artifacti18n library + source resource fileTarget-locale JSON, XLIFF, PO
Failure signalHard-coded strings, broken plurals, mojibakeMissing keys, length overflows, context errors
QA proofPseudo-localization buildLinguistic QA on the real target locale

Where globalization (g11n) fits above both

g11n (globalization) is the umbrella program covering i18n plus l10n plus the business, legal, and go-to-market work that lets a product sell in a new market. For translators, g11n is usually the client's org chart, not their deliverable. The LSP contract still terminates at the resource bundle.

What should a translator check to know an i18n layer is actually ready?

A translator confirms i18n readiness by inspecting 11 upstream decisions: resource format, placeholder syntax, ICU plural coverage, context metadata, locale fallback chain, missing-key behavior, encoding, RTL readiness, length budgets, screenshot delivery, and continuous-sync wiring. Pseudo-localization is the fastest single proof — see our page on Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds.

  1. Resource file format — JSON, XLIFF 2.1, PO, YAML, .strings, .resx
  2. Placeholder syntax — ICU, sprintf, double-curly, named
  3. Plural engine — ICU MessageFormat vs ad-hoc one/other
  4. Context metadata — developer comments, usage notes, descriptions
  5. Flat vs nested keys — namespace strategy and CAT compatibility
  6. RTL token handling — bidi isolates and mirrored assets
  7. Locale fallback chain — fr-CA → fr → en, declared not implicit
  8. Missing-key behavior — render key, fallback string, or empty
  9. Encoding — UTF-8 confirmed in files, APIs, and database
  10. Length budgets — character caps on buttons, labels, titles
  11. Screenshot or pseudo-loc build — context delivered with the keys

Which resource file format arrived, and what does it imply?

Resource format signals the stack. JSON for React, Vue, Next.js; XLIFF 2.1 for TMS bilinguals; gettext PO for WordPress and Django; YAML for Rails; .strings for iOS; .resx for .NET. Each format carries its own placeholder and plural conventions, and each sets what the CAT tool will accept without a filter rewrite.

Are the keys flat or nested — and does it matter for the translator?

Flat JSON keys like common.save are easier to diff and sort. Nested JSON keys like common.buttons.save group context visually. Translators care because deeply nested bundles often lose per-string context when loaded into CAT tools, which flatten the hierarchy into a single key column.

Does every string carry context or screenshots?

Context resolves ambiguity on short strings. 'Open' is a verb or an adjective. 'Post' is a noun or a verb. A developer comment, a usage note, or a screenshot removes the ambiguity. Resource bundles without context force the translator to guess or raise a query, and queries slow the sync by one business day each.

Is pseudo-localization available as a test build?

Pseudo-localization replaces source text with accented, padded, bracketed versions to prove the i18n layer holds before real translation starts. The pseudo-loc build is the fastest i18n-readiness signal a translator can request. Our guide Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds covers how to read one.

How does i18n look in the frameworks translators meet most often?

Translators meet i18n through specific libraries: react-i18next and next-intl in React and Next.js, vue-i18n in Vue, @angular/localize in Angular, Astro content collections, and golang.org/x/text in Go. Each emits different resource formats and enforces different placeholder syntax.

FrameworkLibraryResource formatPlaceholder syntaxTranslator pain point
Reactreact-i18nextJSON (flat or nested){{name}}Trans component segments
Next.jsnext-intlJSONICU {name}Server-component scopes
Vuevue-i18nJSON{name}, pipes for pluralsPlural pipe syntax
Angular@angular/localizeXLIFF 1.2/2.0ICU plural/selectBuild-time locale split
Gogolang.org/x/text (+ go-i18n, gotext)Varies: JSON, TOML, gotextVariesNo dominant library
AstroContent collectionsMarkdown + JSONFramework-chosenMixed content/UI handoff

React i18n (react-i18next, next-intl): JSON keys, interpolation, and inline components

React projects commonly ship JSON resource files via react-i18next or next-intl, using double-curly interpolation like {{name}} and the Trans component for inline markup. A newer pattern translates entire components inline rather than individual string keys — the full JSX fragment becomes the translatable unit. This breaks CAT tools that expect discrete, atomic segments and forces segment-merging on the LSP side.

Vue i18n (vue-i18n): the de facto library and its message format

vue-i18n is the de facto Vue i18n library. It supports flat and nested JSON, named interpolation, and plural pipes. Translators receive one locale JSON per language and keep them aligned as keys change. Named interpolation uses {count}; plural pipes read as "no items | one item | {count} items".

Next.js i18n: routing, locale detection, and the NEXT_LOCALE cookie

Next.js i18n covers sub-path routing (/fr/, /de/), domain routing (example.fr), automatic locale detection from Accept-Language, and the NEXT_LOCALE cookie. These decisions shape the URL inventory the translator sees in multilingual SEO scope and determine whether the locale is a path segment, a subdomain, or a top-level domain.

Angular i18n (@angular/localize): XLIFF out of the box

Angular ships @angular/localize, which extracts translatable strings into XLIFF 1.2 or 2.0. Angular projects usually land in the CAT tool as clean bilingual XLIFF, with ICU plural and select expressions already encoded. The build splits per locale, which means each locale produces its own bundle at compile time rather than at runtime.

Go i18n (golang.org/x/text): the fragmented ecosystem translators quote around

Go has no dominant i18n library. Teams piece solutions together from golang.org/x/text, go-i18n, and gotext, producing resource formats that vary project to project. Agencies quoting Go work ask for the file format and the plural engine upfront, because the quote changes when the format is TOML message catalogs vs flat JSON vs gotext's generated code.

Astro, Shopify, Webflow, and Pendo: i18n for sites and products translators also receive

Beyond app frameworks, translators receive i18n handoffs from Astro content collections, Shopify's Markets and translation API, Webflow's localization panel, and Pendo's in-product strings. Each exposes a different export shape and sync cadence. See our sibling guides on Pseudo Localization: What Translators Need to Know About i18n Test Builds for the shared QA step.

How does translation keep syncing with a live i18n codebase?

Live i18n codebases sync through continuous localization: source JSON or XLIFF changes trigger a TMS webhook, new keys appear in the translator's queue, completed translations push back to the repository, and CI rebuilds the locale bundle. Missing keys fall back on a defined chain.

Translation management systems (TMS) between the repo and the translator

A translation management system (TMS) connects the source repository to the translator's workbench, surfaces new or changed strings, enforces glossary and translation memory, and routes deliveries back to the right branch. The TMS turns one-off handoffs into a continuous workflow and absorbs the diffing work that would otherwise land on a project manager.

Fallback locales and missing-key behavior

A fallback locale is the resource the app renders when a target-locale key is missing — usually the source language, en. A missing-key policy tells the UI whether to render the key name (common.save), the fallback string ("Save"), or an empty slot. A declared fallback chain like fr-CA → fr → en keeps regional variants coherent.

Keeping translation keys DRY as the product changes

Translation keys stay DRY through naming conventions like feature.area.element.state, shared keys for repeated UI patterns, and lint rules against duplicate values. Translators absorb the cost when keys are not DRY: the same "Save" button gets translated five times under five keys, and when the client decides to call it "Apply", five edits ship instead of one.

Pricing

What are the i18n pitfalls that cost translators the most time?

The costliest i18n pitfalls are hard-coded strings, concatenated sentences, missing plural categories, placeholder format drift, no screenshots, nested keys with no context, and retrofitting i18n after launch. Each pitfall adds query loops and QA passes to the localization workflow.

  • Hard-coded strings — text never reaches the resource file and ships in English.
  • Concatenated sentences — "You have " + count + " messages" cannot be reordered in Japanese or German.
  • Missing plural categories — a Russian translation gets 2 forms when the locale needs 4.
  • Placeholder drift — the source switches from %s to {{name}} mid-project and breaks QA regex.
  • No screenshots — short strings like "Open" and "Post" trigger clarifying queries.
  • Deeply nested keys with no context — CAT tools flatten the hierarchy and the context is lost.
  • Retrofitting i18n after launch — every sprint produces new hard-coded strings faster than the i18n cleanup can catch them.
  • CJK encoding edge cases — font fallbacks and line-break rules reveal gaps the pseudo-loc build should have caught.

pages.title: memoQ as a CAT Tool: Features, Licensing, and Certified-Lane Fit
pages.h1: memoQ as a CAT Tool: Features, Licensing, and Certified-Lane Fit
pages.meta_description: memoQ is a desktop-plus-server CAT tool with MQXLIFF bilingual files, LiveDocs corpus reuse, and $620–$900 perpetual licensing — here is how it fits a certified
pages.body_html:
On this page

  • Key points
  • What is memoQ and what are its core features as a CAT tool?
  • How is memoQ licensed and what does it cost in 2025?
  • Does memoQ fit a certified translation production lane?
  • Why do new users find memoQ hard to navigate, and how is that solved?
  • What CAT tool alternatives exist if memoQ does not fit the lane or budget?
  • How does memoQ fit into the wider certified-translation production stack?
  • How we use memoQ on a certified lane — and what we refuse to do
  • Frequently asked questions

memoQ sits in the CAT-tool layer of a certified translation production stack, between the TMS that routes the job and the LQA scorecard that gates the certificate. This page evaluates memoQ as that layer — what it does, what it costs, when the free edition is enough, and whether it holds up on an ISO 17100-aligned lane.

Key points

  • memoQ Translator Pro costs $620–$900 perpetual with annual support, and a free translator edition opens agency-supplied.mqxlz and.mqout project packages — the free edition cannot save back to an agency server, but it gives a freelancer full read and segment-edit access without any additional seat cost.
  • MQXLIFF is memoQ's native bilingual format; it carries segment status, match percentages, and comment threads that a reviewer opens independently of the authoring seat, preserving a complete segment-level audit trail from first draft through sign-off.
  • memoQ supports a wide range of file formats — including Microsoft Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and XML — making it compatible with the document types most seen on certified-translation lanes, from legal briefs to structured data exports.
  • memoQ's three reuse layers — translation memory, term base, and LiveDocs corpus — work together so that every new project draws on approved precedent before the translator types a single character; LiveDocs in particular lets raw reference documents contribute matches without requiring a pre-built TM.
  • memoQ and SDL Trados Studio are the two CAT tools most paired with a TMS on ISO 17100-aligned certified lanes, because both carry a segment-level audit trail and a reliable offline working mode.
  • On this site's certified lanes, memoQ pre-fills at or above a 75% fuzzy floor, with 100% exact and 101% in-context exact matches fully leveraged; a credentialed human reviews and signs every segment page by page before a certificate of accuracy is issued — raw CAT output alone never triggers issuance.
  • LQA runs after the memoQ bilingual file is reviewer-approved, billed at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100.

What we offer

What is memoQ and what are its core features as a CAT tool?

memoQ is a desktop-plus-server CAT tool with a segment-level editor, translation memory, term base, LiveDocs corpus reuse, inline QA checks, and MQXLIFF bilingual export — built so one translator or a packaged project team can produce an auditable bilingual file. The reuse layers stack: TM supplies sentence matches, the term base enforces client terminology, and LiveDocs leverages reference material that is not formal TM. The product belongs to the broader cluster explained CAT Tools Compared: How Translation Memory Software Works.

Pricing

How is memoQ licensed and what does it cost in 2025?

memoQ Translator Pro is licensed perpetually at $620–$900 with annual support, a free translator edition exists for opening and translating assigned packages, and agencies run server seats separately. Pricing published by this site stands at $620–$900 perpetual.

EditionPriceDeploymentWho it fits
Free translator edition$0DesktopFreelancers whose agencies supply a server seat
Translator Pro (perpetual)$620–$900 + annual supportDesktopDirect-client translators, LiveDocs-heavy workflows
Server seat (agency-supplied)Priced to the agency; passed to contractorServer + desktop clientFreelancers inside agency ISO 17100 lanes

The decision matrix below ties the choice to who the paying client is, not to a feature wishlist.

flowchart TD
 A[Who pays for your work?] --> B{Agencies ship memoQ packages?}
 B -- Yes --> C[Free translator edition is enough]
 B -- No --> D{Direct end clients?}
 D -- Yes --> E[Translator Pro perpetual $620-$900]
 D -- No --> F{Mixed, LiveDocs leverage matters?}
 F -- Yes --> E
 F -- No --> C

Is the free version of memoQ enough for a freelance translator?

The free translator edition of memoQ is sufficient for a freelancer whose paying agencies ship memoQ project packages and expect packages back. The licence to translate inside the package is often supplied by the agency's server seat. The free edition opens, translates, and returns the package.

Do agencies provide memoQ licenses to their freelance translators?

Many agencies that standardize on memoQ supply a server-based licence to each contracted translator for the duration of a project. A freelancer working primarily with those agencies rarely needs to buy a Translator Pro perpetual licence. The licence pattern is the one most freelancers encounter first.

When does buying memoQ Translator Pro at $620–$900 pay back?

Buying memoQ Translator Pro at $620–$900 perpetual with annual support pays back when a translator works directly with end clients rather than agencies, when LiveDocs corpus reuse materially leverages prior work, or when offline certified-lane confidentiality rules out server-dependent seats. Three payback cases cover most translators who buy their own licence:

  • Direct corporate accounts where the translator owns the TM and term base.
  • Specialist domains where a LiveDocs corpus of prior deliveries drives new throughput.
  • Jurisdictions where client confidentiality clauses require offline work.
Computer-Assisted Translation Tools: The Working Translator's Field Guide

Does memoQ fit a certified translation production lane?

memoQ fits a certified translation production lane because it carries a segment-level audit trail and a reliable offline working mode — both prerequisites for legally defensible certified delivery. memoQ and SDL Trados Studio are the two CAT tools most paired with a TMS on ISO 17100-aligned certified work. The cross-link to Phrase Alternatives Worth Considering for Your CAT Workflow covers how memoQ sits against cloud CAT tools when the lane rules out cloud posture.

What does ISO 17100 require from the CAT layer and how does memoQ satisfy it?

ISO 17100 requires a documented segment-level audit trail, enforced terminology, and a reviewer step independent of the translator. memoQ satisfies these through MQXLIFF segment status fields, term base enforcement in the editor, and a separate reviewer role that opens the same bilingual file.

ISO 17100 §5 requirementHow memoQ satisfies it
Segment-level audit trailMQXLIFF status fields record draft, confirmed, reviewer-approved per segment
Enforced terminologyTerm base misses raise QA warnings inline during save
Independent reviewer stepReviewer role opens the same bilingual file with its own status column
Offline confidentiality optionDesktop seat works without server dependence for sensitive documents
Record retentionMQXLIFF plus TM and term base kept per project for post-delivery audit

Where does LQA sit after a memoQ draft, and what does it cost?

LQA sits after the memoQ bilingual file is reviewer-approved and before the certificate of accuracy is signed. The gate samples output at $40–$90 per 1,000 words against an MQM-style scorecard aligned to ISO 17100. The gate blocks publish on certified lanes.

Three places LQA fires:

  1. End-of-project sample on every certified job, regardless of translator seniority.
  2. Spot-check during long jobs when a reviewer flags recurring error categories.
  3. Vendor-qualification sample on new translators joining a lane.

What memoQ output is NOT a certified translation on its own?

A raw memoQ bilingual export is not a certified translation on its own. Site policy requires a credentialed human to read every segment against the source and sign for the translation page by page before a certificate of accuracy is issued. The CAT tool produces a draft, not a certificate. On the USCIS certified-translation economics this draft serves — $0.10–$0.25 per source word or $25–$150 per standard 250-word page — a certificate is mandatory on every page.

Why do new users find memoQ hard to navigate, and how is that solved?

New users find memoQ hard to navigate because the project-package model, the resource console, and the dockable editor panes assume prior CAT experience. The fix is a four-step unlock — import the.mqxlz, assign the TM and term base from the resource console, confirm the 75% fuzzy threshold, and open the editor. The perception reverses with repetition.

flowchart TD
 A[.mqxlz or.mqout package arrives] --> B[Install free translator edition]
 B --> C[Double-click package to register in resource console]
 C --> D[Assign TM and term base]
 D --> E[Confirm 75% fuzzy floor]
 E --> F[Open bilingual editor and translate]
 F --> G[Save back to agency server seat]

How do I open a memoQ project package for the first time without a paid license?

To open a memoQ project package for the first time without a paid licence, install the free translator edition, double-click the handoff.mqxlz or.mqout file, let the installer register the project in the local resource console, and open the bilingual view. The agency's server seat authorizes the save-back. The sequence is the same for every subsequent package.

Which parts of the memoQ interface trip up experienced translators?

The parts of the memoQ interface that trip up experienced translators are the resource console's split between light and heavy resources, the server-vs-local distinction for TM and term bases, and the Views feature that merges files into one editor pane. Each is solvable; none is intuitive on day one. The three friction points cover most support tickets a new memoQ user raises in their first week.

What CAT tool alternatives exist if memoQ does not fit the lane or budget?

If memoQ does not fit, four CAT alternatives cover the common lanes: SDL Trados Studio at $400–$900 perpetual for agency pools shipping SDLXLIFF, OmegaT free for solo certified translators, Wordfast lower than Trados for lightweight desktop work, and browser-based tools for zero-cost learners.

ToolPriceDeploymentLane fit
memoQ Translator Pro$620–$900 perpetualDesktop + serverLiveDocs reuse, offline certified lanes
SDL Trados Studio$400–$900 perpetualDesktopAgency pools shipping SDLXLIFF
OmegaTFree, open-sourceDesktopSolo certified translator lane
WordfastLower than TradosDesktopLightweight desktop work
Browser-based toolsFree tier availableCloudNon-certified, learner lane

memoQ vs SDL Trados Studio: which one fits a freelance translator?

memoQ fits a freelancer who prioritizes editor speed, LiveDocs corpus reuse, and a cleaner project view. SDL Trados Studio fits a freelancer whose paying agencies ship SDLXLIFF packages. The client file format decides, not personal taste. The deep comparison lives Trados as a CAT Tool: Features, Costs, and Honest Trade-offs.

Are free or browser-based CAT tools a real memoQ alternative?

Free and browser-based CAT tools are a real alternative when the lane is non-certified and the translator owns the client relationship. They fail the certified-lane test when confidentiality rules out cloud posture or when the receiving authority expects a documented desktop audit trail. OmegaT remains the free option that passes the offline test; browser-based options do not.

How does memoQ fit into the wider certified-translation production stack?

memoQ fits into the CAT-tool layer of a seven-layer production stack — TMS above it, MT engine feeding first drafts, TM and term base inside it, QA automation plus LQA scorecard after it, connectors sideways, and the reviewer-and-certifier workflow sealing the lane. Each layer has a defined handoff point, and memoQ's role is to hold all segment-level intelligence — match percentages, term flags, comment threads, and change history — in a single MQXLIFF bilingual file that every downstream role opens without needing the original source document.

Within that file, memoQ applies three reuse layers simultaneously: the translation memory surfaces fuzzy and exact matches ranked from 75% up through 101% in-context exact; the term base flags controlled vocabulary mid-segment so the translator cannot accidentally drift from approved terminology; and the LiveDocs corpus contributes reference material from past projects or unaligned bilingual documents that have not yet been formally imported into a TM. Together these layers mean that a certified lane running on memoQ inherits institutional memory automatically rather than relying on the individual translator's recall.

After the translator delivers the reviewed MQXLIFF, the stack continues: an automated QA pass checks placeholders, numbers, and tag integrity, then an independent reviewer working inside the same bilingual file applies the ISO 17100 §5 review role before the file moves to LQA scoring at $40–$90 per 1,000 words on an MQM-style scorecard. The certifier — a credentialed human — then signs every segment page by page, and only at that point is a certificate of accuracy issued. No certificate is ever issued on raw memoQ output alone; the full downstream chain must complete first.

How we use memoQ on a certified lane — and what we refuse to do

We treat memoQ as the editor our credentialed translator post-edits an AI first draft inside. It is not a replacement for the translator and not a source of certification. The segment editor pre-fills from TM above 75%, flags term base misses, and runs placeholder and number checks on every save. The reviewer sees the same bilingual file. The LQA sampler scores it against an ISO 17100-aligned scorecard before the certificate is written.

We do not lower the 75% fuzzy floor to force more pre-fills. Below that score, the match is noise and the translator writes from scratch. The threshold is the industry-negotiated line between leverage and rework, and we keep it.

We will not sign a certificate of accuracy on raw CAT output. A memoQ bilingual export is a draft. The certifier reads every segment against the source and signs for the translation page by page. No automation substitutes for that step on our lane.

We do not promote a LiveDocs corpus into formal TM without explicit client scope. Prior certified deliveries carry confidentiality boundaries we respect, which is why they stay in LiveDocs as reference material rather than becoming a cross-client memory a future translator leverages uninstructed.

memoQ is a desktop-plus-server CAT tool with a segment-level editor, translation memory, term base, LiveDocs corpus reuse, inline QA, and MQXLIFF bilingual export.

Frequently asked questions

Is the free version of memoQ enough for freelancers?

The free memoQ Translator Free tier covers basic translation memory and terminology lookups, but it has meaningful limitations that make it insufficient for most professional freelancers. It lacks server connectivity, restricts the number of TMs and term bases you can use simultaneously, and cannot open all project package formats sent by agencies. Freelancers who work regularly with agency-delivered MQXLIFF or MQXLZ packages will almost certainly need the paid Translator Pro license (around €770/year) to maintain a full professional workflow.

Do agencies provide memoQ licenses to translators?

Yes, many agencies provide translators with a memoQ server access license rather than requiring them to purchase their own. Under this model, the agency runs a memoQ Server and grants freelancers a free Translator Pro-equivalent session tied to that server, meaning the translator can only use the license for that agency's projects. Some larger agencies maintain floating seat pools. Translators who work with multiple agencies, or who need an offline workflow, still benefit from owning a personal Translator Pro license.

Why is memoQ considered hard to navigate for beginners?

memoQ's interface exposes a large number of panels, resource managers, and project settings simultaneously, which creates a steep initial learning curve for translators new to CAT tools. Concepts like translation memories, term bases, LiveDocs corpora, and QA profiles must all be configured before a project runs optimally — and each has its own management window. New users often report confusion between local and server projects, and between the translator and project manager views. Most learners need 10–20 hours of deliberate practice before the workflow feels intuitive.

Can I open a memoQ package without a paid license?

You can open a memoQ package (MQXLZ or MQXLIFF) with the free memoQ Translator Free version, but with notable restrictions. Translator Free allows you to work on packages delivered by a memoQ server, yet it blocks features such as full QA runs, certain file filters, and simultaneous use of multiple TMs. If the package requires server check-in or uses resources locked to a Pro license, you will be prompted to upgrade. For straightforward packages from a connected agency server, the free tier is often sufficient.

Is memoQ better than Trados?

memoQ and Trados Studio are the two dominant professional CAT tools, and neither is objectively better — the choice depends on workflow and client base. Trados has a larger market share and is more requested by large LSPs, while memoQ is often preferred for its cleaner project-management features and more responsive vendor support. Pricing is comparable: Trados Freelance runs around €845/year, memoQ Translator Pro around €770/year. Many professional translators maintain familiarity with both, since agencies dictate the tool. For certified translation workflows, the key differentiator is which tool the agency's server runs.

What are examples of CAT tools?

The most widely used CAT tools in professional translation are memoQ, SDL Trados Studio, Wordfast, Déjà Vu, and Memsource (now Phrase). These tools all share core functionality: segmentation, translation memory (TM) leverage, terminology management, and QA checks. Phrase and Memsource are cloud-first and popular with tech-localization teams, while memoQ and Trados dominate agency and certified-translation workflows. Open-source options like OmegaT exist for budget-constrained translators, though they lack the advanced QA and project-management features of commercial tools.

What is memoQ?

memoQ is a professional computer-assisted translation (CAT) tool developed by the Hungarian company memoQ Ltd., widely used by freelance translators, agencies, and language service providers. It combines a translation editor with translation memory, terminology management, machine translation integration, and quality assurance features in a single environment. It is available as a standalone desktop application (memoQ translator) and as a server platform (memoQ Server) that enables collaborative, multi-translator projects. It is particularly common in certified and legal translation workflows where consistency, auditability, and structured QA are critical.

How much should a translation cost?

Professional translation costs between $0.10 and $0.30 per source word for common language pairs, with certified translation often commanding a premium of $0.15–$0.40 per word or a flat per-page rate of $25–$75. Rates vary by language pair (rare languages cost more), subject matter (legal and medical carry premiums), turnaround time, and whether certification or notarization is required. Agencies add a margin on top of translator rates, so end-client prices are higher than direct freelancer rates. Bulk volume and long-term contracts can reduce per-word costs significantly.
